His family told WPTV they do not yet know what happened.“The feeling is unbearable,” his sister, Alexis Hodge, told WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache during an exclusive interview.Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home as they remembered a brother they described as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others.“He’s strong. It’s so much,” Alexis said.Family says Austin appeared normal hours before his deathAlexis said the family has been told Austin appeared to be himself in the hours before he was found unresponsive. They were told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed.“Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said.She said the sudden loss has left the family with questions they cannot yet answer.“It’s a shock to literally all of us,” Alexis said. “Nobody knows what happened.”Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin also worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family.Family loses second firefighter brother in just over a yearAustin’s death comes just over a year after the death of his 26-year-old brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district.The family told WPTV that Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died.“We lost two brothers in one year,” Alexis Hodge said. “I can’t describe to you the pain.”The family said Jairus’ death raised concerns about the medical care he received, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother.“He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”Family seeks answers about Austin’s deathNow, Austin’s family says they are determined to understand what happened in his final hours.“I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said.Alexis said the family wants to know who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive.“We are trying to find out what happened to him, who was around him, who saw him. entry.title: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development
entry.summary: By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. 13. PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Martin County eyes pause on data center development Tuesday's vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday's vote. The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.

entry.title: Florida's U.S. Senate Race: What voters need to know before Election Day
entry.summary: With Election Day just a week away, Florida voters will decide a high-profile race for the U.S. Senate. The special election pits incumbent Republican Ashley Moody against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon, with independent candidate Neil Gillespie also on the ballot. Marco Rubio's term. Rubio left the Senate after becoming U.S. Secretary of State, and Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed Ashley Moody to the seat in January 2025. The winner will serve the final two years of Rubio's term, meaning the seat will be on the ballot again in 2028. Ashley Moody's Campaign Moody, a former two-term Florida attorney general from Plant City, is running as the incumbent Republican. She has highlighted her background as a federal prosecutor, judge and attorney general, frequently emphasizing law enforcement and public safety issues. Moody has framed the race starkly, telling voters the election is a choice between 'safety or chaos' and 'freedom or socialism.' Angie Nixon's Campaign Democratic challenger Angie Nixon is a state representative and labor organizer from Jacksonville. Nixon emerged from a competitive Democratic primary, defeating a more centrist opponent who significantly outraised her campaign. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Nixon has campaigned alongside U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and supports policies including a $25 minimum wage and Medicare for All. entry.title: Frankel, Adeimy outline affordability priorities in race for Florida's redrawn 23rd congressional district
entry.summary: With just a week left until the General Election, the candidates vying for the newly redrawn 23rd congressional district in Florida sat down with WPTV morning anchor Hollani Davis to talk about their priorities for voters here at home if they're elected. U.S. Rep. Louis Frankel, D-Fla., is fighting to continue representing South Florida. She says affordability is at the top of her list to tackle. WATCH REPORT BELOW: District 23 candidates focus on affordability Candidates vying to represent Florida's 23rd District lay out priorities to tackle affordability 'When I'm at the supermarket, and people can't afford their food, that's a pretty big message,' says Frankel. Frankel, who is seeking an eighth term in Congress, says Democrats must seek to end the war with Iran and rein in the Trump administration's tariffs to help bring costs under control. She also says there is another glaring issue that can't be ignored. '(There's) probably nothing more important for the people of Palm Beach County, where we have a big senior population, is (the need) to protect Social Security and Medicare,' Frankel said. Challenging Frankel in the race is Deborah Adeimy. The Republican, is a native of Palm Beach County who's worked as a financial adviser to companies like Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan Chase. She says she'd use her financial acumen to help solve South Florida's affordable housing problem by rewriting the playbook. 'Currently in Palm Beach County, there are real estate developers who are taking advantage of antiquated tax incentives, tax breaks that are driving up costs here in Palm Beach County (including) rent,' says Adeimy. Florida's 23rd congressional district previously straddled the Palm Beach-Broward County line with a heavy focus on Broward County. After the districts were redrawn this year, it now covers a portion of West Palm Beach and extends south to include Boynton Beach.

entry.title: Boca Raton Fire Rescue expands lifesaving whole blood program through new health network partnership
entry.summary: A new partnership between Boca Raton Fire Rescue and Palm Beach Health Network is strengthening a whole blood program that has already saved lives in the field this summer. Boca Raton's fire rescue crews have had access to whole blood since a new program kicked off this summer; paramedics say the capability is transforming how they treat patients before they reach the hospital. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Boca Raton expands whole blood program According to Red Cross Blood Services, whole blood is blood as it flows in our bodies, with none of its components separated or removed. 'Whole blood has been shown to save lives, and now that we have the capability in our arsenal, it's a world of difference in treating patients and getting the right care,' Kacper Palej, Boca Raton firefighter paramedic, said. Jo Thomas was critically injured in a motorcycle crash this summer. Crews administered whole blood for the first time under the new program. 'I've been told I got flown from the bike into a crosswalk pole about 20 to 30 feet and then hit a crosswalk pole with my body,' Thomas said. 'When somebody's bleeding out on the street, the one thing that will really help out is being able to feed blood back into them to keep them alive, just until they can make it to the hospital to be fully treated.' Months later, Thomas is surrounded by fire rescue again, but for a different reason. Crew members who responded to his crash call received a firefighter challenge coin as a token of appreciation. 'Seeing him walking into the station today and we're gonna go and have something to eat, break bread with him... It's a great day,' Steven Wright, driver engineer, said. A recent partnership with Palm Beach Health Network now means that when blood in fire rescue units is close to expiring, crews return it to Palm Beach Health Network for patient care. In exchange, crews receive fresh blood for future emergency calls.

According to authorities, an Audi SUV being pursued by Stuart Police and the Martin County Sheriff's Office was traveling the wrong way on U.S. 1 near NW Federal Highway and Jensen Beach Boulevard when it collided with an oncoming vehicle. The Florida Highway Patrol is investigating the crash. Southbound lanes remain closed, and traffic is backed up in both directions. No fatalities have been reported. entry.summary: A group of faith leaders and immigration advocates gathered near U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody's Palm Beach Gardens office to deliver a message, urging her to support Senate Bill 4814, which would extend Temporary Protected Status for Haitians living in the U.S. for three years. Since 2010, that status has allowed Haitian immigrants to legally live and work in the U.S. because of dangerous conditions in their country. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Advocates urge Sen. Moody to back Haitian TPS extension Homeland Security revoked Haitian TPS in July following a Supreme Court decision allowing it to do so. Advocates say more than 150,000 Haitian TPS beneficiaries live in Florida, contributing $2.6 billion to the state's economy, and that they became unable to legally work when Homeland Security revoked their status. Among those affected is Farah Larrieux, who ran her own marketing company and is now unable to work. I introduced you to Larrieux earlier this year , before TPS was revoked. 'Because of TPS, I'm able to rebuild my life,' Larrieux said in February. I can no longer go out without the fear of being stopped and detained by ICE agents. I live with the constant anxiety of being deported to Haiti, where I can be raped, extorted or even be killed. entry.title: New $17 million Boys & Girls Club opens in West Palm Beach, offering opportunities for hundreds of kids
entry.summary: A new Boys Girls Club officially opened its doors Tuesday in West Palm Beach, bringing a new place for hundreds of children and teens to learn, explore their interests and prepare for their futures. The Julie Mike Connors Boys Girls Club, located at 1150 Southern Blvd., celebrated its grand opening after years of planning. WATCH REPORT BELOW: New Boys Girls Club opens in West Palm Beach 'To have this come to fruition is more beautiful than I ever thought it could be,' Julie Connors said during the celebration. The $17 million, 31,000-square-foot facility is the 21st location for the Boys Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County and is expected to serve approximately 800 children and teens each year, with about 220 attending daily. The club will serve kids ages 6 to 18. For the Connors, however, the bigger story is the need they say exists in the surrounding community. 'People don't realize how big a need there is in West Palm Beach,' Mike Connors said. 'There are a lot of single families that need a lot of help, especially to get kids off the streets.' Inside the new facility are spaces designed for academics, recreation, the arts and career exploration. The club includes a gym and stage, academic center, cultural arts center, computer labs, dance studio, cafeteria, commercial kitchen, sound and recording studio, maker space and outdoor playground. Students will also have access to daily homework help and tutoring programs with certified teachers, along with STEM education, sports, health and fitness programs, cultural arts and leadership programs. For teens, the opportunities extend into career exploration and workforce readiness. They can get hands-on experience in areas such as robotics, health care, content creation, design and culinary arts while being introduced to potential college and career pathways. 'I can be a journalist, a content creator; I can do anything that's possible because we provide essential tools, systems and environment to help them grow,' said Pablo Tejada, Chief Impact Officer for the Boys Girls Club. WPTV reporter Christy Waite spoke with one family who came to the grand opening to tour the new facility. College student Christian Smith said he believes the opportunities being offered could help break cycles of poverty and create new opportunities for young people in the community. entry.title: Powerful waves damage Juno Beach Pier, forcing indefinite closure as officials await full assessment
entry.summary: Powerful waves and strong winds have left their mark on the Juno Beach Pier, forcing officials to close the popular fishing spot indefinitely while crews wait for conditions to improve enough to assess the damage. For people who came to Juno Beach on Tuesday to see the conditions firsthand, the strength of the ocean was impossible to miss. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Rough surf damages Juno Beach Pier, forcing indefinite closure 'It's just amazing the way they roll in and pound and the power,' said Melissa Stolz, who lives in Jupiter but came to Juno Beach to see the rough conditions. 'Between the full moon and the gale-force winds, everything, it's just a perfect storm.' Kristine Galganski lives in North Palm Beach and said Tuesdays are typically her days to visit Juno Beach. After hearing about the damage, she came out to see the pier for herself. 'That's Mother Nature at her best,' Galganski said, 'and she's saying I'm here and I'm ready.' Aerial footage from local photographer Paul Dabill showed floor panels lifted throughout the pier, with some panels missing. Bud Gilfillan, who lives in Jupiter but was visiting Juno Beach, said the conditions stood out to him. 'I'm seeing the heaviest northeast winds and currents that I've seen in a long time,' Gilfillan said. Gilfillan was struck by the amount of force it would take to move the decking. 'I mean, can you imagine the force of those waves pushing that decking up in the air and washing it down,' Gilfillan said. WPTV worked to find answers to understand the extent of the damage the pier had received and contacted Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation Director Jennifer Cirillo. 'The wooden panels are designed to pop out in high surf conditions and in order to save greater structural damage on the pier,' Cirillo said in a statement. The missing panels may be part of the pier's design, but officials believe there could be other damage that would impact when the pier will reopen. 'It does appear during this event, however, that some of the railing may also be damaged, which would require repair,' Cirillo said. For Stolz, seeing the pier closed was difficult. 'I'm just sad it's such a landmark for locals to come down and walk on the fishing pier,' she said. County staff must now wait for the high surf to subside before they can safely assess the entire pier and determine what will need to be repaired. 'It's very damaging,' Gilfillan said. After hearing about the damage, she came out to see the pier for herself."That's Mother Nature at her best," Galganski said, "and she's saying I'm here and I'm ready."Aerial footage from local photographer Paul Dabill showed floor panels lifted throughout the pier, with some panels missing.Bud Gilfillan, who lives in Jupiter but was visiting Juno Beach, said the conditions stood out to him."I'm seeing the heaviest northeast winds and currents that I've seen in a long time," Gilfillan said.Gilfillan was struck by the amount of force it would take to move the decking."I mean, can you imagine the force of those waves pushing that decking up in the air and washing it down," Gilfillan said.WPTV worked to find answers to understand the extent of the damage the pier had received and contacted Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation Director Jennifer Cirillo."The wooden panels are designed to pop out in high surf conditions and in order to save greater structural damage on the pier," Cirillo said in a statement.The missing panels may be part of the pier's design, but officials believe there could be other damage that would impact when the pier will reopen."It does appear during this event, however, that some of the railing may also be damaged, which would require repair," Cirillo said.For Stolz, seeing the pier closed was difficult."I'm just sad it's such a landmark for locals to come down and walk on the fishing pier," she said.County staff must now wait for the high surf to subside before they can safely assess the entire pier and determine what will need to be repaired."It's very damaging," Gilfillan said. "It's going to last a couple more days."Cirillo said it typically takes county crews a few days after high-surf events to retrieve loose panels and put them back into the pier. However, the county won't know whether there will be additional costs to reopen the pier until crews can safely determine the full impact."Once high surf conditions subside, our staff will be able to do a full assessment of this public park infrastructure," Cirillo said. "It typically takes our team a few days following high surf events to retrieve any loose panels and place them back into the pier structure. We will not know what costs above staff time are required for reopening until after we can safely assess the entire event's impacts."For now, there is no clear reopening timeline."It's gonna take time. We can't put a time limit on what she does," Stolz said.The pier isn't the only place where the rough conditions are having an impact. Some stairs at beach access points have also been damaged, and the Town of Jupiter has closed some access points because of erosion.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. entry.title: 15-year-old seriously injured after wrong-way crash following police pursuit in Stuart
entry.summary: A 15-year-old driver and another motorist were seriously injured early Tuesday after a police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department. Police said officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle traveling north at what officers described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted to make a traffic stop, but police said the driver refused to stop and fled. The pursuit eventually continued onto U.S. 1, where police said the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger posed to other motorists, according to the department. Police said officers also attempted to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway. The fleeing vehicle eventually collided with a vehicle traveling south at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said. After the crash, officers learned the driver of the fleeing vehicle was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, while the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash. Police said no additional information would be released at this time because the investigation remains ongoing.

entry.title: 'Really bad' king tide flooding inundates Boynton Beach condo complex, prompting calls for answers
entry.summary: Floodwaters have inundated parking spaces, roads and walkways at a Boynton Beach condominium complex, leaving residents struggling to get in and out as king tides, strong onshore winds and heavy rain push water onto the property. At Coastal Towers Condominium Apartments, located at 730 E. Ocean Avenue, water from the Intracoastal Waterway behind the complex spread throughout portions of the property Tuesday, reaching ankle-deep levels in some areas and knee-deep in others. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: King tide flooding inundates Boynton Beach condo complex Residents say they expect king tide flooding during the fall, but the severity of the conditions has caught them off guard. 'It's really hard to get in and out of the complex,' resident Sophia Cywar said. John Cotanch, who has lived at the complex for 10 years, said he has experienced flooding there before but has never seen it this severe. 'It's been bad before, but this is really bad,' Cotanch said. The flooding has also affected visitors trying to reach the property. Cotanch was waiting for his daughter, Heather, who was visiting from New York. Her Uber driver had to take a detour, and she ultimately had to roll up her pants, put on sandals and wade through the water to reach the complex. Chrissy Ryan, the property's manager, said Coastal Towers installed a new seawall about two years ago, but flooding remains a concern. Ryan said water is entering the property from both sides, including areas near neighboring properties with lower seawalls. 'We've got both properties that have lower seawalls, and now with this king tide they come in from both sides,' Ryan said. Ryan is asking the City of Boynton Beach and the Florida Department of Transportation to investigate the flooding and evaluate the surrounding infrastructure, including neighboring seawalls, drainage outfalls and backflow prevention systems. She also raised concerns about valve checks she said were discussed about a year and a half ago but still need to be addressed. 'I want them to see this so something gets done about it,' Ryan said. In an email, Ryan described the flooding as a serious concern for resident safety and potential property damage. She requested a review of the conditions and clarification on what corrective measures could help prevent or reduce future flooding. Her Uber driver had to take a detour, and she ultimately had to roll up her pants, put on sandals and wade through the water to reach the complex.Chrissy Ryan, the property's manager, said Coastal Towers installed a new seawall about two years ago, but flooding remains a concern.Ryan said water is entering the property from both sides, including areas near neighboring properties with lower seawalls."We've got both properties that have lower seawalls, and now with this king tide they come in from both sides," Ryan said.Ryan is asking the City of Boynton Beach and the Florida Department of Transportation to investigate the flooding and evaluate the surrounding infrastructure, including neighboring seawalls, drainage outfalls and backflow prevention systems.She also raised concerns about valve checks she said were discussed about a year and a half ago but still need to be addressed."I want them to see this so something gets done about it," Ryan said.In an email, Ryan described the flooding as a serious concern for resident safety and potential property damage. She requested a review of the conditions and clarification on what corrective measures could help prevent or reduce future flooding.The City of Boynton Beach said it is aware of the flooding at Coastal Towers and has had crews monitoring and documenting affected areas.In a statement to WPTV, the city said it has been responding as needed, including providing support from its police and fire rescue departments and supplying sandbags.City staff have also been in contact with the condominium association and FDOT, which scheduled a site visit to observe conditions during the king tide.The city said communities throughout South Florida face similar challenges when king tides combine with onshore winds and heavy rainfall, pushing water above levels that much of the region's infrastructure was built to handle.Addressing the flooding, the city said, will require coordination among public agencies and private property owners."The City remains committed to working with the association and these partners," the statement said.While the city has outlined its immediate response, it has not announced specific long-term repairs or a timeline for mitigation at Coastal Towers.For residents, the immediate concern remains navigating the floodwaters — and determining what can be done to reduce the risk of similar conditions during future king tides.

entry.title: Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team
entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program. WATCH REPORT BELOW: IRSC trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming, diving team Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team Instead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community. President Timothy Moore said at Tuesday's meeting that the proposal to cut the programs comes down to money. 'It's a tremendous opportunity to leave this college with that kind of skill, resource and talent here, but it comes at a price,' Moore said. The school president said the program currently costs around $1.4 to $2 million, money that isn't coming in through donations. 'What's required to maintain it as it sits today? We will require $15 to $20 million of an endowment to throw off enough revenue per year to sustain the program as it sits today,' Moore said. There's also a proposal to transition the remaining sports to Division II, resulting in potential savings of around $500,000. But if the swimming and diving program stays, Moore said the school may be forced to cut 50 percent for sports across the board. 'It's elimination of one or impose a penalty across all, and I would imagine that our championships will suffer because of that decision,' Moore said. The administration is expected to present the report at the Board of Trustees Nov. 17 meeting, when recommendations on how to move forward will be considered. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition last week to save the program, which has more than 12,500 signatures.

entry.title: Frankel, Adeimy outline affordability priorities in race for Florida's redrawn 23rd congressional district
entry.summary: With just a week left until the General Election, the candidates vying for the newly redrawn 23rd congressional district in Florida sat down with WPTV morning anchor Hollani Davis to talk about their priorities for voters here at home if they're elected. U.S. Rep. Louis Frankel, D-Fla., is fighting to continue representing South Florida. She says affordability is at the top of her list to tackle. WATCH REPORT BELOW: District 23 candidates focus on affordability Candidates vying to represent Florida's 23rd District lay out priorities to tackle affordability 'When I'm at the supermarket, and people can't afford their food, that's a pretty big message,' says Frankel. Frankel, who is seeking an eighth term in Congress, says Democrats must seek to end the war with Iran and rein in the Trump administration's tariffs to help bring costs under control. She also says there is another glaring issue that can't be ignored. '(There's) probably nothing more important for the people of Palm Beach County, where we have a big senior population, is (the need) to protect Social Security and Medicare,' Frankel said. Challenging Frankel in the race is Deborah Adeimy. The Republican, is a native of Palm Beach County who's worked as a financial adviser to companies like Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan Chase. She says she'd use her financial acumen to help solve South Florida's affordable housing problem by rewriting the playbook. 'Currently in Palm Beach County, there are real estate developers who are taking advantage of antiquated tax incentives, tax breaks that are driving up costs here in Palm Beach County (including) rent,' says Adeimy. Florida's 23rd congressional district previously straddled the Palm Beach-Broward County line with a heavy focus on Broward County. After the districts were redrawn this year, it now covers a portion of West Palm Beach and extends south to include Boynton Beach.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County deputy accused of DUI in Vero Beach crash that injured woman and child    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff's deputy has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left a woman seriously injured and her son hospitalized. The crash happened at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach. Investigators said Tyler Horstman, an off-duty St. Lucie County sheriff's detective, was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying a woman and her son. According to investigators, the SUV's driver ran a red light, while Horstman had a green light. All three individuals involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal. "Given the nature of the vehicles at a decent rate of speed, I mean, I don't want to say it worked out in its best. I mean, obviously injuries were still sustained, possibly long-lasting injuries, but at the end of the day, it's very feasible that a fatality could have occurred," Lt. Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, Horstman stated during his assessment that he had "a few beers" earlier in the evening. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Police also said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash. Horstman turned himself in on Monday. Police explained that the investigation took several months to complete. "It was a matter of investigators going through search warrants, subpoenas, and obtaining all different records," Kerensky said. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro, Horstman subsequently turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail and was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. Sheriff Del Toro released this statement: "Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," said Sheriff Richard R. "The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires." Horstman faces several charges, including DUI, and his arraignment is scheduled for Dec. "Our job is to investigate no matter who's involved, and we're going to do the due diligence to make sure what we do is right. At the end of the day, it happens to be a warrant was issued for Tyler Horstman," Kerensky said. entry.title: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County - WPEC
entry.summary: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

entry.summary: In Florida, you can find a good football game anywhere, but few schools have both great football and amazing band play like Palm Beach Lakes Community High School. 'Seven-time MVP, seven-time FNBC Champs, and seven-time superior-rated band,' said Jazz Velez, the band president. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Palm Beach Lakes band shines on and off field Palm Beach Lakes band shines on and off field If you dont know what that means, let me put it: the Ram Regiment is the best band in the state. 'Its an amazing feeling, but it's a lot of pressure sometimes because we have to put on a show every time we go out there,' said Velez. They put on a show, alright. They've won the state championship, they're the No. 1 superior-rated band in West Palm Beach, and are fresh from a trip to London for the 2026 New Year's Day Parade. If you still don't believe how good they are, the school's quarterback, Jordan Johnson, has one wish ahead of every home and away game: will the band be there? 'The band means everything to our culture. Its just a feeling that you get that gets you out your body at halftime the show that they put on when youre in the game and score a touchdown the band just cranks. It's amazing,' said Palm Beach Lakes quarterback Jordan Johnson. The band isnt just putting on a show on game days; theyre paving the way for countless students to get to colleges for free through countless scholarships. 'It's an honor and a privilege, because not only am I going to the highest level I can get paid to play my instrument. There's no better feeling in the world,' said Trevon Richardson, the band's vice president.

entry.title: 15-year-old seriously injured after wrong-way crash following police pursuit in Stuart
entry.summary: A 15-year-old driver and another motorist were seriously injured early Tuesday after a police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department. Police said officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle traveling north at what officers described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted to make a traffic stop, but police said the driver refused to stop and fled. The pursuit eventually continued onto U.S. 1, where police said the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger posed to other motorists, according to the department. Police said officers also attempted to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway. The fleeing vehicle eventually collided with a vehicle traveling south at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said. After the crash, officers learned the driver of the fleeing vehicle was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, while the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash. Police said no additional information would be released at this time because the investigation remains ongoing.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. "He was a critical part of our team. "Just remember his strength and who he was."The procession offered firefighters, colleagues and members of the community a chance to pay tribute to someone who spent years helping others, both at the fire district and in health care.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County - WPEC
entry.summary: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

entry.title: Surface-to-air missile systems deployed near Trump airport, Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach
entry.summary: New surface-to-air missile systems have been deployed in Palm Beach as part of expanded security around President Donald Trump, with air defense assets visible near Donald J. Trump International Airport and Mar-a-Lago. The North American Aerospace Defense Command has said the deployment was made at the request of the U.S. Secret Service. WATCH: Surface-to-air missiles deployed in Palm Beach Surface-to-air missile systems deployed near Trump airport, Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach The new equipment is attracting attention from people traveling around the airport and near the president's private club. WPTV's Michael Hoffman spoke with aviation experts Dewitt Ingram and Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley about what the systems are designed to do and the types of threats they can counter. What are the air defense systems? 'What you see here are three trailer-mounted anti-aircraft, anti-drone, actually even anti-vehicle defense systems,' Ingram told Hoffman. Ingram said the weapons are surface-to-air missile systems, commonly known as SAMs, and described them as a final layer of protection. entry.article_text: New surface-to-air missile systems have been deployed in Palm Beach as part of expanded security around President Donald Trump, with air defense assets visible near Donald J. Trump International Airport and Mar-a-Lago. The North American Aerospace Defense Command has said the deployment was made at the request of the U.S. Secret Service.WATCH: Surface-to-air missiles deployed in Palm BeachThe new equipment is attracting attention from people traveling around the airport and near the president's private club.WPTV's Michael Hoffman spoke with aviation experts Dewitt Ingram and Matthew "Whiz" Buckley about what the systems are designed to do and the types of threats they can counter."What you see here are three trailer-mounted anti-aircraft, anti-drone, actually even anti-vehicle defense systems," Ingram told Hoffman.Ingram said the weapons are surface-to-air missile systems, commonly known as SAMs, and described them as a final layer of protection."This is the last line of defense that will eliminate the threat to the president of the United States," Ingram said.Hoffman also sat down with Buckley, a decorated former U.S. Navy fighter pilot and graduate of the Navy's elite TOPGUN flight school."I'm surprised those SAMs haven't been there longer," Buckley said.Buckley said the systems are capable of defending against more than conventional aircraft."It's anti-aircraft, anti-drone, anti-anything that's a potential threat," he said.Buckley identified some of the equipment visible near the airport as Avenger systems carrying Stinger missiles. WPTV's independent reporting has also identified Avenger short-range air defense systems among the equipment deployed in the area."It looks like there are a couple Avenger batteries, which are Stinger missiles, and there's four on each side, so a total of eight," Buckley told Hoffman. "I think they might have .50-caliber machine guns on those weapons too."Hoffman previously reported that NORAD and U.S. Northern Command confirmed defense assets had been placed in and around Mar-a-Lago at the Secret Service's request. NORAD declined to provide specific operational information, citing security considerations.The military has not publicly said whether a specific threat prompted the deployment. The developments come amid heightened airspace security around Palm Beach when Trump is in the area.NORAD conducted a planned air defense exercise over Palm Beach on Oct. 14 involving F-16s and Civil Air Patrol aircraft. The command said it routinely uses exercises involving scenarios such as airspace violations, hijackings and unknown aircraft to test its responses, systems and equipment. NORAD also reported an F-16 intercept of an aircraft that violated temporary flight restrictions near Palm Beach on Oct. The latest deployment comes months after WPTV spoke with Buckley about an anti-drone laser defense system at the airport.Buckley told Hoffman then, and maintains now, that one threat deserves particular attention: drone swarms."Most people have seen the movie 'Miracle on the Hudson' with Sully land in the U.S. "That's what a flock of birds did to a couple engines. What do you think a flock of drones — inexpensive, cheap drones — are going to do in front of an airliner?""I'm shocked that we haven't lost an airliner yet due to a drone swarm," he added.For Buckley, the type of technology being deployed is less important than having defenses capable of responding to potential threats."Whether it's directed-energy weapons, laser or an Avenger missile battery, I think, you know, the president's safety is pretty important," Buckley said.The military has not publicly disclosed how long the air defense systems will remain deployed around Mar-a-Lago. entry.summary: St. Lucie County deputy accused of DUI in Vero Beach crash that injured woman and child    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff's deputy has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left a woman seriously injured and her son hospitalized. The crash happened at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach. Investigators said Tyler Horstman, an off-duty St. Lucie County sheriff's detective, was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying a woman and her son. According to investigators, the SUV's driver ran a red light, while Horstman had a green light. All three individuals involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal. "Given the nature of the vehicles at a decent rate of speed, I mean, I don't want to say it worked out in its best. I mean, obviously injuries were still sustained, possibly long-lasting injuries, but at the end of the day, it's very feasible that a fatality could have occurred," Lt. Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, Horstman stated during his assessment that he had "a few beers" earlier in the evening. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Police also said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash. Horstman turned himself in on Monday. Police explained that the investigation took several months to complete. "It was a matter of investigators going through search warrants, subpoenas, and obtaining all different records," Kerensky said. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro, Horstman subsequently turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail and was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. Sheriff Del Toro released this statement: "Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," said Sheriff Richard R. "The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires." Horstman faces several charges, including DUI, and his arraignment is scheduled for Dec. "Our job is to investigate no matter who's involved, and we're going to do the due diligence to make sure what we do is right. At the end of the day, it happens to be a warrant was issued for Tyler Horstman," Kerensky said. entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. They were told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed.“Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said.She said the sudden loss has left the family with questions they cannot yet answer.“It’s a shock to literally all of us,” Alexis said. “Nobody knows what happened.”Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin also worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family.Family loses second firefighter brother in just over a yearAustin’s death comes just over a year after the death of his 26-year-old brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district.The family told WPTV that Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died.“We lost two brothers in one year,” Alexis Hodge said. “I can’t describe to you the pain.”The family said Jairus’ death raised concerns about the medical care he received, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother.“He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”Family seeks answers about Austin’s deathNow, Austin’s family says they are determined to understand what happened in his final hours.“I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said.Alexis said the family wants to know who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive.“We are trying to find out what happened to him, who was around him, who saw him. All those questions that we have,” Alexis said.As the family waits for answers, Alexis said she is relying on her faith.“I just have to lean on God for now and have him direct my path. And direct the path of this investigation most importantly because things that are done in dark will always come to light,” Alexis said.For Alexis, getting those answers is an important part of being able to move forward with her grief.“After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.Siblings promise to carry on their brothers’ legacyAs the Hodge family grieves, Alexis and Javan say they are determined to make both Austin and Jairus proud.For Javan, Austin’s influence is already shaping his future. He said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. Javan is studying to become a nurse and is preparing to graduate in December.Javan said he knows Austin will still be with him when he walks across the stage.“I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”Alexis is also holding on to the plans she shared with Austin.“I’m gonna do everything we talked about. And I’m gonna make him proud,” she said. “I love him and I wish I could just pick up the phone and call him.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Verdict: false Former Social Security Commissioner Martin O Malley was explicit: every current beneficiary could face a 20% reduction in benefits if Congress doesn t act. The cut applies across the board — retirees, disabled recipients, and survivors. Verdict: true O Malley cited polling showing that eliminating or altering the Social Security tax cap is supported by over 80% of people — making it one of the rare proposals with genuine cross-partisan backing. Verdict: false The 1980s presented a similar moment, and Congress ultimately reached a deal — though not until the deadline was just months away. That precedent cuts both ways: a fix is possible, but it may not come early. A report from the Trump administration found that lower fertility rates, higher deportations, and tax changes have contributed to fewer dollars flowing into Social Security. The finding is notable because it ties specific policy decisions — not just demographic trends — to the program s funding pressures.

entry.title: Trump jokes about Ted Cruz Supreme Court nomination on campaign trail
entry.summary: President Donald Trump is crisscrossing the campaign trail in the final days before the midterm elections, making stops in Texas, Ohio and South Carolina as Republicans fight to hold key seats. Trump campaigned in Texas on Tuesday, where Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton is locked in a competitive race against Democrat James Talarico. While there, Trump also took time to talk about another prominent Texas Republican, Sen. Ted Cruz. Trump joked that Cruz would be an easy choice to confirm if a seat opened on the U.S. Supreme Court. I would pick Ted Cruz to be the next Supreme Court justice, Trump said. And I wouldnt have to worry about, I wouldnt even have to make a phone call. Trump went on to joke that Cruz would receive unanimous support for an unusual reason. And the Republicans would 100% vote for it because they cant stand him. They would like to get rid of him. So Id get 100% of the vote. Trumps Texas appearance was part of a late campaign push aimed at turning out Republican voters ahead of Election Day. Trump said the change would save consumers and energy producers $45 billion and unlock an additional 210 million barrels of oil. entry.title: The new renter is getting older
entry.summary: Renting a place to live isn't just for the young anymore. According to a 2026 analysis by Realtor.com , the typical family renter household is headed by a 42-year-old. The data also shows today's long-term renter is 55 years old, with a median household income of $48,500. Experts say for some households, staying in the same rental property is more about affordability and not just preference. However, the dream of homeownership hasn't disappeared. The same research shows around 65% of renters would like to own a home if they had the financial means. WATCH: The new renter is getting older The new renter is getting older Home warranty specialists 'Cinch Home Services' released a list this month of the states where it takes the longest to save for a home down payment. Florida ranks number 5 behind Hawaii, California, Montana and New York. In Florida, the study found it takes about 3.5 years to save up for a 15% down payment of $56,320 for a home valued around the median price of $375,470. Based on these figures, a potential homeowner in Florida would need to save about $1,341 a month. The analysis accounted for household earnings, factoring in the state's median income and the earnings that remain after paying rent, groceries, health care costs and transportation. Across the country, the estimated time to save for a home down payment is around two years and nine months, based on monthly savings of approximately $1,692. Cinch Services asked for a credit. There is nothing that ties directly to this study, but here is their website that was provided in the press release.

entry.title: Heart Walk aims to spread an important message on heart health
entry.summary: WTPV is the proud media sponsor of the American Heart Association 2026 Palm Beach Heart Walk, and we'd like to invite everyone to join the important community gathering! WPTV morning anchor Ashley Glass is glad to emcee the Heart Walk for a second year. entry.title: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuild after Hurricane Milton damage
entry.summary: Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million phase of its campus rebuild after Hurricane Milton spawned a tornado that damaged three main buildings , forcing students and school programs into portable classrooms, according to Martin County school officials. District leaders said improvements to Murray Middle School were already planned, but the hurricane damage added urgency to the project. The new construction will include learning and performing arts spaces, while the school's gym will also be renovated. WATCH: Murray Middle is rebuilding after Hurricane Milton. Students adapt after hurricane damage For Murray Middle student Nicholas Lowe, the transition meant adjusting to a different learning environment. 'It was a big change, but also I had to adapt to it to, like, be better for the choir,' Lowe said. Choir was among the programs that lost permanent space following Hurricane Milton. Dr. Anita Caswell, Murray Middle School's choir and drama director, said the storm destroyed decades of materials used by her programs. 'It was 60 years of drama props,' Caswell said. entry.title: Surface-to-air missile systems deployed near Trump airport, Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach
entry.summary: New surface-to-air missile systems have been deployed in Palm Beach as part of expanded security around President Donald Trump, with air defense assets visible near Donald J. Trump International Airport and Mar-a-Lago. The North American Aerospace Defense Command has said the deployment was made at the request of the U.S. Secret Service. WATCH: Surface-to-air missiles deployed in Palm Beach Surface-to-air missile systems deployed near Trump airport, Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach The new equipment is attracting attention from people traveling around the airport and near the president's private club. WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman spoke with aviation experts Dewitt Ingram and Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley about what the systems are designed to do and the types of threats they can counter. What are the air defense systems? 'What you see here are three trailer-mounted anti-aircraft, anti-drone, actually even anti-vehicle defense systems,' Ingram told Hoffman. Ingram said the weapons are surface-to-air missile systems, commonly known as SAMs, and described them as a final layer of protection. 'This is the last line of defense that will eliminate the threat to the president of the United States,' Ingram said. Hoffman also sat down with Buckley, a decorated former U.S. Navy fighter pilot and graduate of the Navy's elite TOPGUN flight school. 'I'm surprised those SAMs haven't been there longer,' Buckley said. Buckley said the systems are capable of defending against more than conventional aircraft. 'It's anti-aircraft, anti-drone, anti-anything that's a potential threat,' he said. Buckley identified some of the equipment visible near the airport as Avenger systems carrying Stinger missiles. entry.title: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development
entry.summary: By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. 13. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development Tuesday's vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday's vote. The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.

entry.title: Palm Beach County families face a youth mental health gap. A new FAU program aims to fill it.
entry.summary: For years, Palm Beach County has faced a shortage of mental health resources for children, leaving families vulnerable. Now, members of the community are stepping up to fill the need. Florida Atlantic University is launching a new program to provide that support for free. The program, called 'OWLS-FLY' (short for Opportunity, Wellness, Leadership Strength with Families Leading Youth), is being spearheaded by researchers Kelly Emelianchik-Key and Alex Fields inside the education building at FAU. It was made possible by a $1.2 million grant from the Children's Services Council of Palm Beach County. The program will provide free mental health counseling for kids ages 6 through 17 and their families. 'We provide group counseling, individual counseling, family counseling, and we'll have some different parental supports that are going to take place,' Emelianchik-Key said. The space is still coming together with different rooms for family and individual therapy. There's also a room set up to provide care via telehealth. Emelianchik-Key said she anticipates the first clients to be served in January. Fields said the stakes for young people are high. 'If you don't have solid mental health support, you can't build the foundation for a really healthy and high quality of life down the road,' Fields said. The program serves two needs: it helps families who need services, and it provides work experience for the people who are learning to provide them. 'We've worked with clinicians in the community, specifically for youth with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and I've heard how long their wait lists are, and that they're not able to provide services for months and on out,' Fields said. Master's students and graduates will get work experience through the program. Michelle Abarca of the Children's Services Council hopes to take what's learned through FAU's program and scale it in the future. 'Working with FAU is particularly exciting for us because we are a data-driven organization, and with the research that's going to be taking place at FAU, we hope to learn. We hope to be able to replicate some of this at one point,' Abarca said. The program is funded for three years, but Emelianchik-Key and Fields hope to continue it for years to come. 'To be able to do this is a really great honor,' Emelianchik-Key said. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting

entry.title: Black women on the ballot in the midterms could make history across the country
entry.summary: From the U.S. Senate to the governors mansion, dozens of Black women are on the ballot across the country. Dr. Ndidiamaka Okpareke, a pharmacist and Republican newcomer seeking a New Mexico congressional seat, is one of them. We need adequate representation at the table so that we can pull our communities forward, Okpareke told Scripps News. The daughter of Nigerian immigrants and a mother of three, Okpareke would be the first Black woman to represent New Mexico in Congress if she wins her long-shot bid against a three-term incumbent. RELATED STORY | Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges Some 1,500 miles away, 25-year-old Courtney McClain is making a similar bid. The Gen Z Democrat is running in South Carolinas 4th Congressional District in the Upstate, one of the states most conservative districts. She is seeking to become the first Black woman the state has sent to Congress. McClain told Scripps News that many people doubted her candidacy at the start. The Gen Z Democrat is running in South Carolina’s 4th Congressional District in the Upstate, one of the state’s most conservative districts. She is seeking to become the first Black woman the state has sent to Congress.McClain told Scripps News that many people doubted her candidacy at the start.“Now that we are so close to the finish line and with the support that we’ve been able to get people now realize that we can win this race,” McClain said.“STILL CONTINUING TO RUN”Okpareke and McClain are part of a larger group challenging assumptions about Black women’s electability. They’re going to have to deal with a lot of biases and a lot of bigotry. But many of them are able to overcome it, and they’re still continuing to run,” she said.“There definitely has been progress. There always is going to be bigotry, unfortunately, and there’s always going to be barriers,” Austin added. “But I think there are people in today’s society who are a lot more willing to look beyond race and gender when they cast their votes.”“TAKE YOURSELF OUT OF THE BOX”McClain said she doesn’t want her campaign defined by history-making alone.“Representation isn’t just about what the person looks like, but it’s about what that person can actually bring and do for the community,” McClain added.For Okpareke, a medical professional who says she’s bringing firsthand experience to policy that impacts different communities, representation goes beyond race or gender.“There are boxes that are built for us on both sides of the aisle,” Okpareke said. “We've seen that so often where you align yourself with a certain ideology or a certain way to think and you get boxed in and you can never come out of that.”“So take yourself out of the box, be true to who you are, and stand for the people,” she added.INTERACTIVE | How the midterms could shape the future of Social SecurityKelly Dittmar, director of research at CWAP, told Scripps News the election story this year goes beyond the firsts. Some Black women are leaving Congress, so the overall number may not rise sharply, she said. entry.title: Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team
entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program. WATCH REPORT BELOW: IRSC trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming, diving team Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team Instead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community. President Timothy Moore said at Tuesday's meeting that the proposal to cut the programs comes down to money. 'It's a tremendous opportunity to leave this college with that kind of skill, resource and talent here, but it comes at a price,' Moore said. The school president said the program currently costs around $1.4 to $2 million, money that isn't coming in through donations. 'What's required to maintain it as it sits today? We will require $15 to $20 million of an endowment to throw off enough revenue per year to sustain the program as it sits today,' Moore said. There's also a proposal to transition the remaining sports to Division II, resulting in potential savings of around $500,000. But if the swimming and diving program stays, Moore said the school may be forced to cut 50 percent for sports across the board. 'It's elimination of one or impose a penalty across all, and I would imagine that our championships will suffer because of that decision,' Moore said. The administration is expected to present the report at the Board of Trustees Nov. 17 meeting, when recommendations on how to move forward will be considered. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition last week to save the program, which has more than 12,500 signatures.

entry.title: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development
entry.summary: By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. 13. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development Tuesday's vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday's vote. The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.
