entry.article_text: — Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again. The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been 8 years since Lenny passed," she said. Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV’s Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming, it was nerve wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance to our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families.Determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God," she told McRoberts.She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers.When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, "Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us."But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data.When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate."In the White City area," she said. Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll."I haven't given up, it's just you get tired," she said. Millions invested in glioblastoma researchSince WPTV's initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research.Deb has also worked to support research in her son's memory.Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water.The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research.Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers."I'm just glad you have followed through the way that you have," she told McRoberts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. There's no better feeling in the world,' said Trevon Richardson, the band's vice president.

entry.title: Model Your Mission puts Palm Beach County nonprofits on the runway in West Palm Beach
entry.summary: Fashion will share the runway with philanthropy when representatives from about 38+ Palm Beach County nonprofits take part in Model Your Mission on Nov. 5 at the West Palm Beach Marriott. The event, organized by Extraordinary Charities, is designed as an interactive fashion show that gives local nonprofits a chance to showcase their work while their representatives walk the runway. Model Your Mission is a really cool interactive fashion show experience where we put representatives of about 38 small nonprofits paired with fashion partners like the Spark Boutique, and they get to strut their stuff while an MC talks about their incredible work, Christine with Extraordinary Charities said. Model Your Mission runs from 11:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 5, at the West Palm Beach Marriott, 2635 Old Okeechobee Road. A runway filled with Palm Beach County missions The organizations represented at Model Your Mission serve the community in very different ways, from education and literacy to environmental work, music and the arts. Extraordinary Charities describes itself as an accelerator for small nonprofits in Palm Beach County, providing opportunities for education and collaboration. The fashion show offers those organizations a different way to introduce their missions to the community. Among the participating organizations is the Womens Red Apple Foundation, which provides scholarships to women in Palm Beach County, including graduating high school seniors and adult women seeking to re-enter the workforce. Grace Notes Music Foundation provides free music education to underserved students in Palm Beach County. Roots and Wings provides a free after-school literacy program. Friends of Palm Beach combines ocean cleanup efforts with work helping people experiencing homelessness. Digital Vibez empowers young people through dance, fitness, technology, and the arts. Together, the groups illustrate the variety of work being done by smaller nonprofits across Palm Beach County. entry.article_text: King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

entry.title: Palm Beach County deputies shoot at armed person after hours of negotiations near Boca Raton, sheriff says
entry.summary: Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies discharged their firearms following a hours-long negotiation with an armed person who was threatening suicide Wednesday night, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office. Deputies responded shortly before 10 p.m. Wednesday to Sandalfoot Square at 23066 State Road 7 near Boca Raton, after receiving a report of an armed individual threatening suicide, the sheriffs office said. According to PBSO, deputies spent several hours negotiating with the person before the incident resulted in deputies firing their weapons. The sheriffs office did not immediately provide details about what led deputies to open fire or say whether the person was injured or killed. No information about injuries to deputies was included in the release. Sheriff Ric Bradshaw is expected to brief the media about the incident Thursday at the Airport Hilton, where the agency is holding its Annual Awards Ceremony. Additional details about the circumstances surrounding the shooting are expected to be released during the briefing. The incident remains under investigation. entry.title: Alaska governor orders investigation into ‘Dan Sullivan’ ballot controversy
entry.summary: A report alleging efforts to recruit a candidate who shares the same name as Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan has injected fresh controversy into one of the nation's most closely watched U.S. Senate races, where control of the chamber could ultimately be at stake. The controversy centers on a New York Times report detailing efforts by Democrats to encourage another Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher with no major political profile, to enter the race. The move would have placed two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot: the incumbent Republican senator and the retired educator. The report has prompted Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy to order a criminal investigation into the matter, raising questions about whether any state laws may have been violated. Legal experts, however, have expressed skepticism about whether the reported conduct amounts to a crime. Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign has denied involvement. In a statement, the campaign said it had 'no involvement in either Sullivan campaign.' The allegations have become a flashpoint because of Alaska's importance in the battle for Senate control. Political analysts rank the race among the nation's top tier of competitive contests, and even a small shift in votes could prove consequential. Alaska's election system relies heavily on mail voting, with a significant portion of ballots already cast. As voters review their ballots, some Republicans worry that the presence of two candidates with the same name could create confusion and potentially siphon votes from the incumbent senator. While political observers generally expect Republican voters to support the sitting senator, critics argue that even a small number of mistaken votes could influence the outcome if the race is decided by a narrow margin. The controversy gained additional national attention after former President Donald Trump accused Democrats of wrongdoing and called for severe consequences. 'They said they didn't do it, and we caught them cold,' Trump told reporters, adding that Peltola should resign and that those involved should face prosecution. No criminal charges have been filed, and it remains unclear whether investigators will identify any violations of law. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.article_text: Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again.The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.WATCH THE REPORT BELOW: The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.READ THE FULL STATE REPORT BELOW: A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been eight years since Lenny passed," she said.Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God," she told McRoberts.She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers.When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, "Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us."But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data.When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate."In the White City area," she said.Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll."I haven't given up; it's just you get tired," she said.Millions invested in glioblastoma researchSince WPTV's initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research.Deb has also worked to support research in her son's memory.Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water.The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research.Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers."I'm just glad you have followed through the way that you have," she told McRoberts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

entry.title: Family remembers Road Ranger killed on I-95 as loving father, caretaker
entry.summary: The family of Kalibe Combs, a 23-year-old Road Ranger killed while working at an Interstate 95 crash scene near Lantana Road, is remembering the young father as a loving caretaker while calling for changes they hope could protect other roadside workers. Combs was struck early Sunday on northbound I-95 near Lantana Road while working at an existing crash investigation, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. Investigators said an 18-year-old driver entered a closed lane, struck Combs and then collided with a marked FHP cruiser. Combs died at the scene. WATCH: Family remembers Road Ranger killed on I-95 as loving father, caretaker Family remembers Road Ranger killed on I-95 as loving new father Combs leaves behind his fiance, Siarah Rodriguez, and their 3-month-old daughter, Kiara, according to his family and a fundraiser established to support them. 'He brought a lot of light. So losing him, we're losing a lot of light,' his mother, Aretta Combs, told WPTV. 'He was a caretaker' Combs' family told WPTV he was funny, kind and hardworking. His mother said his commitment to his family was at the center of the life he was building. 'He was a caretaker. He lost his life trying to provide for his family, trying to take care of his family,' Aretta Combs said. 'So what's more heartbreaking is that something like this can happen and change the lives of so many people.' entry.title: Florida education data breach may have exposed Social Security numbers of 4.9 million people
entry.summary: A data breach involving a Florida student financial aid website may have exposed personal information, including Social Security numbers, belonging to approximately 4.9 million people, according to the Florida Department of Education (FLDOE). FLDOE said in a Thursday statement that staff became aware Oct. 19 of unauthorized criminal access involving its Florida Student Financial Aid website. The department said the compromised personally identifiable information included Social Security numbers. Officials did not specify what other types of personal information may have been exposed. The breach is believed to have been limited to the Florida Student Financial Aid website, and as many as 4.9 million people potentially were affected, according to FLDOE. The department said it activated its cybersecurity response protocols after detecting the incident, took steps to contain the unauthorized activity and secure its systems, and notified the Florida Attorney General's Office. FLDOE said it is working with the Florida Digital Service and Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The incident remains under criminal investigation. What does the breach mean for financial aid? FLDOE said current financial aid is not at risk and the incident will not delay financial aid disbursements or tuition payments from the department. Officials also said the breach will not affect eligibility for scholarships, grants or student loans from FLDOE. Some department websites and online services, however, may experience temporary disruptions as officials work to restore full functionality. What should people affected by the breach do? FLDOE recommends monitoring financial and online accounts for suspicious activity and regularly reviewing account statements and credit reports. The department also recommends considering a fraud alert or credit freeze with the major credit bureaus. Consumers can obtain free credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com and find additional information about responding to a data breach through the Federal Trade Commission's IdentityTheft.gov website . Anyone with questions about the FLDOE breach can contact the department at databreach@fldoe.org. FLDOE said information could change as the criminal investigation continues. The department is posting updates on its data breach information page .

entry.title: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review - WPEC
entry.summary: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review    WPEC
entry.article_text: Florida health officials notified CBS12 News on Thursday that an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review is available, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma In June and October, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ concerns, interviewing patients and traveling through neighborhoods with Stephanie Ankiel, who helps families through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home in Fort Pierce and another home a few houses away where she said a resident received the same initial diagnosis in 2025: oligodendroglioma. Ankiel previously told CBS12 News that her husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma and that his cancer was later described as glioblastoma. The I-Team asked health officials how their analysis handles changing diagnoses and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. Those points were not explained in the department’s response before the report’s release. The updated report shows two tumor classification codes included in the 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said evolving cancer classifications mean those codes are no longer included in the glioblastoma case definition. The report does not explain how cases initially classified as another tumor type and later described as glioblastoma are handled. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. That means the review does not capture diagnoses such as Laura Cooper’s. Lucie woman told CBS12 News in June that she was diagnosed with glioblastoma in November 2025, years after losing her best friend to the disease. At the time of the interview, she was undergoing treatment and participating in a clinical trial. Environmental records reviewed Health officials reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department reported that its water review did not identify contamination involving chemicals linked by the Environmental Protection Agency to glioblastoma or other brain-related health concerns. It also reported no increase in monitored environmental radiation levels around the plant. The documents describe reviews of existing records and monitoring data. They do not specify whether new environmental samples were collected specifically for this assessment. In Thursday’s email, Sperber highlighted the department’s conclusion that no environmental hazard in the Treasure Coast region has been shown to cause glioblastoma. The report also acknowledges limits to the cancer registry: It lacks environmental exposure information and complete residential histories. A patient’s address at diagnosis may not reflect where a relevant exposure occurred. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners.

entry.title: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library sees $25K boost following WPTV report
entry.summary: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library in Palm Beach County is seeing a boost in both donations and enrollment following WPTV's previous report on the program. After WPTV reporter Christy Waite original story aired, about 250 more children have signed up to receive free books each month, and the program has received more than $25,000 in donations. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Imagination Library sees surge after WPTV report Donation pour into Imagination Library 'Since the story aired, about 250 children have signed up to receive their monthly books, and we have received more than $25,000 in donations,' said Christen Thompson, director of the Palm Beach County Imagination Library. The program sends children a free, age-appropriate book each month, helping families make reading a regular part of their routine at home. 'There are currently 1,600 children in Palm Beach County actively enrolled and getting a free book every single month,' Thompson said. Program leaders and community members hope that number keeps growing. Thompson said about 75,000 children in Palm Beach County are eligible for the program. For some families, having books at home can come with a cost that adds up. 'Unfortunately, for some people, books are a luxury, and this program helps take away that burden,' said Merrell Angstreich, grant writer and public information officer for Lake Park. But the program's impact can go beyond the cost of a book. For mom Coral Rhodes, receiving a new book each month is an opportunity to pass the love of reading she grew up with on to her daughter. 'I was homeschooled growing up, and my mom loved to read, so she instilled that in me,' Rhodes said. 'I want to homeschool her and pass on that love of reading to her.' Program leaders say more than 40,000 books have been distributed to children in Palm Beach County to date. Now, with about 250 more children signed up and more than $25,000 in new donations, leaders hope to continue growing the program and getting books into the hands of more children across Palm Beach County. Community members can also help the program work toward its goal of providing free books to every child under 5 in Palm Beach County. There are three ways to get involved: participate in the Run for Reading 5K, attend a free community movie screening, or sponsor a child for $30, which provides that child with monthly books for an entire year.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

Lucie County: Through Oct. Indian River County: Through Oct. to 4 p.m., with extended hours Thursdays. Okeechobee County: Through Oct. What’s on the ballot Voters across the region will decide races for governor, U.S. The statewide contests include Republican Byron Donalds against Democrat David Jolly for governor, Republican Ashley Moody against Democrat Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate, and Republican James Uthmeier against Democrat Jose Javier Rodriguez for attorney general. Congressional and state legislative races also will appear on ballots. Local races and ballot questions depend on a voter’s address. One statewide ballot question is Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes and lower the annual cap on assessment increases for certain non-homestead properties. It also would limit how local governments can use property tax revenue. Supporters say it would provide tax relief; local governments and public agencies have warned it could reduce funding for services. A proposed constitutional amendment needs at least 60% voter approval to pass. Vote-by-mail deadline The deadline to request a vote-by-mail ballot was Oct. entry.title: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

entry.title: Martin County puts brakes on new large data centers for one year - cw34.com
entry.summary: Martin County puts brakes on new large data centers for one year    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners voted to temporarily halt new applications for large data centers in unincorporated areas of the county for one year on Tuesday. The vote passed 4-0 among Martin County commissioners. The decision gives county officials time to develop regulations governing large data centers, which have raised concerns about electricity consumption and environmental impacts. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana The vote follows an earlier commission meeting in which officials advanced the proposed moratorium for further consideration. The temporary pause applies to new applications for large data centers in areas outside city limits, not throughout the entire county. County officials plan to use the one-year period to review and develop rules for future large data center proposals.

entry.title: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicated its new regional operations center in Fort Pierce Thursday morning, bringing its work under one roof and expanding its capacity to serve people across four counties. The 132,000-square-foot facility at 401 Loop Road supports the organization’s food storage and fresh food programs, prepared meals, nutrition education, benefits assistance and workforce training. The food bank, which began in 1988, is the only food bank serving Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. It reaches about 250,000 people each week and works with hundreds of nonprofit partners. The center’s production kitchen has more than doubled in size, growing from 7,000 to 15,000 square feet. It can produce up to 25,000 meals a day during a disaster, while also preparing nutritious meals for the community. The new freezer area alone could fit one and a half of the food bank’s former facilities. The center is designed to help people build stability for the future as well as meet immediate needs. Adults and children can take nutrition education classes on site, and nutrition information is sent with food boxes delivered to seniors. Its three job-training programs focus on culinary, hospitality and barista skills. Students learn skills such as knife safety, food safety and making pasta from scratch. The programs offer certifications in stages, and some courses are free. See also: Project Thanksgiving: Ruth & Norman Rales Jewish Family Services helps families in need During the dedication, 10 community members took part in a ceremonial First Box packing to represent the network behind the food bank’s work. Robin Safley of Feeding Florida added fresh vegetables on behalf of the statewide hunger-relief network. Donor Dee Locke added fresh fruit, and volunteer Tatiana Rousseau added peanut butter. The food bank’s capital campaign is continuing. To donate, visit the Feed Unite Flourish capital campaign page . Project Thanksgiving The Treasure Coast Food Bank is also a recipient of donations through CBS12 News' Project Thanksgiving . Drop off non-perishable food items at Treasure Coast iTHINK Financial bank branches to help the food bank feed families this holiday season. Treasure Coast Branches Fellsmere: 56 N. entry.title: 'Still in the middle of this': Coastal erosion impacts Vero Beach as king tides and strong winds persist - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Still in the middle of this': Coastal erosion impacts Vero Beach as king tides and strong winds persist    WPBF
entry.article_text: King tides and strong onshore winds have caused significant coastal erosion along the boardwalk in Vero Beach, with officials describing the damage as severe and warning that the weather event is not yet over. I was trying to look it up to see if there was a name, a named storm off the coast or anything, but nope, it's just weather," one observer said. Quintin Bergman is the resource manager with Indian River County. He's monitoring the situation. "So, what we're seeing here is two weather events that have aligned," Bergman said. "We're still in the middle of this. We're not through with the weather event. The forecast is showing elevated winds for a few more days, and the king tide event is still going to be affecting the tide." The erosion has impacted a section of beachfront parking on Ocean Drive, an area official have identified as one of their erosion hot spots. One couple who walked on the beach the day before said they didn’t notice the damage but weren’t surprised by the situation. "That's what nature wants to do, and that's kind of what you need to let nature do, I think. But the problem is we keep building on it. That's the interruption, not nature doing its thing," they said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Officials described the erosion as approaching severe. "I would classify this as leaning more on the severe side of erosion. It's not extreme by any means, but definitely we are very concerned," Bergman said. Authorities are contacting park officials to discuss safety measures to protect the public. Lucie County, beach erosion has also been observed, but officials credited beach replenishment projects with helping protect nearby buildings. "I mean, it certainly helped that we did a renourishment last year. Any time you lose sand, the more you have on there, the better you're going to protect your shoreline," Erick Gill, St. Lucie County public information officer, said. In parts of Martin County, residents are still dealing with flooding caused by the rough conditions. Despite the challenges, some beachgoers in Vero Beach, like Svetlana Ryan, are still enjoying the view and noting the changes to the shoreline. "We noticed because there was so much sand before, and now it's just a wall. But you do with whatever you have to do here in Vero Beach," Ryan said. Officials plan to assess the damage after the weather event passes. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.summary: A newly redrawn congressional district stretching across South Florida is setting up a battle between two candidates with sharply different ideas about how to make life more affordable for Floridians. Republican Casey Askar and Democrat Pia Dandiya are competing to represent District 22, which now connects coastal and inland communities across four counties. Dandiya agreed to an interview. Askar did not respond to multiple requests for comment. However, Askar's campaign website and political advertisements outline his positions on many of those issues and make clear that affordability is at the center of his campaign. 'We're paying too much. For pretty much everything,' Askar says in one campaign ad. The Republican has pledged to cut fuel and property taxes, increase the child tax credit and reduce government regulations he argues are contributing to higher costs. Dandiya is also making affordability a central theme of her campaign. 'People are no longer suffering in silence; they are suffering out loud,' Dandiya told investigative reporter Kate Hussey. Two very different approaches to healthcare The candidates diverge significantly on how they would address healthcare costs. Dandiya, a former teacher and principal, supports allowing Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices and restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies as ways to lower costs. 'Those are real, actionable ways that we can help people make ends meet,' Dandiya said. Askar is taking a different approach. Social Security becomes another dividing line Both candidates say they want to protect Social Security, but their approaches differ. Dandiya told WPTV she believes raising the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes could be one strategy for ensuring the program has enough money to pay promised benefits. entry.summary: An 18-month seawall replacement project on Palm Beach is raising questions from residents and beachgoers about why the entire stretch of Midtown Beach needs to close, what access will remain during construction and what the new seawall will look like. Construction is expected to begin in January 2027 and continue through summer 2028. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Palm Beach answers questions on 18-month Beach closure For people who consider Midtown Beach part of their everyday lives, a year and a half without normal access is a major concern. 'I hope it doesn't get higher though, I don't want to block the view,' said Bridget St. Laurent, a local and owner of Palm Beach Beauty Lab on Palm Beach. 'It's my life, it's my backyard, I grew up here, and the fact I can just take a five-minute drive to the ocean means so much.' Those questions and concerns brought people to a public outreach meeting with project leaders. 'The beach, they're going to take the beach away from us. I've been there for 35 years, and there's always been a beach, and now we can't go to the beach and they can't seem to explain why they have to close the whole Midtown Beach, why can't they do it in sections,' said Sheila Hurley, who lives in a condo along the beach. 'That's a lot of beach to close,' Hurley said. Two weeks ago, the Town Council voted to replace the seawall all at once instead of completing the work in sections. The town says doing the project in sections would have taken twice as long and cost twice as much. When WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked Hurley whether she would have been OK with that alternative, she said, 'I think so, I think people would've been happier. So it's all led to us coming to this progressive design-build, and that's why the time is right," Hurley said.One of the biggest questions WPTV has received is whether people will still be able to use the beach during construction.Hurley said normal access to Midtown Beach will be closed because of safety concerns involving the construction site and heavy equipment."No, I don't think you're gonna want to lay on the beach while it's going on. There's gonna be some heavy equipment, but we have to close the beach access because we don't believe there's a safe way for us to bring people from the roadway onto the beach," Hurley said.However, that doesn't necessarily mean the entire shoreline will be inaccessible at all times."We can't close the ocean, so there will be times when you'll be able to traverse the beach north-south as long as you are more towards the water side," Hurley said.The space he's referring to is east of a berm that's between the ocean and construction activity. Hurley said the barrier will help protect sea turtles from entering the construction area while also keeping people away from the job site."So if you're thinking from the ocean side, it protects the wildlife, mainly the turtles, from coming into the construction site. And then the same with human wildlife, so that people aren't walking onto the construction site," Hurley said. "But no matter what construction method we end up with, there will be some kind of fencing on that side that separates the job site from the ocean."Sea turtle nesting season is also playing a major role in how the work is scheduled."Sea turtle nesting season is a major contributing factor in how we schedule the construction," Hurley said. "We cannot be on the beach unless we have a berm already constructed there."While the project is still in its design phase, Hurley said the new wall is expected to be about six inches higher on average and extend farther east than the existing wall.He also explained that the portion of the existing seawall people see today is largely decorative."The structural component of the wall is actually underground. Everything that we see above ground is decorative," Hurley said.The replacement is intended to provide more protection while maintaining the familiar look of the existing wall."So the intent is for it to be identical to what is out there. So it'll be the same color. We even went out and found the original molds that are the scallops that were put in, I think in the 80s. So it's going to look very similar to what's out there," Hurley said.Hurley said the existing above-ground wall "doesn't actually serve a purpose" and described it as sacrificial."So this new wall is going to actually provide resiliency and protect the community," Hurley said.Plans are also being considered to create walking space around the east side of the Worth Avenue clock tower.Hurley said the location of the existing seawall creates complications around the landmark."So the main reason is that the original seawall butts up directly adjacent to that, so there's no way for us to put the seawall without damaging the clock tower," Hurley said. "So we have to go seaward, and that's what we're permitted for."The project team is also recommending another beach access point on the north end of the project."We do agree that there is a lot of people who are jumping the wall. That's why we did add the, or we're recommending to add the beach access on the north end," Hurley said.The town also plans to relocate fragments of vegetation along the seawall during construction and reinstall cuttings after the replacement is complete.Phase one of the project's design is expected to be completed in fall 2026.The project's guaranteed maximum price has not yet been finalized. Hurley said the town hopes to present that figure to the Town Council in December.Construction is scheduled to begin in January 2027, with completion planned for summer 2028.Project officials plan to host more community meetings as details on the project get finalized.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Some Florida ACA customers are being auto-enrolled in new 2027 health plans without their knowledge
entry.summary: A West Palm Beach woman says she knew she would have to find a health plan offered by the Affordable Care Act since her current insurance was leaving the program at the end of the year. What she didn't realize was that she was automatically signed up in a new plan. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida ACA customers auto-enrolled in new 2027 plans without knowing Florida ACA customers auto-enrolled in new 2027 plans without knowing 'All of a sudden I started getting phone calls, text messages, and emails from another health insurance company saying congrats, you're enrolled, and then getting a bill from them,' Melissa Smith said. 'It took forever to figure out if my doctor was even in their network,' she added. 'My doctor's not in their network, so I don't want to be on their plan.' What happened to Smith does appear to be common. 'If you were enrolled in a plan, there are automatic re-enrollments,' said Scott Darius of Florida Voices for Health. 'If your plan has changed or disappeared, the marketplace will often put you in a plan that they deem to be similar.' It's likely enrolling in another plan on your own can clear out any automatic enrollment. Open enrollment in the ACA in Florida begins on Nov. 1. Darius says most plans have already posted their rates for 2027 and overall rates are up about 10%. He says start by finding someone you trust to help you navigate the enrollment process, which can be done at healthcare.gov 'First, make a list for yourself in terms of what your priorities are,' Darius said. 'If you have doctors that you enjoy seeing, if you have medications that you know you need covered, create that list of priorities for yourself and then work with a trusted source to go through the options and to see what you can get covered.' The enrollment period ends on Jan. 15.

entry.title: Florida mom fights wrongful death law after daughter dies hours after leaving hospital
entry.summary: Two years after her only daughter died just hours after leaving a Florida hospital, Beth Miller says she is still searching for answers. She also wants to make sure another family does not face the same barriers she has encountered. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida mom fights 'free kill' law after daughter's death Florida mom fights 'free kill' law after daughter's death 'I would like to be the only one,' Miller said. 'I know what it feels like. I don't want anybody else to have to go through this.' Miller's daughter, Dawn Miller, was 49 when she died after undergoing gallbladder surgery. A previous WPTV investigation found medical records showed Dawn initially 'tolerated the procedure well.' But her condition later changed. Her hemoglobin dropped. Doctors confirmed sepsis, a potentially life-threatening response to infection, and lab results the morning of her discharge showed decreased kidney function. Records also show Dawn twice resisted leaving the hospital, telling medical staff she felt 'weak' and 'not ready to go home.' She was discharged anyway. Minutes after arriving home, she collapsed. 'I couldn't get her to breathe,' Beth Miller recalled. 'And I just felt so helpless. You know, and then you're staring at your daughter trying to do CPR, and nothing's happening.' Dawn was pronounced dead about two hours after leaving the hospital. Dr. Gerald Feigin, a medical examiner and forensic pathologist who reviewed Dawn's medical records for WPTV, said he believes she should not have been discharged. 'She should have been given emergency transfusions and [they should] figure out why she was bleeding,' Feigin said. 'Possibly had additional surgery.' Feigin also said the hospital should have performed an autopsy. It did not. WPTV previously reported Beth Miller requested an autopsy after her daughter's death, but the hospital declined to perform one. The hospital also declined to answer WPTV's questions about Dawn's case. 'I don't have an answer to this day,' Miller said. 'It's on your mind 24/7.' A legal barrier to seeking damages Miller hoped she might find answers through the legal system. But Florida law creates another obstacle. A provision of the Florida Wrongful Death Act restricts which surviving family members can recover certain damages in medical malpractice cases. Critics have dubbed it Florida's 'free kill' law. Under the provision, parents generally cannot recover certain damages for the medical malpractice death of an adult child age 25 or older.
