"I know what it feels like. I don't want anybody else to have to go through this."Miller's daughter, Dawn Miller, was 49 when she died after undergoing gallbladder surgery.A previous WPTV investigation found medical records showed Dawn initially "tolerated the procedure well." But her condition later changed.Her hemoglobin dropped. Doctors confirmed sepsis, a potentially life-threatening response to infection, and lab results the morning of her discharge showed decreased kidney function.Records also show Dawn twice resisted leaving the hospital, telling medical staff she felt "weak" and "not ready to go home."She was discharged anyway.Minutes after arriving home, she collapsed."I couldn't get her to breathe," Beth Miller recalled. "And I just felt so helpless. You know, and then you're staring at your daughter trying to do CPR, and nothing's happening."Dawn was pronounced dead about two hours after leaving the hospital.Dr. Gerald Feigin, a medical examiner and forensic pathologist who reviewed Dawn's medical records for WPTV, said he believes she should not have been discharged."She should have been given emergency transfusions and [they should] figure out why she was bleeding," Feigin said. "Possibly had additional surgery."Feigin also said the hospital should have performed an autopsy.It did not.WPTV previously reported Beth Miller requested an autopsy after her daughter's death, but the hospital declined to perform one. The hospital also declined to answer WPTV's questions about Dawn's case."I don't have an answer to this day," Miller said. "It's on your mind 24/7."Miller hoped she might find answers through the legal system.But Florida law creates another obstacle.A provision of the Florida Wrongful Death Act restricts which surviving family members can recover certain damages in medical malpractice cases.Critics have dubbed it Florida's "free kill" law.Under the provision, parents generally cannot recover certain damages for the medical malpractice death of an adult child age 25 or older. Adult children also face restrictions on recovering those damages for the death of a parent.Dawn was unmarried, in her 40s, and had no children."Unless she had kids or a spouse, there's nothing I can do," Miller said.Jordan Dulce, a West Palm Beach trial attorney who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is among the critics calling for the law to change."It's completely arbitrary," Dulce said.Dulce said potential liability is something hospitals consider as part of risk management."I can tell you, from a risk management perspective, it's very much on their radar," he said.Critics argue the law can reduce the potential financial consequences when alleged medical negligence results in the death of certain patients compared with others.Dulce argues that it can weaken one of the financial incentives intended to promote accountability and patient safety."It's not meaning that you're intending to hurt someone," he said. "But obviously, when you don't have those guardrails up, certainly the quality of health care suffers."Florida enacted the provision in 1990 amid concerns over the cost and availability of medical malpractice insurance.Federal data show Florida had the sixth-highest number of medical malpractice claim payouts in the country that year.A Yale Journal on Regulation study also found average malpractice premiums had more than quadrupled over a four-year period, from about $4,300 to $18,000.At the time, proponents of the law argued rising malpractice costs were threatening access to doctors and driving physicians out of the state.But some of those claims later came under scrutiny.A 2003 U.S. Government Accountability Office report examined reports of physician shortages in Florida and other states and found some widely cited claims were "anecdotal" or "inaccurate."In one example, medical society officials reported two Florida counties had lost all of their neurosurgeons. GAO investigators found at least five neurosurgeons were still practicing in each county.The report also found the number of new medical licenses in Florida had increased while the number of physicians per capita remained relatively unchanged."There's been no actual studies or evidence or support for this law actually doing what it was intended to do," Dulce said.Florida's medical malpractice insurance market has since stabilized.A 2026 report from Florida's Office of Insurance Regulation found the industry was "doing well," with annual premium increases far below the triple-digit increases seen during the insurance crisis of the late 1980s.The report, however, attributed much of that stabilization to malpractice reforms enacted in 2003 — more than a decade after the wrongful-death provision took effect.Florida also remains among the most expensive states in the country for medical malpractice insurance, ranking third nationwide."No matter what we try to do to limit the victim's right to courts, that has never stopped the insurance industry from continuing to increase their prices because that's their model," Dulce said. "At the end of the day, trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper."WPTV reached out to several local state lawmakers to share Miller's story and ask about the law. None have yet agreed to sit down for an interview.For Miller, the debate is more than a question of insurance rates, liability or state policy.It is about the daughter she still pictures lying on the floor of her home."It will always be difficult," Miller said. "I see her laying on that floor all the time."She said she will continue speaking publicly in hopes of convincing lawmakers to change the law."To get this point across, to make it so other people don't have to go through this suffering," Miller said.Last year, Florida lawmakers passed legislation that would have repealed the provision, but the bill never took effect.In the next part of WPTV's investigation, investigative reporter Kate Hussey examines what happened to that effort — and shares the stories of other Florida families who say they have encountered the same legal barrier.

entry.title: Beef prices squeeze a beloved Texas BBQ joint as midterm voters weigh costs in the Rio Grande Valley
entry.summary: Barbecue is one of the five basic food groups in Texas, and many in the Rio Grande Valley will tell you Teddys is one of the best BBQ joints in the state. But these days, quality meat comes with a high price, and it may impact how people vote in the midterms. Youre talking about the cost of meat itself almost tripling, so its definitely been hard, said co-owner Joel Garcia. Garcia added that every aspect of his business costs more, causing him to close on days he would like to be open and raise prices for customers. RELATED STORY | Increased beef imports still haven't brought relief for high consumer prices According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, beef prices were 3.5% higher in September 2026 than they were a year ago. Overall, the USDA expects beef prices to increase almost 9% in 2026. It is a very fine line that were riding, said Garcia. We raise them too much, we lose customers. We keep our price too low, we lose money. Customers are riding that same line. A few years ago, going out was like, you know, $30, Teddys BBQ customer Adolfo Grimaldo told Scripps News. Now, its like $50 to $60, almost twice the price. Menu prices are up 3.5% from last year, according to the National Restaurant Association. INTERACTIVE | A 109-year-old company is making major changes as beef prices soar With the midterms days away, Adolfo Grimaldo thinks mixing things up, also known as ticket splitting, could be the way to bring political change and lower prices. The way people are right now it seems everyone wants to vote one way or another, and nobody really wants to meet in the middle, said Grimaldo. I always like to vote for a mixture of both. Garcia doesnt put a lot of stock in politicians. With the American cattle herd at historic lows, his faith is in the pastures of South Texas. I trust ranchers, said Garcia. I trust they are, hopefully, still continuing to produce. Ranchers are also dealing with higher costs. Ranchers in the Rio Grande Valley told Scripps News the high price of fuel, labor, and land are all impacting their ability to grow their herd.

entry.title: Florida man receives life sentence for using AI to create child pornography of neighborhood children
entry.summary: A Martin County judge has ordered a sentence equal to life in prison for a man who used artificial intelligence to create child pornography, a case the Martin County Sheriff's Office said it had never seen at that time. Daniel Warren was charged with 75 felony counts of possession of child pornography and seven felony counts of video voyeurism for using AI to create child pornography. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida man receives life sentence for using AI to create child pornography of neighborhood children 'His innocent neighbors, whose parents trusted him to be appropriate with their children, he was taking covert photos of them and then asking for those children to be transformed into some sexualized image which he shared with others,' prosecutor Kristen Chase said. Warren was arrested for these crimes in 2024. At the time, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said it was their first case involving AI and child exploitation. A man who identified himself as an extended family member testified before the judge Wednesday. 'That would be a detriment to the children to have this man even anywhere near a child,' the extended family member said. Before sentencing, Warren showed some remorse. 'My entire community, [I] basically destroyed every friendship I've built,' Warren said. 'I dwell on it every night.' When his defense attorney asked whether he dwells on the decisions he made, Warren said, 'Absolutely.' After listening to the testimony, Judge Elizabeth Metzger decided it was not appropriate to grant a lesser sentence and opted for the minimum allowable sentence by law, at just over 1,000 months per count. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Florida brain tumor patient says nearly $1 million in medical bills are now covered after insurance denial
entry.summary: Five months after an insurance denial threatened to leave a Florida brain tumor patient facing the cost of life-saving surgery, Broqsten Bunt says he has received two pieces of news: He is medically cleared, and the nearly $1 million in medical care billed following his surgery has been wiped down to zero. WATCH FULL STORY HERE: Brain surgery patients gets billed paid for after insurance denial Blessed to be in this position, thank you for all of your help,' Bunt told Tampa Bay 28 Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone recently. 'Everything is working like it used to pre-surgery, and I've got my strength back,No prescriptions ... no future medical needs. Five months earlier When we first met the 36-year-old West Palm Beach man in June, his health and finances were both uncertain. Bunt is a childhood leukemia survivor. But the radiation therapy that helped rid his body of cancer as a child has taken a toll on him as an adult. Hes developed an aggressive brain tumor known as a meningioma. Doctors believe it was connected to the radiation treatment he received as a child. Bunt lives in West Palm Beach. His neurosurgeon near his home said he needed to get the tumor removed and referred him to Tampa General Hospital and a specific neurosurgeon because of the complexity of his case. Then came the denials Although the hospital was in-network with his insurer, Florida Blue, the surgeon was not. As a result, just before his scheduled operation, Florida Blue denied an appeal for additional coverage for the out-of-network care. In June, Bunt moved forward with the surgery anyway. He invited us to speak with him from his hospital recovery room. At the time, Bunt described being caught between his doctors and his insurance company. I'm taking calls from the insurance side, I'm taking calls from the medical office side, he told us. I'm like, I don't write the bills, I don't pay the bills. Why are you calling me? Call each other and figure it out. Then, in the middle of the interview, Bunt's case took a dramatic turn. A Tampa General Hospital spokesperson interrupted our interview with an update, stating that hospital leadership had worked with Florida Blue and the insurer had agreed to cover Bunt's preoperative workup, surgeries, hospital admission and postoperative care. Neither Tampa General Hospital nor Florida Blue explained to us at the time what specifically prompted the reversal. Read our original investigation: Florida brain tumor patient denied insurance coverage

It took the news making the population aware," he said.Neither Florida Blue nor Tampa General Hospital ever explained specifically why the coverage decision changed. Florida Blue told us at the time that it could not discuss individual cases but said it works with members, doctors and hospitals through its appeals process and is “pleased when we reach positive outcomes for our members.” Now, with his surgery behind him and his surgery balance at zero, Bunt has a message for other patients challenging a health insurance denial.“Don't back off the gas,” he said. “You just have to keep pushing and keep reaching out to people. You have to get the care you need so that you can survive,” he added. “You can deal with the details after. If you're not here, you don't have to worry about the details.”If you are dealing with a health insurance denial over medically necessary care, let Katie know about it below.

entry.title: Mattamy Homes donates 125 acres in Martin County to support St. Lucie River restoration
entry.summary: Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River. The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Mattamy Homes donating portion of development to aid in future St. Lucie River clean-up   James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality.   Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres.   Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river. WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project. 'The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project,' Fitzgerald said. 'Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects.' Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

entry.title: Dolphins prepare for Patriots as injuries loom ahead of Sunday's matchup
entry.summary: Ahead of Sunday's matchup between the Dolphins and Patriots, rookie standout offensive lineman Kadyn Proctor's status is unclear after missing Wednesday and Thursday's practices with concussion symptoms. Also, it's unclear if Patriots superstar AJ Brown's will be available for New England. Still, the Dolphins are preparing like everyone is healthy and available. WATCH BELOW: Dolphins gear up for Patriots, could be without OL Proctor Dolphins gear up for Patriots, could be without rookie Kadyn Proctor 'We're just focusing on us and focusing on what I can do better and what I need to do to be able to stop them and what to expect. It's more so on how we do things, so that's just coming off the ball with pad leverage,' said offensive lineman Jonah Savaiinaea. The Patriots have one of the NFL's better defenses, ranking top-10 in scoring defense and total yards allowed, so Savaiinaea and the Dolphins offense know they'll have their hands full. 'Much respect to them; we're playing a physical team, and we know that and are aware of that. We're a physical team as well, so we're excited,' said Savaiinaea. While the offense knows the Patriots defense will be a full go, the Dolphins defense has a lot to prepare for, as AJ Brown is still not fully healed from his ankle injury and his status for Sunday's game is still up in the air. Healthy or not, the defense knows they can't sleep on the Pats. 'AJ Brown has been a premium guy for a long time. They have the other good guys as well, so we got to go in focused,' said cornerback Jason Marshall Jr. Focused best describes the Dolphins' game plan this week, especially rookie safety Michael Taaffe, who's leading the team in interceptions with two coming into this week and knows his ball-hawk skills will be needed. 'Getting so caught up in the solo stats is not what this locker room stands for so I can't stand up here and say that's what I stand for. That's not what our leaders stand for, we care about wins, and that's what we're trying to add to that column,' said Taaffe.

entry.title: CBS12 News Athlete of the Week: Alex Thornton does it all for Jensen Beach - cw34.com
entry.summary: CBS12 News Athlete of the Week: Alex Thornton does it all for Jensen Beach    cw34.com
entry.article_text: When Jensen Beach needs a big play, senior Alex Thornton has a knack for delivering on both sides of the football. Thornton is this week’s CBS12 News Athlete of the Week after a career night helped the Falcons capture the District 13-4A football championship outright. In a 42-21 victory over Fort Pierce Westwood on October 23, Thornton rushed for 215 yards on just 15 carries and scored four touchdowns. He found the end zone on runs of 2, 39, 20 and 7 yards, recording the first four-touchdown game of his career. Three of those scores came in the second half as Jensen Beach pulled away. But Thornton’s impact extends well beyond the offensive backfield. A physical, hard-hitting linebacker, he has built a reputation for setting the tone on defense. His ability to make plays at both running back and linebacker has made him one of Jensen Beach’s most important players. He is the tone-setter, head coach Tim Caffey said in an earlier profile of Thornton, describing the senior’s physical style of play. See also: Dolphins look to build on first win against Patriots Thornton’s contributions are part of a larger winning tradition at Jensen Beach. The Falcons’ victory over Westwood secured the program’s fifth district championship overall and fourth in the past five years under Caffey. It also extended the team’s streak of playoff appearances to five consecutive seasons. Thornton has been part of three district championship teams during his high school career, making him a key figure in the program’s continued success. His potential has also attracted attention at the next level. Before his senior season, Thornton had received eight Division I college football offers, according to TCPalm’s recruiting profile. With the district title secured, Thornton and the Falcons now turn their attention to the postseason. For the senior, the goal is to help Jensen Beach make another deep playoff run before his high school career comes to an end. Thornton’s performance against Westwood showed exactly what makes him stand out: the ability to take over a game, lead by example and deliver when his team needs him most. entry.article_text: Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma Ankiel said she was not surprised by the state’s conclusion. Earlier this month, she drove I-Team reporter Katie Bente through Fort Pierce neighborhoods, pointing out homes where she said brain tumor patients had lived in some cases, only doors apart. Her questions are also personal. Ankiel’s husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012. Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. Now, Ankiel is helping another patient with the same initial diagnosis. Amber Lee, 37, is living with oligodendroglioma, a brain tumor that is distinct from glioblastoma. The first thing I remember thinking of when they told me I had cancer was, I have a daughter, Lee said. Lee also grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Ankiel’s husband. I realized that a lot of those people were family members of people that I grew up with, people that my family, my parents grew up with, Lee said. The shared diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. But Ankiel believes the geographic patterns deserve a closer examination. The state analyzed entire ZIP codes, not individual streets. Maybe the ZIP codes are a little bit too broad, Ankiel said. Let’s actually, let’s look at some of the streets. Why oligodendroglioma was not counted The updated review focuses specifically on glioblastoma. It excludes oligodendroglioma the tumor Lee is living with and the tumor Ankiel said her husband was initially diagnosed with. The report shows two tumor classification codes included in the state’s 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said medical classifications have evolved and those oligodendroglioma codes are no longer included in the current glioblastoma definition. The I-Team previously asked health officials how their analysis handles patients whose diagnoses change and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. The report does not explain how a case initially classified as oligodendroglioma and later diagnosed as glioblastoma would be counted. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis falls outside the period examined. Her tumor also would not be included in the glioblastoma analysis because it is classified as oligodendroglioma. Lee said she wants officials to continue studying brain tumor diagnoses in the area. She is especially concerned about her younger sister, who grew up in the same home. I want to know if my sister can get tested somehow before it’s too late for her, Lee said. The review also does not capture more recent glioblastoma diagnoses previously covered by the I-Team. Lucie resident Laura Cooper told CBS12 News in June that she was diagnosed with glioblastoma in November 2025, years after losing her best friend to the disease. At the time of the interview, she was undergoing treatment and participating in a clinical trial. Street-level limitations The report acknowledges limitations in the Florida Cancer Data System. The registry generally records a patient’s address at the time of diagnosis. It does not contain a complete residential history or detailed information about possible environmental exposures. That means a patient’s address at diagnosis may not reflect where that person lived years earlier or where a potentially relevant exposure occurred. The report also does not analyze whether cases are concentrated on individual streets or within smaller sections of the ZIP codes examined. Environmental records reviewed Health officials reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department reported that its water review did not identify contamination involving chemicals linked by the Environmental Protection Agency to glioblastoma or other brain-related health concerns. It also reported no increase in monitored environmental radiation levels around the plant. The documents describe reviews of existing records and monitoring data. They do not specify whether new environmental samples were collected specifically for this assessment. In Thursday’s email, Sperber highlighted the department’s conclusion that no environmental hazard in the Treasure Coast region has been shown to cause glioblastoma. The scientific journal article provided by the department is a broader review of existing research into environmental hazards and brain tumors. It is not a study of Treasure Coast patients, neighborhoods or environmental conditions. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners. Ankiel said she is not trying to work against health officials and wants to work with them. But for the families she has met, the state’s statistical conclusion does not resolve the questions raised by patients living in the same neighborhoods or sometimes only a few houses apart.

entry.title: Florida District 22 candidates Casey Askar, Pia Dandiya clash over affordability
entry.summary: A newly redrawn congressional district stretching across South Florida is setting up a battle between two candidates with sharply different ideas about how to make life more affordable for Floridians. Republican Casey Askar and Democrat Pia Dandiya are competing to represent District 22, which now connects coastal and inland communities across four counties. WATCH FULL REPORT BELOW: Askar, Dandiya clash over affordability Florida District 22: Askar, Dandiya clash over affordability WPTV reached out to both candidates about some of the biggest issues facing Florida voters, including affordability, insurance and health care. Dandiya agreed to an interview. Askar did not respond to multiple requests for comment. However, Askar's campaign website and political advertisements outline his positions on many of those issues and make clear that affordability is at the center of his campaign. 'We're paying too much. For pretty much everything,' Askar says in one campaign ad. The Republican has pledged to cut fuel and property taxes, increase the child tax credit and reduce government regulations he argues are contributing to higher costs. Dandiya is also making affordability a central theme of her campaign. 'People are no longer suffering in silence; they are suffering out loud,' Dandiya told investigative reporter Kate Hussey. Two very different approaches to healthcare The candidates diverge significantly on how they would address healthcare costs. Dandiya, a former teacher and principal, supports allowing Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices and restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies as ways to lower costs. 'Those are real, actionable ways that we can help people make ends meet,' Dandiya said. Askar is taking a different approach. Dandiya told WPTV she believes raising the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes could be one strategy for ensuring the program has enough money to pay promised benefits. entry.title: Florida brain tumor patient says nearly $1 million in medical bills are now covered after insurance denial
entry.summary: Five months after an insurance denial threatened to leave a Florida brain tumor patient facing the cost of life-saving surgery, Broqsten Bunt says he has received two pieces of news: He is medically cleared, and the nearly $1 million in medical care billed following his surgery has been wiped down to zero. WATCH FULL STORY BELOW: Brain surgery patients gets billed paid for after insurance denial 'Blessed to be in this position, thank you for all of your help,' Bunt told investigative reporter Katie LaGrone recently. 'Everything is working like it used to pre-surgery, and I've got my strength back. No prescriptions ... no future medical needs.' Five months earlier When we first met the 36-year-old West Palm Beach man in June, his health and finances were both uncertain. Bunt is a childhood leukemia survivor. But the radiation therapy that helped rid his body of cancer as a child has taken a toll on him as an adult. He's developed an aggressive brain tumor known as a meningioma. Doctors believe it was connected to the radiation treatment he received as a child. Bunt lives in West Palm Beach. His neurosurgeon near his home said he needed to get the tumor removed and referred him to Tampa General Hospital and a specific neurosurgeon because of the complexity of his case. Then came the denials Although the hospital was in-network with his insurer, Florida Blue, the surgeon was not. As a result, just before his scheduled operation, Florida Blue denied an appeal for additional coverage for the out-of-network care. In June, Bunt moved forward with the surgery anyway. He invited us to speak with him from his hospital recovery room. At the time, Bunt described being caught between his doctors and his insurance company. 'I'm taking calls from the insurance side, I'm taking calls from the medical office side,' he told us. 'I'm like, I don't write the bills, I don't pay the bills. Why are you calling me? Call each other and figure it out.' Then, in the middle of the interview, Bunt's case took a dramatic turn. A Tampa General Hospital spokesperson interrupted our interview with an update, stating that hospital leadership had worked with Florida Blue and the insurer had agreed to cover Bunt's preoperative workup, surgeries, hospital admission and postoperative care. Neither Tampa General Hospital nor Florida Blue explained to us at the time what specifically prompted the reversal. But the radiation therapy that helped rid his body of cancer as a child has taken a toll on him as an adult. He's developed an aggressive brain tumor known as a meningioma. Doctors believe it was connected to the radiation treatment he received as a child. Bunt lives in West Palm Beach. His neurosurgeon near his home said he needed to get the tumor removed and referred him to Tampa General Hospital and a specific neurosurgeon because of the complexity of his case. Then came the denialsAlthough the hospital was in-network with his insurer, Florida Blue, the surgeon was not. As a result, just before his scheduled operation, Florida Blue denied an appeal for additional coverage for the out-of-network care. In June, Bunt moved forward with the surgery anyway. He invited us to speak with him from his hospital recovery room. At the time, Bunt described being caught between his doctors and his insurance company."I'm taking calls from the insurance side, I'm taking calls from the medical office side," he told us. "I'm like, I don't write the bills, I don't pay the bills. Call each other and figure it out."Then, in the middle of the interview, Bunt's case took a dramatic turn.A Tampa General Hospital spokesperson interrupted our interview with an update, stating that hospital leadership had worked with Florida Blue and the insurer had agreed to cover Bunt's preoperative workup, surgeries, hospital admission and postoperative care. Neither Tampa General Hospital nor Florida Blue explained to us at the time what specifically prompted the reversal. Read our original investigation: Florida brain tumor patient denied insurance coverage for surgery gets full reversalFive months laterToday, Bunt said his recovery is going well, and he has been medically cleared.And when asked whether Florida Blue ultimately paid his medical bills, Bunt said, "It appears that way.""So you have zero balance?" LaGrone asked."Zero balance," Bunt said. "$993,000, almost a million dollars, is what the retail value of what was billed."Bunt said Tampa General Hospital continued working with him until his deductible was also reduced to zero. A spokesperson from TGH confirmed his insurer paid the full hospital portion of his claimFor Bunt, the resolution is remarkable. But he also believes his case illustrates how difficult it can be for a patient to challenge an insurance denial.Before the reversal, Bunt had been fighting his insurer for months over the denial. He and his wife turned to social media, appeals and eventually the news media to draw attention to his case.Bunt said he went through two denied appeals before the insurer reversed course."What really changed is when the news stepped in and created the awareness of the severity of my case," he said. "I had two appeals denied, and the condition was always the same. It didn't take any added information for them to change the denial process. It took the news making the population aware," he said.Neither Florida Blue nor Tampa General Hospital ever explained specifically why the coverage decision changed. Florida Blue told us at the time that it could not discuss individual cases but said it works with members, doctors and hospitals through its appeals process and is "pleased when we reach positive outcomes for our members." Now, with his surgery behind him and his surgery balance at zero, Bunt has a message for other patients challenging a health insurance denial."Don't back off the gas," he said. "You just have to keep pushing and keep reaching out to people. You have to get the care you need so that you can survive," he added. "You can deal with the details after. If you're not here, you don't have to worry about the details."If you are dealing with a health insurance denial over medically necessary care, let Katie know about it below.

entry.title: Memorial services announced for St. Lucie County firefighter who died in line of duty
entry.summary: Funeral arrangements have been announced for St. Lucie County Fire District Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge, who died in the line of duty on Saturday. Hodge served the St. Lucie County community for more than nine years, according to the fire district. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Services announced for St. Lucie County firefighter Memorial services announced for St. Lucie County firefighter 'The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to mourn the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge,' the agency said in a statement. 'His loss is deeply felt by his family, friends, fellow firefighters, and the many lives he touched throughout his years of service.' A public viewing will be held Friday, Nov. 6, from 4 to 6 p.m. at River of Life Fellowship Church, located at 3950 Juanita Avenue in Fort Pierce. A memorial service will follow Saturday, Nov. 7, at 10 a.m. at Christ Fellowship Church, located at 10250 SW Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie. The fire district said the arrangements were made in coordination with Hodge's family and Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Officials thanked the community for the support shown to Hodge's family and members of the fire district following his death. 'We remain grateful for the outpouring of love and support extended to Austin's family and our Fire District family during this difficult time,' the agency said. The release did not provide additional details about the circumstances surrounding Hodge's death.

entry.title: Florida education data breach may have exposed Social Security numbers of 4.9 million people
entry.summary: A data breach involving a Florida student financial aid website may have exposed personal information, including Social Security numbers, belonging to approximately 4.9 million people, according to the Florida Department of Education (FLDOE). WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida education data breach may have exposed Social Security numbers FLDOE said in a Thursday statement that staff became aware Oct. 19 of unauthorized criminal access involving its Florida Student Financial Aid website. The department said the compromised personally identifiable information included Social Security numbers. Officials did not specify what other types of personal information may have been exposed. The breach is believed to have been limited to the Florida Student Financial Aid website, and as many as 4.9 million people potentially were affected, according to FLDOE. The department said it activated its cybersecurity response protocols after detecting the incident, took steps to contain the unauthorized activity and secure its systems, and notified the Florida Attorney General's Office. FLDOE said it is working with the Florida Digital Service and Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The incident remains under criminal investigation. What does the breach mean for financial aid? FLDOE said current financial aid is not at risk and the incident will not delay financial aid disbursements or tuition payments from the department. Officials also said the breach will not affect eligibility for scholarships, grants or student loans from FLDOE. Some department websites and online services, however, may experience temporary disruptions as officials work to restore full functionality. What should people affected by the breach do? FLDOE recommends monitoring financial and online accounts for suspicious activity and regularly reviewing account statements and credit reports. The department also recommends considering a fraud alert or credit freeze with the major credit bureaus. Consumers can obtain free credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com and find additional information about responding to a data breach through the Federal Trade Commission's IdentityTheft.gov website . Anyone with questions about the FLDOE breach can contact the department at databreach@fldoe.org. FLDOE said information could change as the criminal investigation continues. The department is posting updates on its data breach information page .

entry.title: CBS12 News Athlete of the Week: Alex Thornton does it all for Jensen Beach - cw34.com
entry.summary: CBS12 News Athlete of the Week: Alex Thornton does it all for Jensen Beach    cw34.com
entry.article_text: When Jensen Beach needs a big play, senior Alex Thornton has a knack for delivering on both sides of the football. Thornton is this week’s CBS12 News Athlete of the Week after a career night helped the Falcons capture the District 13-4A football championship outright. In a 42-21 victory over Fort Pierce Westwood on October 23, Thornton rushed for 215 yards on just 15 carries and scored four touchdowns. He found the end zone on runs of 2, 39, 20 and 7 yards, recording the first four-touchdown game of his career. Three of those scores came in the second half as Jensen Beach pulled away. But Thornton’s impact extends well beyond the offensive backfield. A physical, hard-hitting linebacker, he has built a reputation for setting the tone on defense. His ability to make plays at both running back and linebacker has made him one of Jensen Beach’s most important players. He is the tone-setter, head coach Tim Caffey said in an earlier profile of Thornton, describing the senior’s physical style of play. entry.title: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review - WPEC
entry.summary: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review    WPEC
entry.article_text: Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma Ankiel said she was not surprised by the state’s conclusion. Earlier this month, she drove I-Team reporter Katie Bente through Fort Pierce neighborhoods, pointing out homes where she said brain tumor patients had lived in some cases, only doors apart. Her questions are also personal. Ankiel’s husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012. Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. Now, Ankiel is helping another patient with the same initial diagnosis. Amber Lee, 37, is living with oligodendroglioma, a brain tumor that is distinct from glioblastoma. The first thing I remember thinking of when they told me I had cancer was, I have a daughter, Lee said. Lee also grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Ankiel’s husband. I realized that a lot of those people were family members of people that I grew up with, people that my family, my parents grew up with, Lee said. The shared diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. But Ankiel believes the geographic patterns deserve a closer examination. The state analyzed entire ZIP codes, not individual streets. Maybe the ZIP codes are a little bit too broad, Ankiel said. Let’s actually, let’s look at some of the streets. Why oligodendroglioma was not counted The updated review focuses specifically on glioblastoma. It excludes oligodendroglioma the tumor Lee is living with and the tumor Ankiel said her husband was initially diagnosed with. The report shows two tumor classification codes included in the state’s 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said medical classifications have evolved and those oligodendroglioma codes are no longer included in the current glioblastoma definition. The I-Team previously asked health officials how their analysis handles patients whose diagnoses change and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. The report does not explain how a case initially classified as oligodendroglioma and later diagnosed as glioblastoma would be counted. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis falls outside the period examined. Her tumor also would not be included in the glioblastoma analysis because it is classified as oligodendroglioma. Lee said she wants officials to continue studying brain tumor diagnoses in the area. She is especially concerned about her younger sister, who grew up in the same home. I want to know if my sister can get tested somehow before it’s too late for her, Lee said. The review also does not capture more recent glioblastoma diagnoses previously covered by the I-Team. Lucie resident Laura Cooper told CBS12 News in June that she was diagnosed with glioblastoma in November 2025, years after losing her best friend to the disease. At the time of the interview, she was undergoing treatment and participating in a clinical trial. Street-level limitations The report acknowledges limitations in the Florida Cancer Data System. The registry generally records a patient’s address at the time of diagnosis. It does not contain a complete residential history or detailed information about possible environmental exposures. That means a patient’s address at diagnosis may not reflect where that person lived years earlier or where a potentially relevant exposure occurred. The report also does not analyze whether cases are concentrated on individual streets or within smaller sections of the ZIP codes examined. Environmental records reviewed Health officials reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department reported that its water review did not identify contamination involving chemicals linked by the Environmental Protection Agency to glioblastoma or other brain-related health concerns. It also reported no increase in monitored environmental radiation levels around the plant. The documents describe reviews of existing records and monitoring data. They do not specify whether new environmental samples were collected specifically for this assessment. In Thursday’s email, Sperber highlighted the department’s conclusion that no environmental hazard in the Treasure Coast region has been shown to cause glioblastoma. The scientific journal article provided by the department is a broader review of existing research into environmental hazards and brain tumors. It is not a study of Treasure Coast patients, neighborhoods or environmental conditions. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners. Ankiel said she is not trying to work against health officials and wants to work with them. But for the families she has met, the state’s statistical conclusion does not resolve the questions raised by patients living in the same neighborhoods or sometimes only a few houses apart.

entry.article_text: The deadly shooting of a 30-year-old Army veteran by Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies near Boca Raton is raising familiar questions about how law enforcement officers respond to armed people experiencing a mental health crisis. WPTV's Michael Hoffman sat down with a former federal law enforcement officer and trainer to examine how officers are taught to de-escalate crises and how those encounters can become life-or-death situations.The shooting happened Wednesday night at Sandalfoot Square after deputies responded to a call involving Joshua Senfeld, an Army veteran who Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said was armed and threatening suicide. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said deputies spent more than an hour trying to resolve the encounter peacefully before Senfeld brandished a firearm in their direction and deputies opened fire. Senfeld died at the scene.The incident is under investigation. The deputies involved were placed on administrative leave, and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office and PBSO's Violent Crimes Division are investigating. Bradshaw said Senfeld's family contacted authorities and that Senfeld was suicidal and armed. The sheriff said Senfeld was an Army veteran who authorities understood had post-traumatic stress disorder."He was very suicidal and was armed," Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said deputies negotiated with Senfeld for more than 90 minutes. During that time, one deputy who is also a veteran tried to connect with him."They talked to this guy a long, long time trying to talk him down," Bradshaw said. "Even one of our guys who's a vet kind of connected with him a little bit and told him, 'Hey, you know, we're going to get you the help you need.'"Bradshaw said Senfeld eventually became agitated and began standing with his firearm in what the sheriff described as a "ready position." PBSO said Senfeld brandished the gun in the direction of deputies before they fired. To better understand how officers are trained to handle situations like these, Hoffman sat down with Tim Miller of Lion Heart Protection Strategies.Miller, a former Secret Service agent, former federal law enforcement officer and law enforcement trainer, told Hoffman that Crisis Intervention Training is one way officers are taught to respond to people experiencing crises."There's a program called Crisis Intervention Training where officers are trained specifically for this kind of thing," Miller said.Miller said the training can involve mental health professionals teaching law enforcement officers techniques designed to help them communicate with people during a crisis."We were trained by some of the best psychiatrists, psychologists," Miller told Hoffman. "They're not police training police in many cases. These are professional mental health experts, training officers on how to connect, how to dissuade, how to hear things with the way the person's speaking, to try to understand for exactly the purposes of de-escalating so that everyone goes home safe."Miller, who is also a Marine Corps veteran, pointed to veteran suicide as another part of the tragedy surrounding the encounter.The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs' 2024 National Veteran Suicide Prevention Annual Report found there were 6,407 veteran suicides in 2022, an average of 17.6 per day. Those were the most recent figures available in that edition of the VA's annual report.Miller also spoke about the lasting impact a deadly encounter can have on the officers involved."Whoever had to take that shot is going to have to deal with that the rest of his life, even though he or she didn't have a choice," Miller told Hoffman. "They're going to have to live with that. And that's an unfortunate additional tragedy."The circumstances of Wednesday's shooting remain under investigation, meaning the findings of investigators, rather than the broader training principles discussed by Miller, will ultimately determine what happened during the encounter.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God," she told McRoberts.She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers.When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, "Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us."But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data.When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate."In the White City area," she said.Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll."I haven't given up; it's just you get tired," she said.Millions invested in glioblastoma researchSince WPTV's initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research.Deb has also worked to support research in her son's memory.Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water.The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research.Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers."I'm just glad you have followed through the way that you have," she told McRoberts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: CBS12 News Athlete of the Week: Alex Thornton does it all for Jensen Beach    WPEC
entry.article_text: When Jensen Beach needs a big play, senior Alex Thornton has a knack for delivering on both sides of the football. Thornton is this week’s CBS12 News Athlete of the Week after a career night helped the Falcons capture the District 13-4A football championship outright. In a 42-21 victory over Fort Pierce Westwood on October 23, Thornton rushed for 215 yards on just 15 carries and scored four touchdowns. He found the end zone on runs of 2, 39, 20 and 7 yards, recording the first four-touchdown game of his career. Three of those scores came in the second half as Jensen Beach pulled away. But Thornton’s impact extends well beyond the offensive backfield. A physical, hard-hitting linebacker, he has built a reputation for setting the tone on defense. His ability to make plays at both running back and linebacker has made him one of Jensen Beach’s most important players. He is the tone-setter, head coach Tim Caffey said in an earlier profile of Thornton, describing the senior’s physical style of play. See also: Dolphins look to build on first win against Patriots Thornton’s contributions are part of a larger winning tradition at Jensen Beach. The Falcons’ victory over Westwood secured the program’s fifth district championship overall and fourth in the past five years under Caffey. It also extended the team’s streak of playoff appearances to five consecutive seasons. Thornton has been part of three district championship teams during his high school career, making him a key figure in the program’s continued success. His potential has also attracted attention at the next level. Before his senior season, Thornton had received eight Division I college football offers, according to TCPalm’s recruiting profile. With the district title secured, Thornton and the Falcons now turn their attention to the postseason. For the senior, the goal is to help Jensen Beach make another deep playoff run before his high school career comes to an end. Thornton’s performance against Westwood showed exactly what makes him stand out: the ability to take over a game, lead by example and deliver when his team needs him most. entry.title: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review - cw34.com
entry.summary: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma Ankiel said she was not surprised by the state’s conclusion. Earlier this month, she drove I-Team reporter Katie Bente through Fort Pierce neighborhoods, pointing out homes where she said brain tumor patients had lived in some cases, only doors apart. Her questions are also personal. Ankiel’s husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012. Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. Now, Ankiel is helping another patient with the same initial diagnosis. Amber Lee, 37, is living with oligodendroglioma, a brain tumor that is distinct from glioblastoma. The first thing I remember thinking of when they told me I had cancer was, I have a daughter, Lee said. Lee also grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Ankiel’s husband. I realized that a lot of those people were family members of people that I grew up with, people that my family, my parents grew up with, Lee said. The shared diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. But Ankiel believes the geographic patterns deserve a closer examination. The state analyzed entire ZIP codes, not individual streets. Maybe the ZIP codes are a little bit too broad, Ankiel said. Let’s actually, let’s look at some of the streets. Why oligodendroglioma was not counted The updated review focuses specifically on glioblastoma. It excludes oligodendroglioma the tumor Lee is living with and the tumor Ankiel said her husband was initially diagnosed with. The report shows two tumor classification codes included in the state’s 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said medical classifications have evolved and those oligodendroglioma codes are no longer included in the current glioblastoma definition. The I-Team previously asked health officials how their analysis handles patients whose diagnoses change and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. The report does not explain how a case initially classified as oligodendroglioma and later diagnosed as glioblastoma would be counted. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis falls outside the period examined. Her tumor also would not be included in the glioblastoma analysis because it is classified as oligodendroglioma. Lee said she wants officials to continue studying brain tumor diagnoses in the area. She is especially concerned about her younger sister, who grew up in the same home. I want to know if my sister can get tested somehow before it’s too late for her, Lee said. The review also does not capture more recent glioblastoma diagnoses previously covered by the I-Team. Lucie resident Laura Cooper told CBS12 News in June that she was diagnosed with glioblastoma in November 2025, years after losing her best friend to the disease. At the time of the interview, she was undergoing treatment and participating in a clinical trial. Street-level limitations The report acknowledges limitations in the Florida Cancer Data System. The registry generally records a patient’s address at the time of diagnosis. It does not contain a complete residential history or detailed information about possible environmental exposures. That means a patient’s address at diagnosis may not reflect where that person lived years earlier or where a potentially relevant exposure occurred. The report also does not analyze whether cases are concentrated on individual streets or within smaller sections of the ZIP codes examined. Environmental records reviewed Health officials reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department reported that its water review did not identify contamination involving chemicals linked by the Environmental Protection Agency to glioblastoma or other brain-related health concerns. It also reported no increase in monitored environmental radiation levels around the plant. The documents describe reviews of existing records and monitoring data. They do not specify whether new environmental samples were collected specifically for this assessment. In Thursday’s email, Sperber highlighted the department’s conclusion that no environmental hazard in the Treasure Coast region has been shown to cause glioblastoma. The scientific journal article provided by the department is a broader review of existing research into environmental hazards and brain tumors. It is not a study of Treasure Coast patients, neighborhoods or environmental conditions. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners. Ankiel said she is not trying to work against health officials and wants to work with them. But for the families she has met, the state’s statistical conclusion does not resolve the questions raised by patients living in the same neighborhoods or sometimes only a few houses apart.

entry.title: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

entry.title: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center - cw34.com
entry.summary: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicated its new regional operations center in Fort Pierce Thursday morning, bringing its work under one roof and expanding its capacity to serve people across four counties. The 132,000-square-foot facility at 401 Loop Road supports the organization’s food storage and fresh food programs, prepared meals, nutrition education, benefits assistance and workforce training. The food bank, which began in 1988, is the only food bank serving Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. It reaches about 250,000 people each week and works with hundreds of nonprofit partners. The center’s production kitchen has more than doubled in size, growing from 7,000 to 15,000 square feet. It can produce up to 25,000 meals a day during a disaster, while also preparing nutritious meals for the community. The new freezer area alone could fit one and a half of the food bank’s former facilities. The center is designed to help people build stability for the future as well as meet immediate needs. Adults and children can take nutrition education classes on site, and nutrition information is sent with food boxes delivered to seniors. Its three job-training programs focus on culinary, hospitality and barista skills. Students learn skills such as knife safety, food safety and making pasta from scratch. The programs offer certifications in stages, and some courses are free. See also: Project Thanksgiving: Ruth & Norman Rales Jewish Family Services helps families in need During the dedication, 10 community members took part in a ceremonial First Box packing to represent the network behind the food bank’s work. Robin Safley of Feeding Florida added fresh vegetables on behalf of the statewide hunger-relief network. Donor Dee Locke added fresh fruit, and volunteer Tatiana Rousseau added peanut butter. The food bank’s capital campaign is continuing. To donate, visit the Feed Unite Flourish capital campaign page . Project Thanksgiving The Treasure Coast Food Bank is also a recipient of donations through CBS12 News' Project Thanksgiving . Drop off non-perishable food items at Treasure Coast iTHINK Financial bank branches to help the food bank feed families this holiday season. Treasure Coast Branches Fellsmere: 56 N.
