entry.title: Ramaswamy pulls controversial ad featuring opponent Acton's estranged mother
entry.summary: Ohio governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, is off the air after the Republican spent about a quarter of what his campaign initially said it would invest to run it. Ramaswamy said during a campaign appearance in Vandalia, Ohio, on Thursday that the ads planned run was over. His campaign originally said it would spend $4 million to air the ad, but data from the ad-tracking firm AdImpact showed it spent roughly $1 million. RELATED STORY | Trump in Ohio and Obama in Georgia make closing stretch appeals to midterm voters in pivotal states The divisive spot had provoked backlash in Ohio and among politicians of both parties across the nation. It featured Donna Arthur calling her daughter a lifelong liar. That was despite the two having not seen each other for nearly 50 years. Arthur lost custody of her children in 1978 after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12. Ramaswamy had defended the ad, though a later version trimmed some portions. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said they supported the decision to air the ad. The president said he told Ramaswamy to leave it on the air, adding she's fair game. Ohio governors past and present, alumni of Ramaswamys Catholic high school in Cincinnati and others had urged him to pull it down. RELATED STORY | Trump strongly defends controversial Ramaswamy ad featuring opponent's mother Actons campaign said the ad was despicable and should never have run and that Ramaswamy should have apologized.

entry.title: Jupiter council hears developer's plan for the former Suni Sands waterfront site
entry.summary: Jupiter council members discussed the future of a prime piece of town waterfront in a special town council meeting Thursday evening. In the hours-long meeting, town leaders heard from a developer proposing 44 condos and a 110-room hotel, along with a restaurant and a marina that would take up about 4.5 acres of the 10.5-acre site. WATCH: Jupiter council heard a developer's plan for the former Suni Sands waterfront site Jupiter council heard a developer's plan for 44 condos, a 110-room hotel, a restaurant and a marina at the former Suni Sands waterfront site. The site was once home to the Suni Sands Mobile Home Park off A1A. Development plans stalled after the discovery of Native American archaeological sites, but the town and the developer came to an agreement earlier this year to allow development on part of the parcel, with the town purchasing just over an acre of the waterfront for $10 million. The developer is asking the town for a number of waivers in its plan. He told the council Thursday he's looking to make the space a place the community can enjoy while preserving much of the land. 'We still wanted to work with the town and create something that we could build there that would be something I would be as proud of as I have been with Love Street,' Sperry Parcel Developer Charles Modica said. Dozens of people turned up for the evening meeting to voice concerns over developing one of the town's last waterfront sites. 'Suni Sands is more than a piece of property. It's part of the natural legacy of our community and once it's developed, we can't get it back. Some things are too valuable to replace,' a young resident opposed to the project said. Thursday's special meeting was the first reading of the proposed rule changes that could allow the development. entry.title: Florida mom fights wrongful death law after daughter dies hours after leaving hospital
entry.summary: Two years after her only daughter died just hours after leaving a Florida hospital, Beth Miller says she is still searching for answers. She also wants to make sure another family does not face the same barriers she has encountered. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida mom fights 'free kill' law after daughter's death Florida mom fights 'free kill' law after daughter's death 'I would like to be the only one,' Miller said. 'I know what it feels like. I don't want anybody else to have to go through this.' Miller's daughter, Dawn Miller, was 49 when she died after undergoing gallbladder surgery. A previous WPTV investigation found medical records showed Dawn initially 'tolerated the procedure well.' But her condition later changed. Her hemoglobin dropped. Doctors confirmed sepsis, a potentially life-threatening response to infection, and lab results the morning of her discharge showed decreased kidney function. Records also show Dawn twice resisted leaving the hospital, telling medical staff she felt 'weak' and 'not ready to go home.' She was discharged anyway. Minutes after arriving home, she collapsed. 'I couldn't get her to breathe,' Beth Miller recalled. 'And I just felt so helpless. You know, and then you're staring at your daughter trying to do CPR, and nothing's happening.' Dawn was pronounced dead about two hours after leaving the hospital. Dr. Gerald Feigin, a medical examiner and forensic pathologist who reviewed Dawn's medical records for WPTV, said he believes she should not have been discharged. 'She should have been given emergency transfusions and [they should] figure out why she was bleeding,' Feigin said. 'Possibly had additional surgery.' Feigin also said the hospital should have performed an autopsy. It did not. WPTV previously reported Beth Miller requested an autopsy after her daughter's death, but the hospital declined to perform one. The hospital also declined to answer WPTV's questions about Dawn's case. 'I don't have an answer to this day,' Miller said. 'It's on your mind 24/7.' A legal barrier to seeking damages Miller hoped she might find answers through the legal system. But Florida law creates another obstacle. A provision of the Florida Wrongful Death Act restricts which surviving family members can recover certain damages in medical malpractice cases. Critics have dubbed it Florida's 'free kill' law. Under the provision, parents generally cannot recover certain damages for the medical malpractice death of an adult child age 25 or older.
entry.article_text: Two years after her only daughter died just hours after leaving a Florida hospital, Beth Miller says she is still searching for answers.She also wants to make sure another family does not face the same barriers she has encountered.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida mom fights 'free kill' law after daughter's death"I would like to be the only one," Miller said. "I know what it feels like. I don't want anybody else to have to go through this."Miller's daughter, Dawn Miller, was 49 when she died after undergoing gallbladder surgery.A previous WPTV investigation found medical records showed Dawn initially "tolerated the procedure well." But her condition later changed.Her hemoglobin dropped. Doctors confirmed sepsis, a potentially life-threatening response to infection, and lab results the morning of her discharge showed decreased kidney function.Records also show Dawn twice resisted leaving the hospital, telling medical staff she felt "weak" and "not ready to go home."She was discharged anyway.Minutes after arriving home, she collapsed."I couldn't get her to breathe," Beth Miller recalled. "And I just felt so helpless. You know, and then you're staring at your daughter trying to do CPR, and nothing's happening."Dawn was pronounced dead about two hours after leaving the hospital.Dr. Gerald Feigin, a medical examiner and forensic pathologist who reviewed Dawn's medical records for WPTV, said he believes she should not have been discharged."She should have been given emergency transfusions and [they should] figure out why she was bleeding," Feigin said. "Possibly had additional surgery."Feigin also said the hospital should have performed an autopsy.It did not.WPTV previously reported Beth Miller requested an autopsy after her daughter's death, but the hospital declined to perform one. The hospital also declined to answer WPTV's questions about Dawn's case."I don't have an answer to this day," Miller said. "It's on your mind 24/7."Miller hoped she might find answers through the legal system.But Florida law creates another obstacle.A provision of the Florida Wrongful Death Act restricts which surviving family members can recover certain damages in medical malpractice cases.Critics have dubbed it Florida's "free kill" law.Under the provision, parents generally cannot recover certain damages for the medical malpractice death of an adult child age 25 or older. Adult children also face restrictions on recovering those damages for the death of a parent.Dawn was unmarried, in her 40s, and had no children."Unless she had kids or a spouse, there's nothing I can do," Miller said.Jordan Dulce, a West Palm Beach trial attorney who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is among the critics calling for the law to change."It's completely arbitrary," Dulce said.Dulce said potential liability is something hospitals consider as part of risk management."I can tell you, from a risk management perspective, it's very much on their radar," he said.Critics argue the law can reduce the potential financial consequences when alleged medical negligence results in the death of certain patients compared with others.Dulce argues that it can weaken one of the financial incentives intended to promote accountability and patient safety."It's not meaning that you're intending to hurt someone," he said. "But obviously, when you don't have those guardrails up, certainly the quality of health care suffers."Florida enacted the provision in 1990 amid concerns over the cost and availability of medical malpractice insurance.Federal data show Florida had the sixth-highest number of medical malpractice claim payouts in the country that year.A Yale Journal on Regulation study also found average malpractice premiums had more than quadrupled over a four-year period, from about $4,300 to $18,000.At the time, proponents of the law argued rising malpractice costs were threatening access to doctors and driving physicians out of the state.But some of those claims later came under scrutiny.A 2003 U.S. Government Accountability Office report examined reports of physician shortages in Florida and other states and found some widely cited claims were "anecdotal" or "inaccurate."In one example, medical society officials reported two Florida counties had lost all of their neurosurgeons. GAO investigators found at least five neurosurgeons were still practicing in each county.The report also found the number of new medical licenses in Florida had increased while the number of physicians per capita remained relatively unchanged."There's been no actual studies or evidence or support for this law actually doing what it was intended to do," Dulce said.Florida's medical malpractice insurance market has since stabilized.A 2026 report from Florida's Office of Insurance Regulation found the industry was "doing well," with annual premium increases far below the triple-digit increases seen during the insurance crisis of the late 1980s.The report, however, attributed much of that stabilization to malpractice reforms enacted in 2003 — more than a decade after the wrongful-death provision took effect.Florida also remains among the most expensive states in the country for medical malpractice insurance, ranking third nationwide."No matter what we try to do to limit the victim's right to courts, that has never stopped the insurance industry from continuing to increase their prices because that's their model," Dulce said. "At the end of the day, trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper."WPTV reached out to several local state lawmakers to share Miller's story and ask about the law. None have yet agreed to sit down for an interview.For Miller, the debate is more than a question of insurance rates, liability or state policy.It is about the daughter she still pictures lying on the floor of her home."It will always be difficult," Miller said. "I see her laying on that floor all the time."She said she will continue speaking publicly in hopes of convincing lawmakers to change the law."To get this point across, to make it so other people don't have to go through this suffering," Miller said.Last year, Florida lawmakers passed legislation that would have repealed the provision, but the bill never took effect.In the next part of WPTV's investigation, investigative reporter Kate Hussey examines what happened to that effort — and shares the stories of other Florida families who say they have encountered the same legal barrier.

entry.title: Florida brain tumor patient says nearly $1 million in medical bills are now covered after insurance denial
entry.summary: Five months after an insurance denial threatened to leave a Florida brain tumor patient facing the cost of life-saving surgery, Broqsten Bunt says he has received two pieces of news: He is medically cleared, and the nearly $1 million in medical care billed following his surgery has been wiped down to zero. WATCH FULL STORY BELOW: Brain surgery patients gets billed paid for after insurance denial 'Blessed to be in this position, thank you for all of your help,' Bunt told investigative reporter Katie LaGrone recently. 'Everything is working like it used to pre-surgery, and I've got my strength back. No prescriptions ... no future medical needs.' Five months earlier When we first met the 36-year-old West Palm Beach man in June, his health and finances were both uncertain. Bunt is a childhood leukemia survivor. But the radiation therapy that helped rid his body of cancer as a child has taken a toll on him as an adult. He's developed an aggressive brain tumor known as a meningioma. Doctors believe it was connected to the radiation treatment he received as a child. Bunt lives in West Palm Beach. His neurosurgeon near his home said he needed to get the tumor removed and referred him to Tampa General Hospital and a specific neurosurgeon because of the complexity of his case. Then came the denials Although the hospital was in-network with his insurer, Florida Blue, the surgeon was not. As a result, just before his scheduled operation, Florida Blue denied an appeal for additional coverage for the out-of-network care. In June, Bunt moved forward with the surgery anyway. He invited us to speak with him from his hospital recovery room. At the time, Bunt described being caught between his doctors and his insurance company. 'I'm taking calls from the insurance side, I'm taking calls from the medical office side,' he told us. 'I'm like, I don't write the bills, I don't pay the bills. Why are you calling me? Call each other and figure it out.' Then, in the middle of the interview, Bunt's case took a dramatic turn. A Tampa General Hospital spokesperson interrupted our interview with an update, stating that hospital leadership had worked with Florida Blue and the insurer had agreed to cover Bunt's preoperative workup, surgeries, hospital admission and postoperative care. Neither Tampa General Hospital nor Florida Blue explained to us at the time what specifically prompted the reversal. "I'm like, I don't write the bills, I don't pay the bills. Call each other and figure it out."Then, in the middle of the interview, Bunt's case took a dramatic turn.A Tampa General Hospital spokesperson interrupted our interview with an update, stating that hospital leadership had worked with Florida Blue and the insurer had agreed to cover Bunt's preoperative workup, surgeries, hospital admission and postoperative care. Neither Tampa General Hospital nor Florida Blue explained to us at the time what specifically prompted the reversal. Read our original investigation: Florida brain tumor patient denied insurance coverage for surgery gets full reversalFive months laterToday, Bunt said his recovery is going well, and he has been medically cleared.And when asked whether Florida Blue ultimately paid his medical bills, Bunt said, "It appears that way.""So you have zero balance?" LaGrone asked."Zero balance," Bunt said. "$993,000, almost a million dollars, is what the retail value of what was billed."Bunt said Tampa General Hospital continued working with him until his deductible was also reduced to zero. A spokesperson from TGH confirmed his insurer paid the full hospital portion of his claimFor Bunt, the resolution is remarkable. But he also believes his case illustrates how difficult it can be for a patient to challenge an insurance denial.Before the reversal, Bunt had been fighting his insurer for months over the denial. He and his wife turned to social media, appeals and eventually the news media to draw attention to his case.Bunt said he went through two denied appeals before the insurer reversed course."What really changed is when the news stepped in and created the awareness of the severity of my case," he said. "I had two appeals denied, and the condition was always the same. It didn't take any added information for them to change the denial process. It took the news making the population aware," he said.Neither Florida Blue nor Tampa General Hospital ever explained specifically why the coverage decision changed. Florida Blue told us at the time that it could not discuss individual cases but said it works with members, doctors and hospitals through its appeals process and is "pleased when we reach positive outcomes for our members." Now, with his surgery behind him and his surgery balance at zero, Bunt has a message for other patients challenging a health insurance denial."Don't back off the gas," he said. "You just have to keep pushing and keep reaching out to people. You have to get the care you need so that you can survive," he added. "You can deal with the details after. If you're not here, you don't have to worry about the details."If you are dealing with a health insurance denial over medically necessary care, let Katie know about it below.

entry.title: 5 fun things to do for Halloween in South Florida and beyond
entry.summary: Looking for something fun to do for Halloween? From serious scares and a homegrown haunted yard to kid-friendly trick-or-treating and a Halloween road trip, there are several ways to celebrate across South Florida and beyond. Here are five Halloween experiences to consider: 1. Get your last scare at Fright Nights West Palm Beach | Oct. 30 Friday is the final night of Fright Nights at the South Florida Fairgrounds in West Palm Beach. For people who want the full haunted-attraction experience without leaving South Florida, this is the local option on our list. The hook: One last chance to scream. 2. Brave the Queens Lane Haunted Yard 115 Queens Lane, Royal Palm Beach | Oct. 31 You don't need a theme park to find a Halloween scare. A Royal Palm Beach family is transforming its property into the Queens Lane Haunted Yard, a free walk-through attraction featuring more than 20 animatronics, scares around every corner and free candy. It's a neighborhood Halloween experience that has continued to grow. The hook: A homegrown haunt that keeps getting bigger. 3. Go old-school at Spookyville Oct. 30-31 For families with little ghosts and goblins who aren't ready for the serious scares, Spookyville offers a more traditional Halloween experience. Congressional and state legislative races also will appear on ballots. Local races and ballot questions depend on a voter’s address. entry.title: New Florida survey raises concerns about awareness of rising breast cancer rates among younger women
entry.summary: As Breast Cancer Awareness Month comes to a close, new research is drawing attention to a concerning trend: rising breast cancer rates among younger women. A recent survey of women in Florida found many may not be aware of that increase. The survey, provided to WPTV by TopLine MD Alliance, comes as doctors and survivors continue emphasizing the importance of early detection. I recently sat down with a breast cancer survivor who is now using her experience to educate other women. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Breast cancer survivor shares story as new study of Florida women raises red flag Jamie Howe remembers the phone call in 2023 that changed her life. 'I physically remember sitting up. I'd been lying back. I sat up, and they said we found cancer in your right breast. I remember thinking, it's time,' says Howe. Howe is the 2026 event chair of the Susan G. Komen 'More Than Pink Walk' in Palm Beach County. Before her diagnosis, she already knew what breast cancer could do. Her mother is a three-time cancer survivor. Howe was three months shy of her 43rd birthday when she was diagnosed with Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), a non-invasive stage zero breast cancer. A new survey, conducted by the TopLine MD Alliance, is shedding light on the gaps in public awareness as breast cancer and overall cancer incidence climbs among younger people. It found that more than 1,000 women in Palm Beach, Broward, Miami-Dade, Duval and Hillsborough counties show that too few women are aware that breast cancer rates have been rising among younger women. The study found that close to 52% of respondents, but less than 43% of those aged 30-39, say they are very aware that breast cancer diagnoses are rising among younger patients. Findings show 32% are somewhat aware of this increase, and 17% are either not very aware or not aware at all. Howe said she wants to tell her story so others don't feel like they have to go through it alone. Even though she had a history of breast cancer, she stresses genetics alone aren't a predictor. 'Be vigilant. Do your self breast exam. Do your surveillance,' Howe said.

entry.title: Trump reverses course, will hold rallies in Kansas and Iowa after all
entry.summary: After canceling a pair of rallies planned for this weekend, President Donald Trump has decided to hit the campaign trail after all, with back-to-back stops in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday. On Thursday, Trump aides said the president would hold tele-rallies instead of in-person events as polling showed tight Senate races in Kansas and Iowa. But on Friday, sources familiar with Trump's schedule said the rallies were rescheduled to accommodate dozens of additional tele-rallies recently added to his itinerary. Trump is slated to hold 20 tele-rallies this weekend. In Kansas, Trump will back U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall's reelection campaign against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. A CNN poll showed Hamilton leading Marshall 49% to 45%. Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate election in Kansas since 1932. A Democratic victory in Kansas could further complicate Republican efforts to retain control of the Senate in 2027. Trump is also scheduled to campaign in Iowa this weekend, another state where Republicans could face a competitive Senate race. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek have been separated by only a few points in recent polls. Democrats need a net gain of four Republican-held seats while defending all of their current seats to win a Senate majority.

entry.article_text: Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about an effort to put another candidate on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent as the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation with new grand jury subpoenas.“I just want to clear the air," she said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."RELATED STORY | Report: Peltola campaign linked to effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan in Alaska Senate racePeltola is running against Sen. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters.The race is considered key to control of the U.S. More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.The Justice Department for months has been looking into allegations that Dan J. entered the race to siphon votes from the incumbent Sen. The potential targets of the investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.”“They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said.Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.State attorneys asked a court to rule on the Justice Department’s lawsuit by Monday, saying the case could “cast a cloud over Alaska’s election that is contrary to the public interest.”Alaska's Republican governor has also ordered an investigationSeparately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper's reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens," the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. "It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”Later, as he rallied for Republican Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted."Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’Peltola alluded to the controversy in a fundraising post Thursday. “They can’t win on their record so they’re trying to intimidate me into backing down,” she said, adding later: “This is just another distraction as they avoid answering for the skyrocketing cost of living we’re facing because of their tariffs and forever wars. It won’t work.”RELATED STORY | Alaska governor orders investigation into ‘Dan Sullivan’ ballot controversyIn Juneau, Alaska, independent Carter Bancroft said he voted Thursday for Peltola. “I’m very certain in the candidates I wanted to vote for and I wanted to vote for Mary Peltola,” he said.But he said the latest claims have bothered him. He worries they give “ammunition” to Trump and others to attack Peltola or other Democratic candidates. “And I think I’m bothered by shenanigans on either side," Bancroft said, especially actions intended “to confuse things or try to trick people.”John Delgado, an independent who leans Republican, said he has “warmed up” to Sen. Sullivan, especially in light of the recent claims. He agrees that Peltola should drop out of the race.The situation in Alaska isn't that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”State Supreme Court OK'd the other Sullivan on the ballotEarlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.” He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”

entry.article_text: Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River.The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources.WATCH REPORT BELOW: James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality. Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river.WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project."The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project," Fitzgerald said. "Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects."Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

entry.title: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center - cw34.com
entry.summary: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicated its new regional operations center in Fort Pierce Thursday morning, bringing its work under one roof and expanding its capacity to serve people across four counties. The 132,000-square-foot facility at 401 Loop Road supports the organization’s food storage and fresh food programs, prepared meals, nutrition education, benefits assistance and workforce training. The food bank, which began in 1988, is the only food bank serving Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. It reaches about 250,000 people each week and works with hundreds of nonprofit partners. The center’s production kitchen has more than doubled in size, growing from 7,000 to 15,000 square feet. It can produce up to 25,000 meals a day during a disaster, while also preparing nutritious meals for the community. The new freezer area alone could fit one and a half of the food bank’s former facilities. The center is designed to help people build stability for the future as well as meet immediate needs. Adults and children can take nutrition education classes on site, and nutrition information is sent with food boxes delivered to seniors. Its three job-training programs focus on culinary, hospitality and barista skills. Students learn skills such as knife safety, food safety and making pasta from scratch. The programs offer certifications in stages, and some courses are free. See also: Project Thanksgiving: Ruth & Norman Rales Jewish Family Services helps families in need During the dedication, 10 community members took part in a ceremonial First Box packing to represent the network behind the food bank’s work. Robin Safley of Feeding Florida added fresh vegetables on behalf of the statewide hunger-relief network. Donor Dee Locke added fresh fruit, and volunteer Tatiana Rousseau added peanut butter. The food bank’s capital campaign is continuing. To donate, visit the Feed Unite Flourish capital campaign page . entry.title: WPTV First Alert Weather meteorologist Walter Kelley becomes a firefighter for a day with Jupiter Fire Rescue
entry.summary: My experience at Jupiter Fire Rescue was an unforgettable one! I had the opportunity to learn what it takes to be a firefighter for a day, and let me tell you, there is so much more to this job than meets the eye. WATCH BELOW: Walter Kelley visits Jupiter Fire Rescue Meteorologist Walter Kelley becomes a firefighter for a day From learning about the equipment to understanding the importance of training and teamwork, sliding down the pole, jumping into the heavy gear, leaning into the hose, ringing the bell, blowing the horn, I truly gained a whole new appreciation for the dedication and hard work these incredible heroes put in every single day. One thing that really stood out to me was the importance of safety first! These brave first responders put themselves on the line to protect our families, homes, and community, often in some of the most challenging situations imaginable. I walked away with a tremendous amount of respect for the entire Jupiter Fire Rescue team and all the first responders who work tirelessly to keep us safe. They are true heroes in our community, and their service deserves our gratitude every day, not just during an emergency. The next time you see a firefighter, police officer, paramedic, or another first responder, take a moment to say thank you. Their courage, commitment, and compassion make a real difference in our lives. Thank you, Jupiter Fire Rescue, for letting me experience a little of what you do and for everything you do to keep our community safe!

entry.title: Trump reverses course, will hold rallies in Kansas and Iowa after all
entry.summary: After canceling a pair of rallies planned for this weekend, President Donald Trump has decided to hit the campaign trail after all, with back-to-back stops in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday. On Thursday, Trump aides said the president would hold tele-rallies instead of in-person events as polling showed tight Senate races in Kansas and Iowa. But on Friday, sources familiar with Trump's schedule said the rallies were rescheduled to accommodate dozens of additional tele-rallies recently added to his itinerary. Trump is slated to hold 20 tele-rallies this weekend. In Kansas, Trump will back U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall's reelection campaign against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. A CNN poll showed Hamilton leading Marshall 49% to 45%. Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate election in Kansas since 1932. A Democratic victory in Kansas could further complicate Republican efforts to retain control of the Senate in 2027. Hamilton welcomed the president's visit to Kansas in a statement, suggesting his presence could do more harm than good for his opponent. The president is always welcome in Kansas. I hope he takes the time to meet with Kansans who are being hurt by the policies coming out of Washington. Then I hope he ends this war, ends the chaotic tariffs, and starts working across the aisle to solve the big problems facing our country,' the Democrat said. Trump is also scheduled to campaign in Iowa this weekend, another state where Republicans could face a competitive Senate race. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek have been separated by only a few points in recent polls. Democrats need a net gain of four Republican-held seats while defending all of their current seats to win a Senate majority.

entry.title: Memorial services announced for St. Lucie County firefighter who died in line of duty
entry.summary: Funeral arrangements have been announced for St. Lucie County Fire District Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge, who died in the line of duty on Saturday. Hodge served the St. Lucie County community for more than nine years, according to the fire district. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Services announced for St. Lucie County firefighter Memorial services announced for St. Lucie County firefighter 'The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to mourn the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge,' the agency said in a statement. 'His loss is deeply felt by his family, friends, fellow firefighters, and the many lives he touched throughout his years of service.' A public viewing will be held Friday, Nov. 6, from 4 to 6 p.m. at River of Life Fellowship Church, located at 3950 Juanita Avenue in Fort Pierce. A memorial service will follow Saturday, Nov. 7, at 10 a.m. at Christ Fellowship Church, located at 10250 SW Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie. The fire district said the arrangements were made in coordination with Hodge's family and Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Officials thanked the community for the support shown to Hodge's family and members of the fire district following his death. 'We remain grateful for the outpouring of love and support extended to Austin's family and our Fire District family during this difficult time,' the agency said. The release did not provide additional details about the circumstances surrounding Hodge's death.

entry.title: Breast cancer patient to run New York City Marathon to change the future for her daughters
entry.summary: For Kristen Dugan, running is medicine for the soul. But two years ago, it became something she leaned on even more after a phone call from her doctor changed her life. WATCH BELOW: Breast cancer survivor runs NYC Marathon to change her daughters' future 'I love it, it's a disconnect,' she said. In January 2024, Dugan had just undergone imaging and a biopsy. The results came back that she had cancer. 'It was definite shock and almost like I couldn't work through the words,' Dugan said. 'You're flooded with emotions, you're flooded with how am I going to tell my children, how am I going to tell my mom.' She shared the news with her mother right away. But it wasn't until the night before the West Palm Beach More Than Pink Walk that she sat down with her daughters and told them about her diagnosis. 'They were young at the time, I think 11, 9, and 6, they were young,' Dugan said. 'The word cancer is scary, and I needed to show them that women are living with the disease, they're having fun, there's hope, there's joy.' Dugan said she faced treatment like a bulldog. 'I got lucky. I never got like an infection; I never got sick during treatment. So, I never had to reschedule a treatment,' she said. They gave me enough shots that my blood count always were at the level it needed to be for chemo.' After five months of chemotherapy, Dugan was in remission. But beating cancer was just part of her journey. Now came the challenge of rebuilding her life, both physically and emotionally. And therapy would play an important role in that recovery. 'Anybody that's been through any type of trauma, I believe you're not the same person you were before the trauma,' she said. 'She doesn't exist anymore.' But just 21 months later, while returning from a trip to North Carolina and training for the New York City Marathon, Dugan began experiencing pain in one of her breasts and armpit. It's in a lymph node hiding underneath a muscle, which is why we couldn't feel it," she said.On top of dealing with immune therapy and chemotherapy, she is also training for the New York City Marathon."I had to interview for this race by the way, because Komen, I believe, only had 20 spots on their team and I realized quickly I wanted one," Dugan said.Running the New York City Marathon had never been her dream until it was. She's also serving as this year's event chair for the 36th Susan G. Komen More Than Pink Walk in West Palm Beach on Jan. It's another way she's using her own experience with breast cancer to give hope to others facing the same fight.

entry.title: Martin County man charged with attempted murder after roommate slashed in neck with box cutter
entry.summary: A 32-year-old man is facing an attempted murder charge after deputies say a dispute between roommates ended with a man being slashed in the neck with a box cutter. The Martin County Sheriffs Office said Bradley Martin was arrested Thursday night following the attack in the 2800 block of Southeast Indian St. According to the sheriffs office, Martin used a box cutter to slash an acquaintance, described as a man in his 40s, in the neck during a violent dispute between the roommates. Despite his injuries, the victim attempted to drive himself to a hospital, authorities said. Deputies and Fire Rescue personnel intercepted him and took him to a trauma hospital. The sheriffs office said the victim was in stable condition and is expected to recover. Deputies located Martin shortly after the incident and took him into custody. Martin has been charged with attempted murder. The sheriffs office did not provide additional details about what led to the dispute.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.title: Appeals court rejects DOJ's demand for California to set aside disputed ballots
entry.summary: The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday rejected the Justice Departments request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election. The panels 2-1 ruling is the latest setback for the Trump administrations efforts to assert control over state-run elections. The administration has alleged California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be U.S. citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens. A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Departments demands could disenfranchise citizens. As the district court found and we discern no clear error there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system, the appeals court wrote. The ruling is the latest in an expansive legal battle between the federal government and the state before Election Day in the midterms Tuesday. Millions of people in California have already voted. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Department’s demands could disenfranchise citizens.“As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system,” the appeals court wrote.The ruling is the latest in an expansive legal battle between the federal government and the state before Election Day in the midterms Tuesday. Millions of people in California have already voted.The majority opinion was authored by Judge Mark J. Bennett, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden.The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. Elections officials have said that processed votes are completely anonymized and can’t be matched back to the voters who submitted them.The ruling comes during broader federal scrutiny of local elections, with the Trump administration issuing a raft of subpoenas in Alaska in a spoiler-candidate controversy. They want the list so they can examine who is on the list and assess its impact on eligible voters.It will be the first time that a nongovernment organization will have the opportunity to evaluate the merits of the list of some 20,000 names.Prosecutors with the Trump administration have argued that there is just as much to lose from noncitizens illegally voting, arguing that to tally those votes would dilute the voice of citizens.Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra is an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.The two groups sued the Homeland Security Department in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government’s data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens. It argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote.Another suit seeks to defend election workersA coalition of unions on Friday also joined the growing list of groups challenging the federal government’s efforts.The unions, including the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, are asking a federal judge to temporarily block the Justice Department from demanding that local officials stop counting ballots and to drop threats to criminally prosecute officials who do not comply with their demands.The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli, has warned that “any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.”On Thursday the Associated Press obtained subpoenas issued to election officials in Los Angeles County. The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining the allegations about noncitizen voters. They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. entry.summary: Trick, treat or tech? Students at The Greene School are putting a high-tech twist on Halloween, combining artificial intelligence with traditional art, woodworking, music and theater for an annual Haunted Hall that has been a year in the making. Nearly the entire first floor of the high school has been transformed for the project. Students are serving up tricks, treats and tech, with creations ranging from a handcrafted graveyard to a life-size wooden haunted carriage. 'It really shows how our students can manifest their ideas into reality through collaboration and believing in their imagination,' high school visual arts instructor Sarah Knouse said. But there's more than hocus pocus bringing some of the creations to life; they are using AI. Students in the school's AI Apps and Innovation class created moving portraits and floating heads, using technology to add another dimension to the Haunted Hall. 'We get so much done, and we can do so much more, and we can create such a space where it really looks haunted, and it has that vibe,' senior Lilyana Martin said. entry.summary: For Kristen Dugan, running is medicine for the soul. But two years ago, it became something she leaned on even more after a phone call from her doctor changed her life. WATCH BELOW: Breast cancer survivor runs NYC Marathon to change her daughters' future 'I love it; it's a disconnect,' she said. In January 2024, Dugan had just undergone imaging and a biopsy. The results came back that she had cancer. 'It was definite shock and almost like I couldn't work through the words,' Dugan said. 'You're flooded with emotions, you're flooded with how am I going to tell my children, how am I going to tell my mom.' She shared the news with her mother right away. But it wasn't until the night before the West Palm Beach More Than Pink Walk that she sat down with her daughters and told them about her diagnosis. 'They were young at the time, I think 11, 9, and 6, they were young,' Dugan said. 'The word cancer is scary, and I needed to show them that women are living with the disease, they're having fun, there's hope, there's joy.' Dugan said she faced treatment like a bulldog. 'I got lucky. I never got like an infection; I never got sick during treatment. So, I never had to reschedule a treatment,' she said. They gave me enough shots that my blood count always were at the level it needed to be for chemo.' After five months of chemotherapy, Dugan was in remission. But beating cancer was just part of her journey. Now came the challenge of rebuilding her life, both physically and emotionally. And therapy would play an important role in that recovery. 'Anybody who's been through any type of trauma, I believe you're not the same person you were before the trauma,' she said. 'She doesn't exist anymore.' But just 21 months later, while returning from a trip to North Carolina and training for the New York City Marathon, Dugan began experiencing pain in one of her breasts and armpit. entry.article_text: "She doesn't exist anymore."But just 21 months later, while returning from a trip to North Carolina and training for the New York City Marathon, Dugan began experiencing pain in one of her breasts and armpit. As fate would have it, she was already scheduled for an appointment with her oncologist the following week. What followed was a series of tests, including brain scans, MRIs, ultrasounds and biopsies."My tumor lit right up in my axilla, which is a fancy word for my armpit. It's in a lymph node hiding underneath a muscle, which is why we couldn't feel it," she said.On top of dealing with immune therapy and chemotherapy, she is also training for the New York City Marathon."I had to interview for this race, by the way, because Komen, I believe, only had 20 spots on their team and I realized quickly I wanted one," Dugan said.Running the New York City Marathon had never been her dream until it was. She said her journey helped her find a purpose bigger than herself."I am doing this so that breast cancer is not the inheritance that I leave my children or other people's children," Dugan said. "I'm doing this so that their future is different than mine and hopefully, they live in a world where breast cancer is a disease of the past."And Dugan's commitment to helping others doesn't stop at the finish line. She's also serving as this year's event chair for the 36th Susan G. Komen More Than Pink Walk in West Palm Beach on Jan. It's another way she's using her own experience with breast cancer to give hope to others facing the same fight.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.title: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

entry.title: Thanksgiving on a budget: Florida supermarkets offer holiday meal deals as food inflation bites
entry.summary: Shopping for a Thanksgiving meal could cost a lot this year as inflation hits grocery prices, which is why some supermarkets are offering deals for the big day. According to the Consumer Price Index, the price of turkey is up 8% from a year ago. I discovered at least four stores in Florida offering turkey and trimmings for under $40. Winn-Dixie's deal serves six people for under $40 Target's deal serves six for $30 Aldi serves 10 people for $39 Walmart serves 10 people for $35 Publix has several heat serve meals starting at $69.99 Sam's Club's deal serves 16 people $160 All of the stores' deals include turkey and side dishes. Eric Van Tassel with FAU's College of Business says grocery prices are front and center with consumers. 'Talking to American households, that's the first thing they bring up; naturally, it's something I pay attention to. I'm going to the grocery store after this meeting,' Van Tassel said. Saving money on those holiday meals is important, and it's best to shop around to find the best deal that works for your table.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman, 67, arrested in hoarding of more than 100 cats - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman, 67, arrested in hoarding of more than 100 cats    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie woman was arrested Friday after 124 cats and kittens were rescued from a hoarding situation in her home. Marshals Service arrested Kimberly K. Lucie Police Department detectives obtained an arrest warrant charging her with 29 counts of cruelty to animals, a third-degree felony. Robinson was arrested in Indian River County on the outstanding warrant. The arrest stems from an investigation that began on Oct. Lucie Animal Control responded to a residence in the 2500 block of Southwest Warwick Street, east of Florida's Turnpike, after concerns about the welfare of animals and unsanitary living conditions. Animal Control officers discovered more than 60 cats inside the residence. Officers observed extensive accumulations of animal feces and urine, an overwhelming ammonia odor, and numerous cats suffering from apparent untreated medical conditions. Officers then made multiple visits to the residence and ultimately removed 124 cats, including newborn kittens, juveniles up to 1 year old and adult cats. Animal Control removed the animals over three days. The animals were divided between Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County after Animal Control reached capacity. PSLPD detectives reviewed Animal Control reports, veterinary medical records and other investigative documentation. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory," Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, earlier told WPBF. "The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues." Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. The Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.title: Jupiter council hears developer's plan for the former Suni Sands waterfront site
entry.summary: Jupiter council members discussed the future of a prime piece of town waterfront in a special town council meeting Thursday evening. In the hours-long meeting, town leaders heard from a developer proposing 44 condos and a 110-room hotel, along with a restaurant and a marina that would take up about 4.5 acres of the 10.5-acre site. WATCH: Jupiter council heard a developer's plan for the former Suni Sands waterfront site Jupiter council heard a developer's plan for 44 condos, a 110-room hotel, a restaurant and a marina at the former Suni Sands waterfront site. The site was once home to the Suni Sands Mobile Home Park off A1A. Development plans stalled after the discovery of Native American archaeological sites, but the town and the developer came to an agreement earlier this year to allow development on part of the parcel, with the town purchasing just over an acre of the waterfront for $10 million. The developer is asking the town for a number of waivers in its plan. He told the council Thursday he's looking to make the space a place the community can enjoy while preserving much of the land. 'We still wanted to work with the town and create something that we could build there that would be something I would be as proud of as I have been with Love Street,' Sperry Parcel Developer Charles Modica said. Dozens of people turned up for the evening meeting to voice concerns over developing one of the town's last waterfront sites. 'Suni Sands is more than a piece of property. It's part of the natural legacy of our community and once it's developed, we can't get it back. Some things are too valuable to replace,' a young resident opposed to the project said. Thursday's special meeting was the first reading of the proposed rule changes that could allow the development. The five hour meeting ended with the town council approving the passage of four items. A number of waivers the developer is seeking were met with push-back by the council. Future discussion between town staff and the development team are expected before the second reading of the ordinances. entry.title: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 53-year-old Jensen Beach man was sentenced to more than 84 years in prison on 82 counts of child pornography in Martin County's first arrest in a case involving artificial intelligence in 2024. On Wednesday, Daniel Clark Warren was sentenced by Circuit Judge Elizabeth Metzger to 1,013.1 months in prison with credit for 1,002 days already served. The judge denied the defense's request for a downward departure from the sentence. In July, before a scheduled jury trial, he changed his plea to guilty on all counts of child sexual abuse material and video voyeurism involving a minor. Warren was arrested on Jan. 26, 2024, after detectives received an internet crime tip about child pornography. "It's pretty scary when you look at this stuff," Det. Brian Broughton said at the time about creating the images using AI. "This is our first case in Martin County where we have seen AI taking a regular headshot and then turning them into child porn and it's alarming to us," John Budensiek, chief deputy at the time and now sheriff, said. At least one image was of a child under the age of 5, according to the arrest report. "What he does is he takes the face of a child and then he sexualizes that removes the clothing and poses the child and engages them in certain sexual activity and that's the images that he's making with his AI," Broughton said. It took several months for the state to arrest him. "The reason why we waited this long to put it out is because our detectives have been working with other jurisdictions to try and figure out if there are other cases related to this," Budensiek said. The FBI warns child sexual abuse material created with content manipulation technologies, to include generative artificial intelligence, is illegal. "There's been a couple of years now we've seen the deepfakes with celebrities and politicians," Broughton said. "This is just a new level. This is scary stuff." Since then, AI has become more prominent with even better deepfakes.

entry.article_text: A traffic stop connected to a domestic disturbance investigation led to the seizure of nearly 9 pounds of marijuana and the arrest of a Port St. Lucie man, according to the Port St. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Police said officers with the department's Neighborhood Policing Bureau were investigating a reported domestic disturbance on Oct. 28 when they located a vehicle connected to the case. Officers conducted a traffic stop near Southwest Rice Avenue and Southwest Chartwell Street. During the stop, they observed suspected marijuana in plain view inside the vehicle and requested assistance from the department's Special Investigations Unit. Detectives later discovered about 9 pounds of marijuana, including vacuum-sealed packages and smaller individually packaged bags. Investigators also recovered $1,450 in cash and found additional suspected marijuana throughout the vehicle. According to police, the investigation determined the marijuana had been packaged for distribution. The driver, Samuel Torres, 27, of Port St. Lucie, was arrested and charged with possession of marijuana with intent to sell, manufacture or deliver and possession of drug paraphernalia for retail sale. Police also seized the 2019 Kia Optima involved in the case under the Florida Contraband Forfeiture Act. The investigation remains ongoing. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.
