entry.article_text: Severe flooding along the Treasure Coast has led to several school closures as districts await for conditions to clear. The Martin County School District is reviewing weather impacts and safe conditions before deciding whether schools will operate Wednesday, Nov. Currently, schools within the school district are closed Tuesday, November 3 due to the onslaught of flooding. The district said it will share an update on Wednesday’s schedule as soon as possible after the assessment. It recognized that families and employees are making plans and said the safety and well-being of students, staff and families remain its priority. Lucie schools to close Wednesday as flooding continues The St. Lucie County School District is making its community and students the main concern when it comes to flooding conditions surrounding the schools. On Tuesday, Superintendent Dr. Prince announced the school would be closed on Wednesday. The decision was made in collaboration with local law enforcement and in consultation with the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district anticipates reopening schools on Thursday, November 5. See also: Flooding and severe weather prompt school closures and activity cancellations for Tuesday District school resource officers are supporting efforts on local roadways, and the district has opened a shelter at one of its school sites for families who have been displaced by flooded homes. Lucie Public Schools anticipates reopening Thursday, Nov. 5, and said it looks forward to welcoming students and staff back. The school district of indian river county Wednesday school closures The Indian River County Public Schools and district locations will remain closed on Wednesday, November 4, as flooding continues to make travel unsafe. Although district facilities have been assessed and are operational, 31 roads are closed, and conditions do not allow school buses to run safely, officials said. The district hopes to reopen Thursday, Nov. 5, but has not confirmed that plan. Updates will be shared through the district’s social media channels and Live Feed. District officials shared on social media that they will continue working closely with emergency management officials and share updates as reopening plans are confirmed. Okeechobee County schools to reopen Wednesday Okeechobee County schools will reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, the school district announced. The district thanked families and the community for their patience as crews worked to make sure schools and bus stops were safe and ready for students. It also recognized its operations, maintenance and custodial teams, school administrators and Okeechobee County Emergency Management for their work during the weather event. We look forward to welcoming everyone back tomorrow, the district said.

entry.title: St. Lucie Public Schools to close Wednesday following historic flooding
entry.summary: St. Lucie Public Schools announced they will be closed on Wednesday, Nov. 4, following extreme flooding in the area. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie Public Schools closed Wednesday following flooding Superintendent Dr. Jon R. Prince said the plan is to reopen on Thursday, Nov. 5. He shared the following message with families and staff on Monday afternoon: This is Superintendent Dr. Jon R. Prince calling to inform you that St. Lucie Public Schools will be closed tomorrow, Wednesday, November 4th. The decision was made in collaboration with local law enforcement and consultation with the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. Our school resource officers will be supporting efforts on local roadways, and the district has opened a shelter at one of our school sites for families who have been displaced by flooded homes. We anticipate reopening schools on Thursday, November 5. I also want to address my decision to keep schools open on Monday. I want you to know that our decision-making was based on information received from the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service Sunday evening and early Monday morning. Martin, Indian River and St. Lucie all proceeded as normal as did all local governmental agencies. However, this became an unpredicted and unprecedented once in a century event for our community. As the day unfolded and the rain continued, we faced the difficult decision to call our bus drivers to report early and ask parents to leave work to pick up or meet their children. We never make that call lightly. We know how hard it is for families to change their plans so quickly, and we never want to put children and families on the road in the height of a storm. To our families and employees, I offer my sincerest apologies for the stress you experienced as the day progressed. Words cannot express my gratitude to the teachers and staff who stayed behind to care for our children, the bus drivers who came in early and stayed late to get students home, and the security teams who drove students and employees home after hours. Please stay safe, stay off flooded roads, and take care of one another. We look forward to welcoming our students back on Thursday.

Words cannot express my gratitude to the teachers and staff who stayed behind to care for our children, the bus drivers who came in early and stayed late to get students home, and the security teams who drove students and employees home after hours. Please stay safe, stay off flooded roads, and take care of one another. We look forward to welcoming our students back on Thursday.

entry.summary: Gov. DeSantis declares state of emergency for 7 Florida counties, including Treasure Coast, for flooding    WPTV
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency Monday for Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties as heavy rainfall and flooding continued to affect parts of the Treasure Coast.The three Treasure Coast counties are among seven covered by Executive Order 26-227. The declaration also includes Brevard, DeSoto, Hardee and Highlands counties.The governor's office said flooding has affected and could continue to affect critical infrastructure, including state and county roads, major interstates, airports and schools. Additional heavy rain and thunderstorms were also forecast, potentially worsening flooding in already affected areas.READ THE FULL EXECUTIVE ORDER BELOW: The declaration gives state and local officials additional authority and resources to respond to the flooding. It authorizes the state coordinating officer to carry out response, recovery and mitigation efforts, including logistical, rescue and evacuation operations. The order also allows the Florida National Guard and Florida State Guard to be activated as needed.The order gives the Florida Department of Transportation authority to close roads or manage traffic when necessary and allows tolls to be waived if needed to facilitate emergency assistance or evacuations. Local governments may also waive certain procedures involving public works, contracts, equipment, workers and spending to speed up their emergency response.WATCH BELOW: Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roadsResidents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties are also covered by provisions allowing pharmacists to provide up to a 30-day emergency refill of maintenance medications. State and local facilities may be closed as necessary, and public facilities suitable for shelters must be made available if requested by local emergency management officials.The declaration also activates Florida's price-gouging protections in the affected counties for essential commodities, supplies, services and equipment needed because of the emergency.With Florida's general election scheduled for Tuesday, the order includes a provision addressing potential impacts from the flooding. Any county supervisor of elections who cannot fully comply with certain polling-place requirements must notify the Florida Department of State about proposed partial or substitute measures, which would require approval from the Florida secretary of state.The executive order took effect immediately on Monday and is scheduled to remain in effect for 60 days unless it is extended.

entry.title: Democrat Pia Dandiya wins Florida's 22nd Congressional District
entry.summary: Democrat Pia Dandiya has won Florida's 22nd Congressional District, defeating Republican Casey Askar in Tuesday's general election. Dandiya, a former high school principal and White House Fellow, will represent the newly redrawn congressional district, which stretches across portions of Palm Beach, Broward, Collier and Hendry counties. In a statement released Tuesday night, Dandiya reflected on her family's journey to the United States and her plans for Congress. 'More than 40 years ago, my parents came from India to Palm Beach County, determined to live the American Dream,' Dandiya said. 'And tonight, one generation later, their daughter will become Congresswoman Dandiya.' Dandiya, who was born and raised in Palm Beach County, campaigned on lowering the cost of living, improving education and addressing government corruption. 'I'm not going to Washington to fight with people. I'm going to fight for people,' Dandiya said in her victory statement. She also pledged to work across party lines to address issues facing South Florida families. 'Whether you are from Belle Glade or Marco Island, Parkland or Royal Palm, I will work tirelessly to lower the cost of living and stand up to the corruption in DC,' she said. Dandiya previously worked at Apple and served as a White House Fellow, in addition to her experience as a teacher and high school principal. The 22nd Congressional District was significantly redrawn ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel, who previously represented the district, instead sought reelection in the newly drawn 23rd Congressional District. Dandiya will serve a two-year term in the U.S. House of Representatives. 'Thank you for trusting me with a part in its next chapter,' Dandiya said. 'Let's make it one our children will be proud to read.'

entry.summary: Republican Rep. Byron Donalds was elected Florida's first Black governor on Tuesday in a race that was seen as unexpectedly competitive down the stretch, defeating Democratic nominee David Jolly. FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News Republican Rep. Byron Donalds was elected Florida's first Black governor on Tuesday in a race that was seen as unexpectedly competitive down the stretch, defeating Democratic nominee David Jolly. Donalds will succeed outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who used the office to fan presidential ambitions and steer President Donald Trump's adopted home state further to the right. The race presented a test of whether Trump's unpopularity, which has dragged down Republicans across the U.S., would extend to his backyard and endanger an office in Florida that a Democrat hasn't won in more than 30 years. Jolly is a former Republican congressman who switched parties and ran a centrist campaign. Donalds had sought to define him as an out-of-touch liberal, and he reached out to Black voters who traditionally side with Democrats. Beyond the national political environment, the race centered on issues including high prices and the cost of homeowners insurance, a particularly salient issue in a state with a history of being ravaged by hurricanes. Florida spent a generation as America's prized political battleground, where the interests of big cities, agricultural towns, freshly arrived retirees and diverse Latino communities collided in elections often decided by fractions of a percentage point. That reputation faded under DeSantis, who won his first race in 2018 by less than half a percentage point. But once he was in office, he leaned into culture wars centered on race and gender signing, for instance, legislation often labeled by critics as 'Don't Say Gay' that bars instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through the third grade. By the time he ran for reelection in 2022, DeSantis won in a nearly 20-point landslide that left the state's Democrats in shambles. Jolly faced steep hurdles in his effort to lead the party's rebound. Republicans have a roughly 1.5 million voter registration advantage, and Donalds dominated Jolly in fundraising. But once he was in office, he leaned into culture wars centered on race and gender — signing, for instance, legislation often labeled by critics as "Don't Say Gay" that bars instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through the third grade. By the time he ran for reelection in 2022, DeSantis won in a nearly 20-point landslide that left the state's Democrats in shambles.Jolly faced steep hurdles in his effort to lead the party's rebound. Republicans have a roughly 1.5 million voter registration advantage, and Donalds dominated Jolly in fundraising.Seeking to overcome those challenges, Jolly campaigned in Florida's Democratic strongholds, like Broward County, along with traditionally Republican parts of central Florida and the state's Panhandle.Donalds maintained a steady confidence throughout the campaign, balancing his support for Trump with efforts to create some distance, including minimizing references to the president on his website.

entry.title: Democrat Roy Cooper wins North Carolina Senate race
entry.summary: Democrat Roy Cooper is the projected winner of North Carolina's U.S. Senate race, defeating Republican Michael Whatley, according to The Associated Press. Cooper's victory flips a Republican-held Senate seat and marks his return to elected office after serving two terms as North Carolina's governor. Cooper, one of the state's most recognizable Democrats, served as governor from 2017 to 2025. Before that, he spent nearly 16 years as North Carolina's attorney general, the longest tenure in the state's history. His political career began in the North Carolina General Assembly, where he served from 1987 to 2001. Cooper announced his Senate campaign in July 2025, seeking to replace retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who chose not to run for a third term. Throughout his campaign, Cooper focused on lowering everyday costs for North Carolina families, including groceries, housing, health care, child care and utilities. Cooper's victory gives Democrats a pickup in their effort to gain control of the U.S. Senate. The seat had been held by Tillis since 2015.

entry.title: Okeechobee County to open flood relief distribution Wednesday
entry.summary: Okeechobee County said it is opening flood relief distribution on Wednesday with tarps, cleaning buckets and water for residents. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Significant flooding impacts roads, neighborhoods in Okeechobee The distribution will be held at the Agri-Civic Center, located at 4601 State Rd. 710 E., from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m., while supplies last. Residents picking up supplies should enter the site via State Road 710 only, the county said. The distribution comes after historic rainfall and widespread flooding prompted school closures . Justin Hazellief, public safety director and fire chief for the county, told WPTV's Tyler Hatfield the area experienced a 1-in-200-year rainfall event, receiving around 9 to 10 inches of rain in just six hours on Sunday. 'This is by far in my 25 years this is the worst that I've seen,' Hazellief said. 'Mother nature has a mind of her own, and whenever she brings that amount of rain in that short of time, there's no infrastructure anywhere that would be able to handle that amount of water and not have some consequences.' The widespread flooding Sunday prompted school closures, shelter openings and a state of emergency declaration in Okeechobee County. Okeechobee County Public Schools will reopen on Wednesday after closing Tuesday due to the flooding and severe weather in the region.

entry.title: Ossoff wins reelection in Georgia, delivering Democrats a crucial Senate victory
entry.summary: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection in Georgia on Tuesday, according to a race call from the Association Press. The win is a major victory for Democrats seeking to regain control of the Senate in one of the country's most closely watched midterm contests. The result carries national implications as both parties compete for control of the Senate, where Republicans began the election cycle with a 53-47 majority. Democrats need to gain seats while defending vulnerable incumbents to take control of the chamber. The race centered on the economy and affordability, health care, immigration, abortion and President Donald Trump's policies, with the candidates offering sharply different visions for the country's direction. RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governor Ossoff, first elected to the Senate in a 2021 runoff, made affordability and health care central to his reelection campaign. He criticized Trump's tariffs and Republican-backed changes to federal programs, arguing that the policies put additional pressure on Georgia families. Collins, a Republican congressman representing Georgia's 10th District and a former trucking business owner, campaigned on tax cuts, immigration enforcement, deregulation and support for Trump's agenda. He sought to tie Ossoff to Democratic policies he argued had contributed to higher costs. The candidates clashed during their October debates over inflation, health care, immigration, the war with Iran and election integrity. Their exchanges also became personal, with Ossoff criticizing Collins over controversial associations and social media activity, while Collins attacked Ossoff's policy positions and ties to progressive Democrats.

entry.title: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat - WPEC
entry.summary: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

entry.title: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County officials said Tuesday that emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls as they responded to widespread flooding after historic rainfall. Lucie County Fire District received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period, Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said at a county briefing. The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns, he said. Please use caution and avoid unnecessary travel, Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said. It may take several days for the water to recede. Shelters open; schools closed Wednesday The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. The city said vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000 . The city also warned residents to expect a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. See also: LIST: Flooded St. Lucie, Indian River roads remain hazardous as crews check homes Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Guerrero said emergency dispatchers had received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Officials said call takers were screening requests so emergency vehicles could remain available for urgent situations. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

The Martin County School District is reviewing weather impacts and safe conditions before deciding whether schools will operate Wednesday, Nov. Currently, schools within the school district are closed Tuesday, November 3 due to the onslaught of flooding. Lucie schools to close Wednesday as flooding continues The St. Lucie County School District is making its community and students the main concern when it comes to flooding conditions surrounding the schools. The school district of indian river county Wednesday school closures The Indian River County Public Schools and district locations will remain closed on Wednesday, November 4, as flooding continues to make travel unsafe. Although district facilities have been assessed and are operational, 31 roads are closed, and conditions do not allow school buses to run safely, officials said. The district hopes to reopen Thursday, Nov. 5, but has not confirmed that plan. Updates will be shared through the district’s social media channels and Live Feed. The district thanked families and the community for their patience as crews worked to make sure schools and bus stops were safe and ready for students. entry.title: Democrat Adam Hamilton pulls off upset in Kansas Senate race
entry.summary: Democrat Adam Hamilton is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas' U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press, pulling off a major upset in a state that has overwhelmingly favored Republicans for decades. Hamilton's victory ends a nearly centurylong streak of Republican wins in Kansas' U.S. Senate elections, delivering Democrats an unexpected pickup in their fight for control of the chamber. The result comes amid growing frustration over the economy, with Republicans controlling both Congress and the White House. Hamilton sought to capitalize on concerns about the cost of living, arguing that Kansas families needed new leadership in Washington. Hamiltons victory marks a major setback for President Donald Trump, who visited Kansas ahead of Election Day to campaign for Marshall. Trump carried the state in all three of his presidential campaigns. Hamilton, the founding pastor of one of the nation's largest United Methodist churches, campaigned as a moderate focused on affordability and bringing voters together. The seat is the latest pickup for Democrats in the Senate.

entry.title: Lois Frankel wins 8th term in Congress, says affordability will be top priority
entry.summary: Surrounded by Democratic constituents and fellow Democratic winners celebrating at an election night watch party in West Palm Beach, Lois Frankel was already looking beyond her victory Tuesday night. The Democratic congresswoman won Florida's newly redrawn 23rd Congressional District , defeating Republican Deborah Adeimy and securing an eighth term in Congress. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Lois Frankel wins eighth term in Congress, what's next? FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News Frankel, who has served in Congress since 2013, will return to Washington representing a district that looks different from the one she previously represented. The new 23rd District sits entirely within Palm Beach County and runs from West Palm Beach south to Boca Raton, taking in communities including Boynton Beach, Delray Beach, Greenacres, Lake Worth Beach, Lantana, Palm Beach and Palm Springs. Shortly after the race was called, Frankel told WPTV she was ready to move quickly from campaigning back to governing. 'We're in very complicated times, and I'm ready to roll up my sleeves, get back to it,' Frankel said. At the top of her list is an issue that played a major role throughout the campaign: affordability. Frankel said she wants Democrats in Washington to put a greater focus on the everyday costs affecting families. 'People can't pay their rent. Gas is too expensive. Food is too expensive. Healthcare is too expensive,' Frankel said. 'Democrats are going to get back to Washington, do what we can to lower the costs and let's get the president to come right along with us.' Affordability was also a major theme for Adeimy. The Republican challenger, a Palm Beach County native with a background in finance, focused heavily on housing and insurance costs during the campaign. Frankel had a conciliatory message for her Republican opponent after the votes came in. 'Listen, I think anybody who runs for election today is very brave in Florida. entry.title: Democrat Sherrod Brown defeats GOP's Jon Husted in Ohio Senate race
entry.summary: Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio's U.S. Senate special election Tuesday, according to a race call from the Associated Press. The result gives Democrats an opportunity to strengthen their push to regain control of the Senate as both parties compete for power in Washington. Republicans began the election cycle with a 53-47 Senate majority, and Ohio has emerged as one of the closely watched contests that could determine the chamber's balance. He argued that federal policies favoring wealthy Americans and corporations have left working families struggling with rising costs. He also made the growth of data centers and their potential impact on electricity bills a major issue in his campaign. Husted, a Republican and former Ohio lieutenant governor, was appointed to the Senate in January 2025 after JD Vance left the seat to become vice president. He campaigned on economic growth, tax cuts, immigration enforcement and support for President Donald Trump's agenda. Husted has argued that his record in state government and the Senate makes him better positioned to advance Ohio's interests. The contest drew substantial national attention and spending as both parties sought to influence a race with implications beyond Ohio. Trump campaigned for Husted, while Democrats sought to mobilize union households and voters concerned about affordability. Brown will serve the remainder of Vance's Senate term, which expires in January 2029.

entry.title: Amy Acton defeats Vivek Ramaswamy, becomes Ohio's first female governor
entry.summary: For the first time in 20 years, Ohioans have elected a Democrat to lead the state. Amy Acton, the states former health director who helped lead its response at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, according to a race call from the Associated Press. The race was upended nearly two weeks ago when Ramaswamy ran an advertisement featuring Actons estranged mother, who called Acton a liar. Actons mom reportedly lost custody of Acton when she was 12 years old after a grand jury indicted her stepfather for sexual abuse. The advertisement received bipartisan condemnation, including from Ohios Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, who endorsed Ramaswamy. Acton will replace DeWine, who appointed her state health director in 2019. Although DeWine endorsed Ramaswamy, he defended Actons COVID-19 policies, including decisions to close schools and restaurant dining rooms early in the pandemic. Ramaswamy sought to make the states handling of the pandemic a key issue in the race. Ramaswamy also ran an ad highlighting a 2019 incident in which police were called to Actons residence. Acton cited the ad as a reason she would not participate in a debate with Ramaswamy. Neither Acton nor Ramaswamy had held elected office before entering the governors race. President Donald Trump initially tapped Ramaswamy to co-lead the Department of Government Efficiency with Elon Musk, but Ramaswamy left the effort on the day of Trumps inauguration. Acton becomes the first woman elected governor of Ohio and only the second Democrat elected to the office in 36 years.

His sister, Darline Graham, was subsequently appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remainder of his term.

entry.title: Florida voters approve Amendment 3, bringing major changes to property taxes
entry.summary: Florida voters have approved Amendment 3, a sweeping constitutional amendment that will change the state's property tax system by increasing the homestead exemption, reducing assessment increases on non-homestead properties and restricting how counties and municipalities can use property tax revenue. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida voters approve Amendment 3, increasing homestead exemption FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News With 99% of precincts reporting at 10:13 p.m., 62% voted Yes while 38% voted No. Amendment 3 required support from at least 60% of voters to become part of the Florida Constitution. Under the amendment, the homestead exemption for property taxes other than school district taxes will increase to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Beginning in 2029, the exemption will be adjusted for inflation. The amendment also establishes different rules for newer Florida residents. New residents will receive a smaller exemption until they have lived in the state for five years. Amendment 3 also changes how quickly the assessed value of non-homestead properties, including rental and commercial properties, can rise. The annual assessment cap will decrease from 10% to 5%, except for school district taxes. Another provision restricts how counties and municipalities can spend property tax revenue, directing that revenue toward specified purposes including public safety, education, infrastructure, natural resource and flood-control projects, local bonds, employee retirement benefits and government operations. The proposal was placed on the ballot by the Florida Legislature during a special session in June. The changes will take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

entry.summary: Meltzer wins open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat, succeeding Morgan    WPEC
entry.article_text: Rick Meltzer beat Idony Jean Baptist for the open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat, which covers the city’s eastern and northeastern areas. The winner succeeds three-term Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan, who did not seek reelection. With 58 of 62 precincts reporting, Meltzer won 56.7 percent of the vote to Jean Baptiste's 43.3 percent. Meltzer led the four-candidate August primary with about 42% of the vote, followed by Jean Baptiste at about 22%. Neither reached the majority needed to win outright. Meltzer is a mortgage loan originator, has lived in District 1 for more than 20 years and has coached and mentored youth sports for 17 years. He is a political newcomer who says he would bring an outsider’s perspective to City Hall. His platform focuses on affordability, accountability and infrastructure. Meltzer says he would seek budget cuts and lower property taxes, hold contractors and developers to project deadlines and budgets, and prioritize road, utility and other infrastructure needs before approving new development. He also opposes more zero-lot-line housing and supports building a sports complex. Full local election results Meltzer has also said he is researching the impacts of data centers, including water use, electricity demand and noise. He says their potential tax revenue and jobs could outweigh the concerns if the city protects residents’ interests. Jean Baptiste is a minister and former Indian River County Sheriff’s Office detention deputy. He previously ran for the same seat in 2022 and later briefly filed to run for St. Lucie County sheriff before withdrawing. His campaign emphasizes safer communities, transparent government, listening to residents, helping people in need and supporting small businesses. Jean Baptiste has proposed attracting more businesses to grow city revenue and reduce service costs for residents, along with moving to a double-can automated trash-pickup system that he says could improve service and save money. The choice is between Meltzer’s call for tighter spending oversight and infrastructure-first growth, and Jean Baptiste’s focus on community responsiveness, public safety and service improvements.

Byron Donalds was elected Florida's first Black governor on Tuesday in a race that was seen as unexpectedly competitive down the stretch, defeating Democratic nominee David Jolly. entry.article_text: Okeechobee County and Martin County Public Schools will reopen on Wednesday, Nov. 4, after closing Tuesday due to flooding and severe weather in the region.MARTIN COUNTY SCHOOLSAll Martin County School District-operated schools will reopen on Wednesday, Nov. 4.School officials said in a pres release that they know some families and staff may still be displaced or experiencing difficult travel conditions and they want to provide flexibility to those who need it.Students who are unable to attend school on Wednesday because of weather-related conditions or who need additional time to arrive will have their absence or tardy excused with parent or guardian notification to the school.The district also said families using school district bus transportation should expect delays on Wednesday, and families who are able to safely transport their children to and from school are encouraged to do so.Extended Day programs will operate as scheduled, but any outdoor after-school activities will remain canceled. Indoor after-school activities may resume at the discretion of schools and coaches.No decision has been made yet regarding a make-up day, but they will communicate that information when a decision is reached.The statement read in part, "The District understands that reopening schools is an important step toward returning to normal routines for many families, while others in our community are still navigating very difficult circumstances. Our thoughts remain with those dealing with flooding and other significant impacts, and we encourage every family and employee to make decisions based on the conditions where they live and travel."OKEECHOBEE COUNTY SCHOOLSOkeechobee County district officials announced Tuesday that the schools will reopen on Wednesday, Nov. 4.The statement read in part, "Thank you to our families and the entire Okeechobee community for your patience and understanding over the past two days as we worked to make sure our schools and bus stops are safe and ready for students to return."Officials said the district will also announce in the coming days whether any makeup days will be necessary.

entry.title: Republican Brian Mast wins reelection in Florida's 21st Congressional District
entry.summary: Republican U.S. Rep. Brian Mast has won another term in Congress, defeating Democratic challenger James Martin in Florida's 21st Congressional District. Mast, a U.S. Army veteran who has served in Congress since 2017, secured reelection in the newly redrawn district, which includes portions of Palm Beach, Martin and St. Lucie counties. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Brian Mast wins reelection   Brian Mast wins reelection for Florida House 21 FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News Mast said one of his biggest priorities is to continue the battle for clean water. That is the fight that I'm engaged in every single day,' Mast said. Mast is currently the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. entry.title: St. Lucie Public Schools to close Wednesday following historic flooding
entry.summary: St. Lucie Public Schools announced they will be closed on Wednesday, Nov. 4, following extreme flooding in the area. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie Public Schools closed Wednesday following flooding Superintendent Dr. Jon R. Prince said the plan is to reopen on Thursday, Nov. 5. He shared the following message with families and staff on Monday afternoon: This is Superintendent Dr. Jon R. Prince calling to inform you that St. Lucie Public Schools will be closed tomorrow, Wednesday, November 4th. The decision was made in collaboration with local law enforcement and consultation with the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. Our school resource officers will be supporting efforts on local roadways, and the district has opened a shelter at one of our school sites for families who have been displaced by flooded homes. We anticipate reopening schools on Thursday, November 5. I also want to address my decision to keep schools open on Monday. I want you to know that our decision-making was based on information received from the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service Sunday evening and early Monday morning. Martin, Indian River and St. Lucie all proceeded as normal as did all local governmental agencies. However, this became an unpredicted and unprecedented once in a century event for our community. As the day unfolded and the rain continued, we faced the difficult decision to call our bus drivers to report early and ask parents to leave work to pick up or meet their children. We never make that call lightly. We know how hard it is for families to change their plans so quickly, and we never want to put children and families on the road in the height of a storm. To our families and employees, I offer my sincerest apologies for the stress you experienced as the day progressed. Words cannot express my gratitude to the teachers and staff who stayed behind to care for our children, the bus drivers who came in early and stayed late to get students home, and the security teams who drove students and employees home after hours. Please stay safe, stay off flooded roads, and take care of one another. We look forward to welcoming our students back on Thursday.

entry.title: Fort Pierce restaurant owner finds ways to get young kids to read more books
entry.summary: Big Apple Pizza restaurant owner Scott Van Duzer has been involved with the Read To Succeed program. 'With our Read To Succeed, and after three years, we've gotten 40,000 books out there, but I found a way to get books out there a lot quicker,' said Van Duzer. It's called the New Worlds Reading program. Amy York, and her son Tripp, read together from books he gets in the mail. entry.title: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County officials said Tuesday that emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls as they responded to widespread flooding after historic rainfall. Lucie County Fire District received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period, Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said at a county briefing. The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns, he said. Please use caution and avoid unnecessary travel, Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said. It may take several days for the water to recede. Shelters open; schools closed Wednesday The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. The city said vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000 . The city also warned residents to expect a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. See also: LIST: Flooded St. Lucie, Indian River roads remain hazardous as crews check homes Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Guerrero said emergency dispatchers had received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Officials said call takers were screening requests so emergency vehicles could remain available for urgent situations. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

entry.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed makes history as first Muslim elected to US Senate
entry.summary: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press, keeping the seat in Democratic hands. Abdul El-Sayed delivers victory speech in Michigan Senate win I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect, El-Sayed told supporters in a victory speech late Tuesday. 'I want you to let them know. Let them know that we, together, fighting for something bigger; we won.' El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, made the war in Gaza one of the central issues in his campaign, accusing Israel of committing genocide. He also criticized U.S. support for Israel under President Donald Trump. His background was subject to attack ads from Republicans, who accused him of being part of the Muslim Brotherhood. He shrugged off those attacks and built a coalition of progressive and moderate Democrats that included former President Barack Obama and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. The final days of the campaign took a dramatic turn when El-Sayed's former Democratic primary opponent, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, withdrew her endorsement of him and instead backed Rogers. Stevens said she ultimately could not support El-Sayed, citing differences over Israel and saying she did not feel welcome in his campaign. A former public health official, El-Sayed campaigned on expanding access to affordable health care, including his support for Medicare for All. His platform also focused on lowering everyday costs, expanding access to affordable housing, reducing the influence of money in politics and strengthening environmental protections, including efforts to ensure clean air and water.

entry.title: Democrats will win control of US House, retaking control from Republicans
entry.summary: Democrats will take control of the U.S. House of Representatives after flipping numerous Republican-held seats, according to The Associated Press. The victory, combined with Democrats' takeover of the U.S. Senate, gives the party control of both chambers of Congress. RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governor Votes are still being counted in several House races, leaving the size of Democrats' majority in the next Congress uncertain. Democrats capitalized on voter frustration over affordability, rising gas prices and the war in Iran, issues that dominated the campaign leading up to the midterm elections. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is positioned to become the next speaker of the House. If elected by his colleagues, Jeffries would make history as the first Black person to hold the position. In a speech Tuesday night, Jeffries spoke about how Democrats would lead. 'We understand, as House of Democrats, that we need to deliver dramatic change,' he said. 'Things are broken. We need a Congress that puts the American people first. The wealthy, the well-off, and the well-connected tried to buy this election. The American people have responded in a resounding way and made clear that America is not for sale.' The victory marks Democrats' first return to control of the House since January 2023, when Republicans took the majority after four years of Democratic leadership under former Speaker Nancy Pelosi. In the weeks leading up to Election Day, House Speaker Mike Johnson remained confident that Republicans would retain their majority, dismissing polls that suggested Democrats were positioned for a strong showing. President Donald Trump had promised Americans $5,000 payments if Republicans retained control of both the House and Senate, but the incentive was not enough to prevent the party from losing both chambers.

entry.title: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race - WPEC
entry.summary: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race    WPEC
entry.article_text: Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin in a closely contested race Tuesday, marking a change in leadership for one of Florida's fastest-growing cities. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections , Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Giordano won by 2,601 votes. All 62 precincts have reported, with election-day, early and mail votes marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. Throughout his campaign, he argued that developers should pay their fair share for improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as the city continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion, particularly in St. Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard and Savona Boulevard, and Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway. Taxpayer spending was another major issue in the race. Giordano called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall. Martin pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate. The two candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%. Voters reject twice-weekly trash pickup proposal Port St. Lucie voters also overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to pay more for twice-weekly residential trash collection. According to the latest election results, 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The ballot question asked whether residents would support paying an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly garbage collection. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

entry.title: Angie Nixon concedes Florida Senate race, says progressive movement will continue
entry.summary: Angie Nixons bid to become Florida's first Black U.S. senator ended in defeat Tuesday, but the Jacksonville Democrat told supporters her fight is far from over. 'We may have lost this battle, but the war is not over,' Nixon said during her concession speech. The Associated Press projected Republican Sen. Ashley Moody the winner of the special election. With votes still being counted, Moody had just over 50% of the vote to Nixons approximately 48%. Nixon, a Florida state representative, entered the general election after a surprise victory in the Democratic primary. The progressive candidate campaigned on affordability, championing Medicare for All, free child care and rent freezes. For some supporters, the relatively close race showed an opportunity for Democrats in a state where Republicans have built a substantial advantage. Supporter Mak Manning loved the grassroots campaign Nixon built. 'She's willing to get out there and into the streets and fight,' said Manning. Nixon said Democrats face challenges ahead, including fundraising and closing the voter registration gap with Republicans. 'That 1.5 million gap in registration, we need to fix that,' she told reporters. Asked what comes next, Nixon said her immediate plans included getting some sleep. But she did not rule out another run. 'Im looking forward to 2028 because were getting to work,' she said.

entry.article_text: Lucie County election officials to move six precincts’ polling places on Election Day, including several in Port St. The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves are meant to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Lucie, voters in precincts 49 and 71, who normally cast ballots at Oak Hammock K-8 School, will vote at the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, will also go to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard. Voters in precincts 67 and 86 will not vote at Centennial High School in St. They will vote at Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence, at 500 NW California Blvd. The county says access is from Peacock Boulevard. See also: Inside David Jolly's election night watch party as Florida chooses its next governor In the Tradition area, precinct 83 voters will move from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters will also move from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall. In Fort Pierce, Precinct 12 voters will move from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1. The notice does not list any polling places as closed. It also does not say whether voters who already went to their normal location will be redirected on site. The flooding also disrupted schools. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Jon Prince apologized to families during a news conference Tuesday, after students were seen walking through standing water to get home Monday. We didn’t anticipate anything like what transpired yesterday. Caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry, Prince said. Schools are closed Wednesday. Prince said the district expects to reopen Thursday if roads are clear, and that no school buildings took significant water. A private security company that patrols homeowners associations in the Tradition area joined the rescue effort with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. We had no goal when we came out here. We had just ambition to figure out how we can help anyone and anywhere and do whatever we can with the resources that we have, Matchton said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods, and warned that anyone who preys on flood victims will face zero tolerance. The sheriff said there was no playbook for a storm like this. But the most important thing is we’re all working together with one purpose, which is to serve this community, Del Toro said. The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

entry.title: Meltzer wins open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat, succeeding Morgan - WPEC
entry.summary: Meltzer wins open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat, succeeding Morgan    WPEC
entry.article_text: Rick Meltzer beat Idony Jean Baptist for the open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat, which covers the city’s eastern and northeastern areas. The winner succeeds three-term Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan, who did not seek reelection. With 58 of 62 precincts reporting, Meltzer won 56.7 percent of the vote to Jean Baptiste's 43.3 percent. Meltzer led the four-candidate August primary with about 42% of the vote, followed by Jean Baptiste at about 22%. Neither reached the majority needed to win outright. Meltzer is a mortgage loan originator, has lived in District 1 for more than 20 years and has coached and mentored youth sports for 17 years. He is a political newcomer who says he would bring an outsider’s perspective to City Hall. His platform focuses on affordability, accountability and infrastructure. Meltzer says he would seek budget cuts and lower property taxes, hold contractors and developers to project deadlines and budgets, and prioritize road, utility and other infrastructure needs before approving new development. He also opposes more zero-lot-line housing and supports building a sports complex. Full local election results Meltzer has also said he is researching the impacts of data centers, including water use, electricity demand and noise. He says their potential tax revenue and jobs could outweigh the concerns if the city protects residents’ interests. Jean Baptiste is a minister and former Indian River County Sheriff’s Office detention deputy. He previously ran for the same seat in 2022 and later briefly filed to run for St. Lucie County sheriff before withdrawing. His campaign emphasizes safer communities, transparent government, listening to residents, helping people in need and supporting small businesses. Jean Baptiste has proposed attracting more businesses to grow city revenue and reduce service costs for residents, along with moving to a double-can automated trash-pickup system that he says could improve service and save money. The choice is between Meltzer’s call for tighter spending oversight and infrastructure-first growth, and Jean Baptiste’s focus on community responsiveness, public safety and service improvements.

entry.title: Lois Frankel wins 8th term in Congress, says affordability will be top priority
entry.summary: Surrounded by Democratic constituents and fellow Democratic winners celebrating at an election night watch party in West Palm Beach, Lois Frankel was already looking beyond her victory Tuesday night. The Democratic congresswoman won Florida's newly redrawn 23rd Congressional District , defeating Republican Deborah Adeimy and securing an eighth term in Congress. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Lois Frankel wins eighth term in Congress, what's next? FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News Frankel, who has served in Congress since 2013, will return to Washington representing a district that looks different from the one she previously represented. The new 23rd District sits entirely within Palm Beach County and runs from West Palm Beach south to Boca Raton, taking in communities including Boynton Beach, Delray Beach, Greenacres, Lake Worth Beach, Lantana, Palm Beach and Palm Springs. Shortly after the race was called, Frankel told WPTV she was ready to move quickly from campaigning back to governing. 'We're in very complicated times, and I'm ready to roll up my sleeves, get back to it,' Frankel said. entry.title: Florida voters approve Amendment 3, bringing major changes to property taxes
entry.summary: Florida voters have approved Amendment 3, a sweeping constitutional amendment that will change the state's property tax system by increasing the homestead exemption, reducing assessment increases on non-homestead properties and restricting how counties and municipalities can use property tax revenue. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida voters approve Amendment 3, increasing homestead exemption FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News With 99% of precincts reporting at 10:13 p.m., 62% voted Yes while 38% voted No. Amendment 3 required support from at least 60% of voters to become part of the Florida Constitution. Under the amendment, the homestead exemption for property taxes other than school district taxes will increase to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Beginning in 2029, the exemption will be adjusted for inflation. The amendment also establishes different rules for newer Florida residents. New residents will receive a smaller exemption until they have lived in the state for five years. Amendment 3 also changes how quickly the assessed value of non-homestead properties, including rental and commercial properties, can rise. The annual assessment cap will decrease from 10% to 5%, except for school district taxes. Another provision restricts how counties and municipalities can spend property tax revenue, directing that revenue toward specified purposes including public safety, education, infrastructure, natural resource and flood-control projects, local bonds, employee retirement benefits and government operations. The proposal was placed on the ballot by the Florida Legislature during a special session in June. The changes will take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

entry.title: Steven Giordano defeats incumbent Shannon Martin to win Port St. Lucie mayoral race
entry.summary: Steven Giordano has won the race for Port St. Lucie mayor, defeating incumbent Shannon Martin after a closely watched campaign. Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. He defeated Martin by a margin of just over 2,400 votes. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Steven Giordano defeats incumbent Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race The outcome marked a significant turnaround from the August primary, when Martin finished nearly 13 percentage points ahead of Giordano. Speaking at his election-night watch party, Giordano said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race. 'I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons,' Giordano said. 'I think they watched the debate.' Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician. 'I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people,' he said. 'And I'm proud to be the people's mayor.' The general election followed a contentious August primary that included an FDLE investigation involving campaign signs. The investigation led to Martin's husband and two other Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on paid administrative leave, according to the reporter's script. WPTV reached out to Martin for comment following the election results but had not received a response as of Tuesday night.

entry.title: Republican James Uthmeier wins reelection for attorney general in Florida
entry.summary: Republican James Uthmeier won Florida's attorney general race Tuesday night, securing another term after a closely contested election. Uthmeier, who entered the race as the sitting attorney general, won by about 2 percentage points, according to the latest results. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier wins reelection FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News Speaking to supporters after claiming victory, Uthmeier pointed to his record in office, highlighting arrests and convictions under his leadership and arguing that his experience showed voters he could continue doing the job. He later spoke with WPTV about what the narrow margins in his race and other Republican contests could mean for the future of the GOP in Florida. 'I think Republicans are learning that people across the country, they're facing challenges. They're struggling,' Uthmeier said. WATCH BELOW: Uthmeier speaks about winning attorney general's race James Uthmeier claims victory in Florida attorney general's race Uthmeier acknowledged the financial pressures families are facing, saying he experiences some of those same concerns. 'Look, I've got four little ones at home and I face challenges at the gas pump too. I get it,' he said. 'But at the end of the day, what we learned tonight in our race is that we ultimately have to have public safety.' Public safety was a central theme of Uthmeier's campaign and his election-night remarks. Despite the narrow margin, the reporter said Uthmeier received approximately 4.1 million votes, potentially the highest vote total among Florida Cabinet candidates on the ballot this election.

entry.title: Democrat Pia Dandiya wins Florida's 22nd Congressional District
entry.summary: Democrat Pia Dandiya has won Florida's 22nd Congressional District, defeating Republican Casey Askar in Tuesday's general election and keeping a closely watched congressional seat in Democratic hands. Dandiya's victory comes after a dramatic redrawing of the district, which once reliably favored Democrats but now includes Republican strongholds across Palm Beach, Broward, Collier and Hendry counties. WATCH BELOW: Pia Dandiya says she'll stand up to 'corruption' in D.C. Pia Dandiya wins Florida's 22nd Congressional District The new boundaries created uncertainty over which party would win the seat and made the race significant far beyond South Florida. District 22 was one of four Florida congressional districts redrawn in ways that could help Republicans flip Democratic seats and strengthen their position in Congress. Dandiya's victory denies Republicans one potential pickup in their fight for control of the U.S. House. Supporters erupted in cheers Tuesday night at the Wellington Community Center as Dandiya took the stage to celebrate her victory. The Florida-born former teacher and high school principal thanked voters and pledged to deliver on the promises that shaped her campaign, including lowering the cost of living and tackling what she describes as corruption in Washington. 'My commitment to you is that I will work tirelessly to lower the cost of living, to stand up to the corruption in DC, so you can spend less time worrying about how you will make ends meet and more time building the life for your family that you want,' Dandiya told supporters. Affordability at the center of Dandiya's campaign Throughout her campaign, Dandiya made affordability a central issue, promising to make the American Dream more attainable for South Florida families. In a previous interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Dandiya outlined several proposals aimed at easing financial pressures and protecting federal benefits. Those included expanding Affordable Care Act subsidies, allowing Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices and potentially raising the Social Security payroll tax cap to help preserve benefits. She also pledged to work across party lines to address issues facing families throughout the newly drawn district. 'I'm not going to Washington to fight with people. entry.title: Republican Byron Donalds wins election for governor in Florida
entry.summary: Republican Rep. Byron Donalds was elected Florida's first Black governor on Tuesday in a race that was seen as unexpectedly competitive down the stretch, defeating Democratic nominee David Jolly. Donalds will succeed outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who used the office to fan presidential ambitions and steer President Donald Trump's adopted home state further to the right. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Byron Donalds elected as first Black governor of Florida FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News The race presented a test of whether Trump's unpopularity, which has dragged down Republicans across the U.S., would extend to his backyard and endanger an office in Florida that a Democrat hasn't won in more than 30 years. Jolly is a former Republican congressman who switched parties and ran a centrist campaign. Donalds had sought to define him as an out-of-touch liberal, and he reached out to Black voters who traditionally side with Democrats. WATCH BELOW: Byron Donalds' victory speech Byron Donalds wins Florida governor's race Beyond the national political environment, the race centered on issues including high prices and the cost of homeowners insurance, a particularly salient issue in a state with a history of being ravaged by hurricanes. That reputation faded under DeSantis, who won his first race in 2018 by less than half a percentage point. But once he was in office, he leaned into culture wars centered on race and gender signing, for instance, legislation often labeled by critics as 'Don't Say Gay' that bars instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through the third grade. By the time he ran for reelection in 2022, DeSantis won in a nearly 20-point landslide that left the state's Democrats in shambles. Donalds had sought to define him as an out-of-touch liberal, and he reached out to Black voters who traditionally side with Democrats.WATCH BELOW: Byron Donalds' victory speechBeyond the national political environment, the race centered on issues including high prices and the cost of homeowners insurance, a particularly salient issue in a state with a history of being ravaged by hurricanes.Florida spent a generation as America's prized political battleground, where the interests of big cities, agricultural towns, freshly arrived retirees and diverse Latino communities collided in elections often decided by fractions of a percentage point.That reputation faded under DeSantis, who won his first race in 2018 by less than half a percentage point. But once he was in office, he leaned into culture wars centered on race and gender — signing, for instance, legislation often labeled by critics as "Don't Say Gay" that bars instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through the third grade. By the time he ran for reelection in 2022, DeSantis won in a nearly 20-point landslide that left the state's Democrats in shambles.Jolly faced steep hurdles in his effort to lead the party's rebound. Republicans have a roughly 1.5 million voter registration advantage, and Donalds dominated Jolly in fundraising.Seeking to overcome those challenges, Jolly campaigned in Florida's Democratic strongholds, like Broward County, along with traditionally Republican parts of central Florida and the state's Panhandle.Donalds maintained a steady confidence throughout the campaign, balancing his support for Trump with efforts to create some distance, including minimizing references to the president on his website.
