entry.title: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County officials said Tuesday that emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls as they responded to widespread flooding after historic rainfall. Lucie County Fire District received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period, Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said at a county briefing. The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns, he said. Please use caution and avoid unnecessary travel, Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said. It may take several days for the water to recede. Shelters open; schools closed Wednesday The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. The city said vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000 . The city also warned residents to expect a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. See also: LIST: Flooded St. Lucie, Indian River roads remain hazardous as crews check homes Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Guerrero said emergency dispatchers had received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Officials said call takers were screening requests so emergency vehicles could remain available for urgent situations. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

entry.title: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat - WPEC
entry.summary: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

entry.summary: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race    WPEC
entry.article_text: Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin in a closely contested race Tuesday, marking a change in leadership for one of Florida's fastest-growing cities. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections , Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Giordano won by 2,601 votes. All 62 precincts have reported, with election-day, early and mail votes marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. Throughout his campaign, he argued that developers should pay their fair share for improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as the city continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion, particularly in St. See also: After close win, Byron Donalds turns focus to his first priorities as governor Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard and Savona Boulevard, and Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway. Taxpayer spending was another major issue in the race. Giordano called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall. Martin pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate. The two candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%. Voters reject twice-weekly trash pickup proposal Port St. Lucie voters also overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to pay more for twice-weekly residential trash collection. According to the latest election results, 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The ballot question asked whether residents would support paying an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly garbage collection. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

entry.title: Lauren Boebert trails Democratic challenger in tight Colorado House race
entry.summary: Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert is locked in a tight race to retain her seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, with Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher holding a narrow lead as vote counting continued Wednesday. Boebert has represented Colorado's 4th Congressional District for two years. She previously represented the state's 3rd Congressional District but switched districts in late 2023. Boebert made the switch, referring to the need for a 'fresh start following a difficult year' that included family turmoil and numerous scandals that would have made for a tough reelection bid in her original district. President Donald Trump endorsed Boebert, a staunch ally who has largely supported his agenda. Her Democratic challenger, Laubacher, brings a different background to the race. Laubacher served in the military for more than 30 years, rising to the rank of admiral in the Navy. She said her decision to run for Congress was driven by concerns about the country's future. 'I have never felt as much of a threat to our country, our Constitution, our very democracy, as I do at this time,' Laubacher said.

entry.title: Jeffries claims mandate to address affordability after Democratic Party win
entry.summary: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries vowed to work with Republicans to address affordability issues as he positions himself to become the nation's first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress is seated Jan. 3. Jeffries could become the next speaker after Democrats scored a major victory in Tuesday's midterm elections, securing at least 228 House seats, with the potential to add several dozen more. Jeffries told Scripps News Deputy Political Director Joe St. George that Democrats plan to focus on lowering the costs of housing, health care, groceries, gas and other everyday goods. RELATED STORY | Democrats will win control of US House, retaking control from Republicans 'We've always made clear, as House Democrats, that we will find bipartisan common ground whenever and wherever possible in order to make life better for the American people,' he told St. George. The election results appeared to exceed Jeffries' expectations. 'It was an incredible night,' he said. 'I was very confident that we were going to take back control of the House. I was very confident that we could get to 230, 235, perhaps a little bit more than that. But it looks like we're heading for numbers that could exceed 250 or 255, and we'll have the largest majority of any Congress this century.' He said that the result was 'a massive repudiation of MAGA extremism. RELATED STORY | Trump deflects blame for Republican midterm losses as finger-pointing begins 'We're looking forward, as House Democrats, to getting to work and to finding bipartisan common ground so we can solve this affordability crisis here in America,' he added. Jeffries downplayed the prospect of becoming the first Black speaker of the House. 'Well, we'll cross that bridge when we get to it,' he said. 'America is still in the hands of my colleagues. America is a beautiful country. We are a representative democracy, and I just look forward to trying to bring to life the principle of government of the people, by the people and for the people.'

entry.title: Doctors credit dad's quick CPR with saving son's life after teen is struck by lightning
entry.summary: When lightning struck his 14-year-old son on a soccer field, Kevin Sosa's father didn't hesitate he dropped to the ground and started CPR. Doctors say that decision is the reason Kevin survived. Now, Kevin has reunited with his parents, the first responders and the medical team who brought him back to life during an emotional ceremony at Delray Medical Center. 'Thank you for saving my life,' Kevin said to a room full of medical and emergency staff. According to Kevin's dad, they were playing soccer on a field near their home in Boynton Beach on August 23 when the weather suddenly turned cloudy, and lightning struck. His father was close by when it happened. 'He felt sort of the electricity run through him, but the main impact clearly went to Kevin,' Dr. Pedro Gonzalez said. As Kevin's mother called for help, his father immediately began CPR and doctors said that quick thinking helped save his son's life. Paramedics arrived on scene, took over CPR, and rushed Kevin to Delray Medical Center, where he stayed for weeks and even celebrated his birthday in a hospital room. Doctors said Kevin went into cardiac arrest. Palm Beach Fire Rescue said only about 10% of people who go into cardiac arrest survive and the CPR Kevin received before paramedics arrived made the difference. 'If they hadn't done CPR on him, the time that his brain would've been without oxygen would've been much longer, and I don't think he would've seen this much of a recovery,' Dr. Angela Jones said. 'To see him up, and walking, and talking, it really is a testament to the pre-hospital care that he got both from his parents and from the first responders.' The ceremony brought together everyone who played a part in Kevin's recovery. 'This outcome would not be possible without everyone in this room today,' Heather Havericak said. The reunion was also a reminder that knowing CPR and not being afraid to use it can save a life. entry.title: Washington faces new reality after Democratic wave victory
entry.summary: Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesdays midterm elections, delivering a major setback to President Donald Trump and Republicans while reshaping the political landscape for the final two years of his term. Democrats scored a series of upset victories, including Senate wins in Texas and South Carolina, and expanded their House majority beyond early expectations. Several races remained uncalled Wednesday morning, but the party had already secured enough seats to claim control of both the House and Senate. Voters cited concerns about high prices, the conflict involving Iran and allegations of government corruption as key factors in their decisions. RELATED STORY | Democrat Annie Andrews notches upset win in South Carolina Senate race Political analysts and Democratic leaders described the results as a sweeping rejection of Trumps agenda. The gains extended deep into Republican strongholds, with Democrats also competing strongly in states such as Mississippi and Alaska. The election produced several historic firsts. In Georgia, Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history. Michigan voters elected Abdul El-Sayed, who is set to become the first Muslim member of the Senate. New Hampshire elected its first openly gay U.S. senator, while Ohio elected the first woman to serve as the states governor. In the House, Democrats secured at least 228 seats, surpassing the 218 needed for a majority, with additional gains possible as votes continue to be counted. In the Senate, Democrats won at least 54 seats and could further expand their majority as remaining races are decided. The results position House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries to become speaker when the new Congress is sworn in January. Jeffries said Democrats will focus on lowering the cost of living and pursuing bipartisan solutions where possible. Trump sought to distance himself from the outcome, saying on social media that he was not on the ballot. However, the president campaigned aggressively during the final weeks of the election, holding dozens of rallies across the country and repeatedly urging voters to treat the midterms as a referendum on his administration. entry.title: Troy Ingersoll wins sixth term on St. Lucie County School Board - cw34.com
entry.summary: Troy Ingersoll wins sixth term on St. Lucie County School Board    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County School Board Chairman Troy Ingersoll has won a sixth term, defeating political newcomer Lisa Kessler in the District 5 runoff election. District 5 covers the eastern, coastal portion of the school district. Although School Board candidates must live in their districts, all registered St. Lucie County voters were eligible to vote in the nonpartisan race. The August primary was exceptionally close. Kessler received 37.5% of the vote and Ingersoll received 37.2%, a difference of 167 votes; Charles Cerami received 25.2%. AOL Ingersoll has served on the School Board since 2006 and is its current chairman. He owns Pinch A Penny Pools and Spas in Vero Beach and serves as pastor of Midway Road Baptist Church. He holds a criminology degree from Florida State University and a master’s degree from New Orleans Baptist Theological Seminary. theballotbrief.com Ingersoll says his priorities are safe schools, stronger student achievement and responsible budgeting. He supports maintaining accelerated academic programs through consistent funding, targeted interventions and teacher development. He also cites teacher recruitment and retention, managing rapid population growth and developing leadership as major challenges for the district’s next term. AOL Kessler is a small-business owner, bestselling author and chair of the Fort Pierce Arts and Culture Advisory Board. She spent 26 years in sales and marketing management before writing full time. Her campaign also notes that she is the daughter of two lifelong public-school teachers and has served as a Girl Scout troop leader for 11 years. voterfocus.com Kessler’s platform focuses on academic standards in reading, math, science and career readiness; recruiting and retaining qualified teachers; stronger career and technical education; arts programs; and better communication between schools and families. She says public schools should make their case to families by highlighting certified teachers and programs unavailable elsewhere. AOL She also calls for transparent budgeting and treating parents as partners in school decisions. The race asks voters whether to retain Ingersoll’s long board experience and current direction, or choose Kessler’s call for new leadership focused on teacher retention, core academics and family engagement.

entry.title: Steven Giordano defeats incumbent Shannon Martin to win Port St. Lucie mayoral race
entry.summary: Steven Giordano has won the race for Port St. Lucie mayor, defeating incumbent Shannon Martin after a closely watched campaign. Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. He defeated Martin by a margin of just over 2,400 votes. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Steven Giordano defeats incumbent Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race The outcome marked a significant turnaround from the August primary, when Martin finished nearly 13 percentage points ahead of Giordano. Speaking at his election-night watch party, Giordano said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race. 'I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons,' Giordano said. 'I think they watched the debate.' Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician. 'I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people,' he said. 'And I'm proud to be the people's mayor.' The general election followed a contentious August primary that included an FDLE investigation involving campaign signs. The investigation led to Martin's husband and two other Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on paid administrative leave, according to the reporter's script. WPTV reached out to Martin for comment following the election results but had not received a response as of Tuesday night.

entry.title: Palm Beach County students help scientists track where trash drifts in local waterways
entry.summary: Palm Beach County students are helping scientists answer a deceptively simple question: Where does our trash go once it starts floating through local waterways? ANGARI Foundation plans to release bright orange, eco-friendly drift cards into the water on Nov. 10 at noon as part of its Lagoon Drift Card Study. Members of the public are then being asked to find the cards and report where they ended up. So we're basically trying to track our trash, Laura Jessop with ANGARI Foundation told WPTV. So we put these eco-friendly drift cards in the water. They're going in on November 10 at 12 p.m., and we need the public to go out and find them. The idea is to use the cards as stand-ins for other objects floating on the surface. Everything that floats on the surface, that's what we're sort of tracking right now, Jessop said. Finding the places where floating trash accumulates Each card found by a member of the public becomes another piece of information for the study. Jessop said knowing where the cards eventually turn up can help researchers identify places where floating debris could be accumulating. They're bright orange, and if they report them to us, we can then look at where our trash is accumulating and really target those areas, she said. The project involves Manatee Lagoon, where some of the drift cards will be released. Rachel Shanker with Manatee Lagoon said participating in the project can provide information that may ultimately help protect Florida's environment. Here at Manatee Lagoon, we're so excited to be a part of this study where we can collect data and learn how to better preserve and protect Florida's environment and wildlife for future generations, Shanker said. Students take science from the classroom to the lagoon The study isn't limited to scientists and environmental organizations. Students from Palm Springs Community Middle School are creating their own drift cards and will release them at Manatee Lagoon on Nov. 10. A teacher participating in the project told WPTV the experiment gives students the opportunity to connect what they're studying in class with an actual environmental project. entry.article_text: Palm Beach County students are helping scientists answer a deceptively simple question: Where does our trash go once it starts floating through local waterways?ANGARI Foundation plans to release bright orange, eco-friendly drift cards into the water on Nov. 10 at noon as part of its Lagoon Drift Card Study. Members of the public are then being asked to find the cards and report where they ended up.“So we're basically trying to track our trash,” Laura Jessop with ANGARI Foundation told WPTV. “So we put these eco-friendly drift cards in the water. They're going in on November 10 at 12 p.m., and we need the public to go out and find them.”The idea is to use the cards as stand-ins for other objects floating on the surface.“Everything that floats on the surface, that's what we're sort of tracking right now,” Jessop said.Each card found by a member of the public becomes another piece of information for the study.Jessop said knowing where the cards eventually turn up can help researchers identify places where floating debris could be accumulating.“They're bright orange, and if they report them to us, we can then look at where our trash is accumulating and really target those areas,” she said.The project involves Manatee Lagoon, where some of the drift cards will be released.Rachel Shanker with Manatee Lagoon said participating in the project can provide information that may ultimately help protect Florida's environment.“Here at Manatee Lagoon, we're so excited to be a part of this study where we can collect data and learn how to better preserve and protect Florida's environment and wildlife for future generations,” Shanker said.The study isn't limited to scientists and environmental organizations.Students from Palm Springs Community Middle School are creating their own drift cards and will release them at Manatee Lagoon on Nov. 10.A teacher participating in the project told WPTV the experiment gives students the opportunity to connect what they're studying in class with an actual environmental project.“My students are creating drift cards which they will be releasing on November 10 here at Manatee Lagoon, and they are doing this to track the pollution in the waterways and apply what we're learning in the classroom to the real world,” she said.And the students aren't sending anonymous pieces of orange material into the water.They're making the cards their own.One student decorated a card with water, a sun and a shark, before adding a marine-themed message: “You're 'fintastic.'”Another decorated a card as an ocean scene with a simple message for whoever eventually discovers it: “Love your ocean.”For students, the cards turn an environmental lesson into something tangible.They create the cards, release them, and wait to see where currents carry them. If members of the public find and report their locations, those discoveries become part of the study.That provides a real-world demonstration of something that can otherwise be difficult to visualize in a classroom: What happens to floating material after it enters a waterway?For the broader community, it also turns a walk along the water into an opportunity to participate in local science.If you spot one of the bright orange drift cards, it may be more than something that washed ashore. Its location is precisely the information researchers are looking for.The experiment comes just before another important date for the Lake Worth Lagoon.Manatee season officially begins Nov. 15.Shanker said cooler temperatures help bring manatees back toward Manatee Lagoon.“As the water temperatures drop, they start coming here to Manatee Lagoon for our warm water outflow,” Shanker said.Manatee Lagoon plans to celebrate the beginning of the season with a kickoff event Nov. 21.For the students creating drift cards, meanwhile, the next milestone comes Nov. 10, when their colorful creations leave their hands and begin their journey through South Florida's waterways.Where they end up is part of the experiment.Who finds them could be anyone.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Angie Nixon concedes Florida Senate race, says progressive movement will continue
entry.summary: Angie Nixons bid to become Florida's first Black U.S. senator ended in defeat Tuesday, but the Jacksonville Democrat told supporters her fight is far from over. 'We may have lost this battle, but the war is not over,' Nixon said during her concession speech. The Associated Press projected Republican Sen. Ashley Moody the winner of the special election. With votes still being counted, Moody had just over 50% of the vote to Nixons approximately 48%. Nixon, a Florida state representative, entered the general election after a surprise victory in the Democratic primary. The progressive candidate campaigned on affordability, championing Medicare for All, free child care and rent freezes. For some supporters, the relatively close race showed an opportunity for Democrats in a state where Republicans have built a substantial advantage. Supporter Mak Manning loved the grassroots campaign Nixon built. 'She's willing to get out there and into the streets and fight,' said Manning. Nixon said Democrats face challenges ahead, including fundraising and closing the voter registration gap with Republicans. 'That 1.5 million gap in registration, we need to fix that,' she told reporters. Asked what comes next, Nixon said her immediate plans included getting some sleep. But she did not rule out another run. 'Im looking forward to 2028 because were getting to work,' she said.

entry.article_text: Flooding continues in parts of St. Lucie County as recovery efforts move forward. Lucie police department is getting another look at flooding across the city as the sun rises. Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including : SW Cashmere Boulevard Lake Forest HOA St. Bernadette Church NW Country Club Drive Tradition Parkway SW Community Boulevard Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also working to support recovery efforts and restore normal conditions safely. Officials are reminding residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage people to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. The city thanked residents for their patience and support, noting that helping one another can make a difference as the community recovers. Lucie County moves temporary shelters to new locations St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population and special medical needs shelters to new locations Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter, currently at the Fenn Center, is relocating to the Florida Department of Health’s St. Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s historic flooding. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways Officials warn that it could take several days for water levels to recede. Although public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain. entry.title: New Westlake eye care practice opens as doctor warns of growing nearsightedness in children
entry.summary: WPTV Westlake reporter Christy Waite checked out a new family-owned eye care practice, bringing another healthcare option closer to home for residents of the growing city. Dr. Tuyet-Suong Pham and her husband recently opened Westlake Eye Care, a practice they built from the ground up. The office offers routine eye exams and diagnoses and treats eye diseases. WATCH BELOW: New eye care practice opens in Westlake New eye care practice opens in Westlake Pham said opening her own practice has been a longtime dream, but she also wanted to provide families in Westlake with care closer to home. 'I wanted to provide quality care to the families here so they can get the care they need closer to home,' Pham said. Since opening their doors this fall, the couple said they are already seeing their business grow. 'Over the past two months we have seen a couple hundred patients, and we are accepting new ones,' Pham said. Patient Jeff Cap said having an eye doctor nearby means he no longer has to travel as far for care. Oh! Its so awesome because I dont have to drive 30-40 minutes. Its just right around the corner, Cap said. As more patients come through the doors, Pham said another trend is catching her eye: nearsightedness in children. 'It is projected that by the year 2050 that 50% of the population will be nearsighted,' Pham said. Pham said screen time can play a role, while children are also spending less time outdoors. She is urging parents to make sure their children have their eyes checked, particularly as nearsightedness becomes more common among kids. She said nearsightedness can increase the risk of serious eye complications later in life, including retinal detachment, glaucoma and macular degeneration, and other serious conditions. As Westlake continues to grow, some residents say they would also like to see more medical services grow with it. Cap said he would like to see the existing emergency room eventually expand into a full-scale hospital. 'I would like to see the ER expand. If it could turn into a hospital, that would be awesome,' Cap said. For Pham, the vision is clear: she wants her familys practice to grow alongside the community. 'We are looking to grow and invest in this community for years to come,' Pham said. Westlake EyeCare is located at 4931 Seminole Pratt Whitney Road. They are open Monday and Tuesday 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Wednesday and Thursday 9:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. They are closed Fridays and Sundays but are open on Saturdays 9:30 am- to 3:3

entry.summary: St. Lucie Public Schools will remain closed Thursday as the county continues to recover from flooding caused by this week's severe weather. The school district announced Wednesday that campuses will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5 because of ongoing road conditions, including numerous flooded bus stops and areas where high water remains. District officials said they want to allow additional time for the flooding to subside before returning to normal operations. Essential employees are required to report to work as outlined in the district's Emergency Operations Plan. Schools are expected to reopen Friday, Nov. 6, but the district cautioned that could change depending on conditions. Families are encouraged to check the St. Lucie Public Schools website for updates before schools reopen. 'Thank you for your patience and understanding as our community recovers from this unprecedented weather event,' the district said.

entry.title: Palm Beach County homeowners don't need to reapply for homestead exemption after Florida's Amendment 3 passes
entry.summary: Palm Beach County homeowners who already receive a homestead exemption do not need to reapply following the passage of Amendment 3, according to the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser's Office. The office outlined what property owners can expect after Florida voters approved the amendment Tuesday , including when the increased exemptions will take effect and how they will appear on future property tax notices. WATCH BELOW: Florida voters approve Amendment 3 Florida voters approve Amendment 3, increasing homestead exemption 'If you already have homestead exemption, you do not need to call our office or submit a new application because of Amendment 3,' Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks said in a Wednesday statement. 'Our team will apply the changes to eligible properties and provide clear information every step of the way.' Beginning in 2027, Amendment 3 increases the homestead exemption for non-school taxes to $150,000. It will rise to $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The amendment also lowers the annual cap on assessed-value increases for qualifying non-homestead properties from 10% to 5% for non-school taxes. Those properties include rentals, second homes and commercial properties. The Property Appraiser's Office stressed that the changes do not eliminate property tax bills. When will homeowners see the changes? Amendment 3 will not affect 2026 property tax bills. The higher homestead exemption amounts will first appear on the Notices of Proposed Property Taxes, commonly called TRIM notices, sent in August 2027. Tax bills incorporating the changes will then be issued by the tax collector later that year. How much an individual homeowner ultimately pays will depend in part on the tax rates adopted by local taxing authorities. 'Our responsibility is to value property fairly, administer exemptions and help taxpayers understand their assessments,' Jacks said. 'We do not set tax rates or collect taxes, but we will remain a resource for property owners as the law takes effect.' Who still needs to apply? While existing homestead exemption recipients don't have to do anything because of Amendment 3, first-time applicants must still apply and meet eligibility requirements. Homeowners are also required to report changes that could affect their exemption. Separate residency provisions apply to certain newer Florida residents, according to the Property Appraiser's Office. entry.title: Democrat Manny Rutinel flips competitive Colorado 8th District, unseating GOP Rep. Gabe Evans
entry.summary: Democrat Manny Rutinel will unseat Republican Congressman Gabe Evans in Colorado's 8th Congressional District, flipping one of the most competitive House seats in the country. The projected victory by the Associated Press sends 31-year-old Rutinel, a former Democratic state representative, to Congress. Created after the 2020 Census due to population growth, his district has quickly become one of the nation's premier political battlegrounds. Colorado's 8th Congressional District includes fast-growing suburbs north of Denver, blue-collar communities along the U.S. 85 corridor, agricultural communities and a significant Latino voting population. According to the Colorado Independent Redistricting Commissions, Hispanic or Latino voters make up 38.5% of the district. If you are an able-bodied working-aged adult with no young kids, you have to work, volunteer, or go to school part time, 20 hours a week, 80 hours a month, in order to qualify for Medicaid," Evans said. “We are working to put more money into it, to take care of the truly vulnerable folks, but to make sure the money gets where it belongs instead of disappearing into, again, one of the worst administered programs in the nation."RELATED STORY | Jeffries claims mandate to address affordability after Democratic Party winEvans has campaigned on reducing government spending, including on programs related to the Green New Deal and diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, arguing that doing so could help lower costs for Coloradans. On housing, he has advocated for reducing regulations and barriers to homeownership, citing construction defect liability requirements and building codes as factors that increase building costs.Rutinel, the son of a single mother who immigrated from the Dominican Republic, earned a master's degree in applied economics from Johns Hopkins University and a law degree from Yale. He worked as an economist for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and as an attorney for Earthjustice, an environmental law nonprofit.He campaigned on lowering costs for families. He pledged to reverse cuts to Medicaid, the Affordable Care Act and food assistance in the 2025 Republican tax and spending law that Evans supported.The race drew more than $17 million in outside spending, according to Federal Election Commission filings cited by Colorado Politics in October. House Speaker Mike Johnson campaigned with Evans in the district in late October.This story was originally published by Maggie Bryan and Veronica Acosta with the Scripps News Group in Denver.

"I'm very proud of everyone that had been a part of that."DeSantis said he believes putting the measure on the ballot also benefited Republican candidates further down the ticket."Had Amendment 3 not been on the ballot, I don't know that we turn out the voters that we ended up turning out," DeSantis said. "People wanted to vote yes on that, and then many of them ended up voting Republican later on down the ballot."DeSantis said Florida Republicans benefited from a record of delivering on promises to voters, even as political conditions shifted significantly toward Democrats nationally."We've built up a record of achievement," DeSantis said. "We've earned trust from a number of our voters that even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to hold the line."DeSantis said the next step will be implementing Amendment 3, with a special legislative session expected before he leaves office in January.The governor said he would work with legislative leaders on the timing rather than dictate when lawmakers should return to Tallahassee."We knew this would be something we needed to do," DeSantis said. "There's a lot of ideas that we've been tossing around for the last six months."DeSantis said the legislation would set a schedule for further expansion of homestead tax relief while also seeking to prevent local governments from offsetting the savings with other taxes or fees.He said he wants lawmakers to establish what he described as a "taxpayer bill of rights" and is considering state grants to help local governments, particularly rural communities, cover funding needs for essential services."It's not going to be a tax shift," DeSantis said. "It's going to be a reduction."According to DeSantis, implementing the amendment could involve tens of millions of dollars in state grants for local governments facing shortfalls in funding core services such as sheriff's departments.Amendment 3 must be implemented by Jan. 1.DeSantis also addressed questions about school funding because Amendment 3 does not apply to school districts.He said the implementing legislation will not change that exemption. Instead, he suggested lawmakers could eventually revisit Florida's education funding formula as they consider whether additional property tax relief could be provided to homeowners without reducing support for public schools.DeSantis said his ultimate goal is to move Florida closer to making homesteaded property tax-free, although reaching that point would require additional action after he leaves office."The more we can get the homestead to just be tax free, I think that's the better," DeSantis said.Much of the governor's news conference focused on what he described as disastrous results for Republicans outside Florida.DeSantis argued the election amounted more to a rejection of Republicans in Washington than an endorsement of the Democratic Party."This is probably the political worst-case scenario for a midterm election," he said.He said Republicans need to pay greater attention to voters' economic concerns, including inflation, mortgage rates, gas and grocery prices.DeSantis also criticized Republicans nationally for focusing their campaigns on issues that he believes were more effective in previous elections but did not match voters' concerns this year."The ground shifts and the emphasis then is on different things," DeSantis said. "Republicans, it seemed like in some of the ads I was seeing with how much money they were spending, they really were fighting yesterday's battle."Despite narrower Republican victories in Florida than in recent elections, DeSantis rejected the idea that the results represented a failure for the state GOP. He said he had warned Republican candidates for months that the political environment had moved substantially toward Democrats.DeSantis said strong Democratic turnout and increased participation among no-party-affiliation voters made the election particularly difficult for Republicans.Still, he argued Florida's results showed Republicans could survive an unfavorable national environment if they remain responsive to voters and deliver on policy."Florida is the last main anchor standing," DeSantis said.DeSantis, who is term-limited and will leave office in January, declined to discuss whether he might run for another office in 2028."I still got more work to do," DeSantis said. "We'll work till the lights are out and cross that bridge when we get to it."

entry.title: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race - WPEC
entry.summary: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race    WPEC
entry.article_text: Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin in a closely contested race Tuesday, marking a change in leadership for one of Florida's fastest-growing cities. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections , Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Giordano won by 2,601 votes. All 62 precincts have reported, with election-day, early and mail votes marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. Throughout his campaign, he argued that developers should pay their fair share for improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as the city continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion, particularly in St. Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard and Savona Boulevard, and Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway. Taxpayer spending was another major issue in the race. Giordano called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall. Martin pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate. The two candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%. Voters reject twice-weekly trash pickup proposal Port St. Lucie voters also overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to pay more for twice-weekly residential trash collection. According to the latest election results, 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The ballot question asked whether residents would support paying an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly garbage collection. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

entry.title: Katherine Waldron defeats incumbent Sara Baxter in Palm Beach County Commission District 6 race
entry.summary: Democratic challenger Katherine Waldron has defeated incumbent Palm Beach County Commissioner Sara Baxter in the race for the District 6 seat. Baxter, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, lost her bid for another term on the commission to Waldron, a former state lawmaker and Port of Palm Beach commissioner. FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News The race pitted a first-term Republican incumbent against a Democrat with previous experience in elected office. Baxter was elected to the Palm Beach County Commission in 2022, marking her first elected position. She represented District 6, which covers a large portion of western Palm Beach County. Waldron entered the race with experience in both local and state government. She previously served on the Port of Palm Beach District Board of Commissioners and in the Florida House of Representatives. Waldron's victory flips the District 6 seat from Republican to Democratic control and ends Baxter's tenure on the County Commission after one term.

entry.title: St. Lucie County flips blue after 14 years as voters increase turnout despite floods - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County flips blue after 14 years as voters increase turnout despite floods    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County flipped blue in Tuesday's governor's race for the first time in more than a decade, as voter turnout climbed despite historic flooding that forced last-minute polling place changes. Democrat David Jolly carried the county with approximately 51% of the vote , compared with 48% for Republican Byron Donalds. The result marked the first time since 2012 that a Democratic candidate for governor or president won a majority in St. That year, former President Barack Obama carried the county with 53.42% of the vote. According to TCPalm , voter turnout reached 56.5% in the county, up 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election , when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. Lucie County ranked 51st among Florida's 67 counties, with only 16 counties reporting lower turnout. In 2022, the county had 238,645 registered voters, with 122,361 casting ballots. See also: Neighborhoods in Jensen Beach go underwater as flooding devastates the Treasure Coast Voters turn out despite historic flooding The increase came as widespread flooding forced election officials to relocate several polling places across Port St. Lucie, Tradition and Fort Pierce, per CBS12 reports . Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said the changes were necessary to ensure voters had safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Voters assigned to Oak Hammock K-8 School, Centennial High School and the Paula A. Lewis Library were among those affected, with some redirected to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, Indian River State College's Veterans Center of Excellence and Tradition Town Hall. The changes followed heavy rainfall that submerged roads, stranded vehicles and prompted evacuations across parts of the county. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties, while flooding forced local public schools to close Tuesday and Wednesday. Despite the weather-related challenges, St. Lucie County surpassed its 2022 general election turnout rate while delivering a Democratic majority in the governor's race for the first time in 14 years, when Obama won the county. While the flooding complicated Election Day logistics, the higher turnout suggests those challenges did not prevent overall participation from exceeding the previous gubernatorial election.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie recovery efforts continue after record breaking floods    WPEC
entry.article_text: Flooding continues in parts of St. Lucie County as recovery efforts move forward. Lucie police department is getting another look at flooding across the city as the sun rises. Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including : SW Cashmere Boulevard Lake Forest HOA St. Bernadette Church NW Country Club Drive Tradition Parkway SW Community Boulevard Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also working to support recovery efforts and restore normal conditions safely. Officials are reminding residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage people to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. entry.title: Port St. Lucie offers up to $25,000 to homeowners for flood repairs
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie homeowners whose properties were damaged by this week's flooding could be eligible for up to $25,000 in financial assistance for critical repairs. The city announced Wednesday that it has allocated $1 million to its Disaster Relief Program to help low- and moderate-income homeowners repair their primary residences. WATCH REPORT: Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roads, leaving drivers stranded Pre-applications for the program will open at 8 a.m. Thursday, Nov. 5, and funding will remain available until the $1 million allocation is exhausted. The assistance is being offered through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding provided by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000 through a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years in accordance with program guidelines. What repairs are covered? According to the city, the money may be used for emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable. Eligible expenses may include: Tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability Payment of Homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work Temporary repairs to prevent further property damage, such as: Roof repairs Weatherproofing Water extraction Removal of water-damaged materials Emergency plumbing or electrical work Temporary structural stabilization  Other reasonable and necessary actions required to protect the home from additional damage All work must be directly connected to the declared disaster and approved by the city before assistance is provided. The program does not cover mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal or remediation. If a home requires mold remediation, the homeowner must have that work completed before other approved repairs can proceed. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs and illegal or unpermitted work are also excluded. Who qualifies? To be eligible, applicants must meet the program's income requirements. They must also have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home must have an assessed value of $560,154 or less, and applicants must be current on their mortgage and property tax payments. How to apply The city's pre-application process opens at 8 a.m. Thursday. Residents can apply through the city's housing website. Homeowners who need assistance

entry.title: Palm Beach County firefighters outline 3-day response to widespread flooding
entry.summary: Palm Beach County Fire Rescue crews rescued and evacuated several people during three days of widespread flooding that left vehicles stranded, roads impassable and some neighborhoods covered by several feet of water. The department said its flood response operations began Sunday and continued through Tuesday as crews responded to emergencies in several parts of the county. WATCH BELOW: Aerial video of flooding in Century Village Flooding strands residents in Century Village One of the largest operations unfolded Sunday evening in the Century Village area of unincorporated central Palm Beach County. Beginning around 5 p.m., firefighters responded to more than seventy 911 calls from the area. Nearly 100 residents were trapped in stranded vehicles as water rose rapidly, according to PBCFR. Firefighters reported encountering cars floating with people still inside and water reaching 3 to 4 feet deep in some locations. To help locate people in need of rescue, PBCFR deployed drones over Century Village, Cypress Lakes the Tennis Club and surrounding areas. The drones flew around stranded vehicles and used thermal-imaging cameras to search for people. Using information gathered from the air, firefighters waded through floodwater and deployed high-water vehicles and brush trucks to reach residents and bring them to higher ground. Despite the dangerous conditions, PBCFR said no injuries were reported during those rescues. WATCH BELOW: Aerial video of flooding, rescues in Riviera Beach Riviera Beach residents rescued from flooding More rescues in Riviera Beach The response continued Monday night when PBCFR's Urban Search and Rescue Swiftwater Response Team deployed to flooded neighborhoods in Riviera Beach. The team remained in the area for nearly 24 hours, deploying emergency rafts and boats and going door to door to check on residents where flooded streets had become impassable to normal vehicles. During that operation, PBCFR said crews evacuated 71 people, conducted two medical rescues and evacuated nine pets. The flood response came as the department was also dedicating dozens of personnel and other resources to the aircraft crash site along Military Trail, including a mobile command post. Overall, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said it responded to more than 1,600 emergency calls countywide during the three-day period after the flooding began. That figure includes all 911 calls handled by the department, not just flooding-related emergencies.

entry.title: Six St. Lucie County polling places moved because of flooding on Election Day - WPEC
entry.summary: Six St. Lucie County polling places moved because of flooding on Election Day    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County election officials to move six precincts’ polling places on Election Day, including several in Port St. The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves are meant to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Lucie, voters in precincts 49 and 71, who normally cast ballots at Oak Hammock K-8 School, will vote at the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, will also go to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard. Voters in precincts 67 and 86 will not vote at Centennial High School in St. They will vote at Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence, at 500 NW California Blvd. The county says access is from Peacock Boulevard. See also: Inside David Jolly's election night watch party as Florida chooses its next governor In the Tradition area, precinct 83 voters will move from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters will also move from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall. In Fort Pierce, Precinct 12 voters will move from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1. The notice does not list any polling places as closed. It also does not say whether voters who already went to their normal location will be redirected on site. The flooding also disrupted schools. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Jon Prince apologized to families during a news conference Tuesday, after students were seen walking through standing water to get home Monday. We didn’t anticipate anything like what transpired yesterday. Caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry, Prince said. Schools are closed Wednesday. Prince said the district expects to reopen Thursday if roads are clear, and that no school buildings took significant water. A private security company that patrols homeowners associations in the Tradition area joined the rescue effort with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. We had no goal when we came out here. We had just ambition to figure out how we can help anyone and anywhere and do whatever we can with the resources that we have, Matchton said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods, and warned that anyone who preys on flood victims will face zero tolerance. The sheriff said there was no playbook for a storm like this. But the most important thing is we’re all working together with one purpose, which is to serve this community, Del Toro said. The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

It's called the New Worlds Reading program. Amy York, and her son Tripp, read together from books he gets in the mail. 'Well, it's awesome because they ship the books right to your house.' Van Duzer said it's easy getting books. 'It's real simple. Van Duzer said he wants to help all kids, especially low income children, to have access to books. 'It's just essential that we get books in kids' hands earlier and to have them in the home,' he said, 'I think it's just a huge step in their educational journey.' Van Duzer feels so strongly about kids improving their reading that he is renovating a part of his restaurant into a reading room. 'Once that room is done, I'll have four computers in there designated for New Worlds Reading, where the kid can come out, still get a free book,' he said, 'but at the same time sign up for New Worlds Reading also.' York believes in a strong reading foundation. 'I believe that it's all children's right to read and having access to books is so important,' she said. entry.title: 1 killed, 2 others injured when a helicopter crashes into Biscayne Bay near Bill Baggs State Park
entry.summary: One person was killed, and two others were injured on Wednesday when a helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay near Miami, officials said. The helicopter went down shortly before noon near Bill Baggs State Park, off Key Biscayne, the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said. The U.S. Coast Guard confirmed that one of the three helicopter occupants was reported dead, while the other two were taken to a trauma center. Preliminary information indicates that the Robinson R44 II helicopter appeared to be on a photography flight, the National Transportation Safety Board said. Besides the Coast Guard, firefighters from several local agencies responded to the crash. Television news video of the crash shows the aircraft upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing. Officials didn't immediately identify the helicopter's occupants.

entry.title: Citibank shooting near Tampa, Florida, leaves 2 dead, including suspect, sheriff says
entry.summary: Florida authorities said two people were dead, including a suspect, after witnesses reported a shooting Wednesday at Citibank's sprawling business complex that employs thousands in the Tampa area. Officers swarmed the campus Wednesday afternoon, and TV video showed long lines of workers streaming out of the office buildings. The Hillsborough County Sheriffs Office said in a post on social media that it had 'responded to an active threat and is currently clearing the building.' The sheriff's office said a suspect and one other person were dead. It was not immediately known whether anyone else was injured. 'We believe this is a targeted incident,' Sheriff Chad Chronister posted on the social platform X. The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giants employees. Citigroup said in a statement that it was 'aware of an incident' at the complex and was cooperating with authorities. Doug Merritt said he was startled when his son called him from the Citibank campus Wednesday, saying he had fled after hearing gunshots. 'He was very close to it,' Merritt told The Associated Press. 'He left all this stuff where he was at, and he was able to get out of there.' For around an hour, Merritt said, he didnt know whether his son was safe as he struggled to get in touch over a bad internet connection. 'I wanted him to get to safety,' he said. 'I was upset.' ___ Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story.

entry.title: St. Lucie County flips blue after 14 years as voters increase turnout despite floods - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County flips blue after 14 years as voters increase turnout despite floods    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County flipped blue in Tuesday's governor's race for the first time in more than a decade, as voter turnout climbed despite historic flooding that forced last-minute polling place changes. Democrat David Jolly carried the county with approximately 51% of the vote , compared with 48% for Republican Byron Donalds. The result marked the first time since 2012 that a Democratic candidate for governor or president won a majority in St. That year, former President Barack Obama carried the county with 53.42% of the vote. According to TCPalm , voter turnout reached 56.5% in the county, up 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election , when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. Lucie County ranked 51st among Florida's 67 counties, with only 16 counties reporting lower turnout. In 2022, the county had 238,645 registered voters, with 122,361 casting ballots. See also: Neighborhoods in Jensen Beach go underwater as flooding devastates the Treasure Coast Voters turn out despite historic flooding The increase came as widespread flooding forced election officials to relocate several polling places across Port St. Lucie, Tradition and Fort Pierce, per CBS12 reports . Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said the changes were necessary to ensure voters had safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Voters assigned to Oak Hammock K-8 School, Centennial High School and the Paula A. Lewis Library were among those affected, with some redirected to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, Indian River State College's Veterans Center of Excellence and Tradition Town Hall. The changes followed heavy rainfall that submerged roads, stranded vehicles and prompted evacuations across parts of the county. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties, while flooding forced local public schools to close Tuesday and Wednesday. Despite the weather-related challenges, St. Lucie County surpassed its 2022 general election turnout rate while delivering a Democratic majority in the governor's race for the first time in 14 years, when Obama won the county. While the flooding complicated Election Day logistics, the higher turnout suggests those challenges did not prevent overall participation from exceeding the previous gubernatorial election.

entry.title: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race - WPEC
entry.summary: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race    WPEC
entry.article_text: Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin in a closely contested race Tuesday, marking a change in leadership for one of Florida's fastest-growing cities. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections , Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Giordano won by 2,601 votes. All 62 precincts have reported, with election-day, early and mail votes marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. Throughout his campaign, he argued that developers should pay their fair share for improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as the city continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion, particularly in St. See also: After close win, Byron Donalds turns focus to his first priorities as governor Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard and Savona Boulevard, and Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway. Taxpayer spending was another major issue in the race. Giordano called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall. Martin pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate. The two candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%. Voters reject twice-weekly trash pickup proposal Port St. Lucie voters also overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to pay more for twice-weekly residential trash collection. According to the latest election results, 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The ballot question asked whether residents would support paying an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly garbage collection. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

entry.title: Troy Ingersoll wins sixth term on St. Lucie County School Board - WPEC
entry.summary: Troy Ingersoll wins sixth term on St. Lucie County School Board    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County School Board Chairman Troy Ingersoll has won a sixth term, defeating political newcomer Lisa Kessler in the District 5 runoff election. District 5 covers the eastern, coastal portion of the school district. Although School Board candidates must live in their districts, all registered St. Lucie County voters were eligible to vote in the nonpartisan race. The August primary was exceptionally close. Kessler received 37.5% of the vote and Ingersoll received 37.2%, a difference of 167 votes; Charles Cerami received 25.2%. AOL Ingersoll has served on the School Board since 2006 and is its current chairman. He owns Pinch A Penny Pools and Spas in Vero Beach and serves as pastor of Midway Road Baptist Church. He holds a criminology degree from Florida State University and a master’s degree from New Orleans Baptist Theological Seminary. theballotbrief.com Ingersoll says his priorities are safe schools, stronger student achievement and responsible budgeting. He supports maintaining accelerated academic programs through consistent funding, targeted interventions and teacher development. He also cites teacher recruitment and retention, managing rapid population growth and developing leadership as major challenges for the district’s next term. AOL Kessler is a small-business owner, bestselling author and chair of the Fort Pierce Arts and Culture Advisory Board. She spent 26 years in sales and marketing management before writing full time. Her campaign also notes that she is the daughter of two lifelong public-school teachers and has served as a Girl Scout troop leader for 11 years. voterfocus.com Kessler’s platform focuses on academic standards in reading, math, science and career readiness; recruiting and retaining qualified teachers; stronger career and technical education; arts programs; and better communication between schools and families. She says public schools should make their case to families by highlighting certified teachers and programs unavailable elsewhere. AOL She also calls for transparent budgeting and treating parents as partners in school decisions. The race asks voters whether to retain Ingersoll’s long board experience and current direction, or choose Kessler’s call for new leadership focused on teacher retention, core academics and family engagement.

entry.title: Parents, teachers question why Palm Beach County schools stayed open despite widespread flooding
entry.summary: Parents and teachers across Palm Beach County are questioning why the School District of Palm Beach County only decided to close some schools after flooding made roads difficult or impossible to navigate countywide. Ten of the district's 182 district-operated schools were closed because of flooding. Nine were announced Wednesday, with a tenth Wednesday morning. But WPTV heard from people across the county asking the same question: Why weren't all schools closed? A WPTV Facebook post informing families about the closures quickly filled with comments from people describing conditions in their own neighborhoods. Some said all schools should have been closed, while others shared pictures of flooded roads outside their homes. One person said they work at a school that remained open but live in an area affected by flooding. 'I was texting people in the morning trying to figure out if I can leave, even leave my community,' said Kim Landis. Landis is a fourth-grade teacher at Coral Sunset Elementary School in Boca Raton and is among those who contacted WPTV for help getting answers from the district. Landis still reported to work, but when asked what her route there was like, she didn't hesitate. 'Horrible, horrible,' Landis said. She described encountering vehicles struggling with the conditions, including a school bus. 'There were vehicles that were stuck. There's been vehicles stuck since yesterday on the road. It's just, it's horrible,' Landis said. Her concern goes beyond the conditions immediately surrounding an individual school. Landis said teachers and students in choice programs may have to commute to schools outside the areas where they live, potentially putting them on roads affected by flooding even if their destination school is open. 'Why aren't all the districts closed? We have three hurricane days a year that we didn't even get to, we didn't use,' Landis said. The district sent a message telling families and staff, 'Your personal safety is our top priority,' and announced that students who miss class because of flooding will be excused. For employees, however, the policy is different. Educators who cannot make it to work are required to use a sick or personal day. entry.title: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo
entry.summary: A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago. Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WPTV that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense's second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. hearing held Wednesday. Camerlengo's attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense's amended motion was 'procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.' Wednesday's ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set. Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Her arrest followed a WPTV investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade. A case plagued by delays The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case. During a contentious July hearing , Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo's defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial. 'I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,' Metzger said. 'This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count.' In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial. Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths. 'I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don't think she had all of the facts,' Kaplan previously told WPTV. Dog owners still waiting for answers Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022.
