I don't think she had all of the facts," Kaplan previously told WPTV.Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022.Kirk Csontos filed a police report following Mako's death, but Camerlengo was never charged in connection with it because his necropsy was inconclusive.Necropsies of two other dogs determined they died from blunt force trauma, leading to Camerlengo's arrest."I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn't think it would be two years," Kirk Csontos previously told WPTV.Despite the repeated delays, she said she remains hopeful."I'm still hopeful. Believe it or not, I'm still hopeful that she will be held accountable," she said.Camerlengo's next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. 1.No trial date has been announced.

entry.title: Family of Port St. Lucie teen killed walking to school raises concerns about road safety
entry.summary: WPTV hasn't stopped looking into the tragic death of a Port St. Lucie teen who was killed while walking to school just last month. On Wednesday, WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield sat down with the family for the first time to hear from them about their son and the questions they're still asking. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Family of 14-year old hit and killed by car in Port St. Lucie speak out  Jacory Brown, a freshman at Treasure Coast High School, was struck and killed by a car on Port St. Lucie Boulevard while walking to school early in the morning on Oct. 7. 'He just went to school,' Shelly-Ann Findley-Brown, mother, said. 'He was supposed to come back home. He didn't. His birthday would be on Monday. He would have been 15.' Findley-Brown, father Ainsworth Brown and grandfather Clovis Brown, sat down with WPTV. They're remembering Jacorys smile. 'He's kind, he's a jovial kid, said Findley-Brown. 'He's the life of our party of five.'  Theyre remembering his friendliness to others. '[He] was loved by so many persons, and he has touched everybody he's met,' Finely-Brown said.  And they're remembering his passion for entrepreneurship and graphic design like making cover art, business cards and flyers for friends and family. 'His hand was always up here, mind looking, his eyes all over like he's devising a plan and coming up with his thing,' Findley-Brown said.  But the family still has questions. They say Port St. Lucie Boulevard, with all the construction, makes it a dangerous roadway for kids walking to school. 'The road conditions are horrible,' Findley-Brown said. 'You are walking in puddles. And the night before, it rained. There was water all over the place. There's puddles. There's literally no sidewalks for kids to walk.' FDOT started construction back in 2025 to widen the road from two to four lanes and add new sidewalks and lights. But the project isn't expected to be completed until winter 2028. 'I hope the state takes this into a big consideration because it's not right walking to school when you don't have proper sidewalks,' Findley-Brown said. Jacory Brown will be laid to rest on Nov. 14. Friends have s tarted a GoFundMe to support the family.

entry.title: What Florida homeowners need to know about Amendment 3 property tax savings
entry.summary: The election night victory for Amendment 3 in Florida now sets up property tax savings for homeowners with the state's homestead exemption. 'No one who has homestead today in the state of Florida needs to worry about calling us or coming in or doing anything at this point,' said Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks. WATCH REPORT BELOW: What's next for Florida homeowners after approving Amendment 3 Those homeowners, she said, will automatically see their exemption rise to $150,000 in the first notices going out in August 2027. 'It's important they know that they aren't going to see those savings until the end of 2027,' Jacks said. Tax bills, which are not being eliminated, are sent out in November by the county's tax collector. 'Everyone will continue to pay the school board,' Jacks said. 'In addition, any non-ad valorem assessments, so assessments based usually on fees, the most common one is the solid waste authority, those won't go away.' Only homeowners who claim the homestead exemption by Dec. 31 will be eligible for the new Amendment 3 exemption. New Florida residents in 2027 will have to wait five years for the higher exemption. And renters established in the state by Dec. 31 will be eligible for the higher exemption if they buy a home in the future. For cities and counties in Florida, the future looks uncertain as tax revenues will decrease. Many local government leaders have speculated they will need to turn to budget trimming, cutting services and possibly looking for other revenue streams. 'The first decision they're going to have to make is how do they protect, or if they protect, police and fire,' said former state Sen. Jeff Brandes. Gov. Ron DeSantis, a supporter of Amendment 3, has said he'll call a special session to work out the details of handling Amendment 3. 'I think the first thing they need to do is be honest about what this means for counties and cities,' Brandes said. 'They have to protect the counties. They do not need to protect or have to protect the cities, and frankly, there's gonna be some cities that fail, and they need to let them fail.'

entry.title: Democratic leaders outline agenda after sweeping Congress in midterms
entry.summary: Change is on the horizon in Washington. Democrats swept both the House and Senate in Tuesday's elections, positioning the party to take control of Congress in January for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. The days of the House of Representatives functioning as a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Wednesday. The New York Democrat is widely expected to succeed Republican Mike Johnson as House speaker in January. RELATED STORY | Vance blames Iran war for sweeping Republican midterm losses Jeffries spoke exclusively with Scripps News Chief Washington Correspondent Joe St. George, indicating he would consider cutting deals with President Donald Trump when they can find common ground. In this Congress, Democrats came together with our Republican colleagues in the House and in the Senate to pass a housing affordability bill, because we know we have to build more housing that the American people can afford,' he said. 'That may hopefully provide a foundation for the type of work that can be done together with our Republican colleagues in order to bring about the type of meaningful change the American people demanded. Democrats have also vowed to address what voters across the country cited as top concerns: high costs, the ongoing war in Iran and cracking down on corruption. RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governor In a post on X, congressional Democrats on the Oversight Committee listed some of their top targets. Among them: corporations ripping off Americans, administration officials accused of profiting off the presidency, and associates of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. With control of the Senate, Democrats will have the power to confirm or reject President Donald Trump's nominees for Cabinet positions and other high-level administration posts. They will also control the confirmation process for federal judges, including any future nominees to the U.S. Supreme Court. Asked how Democrats would handle Trump's nominees, Sen. Chuck Schumer, who is expected to become Senate majority leader in January, signaled that his party would closely scrutinize the president's picks. We want judicial nominees, like we showed in 23 and 24, who obey the law, who have fidelity to the rule of law,' he said. 'Too many of Trumps nominees did not have that at all.'

entry.title: FAU men's basketball replaces nearly entire roster but welcomes highest-rated recruit in school history
entry.summary: It's a new season for the FAU Owls basketball team, with a lot of new faces, including the school's highest-rated recruit in school history, Felipe Quinones. 'I'm just grateful to play at a level I could only dream of playing at,' said Quinones, a 6-foot-4, four-star recruit who impresses in transition and can simply put the ball in the basket. WATCH REPORT BELOW: FAU men's basketball rebuilds roster, welcomes highest-rated recruit in school history 'It's a dream come true, and I'm living my dream right now, so it's easy and fun. This is what I always wanted to do,' Quinones said. At this point of the season, FAU stands 1-0 after a 14-point win on Monday against LIU. We got a young team, but we're all learning each other and getting better,' said senior guard Kanaan Carlyle, who's the lone returner from last year's squad, and in his senior year, hes not taking anything for granted. 'I love it. Thats the reason I chose to come back. I got a great staff and great teammates,' Carlyle said. While Carlyle is the coach on the court, John Jakus is the coach of the team, now in his third year. After going 18-15 last season, Jakus was building momentum, but he lost nearly his entire roster. Now, hes starting over and embracing the challenge. 'We're in a great spot, and we're grateful to be able to start with a win and mix in first-year students with transfers. We're just trying to get a little healthy with two of our guards, but well get there, Jakus said.

entry.title: Voters elected governors to curb data centers. Lowering bills for gas and groceries is harder
entry.summary: Voters made their power bills a ballot issue in Tuesday's midterm elections, and the AI industry felt it.  Democrats flipped the governor's offices in Texas, Ohio and Georgia. All three winners campaigned on pausing or reining in the massive data centers that power artificial intelligence, which many voters blame for rising electricity costs. In communities across the country, voters also passed local bans and restrictions on the facilities. But many of the costs squeezing families, from war-driven gas prices to tariffs, are set in Washington, not state capitals. That leaves the new governors with real tools on data centers and utilities, and clear limits on how fast they can lower what people pay. RELATED STORY | Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeats Greg Abbott in historic Texas governor upset The biggest shift came in Texas. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa unseated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, winning 57% to 41% in unofficial results. She will be the state's first Latina governor. Hinojosa campaigned on a moratorium on new data center construction, stricter rules on water and power use, and an end to tax breaks for the industry. Wells Fargo estimates 27% of planned U.S. data center capacity is in the state. Abbott once said he wanted Texas to be the 'epicenter of AI development.' In September, he ordered state environmental regulators to stop issuing data center permits until a grid audit was complete. Hinojosa dismissed the move as an 'election year pause.' In Ohio, Democrat Dr. Amy Acton , the state's former health director, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. Shell become the first woman elected governor in Ohio history and the first Democrat to win the office in 20 years. Acton backs a conditional moratorium: new data centers would have to cover all of their utility costs, use union labor and build on old industrial sites rather than farmland. 'Ohio is open for business, but we are not up for sale,' Acton said when she unveiled the plan. In Georgia, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms beat Republican businessman Rick Jackson. She is the first Democrat to win Georgia's governorship since 1998 and the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history. Bottoms wants a statewide pause on new data center construction to study the effect on power bills, water supplies and communities. Metro Atlanta led the nation in data center space under construction in the first half of 2026, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution . RELATED

Hinojosa dismissed the move as an "election year pause."In Ohio, Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former health director, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. She is the first Democrat to win Georgia's governorship since 1998 and the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. Bottoms wants a statewide pause on new data center construction to study the effect on power bills, water supplies and communities. Metro Atlanta led the nation in data center space under construction in the first half of 2026, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.RELATED STORY | In Kansas, a data center backlash is uniting voters across the political aisleWall Street took notice. AI data center stocks fell as the results came in, and shares of SpaceX dropped 7%."The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers," the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory wrote.Data centers were only part of the picture. About 4 in 10 voters said the economy was the most important issue facing the country, and more than 8 in 10 said they were concerned about the cost of gas, groceries, utilities and health care, according to The AP Voter Poll. About 8 in 10 said inflation had caused their household severe or moderate financial hardship.Fuel was a big part of that pain. Gas prices hit a record high for an Election Day, averaging $4.11 a gallon nationally on Tuesday afternoon, according to GasBuddy. Prices have stayed high because of Iranian attacks and obstruction in the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway that carries much of the world's oil.Electricity bills are climbing too. electricity prices are up roughly 10% since early 2024, and Goldman Sachs analysts expect data center demand to keep pushing them up faster than overall inflation.That's where the new governors run into limits. States can pause data centers, choose who regulates utilities and end the tax breaks that drew many of these projects in the first place. Ohio's data center incentives have reached $1.6 billion, and Acton has promised clawbacks. Ohio's next governor also selects the state's utility regulators, a lever that may matter more for monthly bills than any moratorium.Hinojosa and Acton both promised gas tax relief. Hinojosa wants to suspend Texas' 20-cent-per-gallon gas tax and freeze electricity rates. Acton backed pausing Ohio's 38.5-cent gas tax. But they'll need their legislatures on board, and Republicans still control Ohio's statehouse.What governors can't control are some of the biggest drivers of what families are paying. Oil prices are tied to the war with Iran. Tariffs are set in Washington, where Democrats will now control both chambers of Congress but President Donald Trump has already said he plans to use his veto power.

entry.title: No flood insurance? What Florida homeowners need to know about paying for flood damage
entry.summary: As floodwaters slowly recede across South Florida and the Treasure Coast, homeowners are facing a costly question: Who pays for flood damage if they don't have flood insurance? More than a foot of rain inundated some neighborhoods across the region this week, flooding homes, stranding drivers and forcing some residents to evacuate. WATCH REPORT BELOW: No flood insurance? What homeowners need to know Among the hardest-hit areas was the Ibis neighborhood in West Palm Beach, where floodwaters left dozens of vehicles stranded and streets submerged. But despite the widespread flooding, much of the neighborhood sits outside federally designated high-risk flood zones, leaving some residents without flood insurance. One Ibis resident, Lee, watched as heavy rain transformed her neighborhood into what looked more like a lake. 'It was coming down so hard that you couldn't see the ground,' she said. Lee described the scene as 'apocalyptic,' recalling the shock of seeing cars stranded in floodwaters. 'I was overwhelmed by this whole thing walking and seeing people's cars stranded in the middle,' she said. Like many homeowners who live outside high-risk flood zones, Lee never thought she would need flood insurance. 'Who thought? We moved west so we didn't have to get the flood insurance,' she said. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? According to insurance attorney Aaron Bass, homeowners who don't have separate flood insurance generally cannot rely on their standard homeowners policies to cover damage caused by rising floodwaters. Lee described the scene as "apocalyptic," recalling the shock of seeing cars stranded in floodwaters."I was overwhelmed by this whole thing — walking and seeing people's cars stranded in the middle," she said.Like many homeowners who live outside high-risk flood zones, Lee never thought she would need flood insurance."Who thought? We moved west so we didn't have to get the flood insurance," she said.According to insurance attorney Aaron Bass, homeowners who don't have separate flood insurance generally cannot rely on their standard homeowners policies to cover damage caused by rising floodwaters."There's no loopholes to get flood coverage from your regular homeowner's insurance policy, Kate. It just doesn't exist," Bass said.That means homeowners without flood insurance could be responsible for thousands — or even hundreds of thousands — of dollars in repairs.However, Bass said there are other resources worth exploring.Bass recommends contacting the Federal Emergency Management Agency and nonprofit disaster relief organizations to see what assistance may be available."You're going to have to call FEMA, see if they're going to help you, and you need to call nongovernmental organizations, charities," Bass said.FEMA assistance is not guaranteed. Eligibility depends on several factors, including whether federal disaster assistance has been authorized for the affected area.Some disaster assistance may also be available through low-interest loans, which must be repaid.Yet nonprofit organizations can provide another avenue for help.Jacob Rutz, senior program manager with Samaritan's Purse, said the organization has teams in areas of the southeast helping disaster victims with recovery efforts."Our volunteer teams work on roofs, tarping them, stopping water from coming in," Rutz said.The organization is among several nonprofits that help homeowners recover from disasters, particularly when insurance payments or other assistance are delayed or unavailable.Rutz encourages residents to start by checking with local emergency management agencies to find out what resources are available."The most important thing really is to look at your local emergency services website," he said.He recommended residents also call 211 to connect with local community assistance programs.Bass said the flooding serves as a reminder that living outside a designated high-risk flood zone does not eliminate the risk of flooding.His recommendation? Consider purchasing flood insurance even if your mortgage lender doesn't require it."That $300, $400, $500 a year for a premium for a federal flood insurance policy is small potatoes compared to hundreds of thousands of dollars in damage to your home," Bass said.Actual flood insurance premiums vary depending on the property, location and coverage selected.For homeowners already dealing with damage, experts recommend documenting everything with photos and videos, keeping receipts and contacting local emergency management officials about available assistance.Meanwhile, Lee is finding a little humor in her neighborhood's unexpected waterfront transformation.Her next investment?"I'm going to invest in one of those roll-up boats," she laughed. "So we can get around!"Residents affected by flooding can explore the following resources:FEMA: Visit DisasterAssistance.gov to check whether federal disaster assistance is available in your area.Samaritan's Purse: Visit SamaritansPurse.org for information about disaster relief efforts.211: Dial 211 or visit 211.org to connect with local nonprofit and community resources.U.S. Small Business Administration: Visit SBA.gov for information about disaster loans, which may be available to eligible homeowners and renters, not just business owners.Flood insurance: Visit FloodSmart.gov to learn about flood coverage through the National Flood Insurance Program.Palm Beach County: Visit the County's Individual Disaster and Family Assistance site. St Lucie County: Visit the County's Emergency Preparedness Portal, and scroll to "Report Damage" and/or "After the Emergency" Indian River County: Visit the Emergency Management site for disaster grants, loans, and insurance informationMartin County: Visit the County's Disaster Recovery page for information on insurance, building permits, damage assessment and more. Okeechobee County: Visit the Emergency Homepage for important links to resources like the Red Cross, FEMA Disaster Assistance, and Emergency Contacts.

entry.title: Evacuations underway as flooding swamps Port St. Lucie neighborhood - WPEC
entry.summary: Evacuations underway as flooding swamps Port St. Lucie neighborhood    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community as dangerous waters continue to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. Lucie Police Department said officers and emergency personnel were helping residents affected by ongoing flooding get to safety. The department urged people to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents told CBS12 they were effectively trapped in their homes and unable to get their cars out of their driveways because of flooded streets. Some said water reached their garages but did not enter their homes. CBS12 also observed water 18 inches deep in the street. See also: Two injured, third person believed dead after helicopter crash near Key Biscayne The flooding has continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. Lucie received 16.7 inches of rain from Nov. Lucie County received between 7 and 17 inches during that period, according to the National Weather Service. Residents told CBS12 the flooding was the worst they had seen in their neighborhood. entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that the passage of Amendment 3 helped drive Republican turnout in Florida, arguing the property tax measure played a significant role in allowing the GOP to hold its ground in the state despite major Democratic gains elsewhere in the country.Speaking the day after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, DeSantis called the national results "close to an extinction-level event" for Republicans but said Florida demonstrated the durability of the political coalition Republicans have built during his two terms as governor.WATCH BELOW: Republicans nationally suffer 'close to an extinction-level event,' DeSantis says"In the state of Florida, it got a resounding yes vote," DeSantis said of Amendment 3. "I'm very proud of everyone that had been a part of that."DeSantis said he believes putting the measure on the ballot also benefited Republican candidates further down the ticket."Had Amendment 3 not been on the ballot, I don't know that we turn out the voters that we ended up turning out," DeSantis said. "People wanted to vote yes on that, and then many of them ended up voting Republican later on down the ballot."DeSantis said Florida Republicans benefited from a record of delivering on promises to voters, even as political conditions shifted significantly toward Democrats nationally."We've built up a record of achievement," DeSantis said. "We've earned trust from a number of our voters that even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to hold the line."DeSantis said the next step will be implementing Amendment 3, with a special legislative session expected before he leaves office in January.The governor said he would work with legislative leaders on the timing rather than dictate when lawmakers should return to Tallahassee."We knew this would be something we needed to do," DeSantis said. "There's a lot of ideas that we've been tossing around for the last six months."DeSantis said the legislation would set a schedule for further expansion of homestead tax relief while also seeking to prevent local governments from offsetting the savings with other taxes or fees.He said he wants lawmakers to establish what he described as a "taxpayer bill of rights" and is considering state grants to help local governments, particularly rural communities, cover funding needs for essential services."It's not going to be a tax shift," DeSantis said. "It's going to be a reduction."According to DeSantis, implementing the amendment could involve tens of millions of dollars in state grants for local governments facing shortfalls in funding core services such as sheriff's departments.Amendment 3 must be implemented by Jan. 1.DeSantis also addressed questions about school funding because Amendment 3 does not apply to school districts.He said the implementing legislation will not change that exemption. Instead, he suggested lawmakers could eventually revisit Florida's education funding formula as they consider whether additional property tax relief could be provided to homeowners without reducing support for public schools.DeSantis said his ultimate goal is to move Florida closer to making homesteaded property tax-free, although reaching that point would require additional action after he leaves office."The more we can get the homestead to just be tax free, I think that's the better," DeSantis said.Much of the governor's news conference focused on what he described as disastrous results for Republicans outside Florida.DeSantis argued the election amounted more to a rejection of Republicans in Washington than an endorsement of the Democratic Party."This is probably the political worst-case scenario for a midterm election," he said.He said Republicans need to pay greater attention to voters' economic concerns, including inflation, mortgage rates, gas and grocery prices.DeSantis also criticized Republicans nationally for focusing their campaigns on issues that he believes were more effective in previous elections but did not match voters' concerns this year."The ground shifts and the emphasis then is on different things," DeSantis said. "Republicans, it seemed like in some of the ads I was seeing with how much money they were spending, they really were fighting yesterday's battle."Despite narrower Republican victories in Florida than in recent elections, DeSantis rejected the idea that the results represented a failure for the state GOP. He said he had warned Republican candidates for months that the political environment had moved substantially toward Democrats.DeSantis said strong Democratic turnout and increased participation among no-party-affiliation voters made the election particularly difficult for Republicans.Still, he argued Florida's results showed Republicans could survive an unfavorable national environment if they remain responsive to voters and deliver on policy."Florida is the last main anchor standing," DeSantis said.DeSantis, who is term-limited and will leave office in January, declined to discuss whether he might run for another office in 2028."I still got more work to do," DeSantis said. "We'll work till the lights are out and cross that bridge when we get to it."

entry.title: Six St. Lucie County polling places moved because of flooding on Election Day - WPEC
entry.summary: Six St. Lucie County polling places moved because of flooding on Election Day    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County election officials to move six precincts’ polling places on Election Day, including several in Port St. The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves are meant to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Lucie, voters in precincts 49 and 71, who normally cast ballots at Oak Hammock K-8 School, will vote at the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, will also go to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard. Voters in precincts 67 and 86 will not vote at Centennial High School in St. They will vote at Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence, at 500 NW California Blvd. The county says access is from Peacock Boulevard. See also: Inside David Jolly's election night watch party as Florida chooses its next governor In the Tradition area, precinct 83 voters will move from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters will also move from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall. In Fort Pierce, Precinct 12 voters will move from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1. The notice does not list any polling places as closed. It also does not say whether voters who already went to their normal location will be redirected on site. The flooding also disrupted schools. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Jon Prince apologized to families during a news conference Tuesday, after students were seen walking through standing water to get home Monday. We didn’t anticipate anything like what transpired yesterday. Caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry, Prince said. Schools are closed Wednesday. Prince said the district expects to reopen Thursday if roads are clear, and that no school buildings took significant water. A private security company that patrols homeowners associations in the Tradition area joined the rescue effort with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. We had no goal when we came out here. We had just ambition to figure out how we can help anyone and anywhere and do whatever we can with the resources that we have, Matchton said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods, and warned that anyone who preys on flood victims will face zero tolerance. The sheriff said there was no playbook for a storm like this. But the most important thing is we’re all working together with one purpose, which is to serve this community, Del Toro said. The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

entry.title: Jensen Beach neighborhood submerged as overwhelmed drainage system keeps flooding homes after rain stops
entry.summary: Much of a Jensen Beach neighborhood on Hyline Drive is underwater after this week's heavy rain overwhelmed the local drainage system. As of Wednesday afternoon, water levels inside some homes are still rising long after the rain stopped. For Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid, a kayak has become the way to get around their flooded community. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Jensen Beach neighborhood submerged as overwhelmed drainage system keeps flooding homes At Kincaid's home, the water level is waist-deep. 'We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,' said Kincaid. At French's home, the damage has just begun, with the water level climbing to 4 inches deep. 'My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,' French said. Their homes are among dozens in the neighborhood under water after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and inundated the drainage system. 'We were expecting flooding to go down. There hasn't been rain. Clearly drainage is not things are not draining correctly,' Kincaid said. Martin County told us the neighborhood is uniquely located next to the Savannas Preserve, where water is naturally flowing south from other areas that flooded. For now, the county says it's unable to pump water out of the community because the nearby watershed doesn't have capacity, but relief may be on the horizon. 'As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,' Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said. 'We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.' Residents are hoping relief comes sooner rather than later so they can start the long road to recovery. 'Even after, like, our houses are wrecked,' French said. 'It's just a lot to take in right now for us,' Kincaid said. Lucie County announced Wednesday that South 25th Street is closed to through traffic between Fort Pierce Central High School at Cobra Pride Way and the entrance to Forest Grove Middle School at Bulldog Drive. Anyone with questions about the closure can contact the county's Public Works Engineering Division at 772-462-1707 .

entry.article_text: Flooding continues in parts of St. Lucie County as recovery efforts move forward. Lucie police department is getting another look at flooding across the city as the sun rises. Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including : SW Cashmere Boulevard Lake Forest HOA St. Bernadette Church NW Country Club Drive Tradition Parkway SW Community Boulevard Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also working to support recovery efforts and restore normal conditions safely. Officials are reminding residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage people to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. The city thanked residents for their patience and support, noting that helping one another can make a difference as the community recovers. Lucie County moves temporary shelters to new locations St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population and special medical needs shelters to new locations Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter, currently at the Fenn Center, is relocating to the Florida Department of Health’s St. Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. entry.title: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo - WFLX
entry.summary: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo    WFLX
entry.article_text: A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago. Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WFLX that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense’s second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. Camerlengo’s attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense’s amended motion was “procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.” Wednesday’s ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set. Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Her arrest followed a WFLX investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade. The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case. During a contentious July hearing , Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo’s defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial. “I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,” Metzger said. “This case has been continued so many times, I’ve lost count.” In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial. Camerlengo’s defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths. “I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don’t think she had all of the facts,” Kaplan previously told WFLX. Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022. Kirk Csontos filed a police report following Mako’s death, but Camerlengo was never charged in connection with it because his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs determined they died from blunt force trauma, leading to Camerlengo’s arrest. “I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn’t think it would be two years,” Kirk Csontos previously told WFLX. Despite the repeated delays, she said she remains hopeful. Believe it or not, I’m still hopeful that she will be held accountable,” she said. Camerlengo’s next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. No trial date has been announced.

entry.title: 1 killed, 2 others injured when a helicopter crashes into Biscayne Bay near Bill Baggs State Park
entry.summary: One person was killed, and two others were injured on Wednesday when a helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay near Miami, officials said. The helicopter went down shortly before noon near Bill Baggs State Park, off Key Biscayne, the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: 1 dead, 2 injured in helicopter crash near Miami The U.S. Coast Guard confirmed that one of the three helicopter occupants was reported dead, while the other two were taken to a trauma center. Preliminary information indicates that the Robinson R44 II helicopter appeared to be on a photography flight, the National Transportation Safety Board said. Besides the Coast Guard, firefighters from several local agencies responded to the crash. Television news video of the crash shows the aircraft upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing. Officials didn't immediately identify the helicopter's occupants.

entry.title: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat - WPEC
entry.summary: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie is providing financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners for critical home repairs caused by this week’s flooding through its Disaster Relief Program, funded by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. The program, part of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), offers support to low- and moderate-income homeowners for emergency repairs to their primary residences in Port St. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, payment of homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. These repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, temporary structural stabilization, and other actions necessary to protect the home from additional damage. Eligible homeowners may receive up to $25,000 through 0% interest deferred payment loans, with no monthly payments required. Loans are forgiven over a five-year period in accordance with program guidelines. All work must be directly related to the declared disaster, deemed necessary to preserve the safety and integrity of the property, and approved by the city before assistance is provided. Funding is not available for mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal, or remediation. Homeowners must complete any necessary mold remediation before approved repairs can proceed. Eligible repairs may be funded after remediation is complete. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or non-permitted work are not eligible for assistance. The city has allocated $1 million for the program, which will run until the funds are exhausted. The program’s pre-application will open at 8 a.m. To qualify, applicants must meet income guidelines, have owned and occupied their home within city limits for at least one year, have an assessed home value of $560,154 or less, and be current on mortgage and property tax payments. 5, residents may complete the pre-application online. Assistance is also available by contacting the city’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, emailing Housing@cityofpsl.com, or visiting City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: Evacuations underway as flooding swamps Port St. Lucie neighborhood - WPEC
entry.summary: Evacuations underway as flooding swamps Port St. Lucie neighborhood    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community as dangerous waters continue to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. I think it's part of living in Florida," said Sheri George, a Vitalia resident. Sheri George and her husband Arthur were evacuated by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission on a swamp buggy Wednesday. They had no electricity, no A/C and the food in their refrigerator was spoiling. They were unable to drive out of the neighborhood because roads were flooded. They were thrilled FWC could get them safely out of the neighborhood. This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer," Sheri George said. "I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me," said Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident who was evacuated because of flooding. According to FWC, since Tuesday they've evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater in several areas in St. "I love being able to, when we're at our worst times being able to come and give somebody some ray of hope," said Jon Arnold, an FWC investigator who was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia. "I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety," said Tyson Matthews, FWC Public Information Officer. Lucie Police Department said officers and emergency personnel were helping residents affected by ongoing flooding get to safety. The department urged people to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents told CBS12 they were effectively trapped in their homes and unable to get their cars out of their driveways because of flooded streets. Some said water reached their garages but did not enter their homes. CBS12 also observed water 18 inches deep in the street. See also: Two injured, third person believed dead after helicopter crash near Key Biscayne The flooding has continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. Lucie received 16.7 inches of rain from Nov. Lucie County received between 7 and 17 inches during that period, according to the National Weather Service. Residents told CBS12 the flooding was the worst they had seen in their neighborhood. Police urged residents to never drive or walk through floodwaters, follow evacuation instructions, stay away from closed roads and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones if they can do so safely.

entry.title: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County officials said Tuesday that emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls as they responded to widespread flooding after historic rainfall. Lucie County Fire District received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period, Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said at a county briefing. The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns, he said. Please use caution and avoid unnecessary travel, Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said. It may take several days for the water to recede. Shelters open; schools closed Wednesday The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. The city said vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000 . The city also warned residents to expect a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. See also: LIST: Flooded St. Lucie, Indian River roads remain hazardous as crews check homes Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Guerrero said emergency dispatchers had received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Officials said call takers were screening requests so emergency vehicles could remain available for urgent situations. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

entry.title: Former Top Gun pilot, recovering addict paying it forward
entry.summary: November marks National Veterans and Military Families Month, and WPTV is examining ways to celebrate and support our service members. Former Top Gun pilot Chris Claflin is doing his part and paying it forward to fellow veterans struggling with addiction issues. After a WPTV Let's Hear It story presented by morning anchor Ashley Glass, a viewer reached out and invited Claflin to speak at the Called to Freedom Veterans Retreat. He happily accepted the invitation. 'Serving in the military, no matter what your service is, theres something about meeting other people who are willing to put their lives on the line for the nation. It was an immediate bond right there,' Claflin said. Claflin graduated from Harvard Business School. He was also a U.S. Navy pilot and flew jets in combat, but all of that success fell apart when he became drug addicted for eight years. Claflin traced the onset of the drug addiction, in part, back to not dealing with trauma he experienced as a child. He is currently more than a year sober, and has a message for anyone struggling, especially veterans. Get help,' Claflin said. 'You have to get help. You cant do this on your own. Its not something you can figure out. Once you get so far down the rabbit hole, you cant pull yourself out on your own. Claflin has been greatly supported by the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach, a community resource to support the mental health and well-being of service members or anyone struggling. He is currently working to become a certified addiction counselor and aims to have that certificate by spring.

entry.title: Greenacres mom loses home after deadly jet crash, asks community for help
entry.summary: A Greenacres mother says her family lost their home after a deadly Learjet 60 crash Sunday sent flames and burning debris onto their property. Days later, Stephanie Platts told WPTV she is grateful her family escaped but is now turning to the community for help as they try to rebuild. It was absolute chaos, Platts said. There was a lot of fire, a lot of debris, a lot of screaming. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Greenacres family loses home after deadly jet crash, seeks community help Family rushed to safety as flames spread Platts told WPTV she was home with her family when the jet crashed just yards away. We didnt have time to think, we didnt have time to process it, Platts said. The only thing that we had time to do was get to safety. Platts said she didn't immediately understand what had happened until she encountered the flames. I didnt realize that it was an actual explosion until I was faced with flames, she said. She described large pieces of burning debris hitting the roof of her home as the fire spread. There were giant chunks of debris that were on fire that pelted my roof, Platts said. Her home was devastated by the fire, leaving her family displaced. Platts also says she suffered a burn to her foot during the chaos, leaving it swollen. NTSB: Learjet reported icing, turbulence before deadly crash Greenacres mother asks community for help Now, Platts is trying to figure out how her family can move forward and eventually return home. I want to be able to go back home and enjoy the holidays coming around, she said. Platts told WPTV that Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Palm Beach has assisted her while she temporarily stays at the Greenacres Community Center. A GoFundMe has also been set up to support Platts after the crash. Help Stephanie Platts through the GoFundMe Remembering the lives lost Even as she copes with losing her home, Platts said she is thinking about the nine lives lost in the crash just steps from where her family lived. Its very heartbreaking for me, Platts said. But at the same time, it could have been worse. But every life is important. It doesnt matter if it was nine or 100, its still a life. Platts said the tragedy has changed how she looks at life. Life is very short and it can change instantaneously, she said. Her message to others is simple: Just embrace it and enjoy it because you dont know whats gonna happen tomorrow. Crews continue to investigate the deadly crash. entry.title: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo
entry.summary: A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago. Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WPTV that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense's second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. hearing held Wednesday. Camerlengo's attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense's amended motion was 'procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.' Wednesday's ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set. Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Her arrest followed a WPTV investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade. A case plagued by delays The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case. During a contentious July hearing , Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo's defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial. 'I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,' Metzger said. 'This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count.' In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial. Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths. 'I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don't think she had all of the facts,' Kaplan previously told WPTV. entry.title: Port St. Lucie offers up to $25,000 to homeowners for flood repairs
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie homeowners whose properties were damaged by this week's flooding could be eligible for up to $25,000 in financial assistance for critical repairs. The city announced Wednesday that it has allocated $1 million to its Disaster Relief Program to help low- and moderate-income homeowners repair their primary residences. WATCH REPORT: Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roads, leaving drivers stranded Pre-applications for the program will open at 8 a.m. Thursday, Nov. 5, and funding will remain available until the $1 million allocation is exhausted. The assistance is being offered through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding provided by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000 through a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years in accordance with program guidelines. What repairs are covered? According to the city, the money may be used for emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable. Eligible expenses may include: Tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability Payment of Homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work Temporary repairs to prevent further property damage, such as: Roof repairs Weatherproofing Water extraction Removal of water-damaged materials Emergency plumbing or electrical work Temporary structural stabilization  Other reasonable and necessary actions required to protect the home from additional damage All work must be directly connected to the declared disaster and approved by the city before assistance is provided. The program does not cover mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal or remediation. If a home requires mold remediation, the homeowner must have that work completed before other approved repairs can proceed. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs and illegal or unpermitted work are also excluded. Who qualifies? To be eligible, applicants must meet the program's income requirements. They must also have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home must have an assessed value of $560,154 or less, and applicants must be current on their mortgage and property tax payments. entry.article_text: Lucie voters who were assigned to vote in Precinct 90, Legacy High School are now being told the polling place is changing locations. Voters were directed to Precinct 89 at Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. It was a confusing day for voters assigned to the precinct, due to flooding impacting travel to Legacy High School. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections instructed voters to take Midway Road and Glade Extension to reach Legacy High School. entry.title: Vitalia evacuations paused overnight as crews pump floodwater in Port St. Lucie - WPEC
entry.summary: Vitalia evacuations paused overnight as crews pump floodwater in Port St. Lucie    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community as dangerous waters continue to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. I think it's part of living in Florida," said Sheri George, a Vitalia resident. Sheri George and her husband Arthur were evacuated by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission on a swamp buggy Wednesday. They had no electricity, no A/C and the food in their refrigerator was spoiling. They were unable to drive out of the neighborhood because roads were flooded. They were thrilled FWC could get them safely out of the neighborhood. This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer," Sheri George said. "I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me," said Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident who was evacuated because of flooding. According to FWC, since Tuesday they've evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater in several areas in St. "I love being able to, when we're at our worst times being able to come and give somebody some ray of hope," said Jon Arnold, an FWC investigator who was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia. "I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety," said Tyson Matthews, FWC Public Information Officer. Lucie Police Department said officers and emergency personnel were helping residents affected by ongoing flooding get to safety. The department urged people to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents told CBS12 they were effectively trapped in their homes and unable to get their cars out of their driveways because of flooded streets. Some said water reached their garages but did not enter their homes. CBS12 also observed water 18 inches deep in the street. See also: Two injured, third person believed dead after helicopter crash near Key Biscayne The flooding has continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. Lucie received 16.7 inches of rain from Nov. Lucie County received between 7 and 17 inches during that period, according to the National Weather Service. Residents told CBS12 the flooding was the worst they had seen in their neighborhood. Police urged residents to never drive or walk through floodwaters, follow evacuation instructions, stay away from closed roads and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones if they can do so safely. As of Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District says it has responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide. In the Vitalia community, the City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department has installed a 12-inch pump, which began operating at approximately 8:00 p.m. tonight, the fire district said. The pump is moving an estimated 7,000 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce flooding in the neighborhood. Additionally, SLCFD says routine evacuation operations in Vitalia have been suspended overnight and are scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Emergency responders remain available for fire and medical emergencies. Residents experiencing immediate safety or serious medical concerns requiring assistance should call 911.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie is providing financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners for critical home repairs caused by this week’s flooding through its Disaster Relief Program, funded by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. The program, part of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), offers support to low- and moderate-income homeowners for emergency repairs to their primary residences in Port St. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, payment of homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. These repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, temporary structural stabilization, and other actions necessary to protect the home from additional damage. Eligible homeowners may receive up to $25,000 through 0% interest deferred payment loans, with no monthly payments required. Loans are forgiven over a five-year period in accordance with program guidelines. All work must be directly related to the declared disaster, deemed necessary to preserve the safety and integrity of the property, and approved by the city before assistance is provided. Funding is not available for mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal, or remediation. Homeowners must complete any necessary mold remediation before approved repairs can proceed. Eligible repairs may be funded after remediation is complete. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or non-permitted work are not eligible for assistance. The city has allocated $1 million for the program, which will run until the funds are exhausted. The program’s pre-application will open at 8 a.m. To qualify, applicants must meet income guidelines, have owned and occupied their home within city limits for at least one year, have an assessed home value of $560,154 or less, and be current on mortgage and property tax payments. 5, residents may complete the pre-application online. Assistance is also available by contacting the city’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, emailing Housing@cityofpsl.com, or visiting City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: Boca Raton expanding school zone speed camera program to 3 more locations
entry.summary: The City of Boca Raton is expanding its school zone speed camera program to three additional locations beginning Nov. 9. The city said the expansion will add speed cameras in school zones serving Calusa Elementary School, Blue Lake Elementary School, and Omni Middle School/Spanish River High School, bringing the total number of participating school zones in the city to six. Westlake considers school zone speed cameras near Seminole Ridge High School to improve student safety The city operates the School Zone Safety Program in partnership with RedSpeed. Cameras are designed to deter speeding and will capture violations only while school zone flashing lights are activated. The new locations and enforcement times are: Calusa Elementary School 2051 Clint Moore Road Morning: 7:05 a.m. to 8:05 a.m. Afternoon: 2 p.m. to 2:35 p.m. Blue Lake Elementary School Military Trail and Potomac Road Morning: 7:20 a.m. to 8:05 a.m. Afternoon: 2 p.m. to 2:35 p.m. Omni Middle School/Spanish River High School Jog Road and Yamato Road Morning: 7 a.m. to 9:35 a.m. Afternoon: 2:45 p.m. to 4:35 p.m. Each school zone will have a 30-day warning period when its cameras are first activated. After the warning period ends, drivers traveling at least 11 mph over the posted speed limit while the school zone lights are flashing can receive a $100 civil penalty. Delray Beach school zone cameras issue nearly 5,000 speeding tickets More than 200 drivers ticketed in first week of Boca Raton school zone speed cameras According to the city, citations issued through the program do not add points to a driver's license or affect auto insurance rates. Boca Raton previously implemented the program in the school zones for Addison Mizner School, Boca Raton Community High School and J.C. Mitchell Elementary School. For more information, visit their website .

entry.title: GOP meltdown sparks battle over who's to blame
entry.summary: Even as key Senate races remain unresolved in Mississippi and Alaska, Republicans have already begun searching for someone to blame after a devastating midterm election defeat. With Democrats securing control of the Senate and on track for major gains in the House, the conversation in Washington has quickly shifted from counting ballots to assigning responsibility. The outstanding races remain extraordinarily close. In Mississippi, just over 1,000 votes separate the candidates, with additional mail ballots still eligible to arrive under state law. Alaska's contest may take even longer to resolve because of its ranked-choice voting system, where second- and third-choice preferences could ultimately determine the winner. But while election officials continue tallying votes, Republicans are increasingly focused on what many in the party view as one of the worst electoral setbacks in decades. RELATED STORY | Democratic leaders outline agenda after sweeping Congress in midterms The finger-pointing has already begun. One of the first casualties appears to be House Republican leadership. Speaker Mike Johnson has announced he will not seek another term as the party's leader in the House, guaranteeing a new face at the helm as Republicans attempt to regroup. Attention is also turning toward the White House and Trump's inner circle. Vice President JD Vance sparked discussion across Washington after publicly arguing that the party's losses were primarily tied to the conflict with Iran. In a social media post, Vance argued that the war was the central reason for the GOP's defeat and suggested any effort to rebuild the party must begin with an honest assessment of that decision. The comments have intensified scrutiny on senior administration officials, particularly Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Some Republicans are openly questioning whether changes at the Pentagon or elsewhere in the administration are necessary after the election results. The debate echoes a familiar chapter in modern political history. Following Republican losses in the 2006 midterm elections, President George W. Bush replaced Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld amid growing criticism over the Iraq War. Some Republicans are drawing parallels between that election and the party's current predicament. entry.title: Former Top Gun pilot, recovering addict paying it forward
entry.summary: November marks National Veterans and Military Families Month, and WPTV is examining ways to celebrate and support our service members. Former Top Gun pilot Chris Claflin is doing his part and paying it forward to fellow veterans struggling with addiction issues. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Former Top Gun pilot pays it forward After a WPTV Let's Hear It story presented by morning anchor Ashley Glass, a viewer reached out and invited Claflin to speak at the Called to Freedom Veterans Retreat. He happily accepted the invitation. 'Serving in the military, no matter what your service is, theres something about meeting other people who are willing to put their lives on the line for the nation. It was an immediate bond right there,' Claflin said. Claflin graduated from Harvard Business School. He was also a U.S. Navy pilot and flew jets in combat, but all of that success fell apart when he became drug addicted for eight years. Claflin traced the onset of the drug addiction, in part, back to not dealing with trauma he experienced as a child. He is currently more than a year sober, and has a message for anyone struggling, especially veterans. 'Get help,' Claflin said. 'You have to get help. You cant do this on your own. It's not something you can figure out. Once you get so far down the rabbit hole, you cant pull yourself out on your own.' Claflin has been greatly supported by the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach, a community resource to support the mental health and well-being of service members or anyone struggling. He is currently working to become a certified addiction counselor and aims to have that certificate by spring.

They had no electricity, no A/C and the food in their refrigerator was spoiling. They were unable to drive out of the neighborhood because roads were flooded. They were thrilled FWC could get them safely out of the neighborhood. This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer," Sheri George said. "I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me," said Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident who was evacuated because of flooding. According to FWC, since Tuesday they've evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater in several areas in St. "I love being able to, when we're at our worst times being able to come and give somebody some ray of hope," said Jon Arnold, an FWC investigator who was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia. "I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety," said Tyson Matthews, FWC Public Information Officer. Lucie Police Department said officers and emergency personnel were helping residents affected by ongoing flooding get to safety. The department urged people to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents told CBS12 they were effectively trapped in their homes and unable to get their cars out of their driveways because of flooded streets. Some said water reached their garages but did not enter their homes. CBS12 also observed water 18 inches deep in the street. See also: Two injured, third person believed dead after helicopter crash near Key Biscayne The flooding has continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. Lucie received 16.7 inches of rain from Nov. Lucie County received between 7 and 17 inches during that period, according to the National Weather Service. Residents told CBS12 the flooding was the worst they had seen in their neighborhood. Police urged residents to never drive or walk through floodwaters, follow evacuation instructions, stay away from closed roads and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones if they can do so safely. As of Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District says it has responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide. In the Vitalia community, the City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department has installed a 12-inch pump, which began operating at approximately 8:00 p.m. tonight, the fire district said. The pump is moving an estimated 7,000 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce flooding in the neighborhood. Additionally, SLCFD says routine evacuation operations in Vitalia have been suspended overnight and are scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Emergency responders remain available for fire and medical emergencies. Residents experiencing immediate safety or serious medical concerns requiring assistance should call 911.
