This targeted approach prevents unaffected students from losing valuable instructional time.For our educators and staff, personal safety comes first. entry.title: What Florida homeowners need to know about Amendment 3 property tax savings
entry.summary: The election night victory for Amendment 3 in Florida now sets up property tax savings for homeowners with the state's homestead exemption. 'No one who has homestead today in the state of Florida needs to worry about calling us or coming in or doing anything at this point,' said Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks. WATCH REPORT BELOW: What's next for Florida homeowners after approving Amendment 3 Those homeowners, she said, will automatically see their exemption rise to $150,000 in the first notices going out in August 2027. 'It's important they know that they aren't going to see those savings until the end of 2027,' Jacks said. Tax bills, which are not being eliminated, are sent out in November by the county's tax collector. 'Everyone will continue to pay the school board,' Jacks said. 'In addition, any non-ad valorem assessments, so assessments based usually on fees, the most common one is the solid waste authority, those won't go away.' Homeowners who have established Florida residency and apply by Dec. 31 are eligible for the new exemption. New Florida residents in 2027 will have to wait five years for the higher exemption. And renters established in the state by Dec. 31 will be eligible for the higher exemption if they buy a home in the future. For cities and counties in Florida, the future looks uncertain as tax revenues will decrease. Many local government leaders have speculated they will need to turn to budget trimming, cutting services and possibly looking for other revenue streams. 'The first decision they're going to have to make is how do they protect, or if they protect, police and fire,' said former state Sen. Jeff Brandes. Gov. Ron DeSantis, a supporter of Amendment 3, has said he'll call a special session to work out the details of handling Amendment 3. 'I think the first thing they need to do is be honest about what this means for counties and cities,' Brandes said. 'They have to protect the counties. They do not need to protect or have to protect the cities, and frankly, there's gonna be some cities that fail, and they need to let them fail.'

entry.title: Nearly two-year investigation targets 23rd Street Gang in St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: Nearly two-year investigation targets 23rd Street Gang in St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street Gang has led to a law enforcement operation in St. Lucie County, the sheriff’s office said. Officials are expected to discuss the operation, criminal charges and the group’s alleged involvement in violent crimes and drug trafficking at a news conference Thursday. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. The sheriff’s office did not provide details about arrests or charges in its release. Officials scheduled a news conference for 2:30 p.m. Thursday at sheriff’s office headquarters. Sheriff Richard Del Toro , Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith and representatives from participating agencies are expected to speak. CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized. The sheriff’s office said Thursday’s briefing will provide further details about the investigation and enforcement operation. CBS12 News will provide updates from the news conference later today.

entry.title: 1 killed, 2 others injured when a helicopter crashes into Biscayne Bay near Bill Baggs State Park
entry.summary: One man was killed, and two others were critically injured on Wednesday when their helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay near Miami, officials said. The Robinson R44 II helicopter went down late Wednesday morning near Bill Baggs State Park, off Key Biscayne, while on a trip to film boats on the water, the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: 1 dead, 2 injured in helicopter crash near Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during an afternoon news conference that the two survivors were taken to a nearby trauma center in critical but stable condition. Rescue workers from several local agencies, as well as the U.S. Coast Guard and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, responded to the crash. When the sheriff's office marine patrol units reached the scene, they reported finding a Good Samaritan trying to help one of the victims and take him to shore. Miami firefighters attempted to save his life, but he didn't survive, Cordero-Stutz said. Meanwhile, border protection officers found the two other men from the helicopter and turned them over to Miami-Dade rescue workers for transport to the hospital. Cordero-Stutz said the cause of the crash remains under investigation. South Florida has experienced heavy showers over the past few days, but it wasn't known if the weather contributed to the crash. Television news video of the crash shows the aircraft upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing. Officials didn't immediately identify the helicopter's occupants. The sheriff said they were still working to notify family members. On Sunday, nine people died when a Learjet plummeted into the ground near West Palm Beach, Florida, with enough force to create a crater and pulverize the airplane. The NTSB is also investigating that crash.

entry.title: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat - WPEC
entry.summary: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie is providing financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners for critical home repairs caused by this week’s flooding through its Disaster Relief Program, funded by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. The program, part of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), offers support to low- and moderate-income homeowners for emergency repairs to their primary residences in Port St. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, payment of homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. These repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, temporary structural stabilization, and other actions necessary to protect the home from additional damage. Eligible homeowners may receive up to $25,000 through 0% interest deferred payment loans, with no monthly payments required. Loans are forgiven over a five-year period in accordance with program guidelines. All work must be directly related to the declared disaster, deemed necessary to preserve the safety and integrity of the property, and approved by the city before assistance is provided. Funding is not available for mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal, or remediation. Homeowners must complete any necessary mold remediation before approved repairs can proceed. Eligible repairs may be funded after remediation is complete. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or non-permitted work are not eligible for assistance. The city has allocated $1 million for the program, which will run until the funds are exhausted. The program’s pre-application will open at 8 a.m. To qualify, applicants must meet income guidelines, have owned and occupied their home within city limits for at least one year, have an assessed home value of $560,154 or less, and be current on mortgage and property tax payments. 5, residents may complete the pre-application online. Assistance is also available by contacting the city’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, emailing Housing@cityofpsl.com, or visiting City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.article_text: Lucie County over the past few days has left dozens of vehicles stranded and some homes without power. entry.summary: Six St. Lucie County polling places moved because of flooding on Election Day    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County election officials to move six precincts’ polling places on Election Day, including several in Port St. The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves are meant to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Lucie, voters in precincts 49 and 71, who normally cast ballots at Oak Hammock K-8 School, will vote at the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, will also go to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard. Voters in precincts 67 and 86 will not vote at Centennial High School in St. They will vote at Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence, at 500 NW California Blvd. The county says access is from Peacock Boulevard. See also: Inside David Jolly's election night watch party as Florida chooses its next governor In the Tradition area, precinct 83 voters will move from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters will also move from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall. In Fort Pierce, Precinct 12 voters will move from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1. The notice does not list any polling places as closed. It also does not say whether voters who already went to their normal location will be redirected on site. The flooding also disrupted schools. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Jon Prince apologized to families during a news conference Tuesday, after students were seen walking through standing water to get home Monday. We didn’t anticipate anything like what transpired yesterday. Caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry, Prince said. Schools are closed Wednesday. Prince said the district expects to reopen Thursday if roads are clear, and that no school buildings took significant water. A private security company that patrols homeowners associations in the Tradition area joined the rescue effort with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. We had no goal when we came out here. We had just ambition to figure out how we can help anyone and anywhere and do whatever we can with the resources that we have, Matchton said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods, and warned that anyone who preys on flood victims will face zero tolerance. The sheriff said there was no playbook for a storm like this. But the most important thing is we’re all working together with one purpose, which is to serve this community, Del Toro said. The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

entry.title: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County reports 120 water rescues; schools closed Wednesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County officials said Tuesday that emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls as they responded to widespread flooding after historic rainfall. Lucie County Fire District received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period, Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said at a county briefing. The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns, he said. Please use caution and avoid unnecessary travel, Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said. It may take several days for the water to recede. Shelters open; schools closed Wednesday The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. The city said vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000 . The city also warned residents to expect a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. See also: LIST: Flooded St. Lucie, Indian River roads remain hazardous as crews check homes Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Guerrero said emergency dispatchers had received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Officials said call takers were screening requests so emergency vehicles could remain available for urgent situations. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

entry.title: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, most homes evacuated
entry.summary: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Aerial video of flooding in the Creekside community of St. Lucie County Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. 'If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies,' Del Toro said. Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff. Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power Light's equipment remains underwater. 'We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else,' FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. 'Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety.' Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high. Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede. Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

entry.title: Democrat clings to razor-thin lead in Mississippi Senate race
entry.summary: Mississippi voters could send a Democrat to the U.S. Senate for the first time in decades, with Scott Colom holding a narrow lead over Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. As of Thursday, Colom's lead over Hyde-Smith grew to more than 1,7000 votes, with nearly 1 million ballots counted. In many states, a race this close would trigger an automatic recount. However, Mississippi has no law requiring automatic recounts in federal elections. Instead, a court would have to order one. RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governor The race remains too close to call, with as many as 3,500 mail-in ballots still outstanding, according to the Mississippi secretary of state's office. Mississippi allows mail-in ballots to arrive after Election Day as long as they are postmarked by Election Day. However, not all outstanding ballots are necessarily expected to arrive, as some voters who requested ballots may not have returned them. In addition to mail-in ballots, election officials must review provisional ballots, known in Mississippi as affidavit ballots. Voters may cast affidavit ballots for several reasons, including failing to present identification at the polls. Those voters must provide the required identification to county election officials after Election Day for their ballots to count. Other affidavit ballots may have been cast by voters listed as inactive on the state's voter rolls. Those ballots can be counted once officials confirm the voters' eligibility through the state's registration system, without requiring additional action from the voters. Counties have until Nov. 13 to submit their certified election results to the Mississippi secretary of state's office, meaning an official winner may not be determined for several more days. Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982.

At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. entry.title: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo - WFLX
entry.summary: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo    WFLX
entry.article_text: A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago. Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WFLX that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense’s second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. Camerlengo’s attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense’s amended motion was “procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.” Wednesday’s ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set. Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Her arrest followed a WFLX investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade. The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case. During a contentious July hearing , Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo’s defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial. “I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,” Metzger said. “This case has been continued so many times, I’ve lost count.” In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial. Camerlengo’s defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths. “I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don’t think she had all of the facts,” Kaplan previously told WFLX. Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022. Kirk Csontos filed a police report following Mako’s death, but Camerlengo was never charged in connection with it because his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs determined they died from blunt force trauma, leading to Camerlengo’s arrest. “I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn’t think it would be two years,” Kirk Csontos previously told WFLX. Despite the repeated delays, she said she remains hopeful. Believe it or not, I’m still hopeful that she will be held accountable,” she said. Camerlengo’s next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. No trial date has been announced.

entry.title: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo
entry.summary: A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago. Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WPTV that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense's second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. hearing held Wednesday. Camerlengo's attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense's amended motion was 'procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.' Wednesday's ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set. Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Her arrest followed a WPTV investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade. A case plagued by delays The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case. During a contentious July hearing , Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo's defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial. 'I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,' Metzger said. 'This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count.' In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial. Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths. 'I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don't think she had all of the facts,' Kaplan previously told WPTV. entry.title: Family of Port St. Lucie teen killed walking to school raises concerns about road safety
entry.summary: WPTV hasn't stopped looking into the tragic death of a Port St. Lucie teen who was killed while walking to school just last month. On Wednesday, WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield sat down with the family for the first time to hear from them about their son and the questions they're still asking. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Family of 14-year old hit and killed by car in Port St. Lucie speak out  Jacory Brown, a freshman at Treasure Coast High School, was struck and killed by a car on Port St. Lucie Boulevard while walking to school early in the morning on Oct. 7. 'He just went to school,' Shelly-Ann Findley-Brown, mother, said. 'He was supposed to come back home. He didn't. His birthday would be on Monday. He would have been 15.' Findley-Brown, father Ainsworth Brown and grandfather Clovis Brown, sat down with WPTV. They're remembering Jacorys smile. 'He's kind, he's a jovial kid, said Findley-Brown. 'He's the life of our party of five.'  Theyre remembering his friendliness to others. '[He] was loved by so many persons, and he has touched everybody he's met,' Finely-Brown said.  And they're remembering his passion for entrepreneurship and graphic design like making cover art, business cards and flyers for friends and family. 'His hand was always up here, mind looking, his eyes all over like he's devising a plan and coming up with his thing,' Findley-Brown said.  But the family still has questions. They say Port St. Lucie Boulevard, with all the construction, makes it a dangerous roadway for kids walking to school. 'The road conditions are horrible,' Findley-Brown said. 'You are walking in puddles. And the night before, it rained. There was water all over the place. There's puddles. There's literally no sidewalks for kids to walk.' FDOT started construction back in 2025 to widen the road from two to four lanes and add new sidewalks and lights. But the project isn't expected to be completed until winter 2028. 'I hope the state takes this into a big consideration because it's not right walking to school when you don't have proper sidewalks,' Findley-Brown said. Jacory Brown will be laid to rest on Nov. 14. Friends have s tarted a GoFundMe to support the family.

entry.title: New reimagined Florida Panthers JetBlue plane debuts in Fort Lauderdale
entry.summary: 'Go Cats Go' is the name of the newly decorated JetBlue commercial plane revealed in Fort Lauderdale on Thursday. The 162-seat plane was shown to a group of media members, including WPTV Panthers anchor Mike Trim, at the Jetscape hangar at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. You guys see my new plane? joked Panthers star forward Brad Marchand. Marchand was joined at the ceremony by Panthers captain Alexsander Barkov and Panthers General Manager Bill Zito. The commercial airliner is capable of flying to all 130 JetBlue destinations and will fly locally out of South Florida, including Donald J. Trump International Airport. There's an energy from it. It's so beautiful. It's so cool, and I'm already proud of it, and I really have no reason to be proud of it. It's just really special and really cool, said Zito. The plane features Panthers logos old and new. The current Panthers shield is featured on the tail while the classic jumping cat logo is on the underbelly. Marchand, Barkov and Zito added a special touch at the ceremony by signing the jumping cat logo with Sharpies. For Barkov, its another step is seeing the Panthers brand grow. I love it. It's been fun to see this community grow, get more and more fans, more and more involved in here, and just seeing Florida Panthers everywhere. You see it on the highways, you see like, everywhere and now this plane, said Barkov. The plane's first flight will be to Boston Thursday. Its a city with a Panthers rival team, the Boston Bruins. Marchand captained that team for years and told Trim and a group of reporters, I almost feel like they might have done that on purpose. You know, because it's not a plane that you're going to miss. It all stands out. They did an incredible job with it.  Representatives from JetBlue told Trim the plane's Panthers livery will stay for at least five years.

entry.title: Panthers Figure Skating Club member chases nationals berth with dreams of Team USA, Olympics
entry.summary: Several athletes with the Panthers Figure Skating Club are competing in the Eastern Sectional Finals this week in Boston, and for some skaters it's the final stop before nationals. One athlete competing is figure skater Skylar Zaglul. 'I'm really excited. I've worked really hard this whole year just for this moment, so I'm really looking forward to it,' Zaglul said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Panthers figure skater chases Olympic dream 'I would definitely describe it as being harder than it looks,' Zaglul said. 'People look at the jumps and the spins like, wow, it's so impressive. It is, but a really hard part about it is also just the skating skills.' The 15-year-old said she trains six days a week a lot of practice to perfect her technique. 'I really love how skating brings out the toughness in me, and I just love how challenging it is,' Zaglul said. When asked what goes through her mind during a performance, she described her approach to staying present. 'I try to stay focused on one element at a time or else I can start thinking ahead too much, and it just goes,' Zaglul said. Zaglul is one of 30 high-performance skaters. The Panthers program has over 300 athletes in the figure skating club and 2,800 more kids in learn to skate. 'I love how I get to train alongside all my best friends,' Zaglul said. 'I think having good team bonding and my coaches, they're all what keeps me going,' Zaglul said. Asked about the end goal of her figure skating career, Zaglul pointed to the sport's highest stage. 'Well, I've always dreamed about being on Team USA. That's like something I've always wanted to do. Of course, being at the Olympics,' Zaglul said. Zaglul says her sights are set on the Olympics, but the first stop is getting to nationals. Her coaches and teammates tell me they'll be cheering her on the entire way.

entry.title: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat - WPEC
entry.summary: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

entry.title: St. Lucie Public Schools to remain closed Thursday because of flooding
entry.summary: St. Lucie Public Schools will remain closed Thursday as the county continues to recover from flooding caused by this week's severe weather. The school district announced Wednesday that campuses will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, because of ongoing road conditions, including numerous flooded bus stops and areas where high water remains. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie Public Schools to remain closed Thursday District officials said they want to allow additional time for the flooding to subside before returning to normal operations. Essential employees are required to report to work as outlined in the district's Emergency Operations Plan. Schools are expected to reopen Friday, Nov. 6, but the district cautioned that could change depending on conditions. Families are encouraged to check the St. Lucie Public Schools website for updates before schools reopen. 'Thank you for your patience and understanding as our community recovers from this unprecedented weather event,' the district said.

entry.title: Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman ousts embattled Mayor Karen Bass
entry.summary: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nations second-largest city. The India-born Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at City Hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign. Her entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, once her ally. entry.article_text: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation’s second-largest city.The India-born Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at City Hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign.Her entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, once her ally. She said the city had reached a “breaking point” and announced her own candidacy just before the filing deadline.Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory.“While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said. “I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for reelection. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered.Raman's rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals.Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating with federal immigration authorities. She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years and left neighborhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights.Raman called Bass’ efforts to reduce homelessness ineffective. She's promising a new approach on the crisis that would expand medical teams for people who live in encampments and on the streets in an effort to build trust and eventually bring them indoors. Raman also wants to provide more housing to move people out of hotels rented by the city for those who are homeless.She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region.RELATED STORY | Keisha Lance Bottoms to become Georgia’s first Black governor, first woman governorRaman offered changeRaman, 45, was the face of change in a year when voters were restless over long-running problems that persisted under Bass, 73. A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted from Oct. 19 to 25 found that about 4 in 10 likely voters said reducing the number of homeless encampments should be a top priority for the next mayor to address, while about 3 in 10 said that about ensuring public safety or building more affordable housing.She was able to overcome criticism from Bass that she was “not ready for primetime” and too inexperienced to run a city with 3.8 million people, and she capitalized on anxiety over the future.“Our city is in crisis,” she said in one ad. The ad showed a lectern with no one behind it at the site of a massive warehouse fire from last summer, the homeless epicenter of Skid Row and shuttered malls and storefronts. “Where is our mayor?” Raman asked.Bass argued that she made enough progress to merit a second four-year term, and she branded Raman’s views on policing and homelessness as “extreme.”RELATED STORY | Xavier Becerra wins California gubernatorial race, making history as the state’s second Latino leaderTop Democrats lined up with BassRaman's victory came despite limited backing from the Democratic establishment. Bass had support from Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the City Council. Bass served in the state Legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former President Joe Biden’s running mate in 2020.In an important signal to the business community, billionaire developer Rick Caruso said he was voting for Bass, but stopped short of formally endorsing the candidate he lost to in the 2022 mayoral race.Raman, an urban planner, picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. But she was thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians.She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, who was not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle. Expanding her network of allies could be crucial as she begins governing a city that's home to a struggling entertainment industry, a major port, world-class universities and research institutions and serves as a major tourist destination.

entry.title: Democrat clings to razor-thin lead in Mississippi Senate race
entry.summary: Mississippi voters could send a Democrat to the U.S. Senate for the first time in decades, with Scott Colom holding a narrow lead over Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. As of Thursday, Colom's lead over Hyde-Smith grew to more than 1,700 votes, with nearly 1 million ballots counted. In many states, a race this close would trigger an automatic recount. However, Mississippi has no law requiring automatic recounts in federal elections. Instead, a court would have to order one. RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governor The race remains too close to call, with as many as 3,500 mail-in ballots still outstanding, according to the Mississippi secretary of state's office. Mississippi allows mail-in ballots to arrive after Election Day as long as they are postmarked by Election Day. However, not all outstanding ballots are necessarily expected to arrive, as some voters who requested ballots may not have returned them. In addition to mail-in ballots, election officials must review provisional ballots, known in Mississippi as affidavit ballots. Voters may cast affidavit ballots for several reasons, including failing to present identification at the polls. Those voters must provide the required identification to county election officials after Election Day for their ballots to count. Other affidavit ballots may have been cast by voters listed as inactive on the state's voter rolls. Those ballots can be counted once officials confirm the voters' eligibility through the state's registration system, without requiring additional action from the voters. Counties have until Nov. 13 to submit their certified election results to the Mississippi secretary of state's office, meaning an official winner may not be determined for several more days. Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982.

entry.title: Nearly two-year investigation targets 23rd Street Gang in St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: Nearly two-year investigation targets 23rd Street Gang in St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street gang has led to nearly 40 arrests and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash, law enforcement officials said Thursday. The multi-agency investigation, called Operation Score Board, focused on alleged gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas. Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also found that gang members allegedly kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. Officials said about 70 to 80 people are documented as members of the gang. The investigation focused on people police described as shot callers who allegedly directed its activities. Authorities said the 23rd Street gang has been a problem in the Fort Pierce area for decades and was the most violent of several gangs in the city. 4, officers served five search warrants four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie beginning around 5 a.m. The operation led to 11 arrests on racketeering charges, with two people still wanted on warrants, and four additional probable-cause arrests, officials said. Authorities said some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages. 4 searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474. Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV. Authorities did not identify the people they believe led the gang, but said they believe they have arrested most of the key players. They said some people connected to the investigation have faced murder charges, but declined to discuss active cases. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro called the operation an unusually large collaboration among local, state and federal agencies. He said investigators took significant players off the streets and that more operations are expected. The sheriff said the case took extensive work to connect years of records and evidence, and involved a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case. History of problems CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized. The sheriff’s office said Thursday’s briefing will provide further details about the investigation and enforcement operation. CBS12 News will provide updates from the news conference later today.

entry.title: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo - WFLX
entry.summary: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo    WFLX
entry.article_text: A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago. Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WFLX that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense’s second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. Camerlengo’s attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense’s amended motion was “procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.” Wednesday’s ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set. Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Her arrest followed a WFLX investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade. The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case. During a contentious July hearing , Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo’s defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial. “I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,” Metzger said. “This case has been continued so many times, I’ve lost count.” In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial. Camerlengo’s defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths. “I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don’t think she had all of the facts,” Kaplan previously told WFLX. Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022. Kirk Csontos filed a police report following Mako’s death, but Camerlengo was never charged in connection with it because his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs determined they died from blunt force trauma, leading to Camerlengo’s arrest. “I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn’t think it would be two years,” Kirk Csontos previously told WFLX. Despite the repeated delays, she said she remains hopeful. Believe it or not, I’m still hopeful that she will be held accountable,” she said. Camerlengo’s next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. No trial date has been announced.

entry.title: New reimagined Florida Panthers JetBlue plane debuts in Fort Lauderdale
entry.summary: 'Go Cats Go' is the name of the newly decorated JetBlue commercial plane revealed in Fort Lauderdale on Thursday. The 162-seat plane was shown to a group of media members, including WPTV Panthers anchor Mike Trim, at the Jetscape hangar at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. WATCH REPORT BELOW: JetBlue unveils Florida Panthers-themed plane 'You guys see my new plane?' joked Panthers star forward Brad Marchand. Marchand was joined at the ceremony by Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov and Panthers General Manager Bill Zito. The commercial airliner is capable of flying to all 130 JetBlue destinations and will fly locally out of South Florida, including Donald J. Trump International Airport. 'There's an energy from it. It's so beautiful. It's so cool, and I'm already proud of it, and I really have no reason to be proud of it. It's just really special and really cool,' said Zito. The plane features Panthers logos old and new. The current Panthers shield is featured on the tail while the classic jumping cat logo is on the underbelly. Marchand, Barkov and Zito added a special touch at the ceremony by signing the jumping cat logo with Sharpies. For Barkov, it's another step in seeing the Panthers brand grow. 'I love it. It's been fun to see this community grow, get more and more fans, more and more involved in here, and just seeing Florida Panthers everywhere. You see it on the highways, you see like, everywhere and now this plane,' said Barkov. The plane's first flight will be to Boston on Thursday, home of the rival Bruins. Marchand captained that team for years and told Trim and a group of reporters, 'I almost feel like they might have done that on purpose. You know, because it's not a plane that you're going to miss. It all stands out. They did an incredible job with it.'  Representatives from JetBlue told Trim the plane's Panthers livery will stay for at least five years.

We're just trying to get a little healthy with two of our guards, but well get there, Jakus said.

entry.title: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat - WPEC
entry.summary: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. entry.article_text: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. "If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies," Del Toro said. Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff. Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power Light's equipment remains underwater. "We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else," FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. "Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety." Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high. Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede. Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

entry.summary: Six St. Lucie County polling places moved because of flooding on Election Day    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County election officials to move six precincts’ polling places on Election Day, including several in Port St. The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves are meant to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Lucie, voters in precincts 49 and 71, who normally cast ballots at Oak Hammock K-8 School, will vote at the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, will also go to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard. Voters in precincts 67 and 86 will not vote at Centennial High School in St. They will vote at Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence, at 500 NW California Blvd. The county says access is from Peacock Boulevard. See also: Inside David Jolly's election night watch party as Florida chooses its next governor In the Tradition area, precinct 83 voters will move from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters will also move from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall. In Fort Pierce, Precinct 12 voters will move from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1. The notice does not list any polling places as closed. It also does not say whether voters who already went to their normal location will be redirected on site. The flooding also disrupted schools. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Jon Prince apologized to families during a news conference Tuesday, after students were seen walking through standing water to get home Monday. We didn’t anticipate anything like what transpired yesterday. Caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry, Prince said. Schools are closed Wednesday. Prince said the district expects to reopen Thursday if roads are clear, and that no school buildings took significant water. A private security company that patrols homeowners associations in the Tradition area joined the rescue effort with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. We had no goal when we came out here. We had just ambition to figure out how we can help anyone and anywhere and do whatever we can with the resources that we have, Matchton said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods, and warned that anyone who preys on flood victims will face zero tolerance. The sheriff said there was no playbook for a storm like this. But the most important thing is we’re all working together with one purpose, which is to serve this community, Del Toro said. The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

entry.title: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat - WPEC
entry.summary: Roberts beats White for Martin County School Board District 1 seat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

entry.title: Amendment 3 promises property tax savings, but Florida cities now face tough budget choices
entry.summary: The passing of Amendment 3 has now put Florida cities on notice to find ways to handle the anticipated loss of revenue. 'I was interviewed a couple of years ago when this first came up, and I said, 'What are we going to do, have a bake sale,' and here we are,' says Lake Worth Beach Mayor Betty Resch. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida Cities Chart Uncertain Future Under Amendment 3 According to Florida Tax Watch, Lake Worth Beach stands to lose $2.9 million in the first year of the higher homestead exemption and $5 million in the second year. 'We can't just keep raising the fees. We can't charge somebody if they want to go to the library,' Resch said. Voters made a statement on affordability, with 62% approving the referendum. The measure raises the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, which will mean savings on property tax bills. Local governments that depend on property tax revenue now face tightening budgets by making cuts, reducing services and possibly finding new ways to raise revenue. 'We don't charge yet for parking downtown, and every time we talk about it, everybody flips out because they don't want it and neither do I,' Resch said. 'I don't know where we're going to go. I don't know what we're going to do.'

entry.title: NTSB recovers part of Learjet engine, asks public to report crash debris
entry.summary: Investigators have recovered a portion of an engine from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres on Sunday as crews continue excavating the crash site, according to the National Transportation Safety Board. The NTSB said excavation work began late Wednesday and continued Thursday as investigators and local officials worked to recover wreckage from the crash that killed nine people. Debris from the aircraft has been found away from the main impact site, including on the roofs of nearby homes and buildings, according to the NTSB. All recovered wreckage will be taken to a secure location for further examination. Investigators are also asking residents who find debris believed to be from the Learjet not to keep it or attempt to move, alter or dispose of it. The agency said even small pieces of wreckage could contain evidence that helps investigators determine what happened. Anyone who has found or collected debris from the crash is asked to email witness@ntsb.gov to arrange for its recovery. The NTSB is asking people to include a photograph of the debris in the email, if possible. The NTSB said recovering as much of the aircraft wreckage as possible is critical to its investigation and efforts to determine the cause of the crash.

'We appreciate the flexibility, patience, and understanding as we've worked through these severe weather conditions and flooding,' the district said. entry.title: Flooding hits farms, nurseries hard in Martin and Palm Beach counties
entry.summary: Days after heavy rain moved through the area, floodwaters are still creating problems for local farms and nurseries, forcing some to close to visitors and adding to months of weather-related challenges. WPTV reporter Christy Waite visited Happy Place Ranch in Palm City, where standing water surrounds much of the property as the owners work to recover from the flooding. 'It's crushing,' Cimorelli said as she fought back tears. 'It's sad.' She said they expected rain, but not the amount that ultimately fell. 'We figured it was just rain. It just didn't stop. It was relentless,' she said. For seven years, Happy Place Ranch has hosted horse shows, riding lessons, birthday parties and other activities. Now, the flooding has forced the ranch to close, costing the business money while adding new expenses. Cimorelli said the ranch has been losing revenue since October as weather forced it to cancel activities, including its fall festival and horse shows. The flooding could now force the ranch to cancel two upcoming birthday parties, something Cimorelli said has never happened in the seven years they have been there. entry.summary: Elon Musk spent more money on the 2026 midterm elections than any political donor in American history. In Texas, the state his companies call home, it didn't buy him the results he wanted. The world's richest man spent at least $474 million on the midterms, including about $224 million in Texas, according to campaign finance records. On Tuesday, Texas voters elected Democrat James Talarico to the U.S. Senate over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, the candidate Musk spent the most to support. They also ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in favor of Democrat Gina Hinojosa. The day after each donation, the fund transferred the exact same amount to Texas PAC, a super PAC supporting Paxton.
