entry.article_text: Thomas Wayne Markle, the father of Meghan Markle, was arrested Friday morning at an assisted living facility in Lakeland, Florida, on a federal charge of possessing child pornography after investigators said they found suspected child sexual abuse material in two Los Angeles-area storage units he had rented for nearly two decades.The 82-year-old Lakeland resident is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to federal prosecutors. He was expected to make his initial appearance Friday in federal court in Tampa.The FBI investigation began after authorities learned in October that a person had signed an affidavit describing the discovery of suspected child sexual abuse material among Thomas Markle's belongings in the Philippines, according to an affidavit filed with the criminal complaint.Investigators later learned Thomas Markle rented a storage unit in the Los Angeles area. Information provided by the person who reported the material in the Philippines eventually led authorities to a second storage unit, according to the affidavit.Federal agents obtained search warrants for both units, which investigators said Thomas Markle had rented since 2008. According to prosecutors, his most recent payments for the units were made through automatic payments last month.During searches of the units, FBI agents seized roughly 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books containing suspected child sexual abuse material, according to the news release.Federal authorities allege some of the photographs show an adult man, identified by a witness as Thomas Markle, with prepubescent girls. Investigators said other photographs appeared to depict Markle with children in various stages of undress."These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.FBI officials said the case demonstrates the importance of reporting suspected child exploitation to law enforcement."This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it's a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office, said.Thomas Markle is the estranged father of Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex and wife of Prince Harry.The FBI is investigating the case. If convicted, Thomas Markle faces a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.His arrest follows reports by The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan's half-brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out the home of their father in the Philippines.Meghan recently said she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018."It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. "I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits,” married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.Thomas Markle Sr. was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr. recently found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s former home in Cebu City, in the Philippines, when he was clearing out the property.Markle Jr. told the newspaper that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI."I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him."

entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: St. Lucie County flips blue after 14 years as voters increase turnout despite floods - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County flips blue after 14 years as voters increase turnout despite floods    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County flipped blue in Tuesday's governor's race for the first time in more than a decade, as voter turnout climbed despite historic flooding that forced last-minute polling place changes. Democrat David Jolly carried the county with approximately 51% of the vote , compared with 48% for Republican Byron Donalds. The result marked the first time since 2012 that a Democratic candidate for governor or president won a majority in St. That year, former President Barack Obama carried the county with 53.42% of the vote. According to TCPalm , voter turnout reached 56.5% in the county, up 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election , when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. Lucie County ranked 51st among Florida's 67 counties, with only 16 counties reporting lower turnout. In 2022, the county had 238,645 registered voters, with 122,361 casting ballots. See also: Neighborhoods in Jensen Beach go underwater as flooding devastates the Treasure Coast Voters turn out despite historic flooding The increase came as widespread flooding forced election officials to relocate several polling places across Port St. Lucie, Tradition and Fort Pierce, per CBS12 reports . Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said the changes were necessary to ensure voters had safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Voters assigned to Oak Hammock K-8 School, Centennial High School and the Paula A. Lewis Library were among those affected, with some redirected to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, Indian River State College's Veterans Center of Excellence and Tradition Town Hall. The changes followed heavy rainfall that submerged roads, stranded vehicles and prompted evacuations across parts of the county. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties, while flooding forced local public schools to close Tuesday and Wednesday. Despite the weather-related challenges, St. Lucie County surpassed its 2022 general election turnout rate while delivering a Democratic majority in the governor's race for the first time in 14 years, when Obama won the county. While the flooding complicated Election Day logistics, the higher turnout suggests those challenges did not prevent overall participation from exceeding the previous gubernatorial election.

entry.title: 'Life turned upside down': Family retains attorney after losing home, livelihood in deadly Learjet crash
entry.summary: Nine people lost their lives when a Learjet crashed into Military Trail in Greenacres on Sunday. But the devastation extends beyond those on board, leaving at least one family on the ground without access to their home, their business and the life they knew before the crash. Now, that family has hired an attorney to investigate what went wrong and determine whether anyone could be held legally responsible. Ricardo Martinez-Cid, a partner at Miami law firm Podhurst Orseck, told WPTV his clients were inside the area impacted by the crash when debris struck, injuring family members and sending them to the hospital. Their home was damaged and remains inaccessible. Their food truck, which they relied on for their livelihood, was also lost. 'We want to be really sensitive in talking about how this has impacted their lives because it's been horrific for them,' Martinez-Cid said. 'But they're sensitive to the fact that nine people lost their lives on board that aircraft, and this is a horrible tragedy.' Martinez-Cid said the family is now grappling with the emotional and financial consequences of a disaster they never saw coming. 'Although my clients, you know, lost their home, they lost their livelihood in the food truck that they operated. They were injured and went to the hospital, and they're dealing with the trauma of what they witnessed and experienced,' he said. 'They're lucky, they're blessed because nine folks lost their lives.' Searching for answers and accountability Martinez-Cid, a board-certified aviation attorney with more than two decades of experience, said his firm is conducting its own investigation into the crash. The goal is to determine what caused the Learjet to go down and whether any individual, company or other entity bears legal responsibility. 'You don't want to jump to conclusions,' Martinez-Cid said. 'But in every aviation disaster ... you're really looking at man, the machine and the environment.' That means examining several potential factors, including weather conditions, pilot decisions, air traffic control communications and the aircraft's mechanical performance. 'We're looking at the weather, we're looking at the piloting, we're looking at how the aircraft responds, we're looking at the communications between the tower and with the pilots,' he said. 'We're going to look very closely at how the aircraft responded to what was going on as well.' Martinez-Cid said his firm has previously handled aviation cases involving aircraft manu
entry.article_text: So families need to get their own answers."Martinez-Cid said his firm plans to work with aviation experts to independently analyze available data, including communications, weather information and the aircraft's performance."So we look at it from all angles, and we make sure our experts get all the data that they can," he said.Martinez-Cid confirmed his firm has also been in contact with attorneys connected to families of people killed aboard the Learjet."We've been contacted by, which is often the case, attorneys that either are friends with the family or have been contacted by the family because of our expertise globally on these issues," he said. "And so we've been speaking to some."He said those conversations are not necessarily limited to potential lawsuits."We have experts that can talk to the families and explain the different things that they're hearing and what's going on, and I think that's an important thing for the family to have."Martinez-Cid previously served as lead counsel for death and injury cases stemming from the 2021 Champlain Towers South condominium collapse in Surfside.He said that experience reinforced the importance of recognizing the different kinds of losses families endure after a disaster.For the family Martinez-Cid represents in Greenacres, the immediate future remains uncertain.Their home is inaccessible, their source of income is gone, and they are recovering from injuries and the trauma of witnessing a deadly plane crash.Martinez-Cid declined to identify the family, saying they are still struggling emotionally with the aftermath.But he emphasized that while his clients recognize how fortunate they are to have survived, their lives have been permanently changed."Their life has been turned upside down," he said. "They're going to be living with this trauma forever. They've lost their livelihood."Still, he said the family remains deeply aware of the grief experienced by those who lost loved ones."Their hearts really go out to those who have lost loved ones," Martinez-Cid said.He hopes the investigation will eventually provide answers for everyone affected by the crash, regardless of whether they were aboard the plane or on the ground."They all suffer loss, and you have to respect each individual family member, and you have to respect each individual case and treat them all with the care and the respect that they deserve," he said.The NTSB investigation remains ongoing, and the cause of the crash has not been determined.

She was gifted, and my soulmate," Allan Filgueiras said Friday, fighting back tears as he remembered his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras.Nathalia was one of nine people killed Sunday when the aircraft crashed into Military Trail near 10th Avenue North in Greenacres, leaving a crater in the roadway and scattering debris across nearby homes and businesses. A driver on the ground was also injured.Five days later, wreckage remained at the scene as investigators continued working to determine what caused the crash.For Nathalia's father, the search for answers is deeply personal. But he wants the world to remember his daughter not for how she died, but for how she lived.Standing alongside his attorneys Friday, Filgueiras spoke publicly about his daughter's life, her love of aviation and the final moments he has replayed in his mind since the crash.His attorney, Stuart Grossman of Grossman, Yaffa & Cohen, said the family has retained legal counsel but has not filed a lawsuit."It is customary among law firms that the moment they file a lawsuit, to call a press conference," Grossman said. "This is not today's topic. We're suing no one yet."Instead, Grossman said the family wanted to express its condolences to the other eight families grieving loved ones and thank the National Transportation Safety Board for its ongoing investigation."We're not making allegations against anybody at this time," Grossman said. "We're going to do the right thing, and we're going to listen to what the government uncovers. Then we'll have our experts look at it and say they agree or not."But Grossman said the family's decision to speak publicly also serves another purpose: protecting Nathalia's reputation."The purpose of this is to preserve not just her memory but her reputation," Grossman said. "Nathalia was beyond an average pilot; she was extraordinary."Despite her young age, Grossman said Nathalia was highly trained and qualified to serve as co-pilot."She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years," he said.Grossman also addressed questions about how someone so young could be flying a jet."When you read that someone's 20 years old, and a co-pilot in a jet plane, you say, 'How can this be?'" Grossman said. "Well, wait until you see her hours, and what the government proves about her capabilities and what her instructors had to say."He described her death as a loss not only to her family but to the aviation community."This is a loss to aviation," Grossman said.Long before Nathalia was flying jets, she was a 12-year-old girl discovering her passion for aviation alongside her father.Allan, a pilot himself, introduced his daughter to flying before she was old enough to drive.Grossman said that the early bond between father and daughter made the tragedy even more painful."My client Allan, who is her father, was the reason why she flew," Grossman said. "From the time she was 12 years old, she, who was a pilot, Allan would take her up, and she fell in love with flying."As Nathalia grew older, that childhood passion became her career.Her father recalled how she would marvel at being paid to do something she loved so much."She said, 'Dad, can you believe? Can you believe that I would pay for this, but they're actually paying me,'" Filgueiras recalled. "It was her happiest moment to fly." Eventually, the roles between father and daughter reversed. Allan, who had once taught Nathalia to fly, found himself learning from her."When we were flying together, I used to instruct her, but then she became my instructor," he said. Now, the same father who taught Nathalia to fly is struggling to understand how her life ended.Filgueiras said he has listened repeatedly to air traffic control recordings from the aircraft's final moments, searching for answers. "I did listen to that many times, trying to find a clue in my head how that happened," he said. "And wow, she's tough."He said hearing his daughter's final moments left him proud of her determination."She made me so proud," Filgueiras said. "She showed me what it is to be a hero."The NTSB has not yet determined the cause of the crash. Investigators are examining the circumstances surrounding the aircraft's final flight.Grossman said the family's legal team intends to wait for the federal investigation before reaching its own conclusions."We'll let you know when the report comes out what our point of view is on it," he said.The attorney also acknowledged the families on the ground whose homes and lives were disrupted by the crash, expressing sympathy for those displaced while investigators continue their work.For now, Filgueiras is focused on remembering his daughter and finding a way forward for his wife and surviving children.Speaking partly in Spanish, he described the loss as having his heart ripped from his chest.He said he knows he must find a way to keep going for his family — and for Nathalia. "Nathalia doesn't want to see a father falling apart," he said in Spanish. "So I gotta — I'm gonna find a way. I'm gonna find a way to make her proud."He also recalled their spontaneous flights together, traveling to places like Key West and Naples just to grab a cup of coffee or something to eat.Those simple moments are now memories he will carry for the rest of his life.And while some families grieve privately, Filgueiras chose to share his heartbreak in front of cameras Friday — not to assign blame, but to honor the daughter he wishes he could have protected.When Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey asked what he would say to Nathalia if he could speak to her again, the grieving father broke down."I wanted to be by her side. To be by her teammates," he said through tears. "I had to be next to her."For a father who spent years sharing the skies with his daughter, it is the one flight he wishes he could have taken with her.The NTSB's investigation into the crash remains ongoing. No cause has yet been determined.

entry.title: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, most homes evacuated
entry.summary: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. 'If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies,' Del Toro said. Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff. WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Aerial video of flooding in the Creekside community of St. Lucie County Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power Light's equipment remains underwater. 'We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else,' FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. 'Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety.' Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high. Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede. Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: New $48 million Westlake elementary school stays on track despite heavy rain, flooding
entry.summary: A new elementary school in Westlake is quickly taking shape, with project leaders saying construction remains on time and on budget despite recent heavy rain and flooding. WPTV reporter Christy Waite first toured the construction site in August , when much of the school was still a concrete slab. She returned to the site on Friday and found a much different scene, with the building now taking shape. WATCH REPORT BELOW: PROGRESS ON WESTLAKES NEW SCHOOL Site Superintendent Brad Stapleton said recent weather created challenges for crews, with parts of the construction site underwater. 'We joked that we should have brought kayaks and canoes to work to get from our trailer and parking to the building because a lot of this area that we are standing in now was underwater,' Stapleton said. Despite those conditions, Stapleton said construction has stayed on track. 'We are looking great for meeting the August turnover for the next school year,' he said. Principal Darline Winewski has watched the school rise from the ground up and said seeing the individual spaces inside the building is making the project feel more real. 'To actually see the walls come up and really be able to see the individual spaces, I'm just so excited,' Winewski said. As Westlake continues to grow, the $48 million school will have room for 972 students in pre-K through fifth grade. Winewski said the new school will fill a need for families whose children currently attend two different schools. 'We really have a need for this school in our community. Our families deserve that. Our kids deserve that. They are going to two different schools right now,' Winewski said. Waite also connected with parent Krystal Lexima, whose daughter is looking forward to the new school opening. 'She's so excited to walk the halls for the first time,' Lexima said. Another milestone is coming soon. The school's official name, mascot and colors are expected to be revealed next month. 'We submitted our names to the board and we will find out soon enough and start identifying ourselves officially,' Winewski said.

entry.title: Father of 20-year-old pilot killed in Greenacres Learjet crash shares heartbreaking grief
entry.summary: Five days after a Learjet crashed into Military Trail , killing all nine people on board, the father of a 20-year-old co-pilot is breaking his silence, sharing his grief publicly for the first time and vowing to preserve his daughter's legacy. 'She was gifted. She was gifted, and my soulmate,' Allan Filgueiras said Friday, fighting back tears as he remembered his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Father of pilot killed in Learjet crash shares heartbreaking grief Nathalia was one of nine people killed Sunday when the aircraft crashed into Military Trail near 10th Avenue North in Greenacres, leaving a crater in the roadway and scattering debris across nearby homes and businesses. A driver on the ground was also injured. Five days later, wreckage remained at the scene as investigators continued working to determine what caused the crash. For Nathalia's father, the search for answers is deeply personal. But he wants the world to remember his daughter not for how she died, but for how she lived. 'She was extraordinary' Standing alongside his attorneys Friday, Filgueiras spoke publicly about his daughter's life, her love of aviation and the final moments he has replayed in his mind since the crash. His attorney, Stuart Grossman of Grossman, Yaffa Cohen, said the family has retained legal counsel but has not filed a lawsuit. 'It is customary among law firms that the moment they file a lawsuit, to call a press conference,' Grossman said. 'This is not today's topic. We're suing no one yet.' Instead, Grossman said the family wanted to express its condolences to the other eight families grieving loved ones and thank the National Transportation Safety Board for its ongoing investigation. 'We're not making allegations against anybody at this time,' Grossman said. 'We're going to do the right thing, and we're going to listen to what the government uncovers. Then we'll have our experts look at it and say they agree or not.' But Grossman said the family's decision to speak publicly also serves another purpose: protecting Nathalia's reputation. 'The purpose of this is to preserve not just her memory but her reputation,' Grossman said. 'Nathalia was beyond an average pilot; she was extraordinary.' Despite her young age, Grossman said Nathalia was highly trained and qualified to serve as co-pilot. 'She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years,' he said.

She was gifted, and my soulmate," Allan Filgueiras said Friday, fighting back tears as he remembered his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Nathalia was one of nine people killed Sunday when the aircraft crashed into Military Trail near 10th Avenue North in Greenacres, leaving a crater in the roadway and scattering debris across nearby homes and businesses. A driver on the ground was also injured.Five days later, wreckage remained at the scene as investigators continued working to determine what caused the crash.For Nathalia's father, the search for answers is deeply personal. But he wants the world to remember his daughter not for how she died, but for how she lived.Standing alongside his attorneys Friday, Filgueiras spoke publicly about his daughter's life, her love of aviation and the final moments he has replayed in his mind since the crash.His attorney, Stuart Grossman of Grossman, Yaffa & Cohen, said the family has retained legal counsel but has not filed a lawsuit."It is customary among law firms that the moment they file a lawsuit, to call a press conference," Grossman said. "This is not today's topic. We're suing no one yet."Instead, Grossman said the family wanted to express its condolences to the other eight families grieving loved ones and thank the National Transportation Safety Board for its ongoing investigation."We're not making allegations against anybody at this time," Grossman said. "We're going to do the right thing, and we're going to listen to what the government uncovers. Then we'll have our experts look at it and say they agree or not."But Grossman said the family's decision to speak publicly also serves another purpose: protecting Nathalia's reputation."The purpose of this is to preserve not just her memory but her reputation," Grossman said. "Nathalia was beyond an average pilot; she was extraordinary."Despite her young age, Grossman said Nathalia was highly trained and qualified to serve as co-pilot."She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years," he said.Grossman also addressed questions about how someone so young could be flying a jet."When you read that someone's 20 years old, and a co-pilot in a jet plane, you say, 'How can this be?'" Grossman said. "Well, wait until you see her hours, and what the government proves about her capabilities and what her instructors had to say."He described her death as a loss not only to her family but to the aviation community."This is a loss to aviation," Grossman said.Long before Nathalia was flying jets, she was a 12-year-old girl discovering her passion for aviation alongside her father.Allan, a pilot himself, introduced his daughter to flying before she was old enough to drive.Grossman said that the early bond between father and daughter made the tragedy even more painful."My client Allan, who is her father, was the reason why she flew," Grossman said. "From the time she was 12 years old, she, who was a pilot, Allan would take her up, and she fell in love with flying."As Nathalia grew older, that childhood passion became her career.Her father recalled how she would marvel at being paid to do something she loved so much."She said, 'Dad, can you believe? Can you believe that I would pay for this, but they're actually paying me,'" Filgueiras recalled. "It was her happiest moment to fly." Eventually, the roles between father and daughter reversed. Allan, who had once taught Nathalia to fly, found himself learning from her."When we were flying together, I used to instruct her, but then she became my instructor," he said. Now, the same father who taught Nathalia to fly is struggling to understand how her life ended.Filgueiras said he has listened repeatedly to air traffic control recordings from the aircraft's final moments, searching for answers. "I did listen to that many times, trying to find a clue in my head how that happened," he said. "And wow, she's tough."He said hearing his daughter's final moments left him proud of her determination."She made me so proud," Filgueiras said. "She showed me what it is to be a hero."The NTSB has not yet determined the cause of the crash. Investigators are examining the circumstances surrounding the aircraft's final flight.Grossman said the family's legal team intends to wait for the federal investigation before reaching its own conclusions."We'll let you know when the report comes out what our point of view is on it," he said.The attorney also acknowledged the families on the ground whose homes and lives were disrupted by the crash, expressing sympathy for those displaced while investigators continue their work.For now, Filgueiras is focused on remembering his daughter and finding a way forward for his wife and surviving children.Speaking partly in Spanish, he described the loss as having his heart ripped from his chest.He said he knows he must find a way to keep going for his family — and for Nathalia. "Nathalia doesn't want to see a father falling apart," he said in Spanish. "So I gotta — I'm gonna find a way. I'm gonna find a way to make her proud."He also recalled their spontaneous flights together, traveling to places like Key West and Naples just to grab a cup of coffee or something to eat.Those simple moments are now memories he will carry for the rest of his life.And while some families grieve privately, Filgueiras chose to share his heartbreak in front of cameras Friday — not to assign blame, but to honor the daughter he wishes he could have protected.When Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey asked what he would say to Nathalia if he could speak to her again, the grieving father broke down."I wanted to be by her side. To be by her teammates," he said through tears. "I had to be next to her."For a father who spent years sharing the skies with his daughter, it is the one flight he wishes he could have taken with her.The NTSB's investigation into the crash remains ongoing. No cause has yet been determined.

entry.title: NFL legends from the Dolphins and Lions honor military service members in Broward County
entry.summary: With the Miami Dolphins and Detroit Lions set to play Sunday, retired legends from both teams met up in Broward County for a little competition while honoring America's heroes. NFL legends from the Dolphins and Lions met up Friday to host military veterans for a fun day ahead of Sunday's showdown. The event saluted 50 active-duty service members through the NFL's Salute to Service. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Dolphins and Lions legends honor military members The service members were put to the test running the 40-yard dash, throwing drills and a shuttle drill. It was hard, but Michael Capozzi looked legit. 'You have insight from NFL legends, and it's cool to play with them and get insight on football. I really like playing, so any chance I get, I'll play,' Capozzi said. While Capozzi is still in his physical prime, you can't say the same about the former NFL guys. 'Hey, this is awesome man, and this is what it's all about for guys that have given so much to come back and give like we are,' retired Detroit Lions offensive lineman Lomas Brown said. 'This is two teams coming together to do a great job of entertaining our military and hanging out with them,' Nat Moore said. 'Well, everybody is having a blast, and the guys that can still run are out running.' 'You right, man big fella used to handle those drills; now I just look at them because I done got a little up there in age. I don't want to pull or tear anything,' Brown said. entry.title: Port St. Lucie grandmother grateful after flood rescue from van swept into canal - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie grandmother grateful after flood rescue from van swept into canal    WPEC
entry.article_text: Maria Andrade-Vasquez of Port St. Lucie has overcome plenty of challenges in her life. The mother of four, grandmother of 10, cancer survivor and dialysis patient never imagined a routine ride home from treatment would turn into a fight for survival. On Monday, Andrade-Vasquez was riding home from dialysis when floodwaters swept the transport van she was in off the road near Lakehurst Drive and into a canal in Port St. Lucie's Swan Park community. Speaking with CBS12 News through her son, Raul Morales, who translated from Spanish, Andrade-Vasquez said she feared she would not survive. "Yes, very, very scared," she said. Morales said as floodwaters rose around the van, his mother thought she might be living her final moments. Also see: Officer, firefighters rescue two from vehicle swept into Port St. Lucie canal "Seeing all the water go up, she was thinking, what's going to happen? Is this it?" Morales said. Police body camera video released this week shows how quickly first responders reacted. Lucie police said Officer Peterson arrived just 100 seconds after being dispatched to reports of a transport van that had gone into a canal off Southwest Hogan Street. Video captured the officer rushing into the water and rescuing the driver first before learning another passenger was still trapped inside. That passenger was Andrade-Vasquez. As water surrounded the vehicle, rescuers say the van tilted into the canal, leaving her trapped in the back. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the same wheelchair equipment used to help Andrade-Vasquez after dialysis treatments was now blocking her escape. "She's wheelchair bound, so the equipment that came out of the back of the van was up in place blocking her in," Niemczyk said. "They had to get her out of the wheelchair and pull her up over the equipment to get her out of the van." According to police, firefighters with St. Lucie County Fire District joined the officer at the scene and worked together to free Andrade-Vasquez from the vehicle. Morales said his mother still struggles to understand how rescuers were able to get her out so quickly. "She said, 'I don't know how they did it, but they quickly released her,'" Morales said. "To me it was amazing to see how quick they did what they did." Both Andrade-Vasquez and the driver were rescued safely. Her rescue was one of dozens of flood-related emergencies first responders handled as rainfall inundated roads and neighborhoods across Port St. Now recovering at home with her family, Andrade-Vasquez remains grateful to the first responders who helped save her life. The way I see it, you guys went the extra mile," Morales said. So thank you." Morales said his mother is still processing the trauma of the rescue but plans to continue her dialysis treatments three times a week as she focuses on her recovery.

entry.title: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, most homes evacuated - WFLX
entry.summary: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, most homes evacuated    WFLX
entry.article_text: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. "If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies," Del Toro said. Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff. WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power Light's equipment remains underwater. "We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else," FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. "Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety." Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high. Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede. Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

entry.title: 'Life turned upside down': Family retains attorney after losing home, livelihood in deadly Learjet crash
entry.summary: Nine people lost their lives when a Learjet crashed into Military Trail in Greenacres on Sunday. But the devastation extends beyond those on board, leaving at least one family on the ground without access to their home, their business and the life they knew before the crash. Now, that family has hired an attorney to investigate what went wrong and determine whether anyone could be held legally responsible. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Family retains attorney after losing home in Learjet crash Ricardo Martinez-Cid, a partner at Miami law firm Podhurst Orseck, told WPTV his clients were inside the area impacted by the crash when debris struck, injuring family members and sending them to the hospital. Their home was damaged and remains inaccessible. Their food truck, which they relied on for their livelihood, was also lost. 'We want to be really sensitive in talking about how this has impacted their lives because it's been horrific for them,' Martinez-Cid said. 'But they're sensitive to the fact that nine people lost their lives on board that aircraft, and this is a horrible tragedy.' Martinez-Cid said the family is now grappling with the emotional and financial consequences of a disaster they never saw coming. 'Although my clients, you know, lost their home, they lost their livelihood in the food truck that they operated. They were injured and went to the hospital, and they're dealing with the trauma of what they witnessed and experienced,' he said. 'They're lucky; they're blessed because nine folks lost their lives.' Searching for answers and accountability Martinez-Cid, a board-certified aviation attorney with more than two decades of experience, said his firm is conducting its own investigation into the crash. The goal is to determine what caused the Learjet to go down and whether any individual, company or other entity bears legal responsibility. 'You don't want to jump to conclusions,' Martinez-Cid said. 'But in every aviation disaster ... you're really looking at man, the machine and the environment.' That means examining several potential factors, including weather conditions, pilot decisions, air traffic control communications and the aircraft's mechanical performance. 'We're looking at the weather, we're looking at the piloting, we're looking at how the aircraft responds, we're looking at the communications between the tower and with the pilots,' he said. 'We're going to look very closely at how the aircraft responded to what was going on as well.' Martinez-
entry.article_text: So families need to get their own answers."Martinez-Cid said his firm plans to work with aviation experts to independently analyze available data, including communications, weather information and the aircraft's performance."So we look at it from all angles, and we make sure our experts get all the data that they can," he said.Martinez-Cid confirmed his firm has also been in contact with attorneys connected to families of people killed aboard the Learjet."We've been contacted by, which is often the case, attorneys that either are friends with the family or have been contacted by the family because of our expertise globally on these issues," he said. "And so we've been speaking to some."He said those conversations are not necessarily limited to potential lawsuits."We have experts that can talk to the families and explain the different things that they're hearing and what's going on, and I think that's an important thing for the family to have."Martinez-Cid previously served as lead counsel for death and injury cases stemming from the 2021 Champlain Towers South condominium collapse in Surfside.He said that experience reinforced the importance of recognizing the different kinds of losses families endure after a disaster.For the family Martinez-Cid represents in Greenacres, the immediate future remains uncertain.Their home is inaccessible, their source of income is gone, and they are recovering from injuries and the trauma of witnessing a deadly plane crash.Martinez-Cid declined to identify the family, saying they are still struggling emotionally with the aftermath.But he emphasized that while his clients recognize how fortunate they are to have survived, their lives have been permanently changed."Their life has been turned upside down," he said. "They're going to be living with this trauma forever. They've lost their livelihood."Still, he said the family remains deeply aware of the grief experienced by those who lost loved ones."Their hearts really go out to those who have lost loved ones," Martinez-Cid said.He hopes the investigation will eventually provide answers for everyone affected by the crash, regardless of whether they were aboard the plane or on the ground."They all suffer loss, and you have to respect each individual family member, and you have to respect each individual case and treat them all with the care and the respect that they deserve," he said.The NTSB investigation remains ongoing, and the cause of the crash has not been determined.

entry.title: Viral video of student swimming home raises safety concerns in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: Viral video of student swimming home raises safety concerns in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: A viral video showing a student swimming home from a school bus in flooded Port St. Lucie streets has raised questions about why schools opened during Monday’s severe weather. The video, filmed in a neighborhood where water has since receded, shows the student navigating deep floodwaters after exiting the bus. "He literally almost went completely underwater," said Lucinda Lopez, a Port St. Another neighbor, Ariel Abel, described the scene: "We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water." The incident has left parents questioning why schools opened on Monday despite the flooding. Concerns include why buses were sent into severely flooded streets and whether students should have sheltered in place at school until conditions improved. "Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay," Lopez said. Abel added, "They really dropped the ball on this. The community is disappointed." On Tuesday, St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince addressed the situation during a news conference, apologizing to families for the district’s response. The first flood advisory for the county came in just after 8 a.m. Monday, with the first flash flood warning issued at 10:41 a.m. "I completely understand the frustration families feel," Prince said. "It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry." Despite the apology, some parents remain unsatisfied. "An apology doesn’t fix what is happening," Abel said. Lopez emphasized the need for change: "We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs." WPBF is working to hear from the school district to address these concerns and questions. entry.title: Thomas Markle, father of Meghan Markle, arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse material in Florida
entry.summary: Thomas Wayne Markle, the father of Meghan Markle, was arrested Friday morning at an assisted living facility in Lakeland, Florida, on a federal charge of possessing child pornography after investigators said they found suspected child sexual abuse material in two Los Angeles-area storage units he had rented for nearly two decades. The 82-year-old Lakeland resident is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to federal prosecutors. He was expected to make his initial appearance Friday in federal court in Tampa. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Meghan Markle's father arrested in Florida The FBI investigation began after authorities learned in October that a person had signed an affidavit describing the discovery of suspected child sexual abuse material among Thomas Markle's belongings in the Philippines, according to an affidavit filed with the criminal complaint. Investigators later learned Thomas Markle rented a storage unit in the Los Angeles area. Information provided by the person who reported the material in the Philippines eventually led authorities to a second storage unit, according to the affidavit. Federal agents obtained search warrants for both units, which investigators said Thomas Markle had rented since 2008. According to prosecutors, his most recent payments for the units were made through automatic payments last month. During searches of the units, FBI agents seized roughly 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books containing suspected child sexual abuse material, according to the news release. Federal authorities allege some of the photographs show an adult man, identified by a witness as Thomas Markle, with prepubescent girls. Investigators said other photographs appeared to depict Markle with children in various stages of undress. 'These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law,' First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.summary: Vitalia evacuations paused overnight as crews pump floodwater in Port St. Lucie    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community as dangerous waters continue to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. I think it's part of living in Florida," said Sheri George, a Vitalia resident. Sheri George and her husband Arthur were evacuated by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission on a swamp buggy Wednesday. They had no electricity, no A/C and the food in their refrigerator was spoiling. They were unable to drive out of the neighborhood because roads were flooded. They were thrilled FWC could get them safely out of the neighborhood. This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer," Sheri George said. "I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me," said Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident who was evacuated because of flooding. According to FWC, since Tuesday they've evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater in several areas in St. "I love being able to, when we're at our worst times being able to come and give somebody some ray of hope," said Jon Arnold, an FWC investigator who was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia. "I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety," said Tyson Matthews, FWC Public Information Officer. Lucie Police Department said officers and emergency personnel were helping residents affected by ongoing flooding get to safety. The department urged people to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents told CBS12 they were effectively trapped in their homes and unable to get their cars out of their driveways because of flooded streets. Some said water reached their garages but did not enter their homes. CBS12 also observed water 18 inches deep in the street. See also: Two injured, third person believed dead after helicopter crash near Key Biscayne The flooding has continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. Lucie received 16.7 inches of rain from Nov. Lucie County received between 7 and 17 inches during that period, according to the National Weather Service. Residents told CBS12 the flooding was the worst they had seen in their neighborhood. Police urged residents to never drive or walk through floodwaters, follow evacuation instructions, stay away from closed roads and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones if they can do so safely. As of Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District says it has responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide. In the Vitalia community, the City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department has installed a 12-inch pump, which began operating at approximately 8:00 p.m. tonight, the fire district said. The pump is moving an estimated 7,000 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce flooding in the neighborhood. Additionally, SLCFD says routine evacuation operations in Vitalia have been suspended overnight and are scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Emergency responders remain available for fire and medical emergencies. Residents experiencing immediate safety or serious medical concerns requiring assistance should call 911.

entry.article_text: Votes are still being counted in Mississippi, in the tight senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.Part of the delay in counting is because thousands of voters cast their ballots by affidavit rather than a traditional ballot. Many voters said they were caught by surprise when they learned they would have to vote by affidavit because their registration was marked inactive. “It was very disheartening to be labeled inactive,” voter Kevin Green, a Mississippi voter, told Scripps News this week. “And there was no real rationale behind it.”Green said he has voted consistently since moving back to his home state of Mississippi in 2020. He said he received a notice from the NAACP telling him to look up his registration status in the days before the election. When he did, he was shocked to see his status was inactive. After speaking to the county clerk, he learned he would have to vote by affidavit because he had not responded to a mailer seeking to verify his address. After successfully voting on Election Day by affidavit, Green posted about his experience on social media. “We know there was some shady business going on there,” Green told Scripps News, pointing to the state’s history of disenfranchising Black voters. “It's really not a good look for our state when we've come so far, and the fact that this election is now so close speaks volumes about where we've come.”Ralph Sandidge said he was disappointed to find out he had been purged from the voter rolls when he arrived to cast his ballot this year.“I said, ‘Well, who did that? Under what authority?’” Sandidge said. Sandidge said he was told he was no longer registered to vote because he had not voted in several elections. Election experts told Scripps News the large number of inactive voters this election in Mississippi may be due in part to the state’s reliance on consumer data provided by Experian to maintain its voter rolls. The state used the data to check voter addresses, but experts said the data may have contained errors affecting thousands of voters. “Everything we've heard from the Secretary of State's office is that this was a good faith effort to keep the voter rolls accurate,” said Daniel Griffith, the senior director of policy at Secure Democracy. “Because it wasn't based on the best practices, and because the credit agency data is not reliable, it has had an unfortunate outcome for a lot of individuals.”Thomas Minor said he encountered such an error when he attempted to vote in the primary election earlier this year. He told Scripps News the clerk told him his registration was inactivated because Experian data said he lived in another city. However, he told Scripps News, he has not moved for a decade. He was able to fix the error and vote normally during the general election on Tuesday but was dismayed to see so many other voters encounter the same problem he had months ago. “It feels like somebody’s trying to pull strings somewhere and mess things up,” Minor said. “We have no evidence that there is something sinister (happening), and election officials are very, very careful and very committed to protect elections and not disenfranchise voters,” said Thessalia Merivaki, a distinguished professor of government at Washington State University. “Sometimes your data are bad, and this is what happens.”An Experian spokesperson said its company has not provided services to the state since 2025.“The solution provided at that time consisted of supplemental address information and was not designed or intended to validate voter records,” said Scott Anderson, vice president of corporate communications for Experian, in a statement sent Friday to Scripps News. “Decisions regarding voter registration policies, procedures and record updates are made solely by election officials in accordance with applicable local, state and federal laws.”The Mississippi Secretary of State’s Office did not respond to multiple voice messages and emails from Scripps News.RELATED STORY | Democrat clings to razor-thin lead in Mississippi Senate raceIn a Friday interview with Democracy Docket, Colom criticized the state for its use of Experian data and said voters experiencing ballot problems should contact his campaign for help. Merivaki said she expects the Secretary of State’s office will investigate what went wrong. In the meantime, election clerks across Mississippi are counting affidavit ballots to determine the winners of Tuesday’s election. Voters who provided identification and voted by affidavit do not need to take any further action for their votes to be counted. Those who did not have ID with them have until Tuesday to rectify their affidavits. The Secretary of State’s office posted a tracker online for voters who voted absentee or by affidavit to ensure their ballot is being counted.Kevin Green said he’s happy to know his vote will count, but wants the process to change going forward. “Obviously there are some gaps there, and we need to revisit that and ensure that we have effective policies that are in place,” he said.

entry.article_text: Nearly a week after a Learjet crash killed nine people in Greenacres and forced hundreds from their homes, some residents are still waiting for an answer to the question that has consumed their lives since the crash.For those who haven't been allowed to return, the cost of being displaced is adding up.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "When are they going to let us back home?" Joseph Santana Quiroz asked WPTV.He hasn't been allowed home all week.He told WPTV he has also had to miss work without pay."If you can't work, they can't pay you?" WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked."Exactly," Santana Quiroz said.But even without a paycheck, the bills don't stop."We can't tell the bank we can't pay because this happened," Santana Quiroz said.He is one of 31 people still sheltering at the Greenacres Community Center as the investigation continues.Now, organizations are stepping in to help with everything from those immediate financial pressures to the challenges residents could face when they are finally allowed back home.The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched the People First Fund for Green Acres Mobile Home Community Learjet Crash to provide direct financial assistance to eligible residents impacted by the crash."We actually are ready and prepared to start taking in grant applications at this time," said Josselyn Hodges, director of the People First Fund Initiative at Emergency Assistance Foundation.She told WPTV the organization normally responds to disasters and hardships around the world, but this time the need is close to home."We are a global public charity that does financial assistance to impacted individuals after disasters around the world. However, we're headquartered here in West Palm Beach, so we felt compelled to help our neighbors," Hodges said.The organization plans to provide $1,000 cash grants to eligible individuals, allowing residents to decide where that money is needed most."Our goal is to be able to provide that financial assistance so people can take care of their most urgent self-assessed needs," Hodges said. "We understand that when people get displaced from their homes, you know, they experience financial hardship in seeking temporary housing, in seeking food and other personal hardships."Hodges said the cash assistance is intended to complement the food, shelter and other services being provided by different organizations."While there may be other organizations that support with food or housing, you know, this financial assistance and cash assistance that will be, you know, landing directly into the hands of individuals is meant to be able to help those individuals, you know, take, you know, buy supplies or take care of whatever items are, you know, heaviest in their mind at this time," Hodges said.Through donations from community foundations and individual donors, Hodges said the fund currently has enough money to provide $1,000 grants to 18 people.But the organization wants to go further."We understand that there are about 68 impacted individuals from the mobile home community, the Green Acres mobile home community, so we are calling on to the community to come together and be able to, you know, turn that compassion into tangible support and help us reach every single one of these members," Hodges said.Hodges said the goal is to raise enough money to provide a grant to all 68 individuals the organization has identified.Residents looking for assistance won't simply have to navigate the process on their own. Hodges said EAF is working with members of the Emergency Operations Center to identify people with the greatest needs and provide them with a direct link to apply.For residents who don't know when they'll be able to return home, Hodges said the goal is to provide some immediate relief while other assistance is still coming together."We believe in the power of community. We know that people wanna come together and help community members in the wake of hardships and disasters, so we have a way to be able to provide that immediate impact now while other resources are still mobilizing," Hodges said. "That is our goal, to be able to support people in the very first critical days of their recovery process."Preparing for what happens when residents return homeThe financial fallout may not end when people are finally able to return.State Rep. Debra Tendrich is working through her organization, Eat Better Live Better, to prepare for another expense some families could face: replacing spoiled food."If you look at what's happening with their electricity being cut off and the power grid shut down, you're looking at people returning to their homes and having to throw out their entire refrigerator full of food that they might have just purchased or or that they need to fill now," Tendrich said.For families already dealing with displacement and lost income, Tendrich wants to make replacing those groceries one less thing they have to worry about."I'm really working right now to make sure that we are able to help fill those refrigerators," Tendrich said.Tendrich's nonprofit operates an affordable farmers market-style food pantry with fresh and healthy items.She said her organization was already seeing an increased demand for grocery assistance before the crash."We, we've been seeing an increased need as is. My organization has received between 25 and 100 new applications every week needing grocery assistance," Tendrich said. "So to pile that up with having to now, have your entire refrigerator needs to be thrown out and then also replenish that just doubles down on how hard times are right now for my community."For Tendrich, it's about helping families move toward some sense of normalcy after days of uncertainty."The last thing that you want to worry about is how are you going to feed yourself, your family and your children after a tragedy like this," Tendrich said.Tendrich said displaced families are also dealing with needs that can easily be overlooked during a prolonged evacuation, including getting to doctor's appointments and accessing medications."Families with their children are trying to get to doctor's appointments, get their medications that they need, uh, we're really trying to make sure that people are accessing everything they need at this moment to get through this while they're displaced from their homes," Tendrich said. "We're doing everything we can between the county, the police, the fire and my office. We're working hard to make sure not only while you're, you're displaced, but once you get back home, we're trying to make sure that you're supported as much as possible during this, this tough time."While groups are getting to work countywide, help continues while families wait as other organizations are addressing needs at the shelter itself.Many other organizations like the Red Cross, and community members have dropped off supplies this week.Dare to Care has been providing mobile showers and laundry services at the Greenacres Community Center."They called us on Monday and said, ‘Can you come out?’ We've been here ever since," said Timothy Murphy, with the organization Dare to Care. "My message to residents is that there are people who care. We're here for those in need no matter what," he said. "When crisis happen it just complies, so we're here to relieve some of the loss."It remains unclear how long all of the impacted residents will be displaced.Click here if you'd like to help make monetary donations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Who will lead Congress? Leadership battles take center stage after midterms
entry.summary: With Democrats poised to take control of both chambers of Congress, attention is quickly turning from the 2026 midterm elections to the leadership battles that will determine who guides the new House and Senate majorities. Leadership elections are expected to begin next week, with Democrats facing some internal pressure over their current leaders and House Republicans preparing for a potentially tight contest of their own. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries are expected to remain at the top of their respective caucuses. Jeffries would be in position to become House speaker, while Schumer would become Senate majority leader. Both, however, have faced calls from some progressive activists and incoming lawmakers for a change in leadership. Critics argue Democratic leaders did not push back aggressively enough against President Donald Trump while the party was in the minority. entry.title: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street gang has led to nearly 40 arrests and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash, law enforcement officials said Thursday. The multi-agency investigation, called Operation Score Board, focused on alleged gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas. Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also found that gang members allegedly kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. "Hundreds of shootings over the last decade, violent crime terrorizing the north end of this county, and our community deserves better, and they're getting better because of the hard work of the men and women with the special investigation units that the chief mentioned, and our federal partners here," said Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Officials said about 70 to 80 people are documented as members of the gang. The investigation focused on people police described as shot callers who allegedly directed its activities. Authorities said the 23rd Street gang has been a problem in the Fort Pierce area for decades and was the most violent of several gangs in the city. 4, officers served five search warrants four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie beginning around 5 a.m. The operation led to 11 arrests on racketeering charges, with two people still wanted on warrants, and four additional probable-cause arrests, officials said. Authorities said some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages. 4 searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474. Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV. "We remain committed to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those responsible for bringing violence and criminal activity into our neighborhoods," Chief Smith said. "Our message is clear: We will not tolerate organized criminal activity that threatens the safety of our residents." Authorities did not identify the people they believe led the gang, but said they believe they have arrested most of the key players. They said some people connected to the investigation have faced murder charges, but declined to discuss active cases. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro called the operation an unusually large collaboration among local, state and federal agencies. He said investigators took significant players off the streets and that more operations are expected. The sheriff said the case took extensive work to connect years of records and evidence, and involved a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case. History of problems CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized.

entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.title: Boynton Beach police seek driver who ran over, killed 6-month-old puppy
entry.summary: Police are asking for the public's help identifying a driver after a 6-month-old dog was found dead in a Boynton Beach parking lot earlier this week. Shortly after 2:30 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3, Boynton Beach Police received a report of a dead dog in a parking space at the back of a parking lot at 1500 Southwest 8th Street. WATCH VIDEO BELOW: Police seek driver after puppy found dead in Boynton Beach An animal cruelty officer responded and found a small white dog that appeared to have been run over, according to police. Investigators described the dog as a female Jack Russell Terrier, approximately 6 months old, with white fur and light tan or brown spots. Detectives obtained surveillance video that police said shows a dark-colored sedan, believed to possibly be a Tesla, entering the parking lot at about 1:35 p.m. According to police, the driver parked and got out before walking around the back of the vehicle toward the passenger side. The dog was then seen walking from the passenger side toward the front of the vehicle while the driver walked back around the car and returned to the driver's seat. Police said the dog then walked back toward the passenger side of the vehicle. At about 1:38 p.m., the sedan drove away. The dog was subsequently seen lying motionless on the ground, according to investigators. Police have not identified the driver, and the news release did not specify whether investigators believe the dog was struck intentionally. Detectives are asking anyone who saw anything suspicious near 1500 Southwest 8th Street on Nov. 3, or anyone who recognizes the driver or dog, to contact Detective Sala at 561-742-6818 or SalaN@bbfl.us.
