entry.title: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey
entry.summary: St. Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie, St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. Lucie County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County asks residents to report flood damage County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. 20. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roads, leaving drivers stranded County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

entry.summary: Flooding shuts down South 25th Street near two St. Lucie County schools    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Flooding continues to plague St. Lucie County roads, with officials closing a stretch of South 25th Street near two schools as the district extends school closures through Thursday. Lucie County announced Wednesday that South 25th Street is closed to through traffic between Fort Pierce Central High School at Cobra Pride Way and the entrance to Forest Grove Middle School at Bulldog Drive. County officials said the closure is due to unsafe road conditions caused by flooding. See also: Evacuations underway as flooding swamps Port St. Lucie neighborhood The road closure comes as St. Lucie Public Schools announced that schools will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, for another day as the county continues dealing with widespread flooding. entry.title: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street gang has led to nearly 40 arrests and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash, law enforcement officials said Thursday. The multi-agency investigation, called Operation Score Board, focused on alleged gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas. Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also found that gang members allegedly kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. "Hundreds of shootings over the last decade, violent crime terrorizing the north end of this county, and our community deserves better, and they're getting better because of the hard work of the men and women with the special investigation units that the chief mentioned, and our federal partners here," said Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Officials said about 70 to 80 people are documented as members of the gang. The investigation focused on people police described as shot callers who allegedly directed its activities. Authorities said the 23rd Street gang has been a problem in the Fort Pierce area for decades and was the most violent of several gangs in the city. 4, officers served five search warrants four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie beginning around 5 a.m. The operation led to 11 arrests on racketeering charges, with two people still wanted on warrants, and four additional probable-cause arrests, officials said. Authorities said some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages. 4 searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474. Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV. "We remain committed to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those responsible for bringing violence and criminal activity into our neighborhoods," Chief Smith said. "Our message is clear: We will not tolerate organized criminal activity that threatens the safety of our residents." Authorities did not identify the people they believe led the gang, but said they believe they have arrested most of the key players. They said some people connected to the investigation have faced murder charges, but declined to discuss active cases. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro called the operation an unusually large collaboration among local, state and federal agencies. He said investigators took significant players off the streets and that more operations are expected. The sheriff said the case took extensive work to connect years of records and evidence, and involved a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case. History of problems CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized.

entry.title: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue    WPBF
entry.article_text: Floodwaters are receding in Indian River County, but some areas remain affected by standing water as crews and officials work to address the aftermath of this week’s severe downpours. Law enforcement officials said County Roads 510 and 512 were reduced to one lane at one point due to flooding. Crews installed an emergency pipe under the roadway Thursday night to help drain the area. Dave Kubacki, a resident of Sebastian, shared cellphone video of the flooding outside his home. "Holy smoke, I can't believe how much water was out there, and I can't believe how fast it disappeared," Kubacki said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates He said he was surprised by the flooding, noting that the only time it had been this bad was during a hurricane. "The hurricanes were bad, but I've never seen rain come down like this for such a long period of time and so heavy," Kubacki said. Officials shared video of flooded roads taken just after the severe downpours, along with body camera footage showing deputies responding to incidents caused by the high water. Deputies were called to a residential driveway to secure an alligator that had been pushed out of its usual habitat by the flooding. The alligator was safely relocated to another area within the county. County leaders said assessment teams were out Friday surveying the damage, and results are still pending. Schools in Indian River County were closed Friday but are expected to reopen Monday. Kubacki said he shared the news with his granddaughter. "I said, 'Are you mad that schools are closed?' and she said, 'Oh no!' I said, 'What about your friends?' She said, 'That's OK, I'll see them on Monday,'" Kubacki said. Officials are reminding residents to avoid flooded roads as cleanup efforts continue. entry.title: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: Five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still dealing with several feet of standing water inside their homes, with little indication of when it will recede. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, with floodwaters reaching mailboxes and entering most homes along the road. For longtime resident Linda Weisbecker, the flooding has left decades of memories and belongings underwater. “Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said. Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, preventing her from beginning the cleanup process. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials told WPBF 25 News that crews will be working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. entry.title: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary seeks help after historic flooding
entry.summary: Save the Chimps, a 150-acre chimpanzee sanctuary in Fort Pierce, is asking the community for help after historic flooding left parts of its property underwater, damaged equipment and disrupted normal operations. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary seeks help after historic flooding The sanctuary's more than 200 chimpanzees are safe and continue to receive food, medication, enrichment and other daily care, according to Mark Yohannan, the organization's director of facilities. But Yohannan told WPTV the sanctuary faces a long recovery after receiving 19 inches of rain. 'We've got a long way to go,' Yohannan said. He said it is the worst flooding the sanctuary has experienced in its 25 years in Fort Pierce. 'We're absolutely shut down until we get the water gone,' Yohannan said. Staff adapts to care for chimpanzees Since Tuesday, Save the Chimps staff members have had to find new ways to reach parts of the flooded sanctuary. Workers have used tractors and trailers to navigate the property and deliver supplies. Video shared with WPTV shows staff using a drone to drop food to a chimpanzee during the flooding. Despite the difficult conditions, Yohannan said the chimpanzees have continued receiving their normal care. 'They're doing great. The care staff have been on their game,' Yohannan said. 'They're getting everything they would get normally: enrichment, all their food, all their medication, blankets. They haven't missed a beat.' Yohannan said some staff members have been unable to get to work because of the flooding, but those who can reach the sanctuary have come together to keep operations moving. 'It's heavy, but it's good heavy,' Yohannan said. 'Everyone's come together.' Flooding damages vehicles and equipment The flooding has also taken a toll on equipment used for everyday operations. Yohannan said nearly 15 golf carts used to transport food, supplies and staff around the 150-acre property have broken down. 'We'd seen the water and we figured, well, no big deal, we'll drive through it, and that became impossible immediately,' he said. Yohannan said the sanctuary is looking for taller four-wheel-drive vehicles that can safely move people and supplies through the property while floodwaters remain. 'We need four-wheel-drive vehicles that are taller that can move supplies and people,' Yohannan said. He said the vehicles could be rented or donated for a short period. "Everyone's come together."Flooding damages vehicles and equipmentThe flooding has also taken a toll on equipment used for everyday operations.Yohannan said nearly 15 golf carts used to transport food, supplies and staff around the 150-acre property have broken down."We'd seen the water and we figured, well, no big deal, we'll drive through it, and that became impossible immediately," he said.Yohannan said the sanctuary is looking for taller four-wheel-drive vehicles that can safely move people and supplies through the property while floodwaters remain."We need four-wheel-drive vehicles that are taller that can move supplies and people," Yohannan said. He said the vehicles could be rented or donated for a short period.Save the Chimps asks community for helpAs the sanctuary works to recover, staff members are preparing to bring their concerns to the St. Lucie County Commission at a meeting next week.In the meantime, Save the Chimps is asking the community for support, including temporary access to vehicles and financial donations."A donation goes a long way," Yohannan said.Even as employees deal with challenges at the sanctuary, Yohannan acknowledged that some staff members and Treasure Coast residents are facing flooding problems of their own."There's a lot of people, including our own staff, that have much bigger problems with this water than we have here," he said. "Nobody brings that with them. They just get together, we get to work. We work on that plan, we execute."For a sanctuary that has called Fort Pierce home for 25 years, Yohannan said community support could make a meaningful difference as the water recedes and the recovery continues.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.title: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street gang has led to nearly 40 arrests and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash, law enforcement officials said Thursday. The multi-agency investigation, called Operation Score Board, focused on alleged gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas. Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also found that gang members allegedly kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. "Hundreds of shootings over the last decade, violent crime terrorizing the north end of this county, and our community deserves better, and they're getting better because of the hard work of the men and women with the special investigation units that the chief mentioned, and our federal partners here," said Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Officials said about 70 to 80 people are documented as members of the gang. The investigation focused on people police described as shot callers who allegedly directed its activities. Authorities said the 23rd Street gang has been a problem in the Fort Pierce area for decades and was the most violent of several gangs in the city. 4, officers served five search warrants four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie beginning around 5 a.m. The operation led to 11 arrests on racketeering charges, with two people still wanted on warrants, and four additional probable-cause arrests, officials said. Authorities said some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages. 4 searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474. Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV. "We remain committed to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those responsible for bringing violence and criminal activity into our neighborhoods," Chief Smith said. "Our message is clear: We will not tolerate organized criminal activity that threatens the safety of our residents." Authorities did not identify the people they believe led the gang, but said they believe they have arrested most of the key players. They said some people connected to the investigation have faced murder charges, but declined to discuss active cases. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro called the operation an unusually large collaboration among local, state and federal agencies. He said investigators took significant players off the streets and that more operations are expected. The sheriff said the case took extensive work to connect years of records and evidence, and involved a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case. History of problems CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized.

entry.title: Martin County flooding leaves cattle farmers struggling, residents demanding solutions - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County flooding leaves cattle farmers struggling, residents demanding solutions    WPBF
entry.article_text: Floodwaters continue to inundate properties in Martin County, leaving cattle farmers struggling to care for their animals and residents concerned about how much longer the water will remain. Residents in the Trailside community say water from neighboring properties is flowing into their drainage system, causing widespread flooding. Flooding threatens cattle, farm operations Hungryland Farms normally operates a 20-acre rotational grazing system for its Florida Cracker cattle. The owner, Melissa, said much of the pasture is now underwater, forcing the animals onto the farm’s elevated driveway. "We're starting to lose big sections of the driveway. We have them concentrated up the house pad, but if we lose too much more, we're just going to have to figure out a way to evacuate them somewhere," she said. Some cattle have struggled to navigate the water, and Melissa said the farm is concerned about losing access to its property as flooding continues. For now, the farm is bringing in hay and hay cubes to keep the cattle on their regular diet while monitoring potential health risks from floodwaters. "We’re more just concerned with the health and safety of our cattle," Melissa said. Melissa said the farm has an emergency contact with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service if the animals face imminent danger. "We don’t know how long we’re going to be here," she said. HOA says solution is unclear Kyla Shay, president of the Trailside Homeowners Association, said the community’s drainage system is designed to handle water from its 41 lots and designated neighboring properties. However, Shay said water from outside that system is now flowing through county-owned land and other neighboring properties before reaching the community’s southern canal. We can’t handle theirs," Shay said. The flooding has also affected neighboring pastures and reached areas near Bridge Road and an electrical substation, according to Shay. She said some electrical transformers are partially underwater, septic systems are overwhelmed and residents have been warned their well water could be compromised. "The health department issued warnings this morning to me that our water wells could be compromised because of bacteria, because of the standing water," Shay said. Since their septic systems are submerged, Shay said homeowners have been unable to shower or do laundry. County says repairs must wait WPBF 25 News reached out to Martin County about their concerns and learned the county recently acquired approximately 315 acres of land in the area, known as the Elise J. A county spokesperson said establishing access has been their immediate priority so staff can assess conditions and respond. The county said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District to address a breach affecting drainage into its irrigation canal and that the agencies jointly determined repairs should wait until water levels recede. The county said current conditions make hauling and placing sand unsafe and potentially damaging to the levee. Material could also wash into the canal before crews establish a stable repair. "County staff will continue to monitor water levels and site conditions in close coordination with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District," a county spokesperson said. The county said it will move forward with repairs when conditions allow safe work without compromising the levee. It is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce the risk of flooding happening again. Residents want a long-term solution Shay said the homeowners association has been working with water engineers and other experts to understand how long the flooding could last. "It's probably going to be late January, February before we can see a break, and that's assuming that the south canal wall does not collapse and immediately dump all the water on us," she said. Melissa said the farm’s drainage system normally provides room for water to collect during the rainy season, but the amount coming from outside the property has overwhelmed it. "We have a very extensive drainage system, but it’s just not equipped to handle this amount of water," Melissa said. Both women said they want neighboring properties and the agencies responsible for drainage to address the problem. For now, Martin County said it will continue monitoring conditions and coordinating with the conservancy district before attempting repairs. Meanwhile, Melissa said the farm is focused on keeping its cattle safe as water continues to surround the property.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: Five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still dealing with several feet of standing water inside their homes, with little indication of when it will recede. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, with floodwaters reaching mailboxes and entering most homes along the road. For longtime resident Linda Weisbecker, the flooding has left decades of memories and belongings underwater. “Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said. Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, preventing her from beginning the cleanup process. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials told WPBF 25 News that crews will be working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. entry.article_text: Nearly a week after a Learjet crash killed nine people in Greenacres and forced hundreds from their homes, some residents are still waiting for an answer to the question that has consumed their lives since the crash.For those who haven't been allowed to return, the cost of being displaced is adding up.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "When are they going to let us back home?" Joseph Santana Quiroz asked WPTV.He hasn't been allowed home all week.He told WPTV he has also had to miss work without pay."If you can't work, they can't pay you?" WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked."Exactly," Santana Quiroz said.But even without a paycheck, the bills don't stop."We can't tell the bank we can't pay because this happened," Santana Quiroz said.He is one of 31 people still sheltering at the Greenacres Community Center as the investigation continues.Now, organizations are stepping in to help with everything from those immediate financial pressures to the challenges residents could face when they are finally allowed back home.The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched the People First Fund for Green Acres Mobile Home Community Learjet Crash to provide direct financial assistance to eligible residents impacted by the crash."We actually are ready and prepared to start taking in grant applications at this time," said Josselyn Hodges, director of the People First Fund Initiative at Emergency Assistance Foundation.She told WPTV the organization normally responds to disasters and hardships around the world, but this time the need is close to home."We are a global public charity that does financial assistance to impacted individuals after disasters around the world. However, we're headquartered here in West Palm Beach, so we felt compelled to help our neighbors," Hodges said.The organization plans to provide $1,000 cash grants to eligible individuals, allowing residents to decide where that money is needed most."Our goal is to be able to provide that financial assistance so people can take care of their most urgent self-assessed needs," Hodges said. "We understand that when people get displaced from their homes, they experience financial hardship in seeking temporary housing, in seeking food and other personal hardships."Hodges said the cash assistance is intended to complement the food, shelter and other services being provided by different organizations."While there may be other organizations that support with food or housing, this financial assistance and cash assistance that will be, landing directly into the hands of individuals is meant to be able to help those individuals, take, buy supplies or take care of whatever items are, heaviest in their mind at this time," Hodges said.Through donations from community foundations and individual donors, Hodges said the fund currently has enough money to provide $1,000 grants to 18 people.But the organization wants to go further."We understand that there are about 68 impacted individuals from the mobile home community, the Green Acres mobile home community, so we are calling on to the community to come together and be able to, turn that compassion into tangible support and help us reach every single one of these members," Hodges said.Hodges said the goal is to raise enough money to provide a grant to all 68 individuals the organization has identified.Residents looking for assistance won't simply have to navigate the process on their own. Hodges said EAF is working with members of the Emergency Operations Center to identify people with the greatest needs and provide them with a direct link to apply.For residents who don't know when they'll be able to return home, Hodges said the goal is to provide some immediate relief while other assistance is still coming together."We believe in the power of community. We know that people wanna come together and help community members in the wake of hardships and disasters, so we have a way to be able to provide that immediate impact now while other resources are still mobilizing," Hodges said. "That is our goal, to be able to support people in the very first critical days of their recovery process."Preparing for what happens when residents return homeThe financial fallout may not end when people are finally able to return.State Rep. Debra Tendrich is working through her organization, Eat Better Live Better, to prepare for another expense some families could face: replacing spoiled food."If you look at what's happening with their electricity being cut off and the power grid shut down, you're looking at people returning to their homes and having to throw out their entire refrigerator full of food that they might have just purchased or or that they need to fill now," Tendrich said.For families already dealing with displacement and lost income, Tendrich wants to make replacing those groceries one less thing they have to worry about."I'm really working right now to make sure that we are able to help fill those refrigerators," Tendrich said.Tendrich's nonprofit operates an affordable farmers market-style food pantry with fresh and healthy items.She said her organization was already seeing an increased demand for grocery assistance before the crash."We, we've been seeing an increased need as is. My organization has received between 25 and 100 new applications every week needing grocery assistance," Tendrich said. "So to pile that up with having to now, have your entire refrigerator needs to be thrown out and then also replenish that just doubles down on how hard times are right now for my community."For Tendrich, it's about helping families move toward some sense of normalcy after days of uncertainty."The last thing that you want to worry about is how are you going to feed yourself, your family and your children after a tragedy like this," Tendrich said.Tendrich said displaced families are also dealing with needs that can easily be overlooked during a prolonged evacuation, including getting to doctor's appointments and accessing medications."Families with their children are trying to get to doctor's appointments, get their medications that they need, uh, we're really trying to make sure that people are accessing everything they need at this moment to get through this while they're displaced from their homes," Tendrich said. "We're doing everything we can between the county, the police, the fire and my office. We're working hard to make sure not only while you're, you're displaced, but once you get back home, we're trying to make sure that you're supported as much as possible during this, this tough time."While groups are getting to work countywide, help continues while families wait as other organizations are addressing needs at the shelter itself.Many other organizations like the Red Cross, and community members have dropped off supplies this week.Dare to Care has been providing mobile showers and laundry services at the Greenacres Community Center."They called us on Monday and said, ‘Can you come out?’ We've been here ever since," said Timothy Murphy, with the organization Dare to Care. "My message to residents is that there are people who care. We're here for those in need no matter what," he said. "When crisis happen it just complies, so we're here to relieve some of the loss."It remains unclear how long all of the impacted residents will be displaced.Click here if you'd like to help make monetary donations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County, the district said flooding has left some bus stops and roads inaccessible and affected access to some campuses. entry.summary: Floodwaters leave Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary relying on tractors and a drone for care    WPEC
entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

entry.article_text: Richard Acosta of Pinewood Elementary School has been named the 2026-2027 Martin County Teacher of the Year, the Martin County School District and the Education Foundation of Martin County announced. Acosta was selected from 24 educators representing schools throughout the district. He was earlier named the Elementary Teacher of the Year. The announcement was made during the Education Foundation of Martin County’s Teacher of the Year Awards Celebration on Friday at the MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center in Port St. About 800 people attended the event. It was the 42nd year of the Teacher of the Year Award. “The Teacher of the Year celebration is a special tradition that allows us to pause and celebrate the educators who give so much to their students, colleagues and school communities,” Superintendent Michael Maine said. “We are incredibly proud of all of our school-level honorees and especially proud to recognize Richard Acosta as the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year. Thank you to the Education Foundation of Martin County and our sponsors for helping make this evening such a meaningful celebration of our teachers.” “On behalf of the Education Foundation of Martin County, I am thrilled to congratulate Richard Acosta on being named the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year,” Kelley Decowski, president of the Education Foundation of Martin County, said. “We are fortunate to have so many exceptional educators who inspire and empower students every day. Selecting just one to represent Martin County's public schools is no easy task. Acosta exemplifies the passion and dedication that make our teachers so extraordinary.” An educator since 1991, Acosta joined the Martin County School District in 2019 and serves at Pinewood Elementary School as the Related Arts-Science teacher. Acosta brings a hands-on approach to learning that connects classroom instruction to real-world discovery, including helping students tackle challenging concepts or encouraging them to explore the world through scientific inquiry. “After I teach a lesson, I’m always thinking of as I teach that lesson, how can I make it better," Acosta said. "And I’m never tired of it because I teach science. And I’m always one-upping the lesson, and I’m always striving to be better than I was the day before.” At Pinewood, Acosta has helped lead schoolwide STEAM initiatives, chaired the STEAM School Improvement Team, and secured two Martin County Education Foundation grants to support innovative science projects. He also developed a Birds of the Everglades curriculum in partnership with Friends of the Everglades and Inwater Research Group, scheduled to be piloted at Pinewood in fall 2026. His efforts have helped strengthen science instruction and contributed to an increase in fifth-grade science proficiency by 12 percentage points. Acosta exemplifies what it means to be a passionate educator. His love for teaching is evident in every learning experience he creates,” former Principal Susanna Deutsch shared. “His ability to make complex concepts accessible, engaging and meaningful has fostered authentic excitement for learning, with students eagerly sharing their discoveries and newfound knowledge throughout the school.” Miriam Hernandez, an intensive reading teacher at Indiantown Middle School, was named Middle School Teacher of the Year. Hernandez’s career with the Martin County School District began in 2006 as a paraprofessional before she became a teacher in 2012. Since joining Indiantown Middle School in 2018, she has served students in a variety of roles, including Spanish and Intensive Reading, building a reputation as a trusted educator who believes deeply in every student’s ability to grow. “In every role, she has approached her work with professionalism, compassion, and an unwavering belief that every student is capable of growth and success,” Assistant Principal Kellie Siters shared. “She meets students where they are, builds meaningful relationships with them, and works tirelessly to ensure they receive the support they need to thrive both academically and personally.” Marc Turull, an International Baccalaureate physics and chemistry teacher at South Fork High School, was named High School Teacher of the Year. An educator since 2007, Mr. Marc Turull has served students at South Fork High School since 2011. He brings science to life through real-world applications, career exploration and hands-on learning. Outside the classroom, he has been involved in the Engineering Club, First Priority Club and Architecture, Construction and Engineering Mentorship Program, as well as annual STEM experiences that connect students with opportunities and careers in their community. “Marc is widely admired for his ability to foster a positive, inclusive, and engaging learning environment,” South Fork High School Principal Jaime Thompson shared. “He believes that every student can achieve at high levels when provided with meaningful, challenging, and supportive instruction – and he brings that belief to life daily in his classroom.” Felix A. Williams Elementary School earned the Spirit Award for the team that displays the most school spirit. The event’s presenting sponsors were Audi Stuart and Infiniti Stuart, along with Cigna Healthcare, Publix Super Markets Charities, and Keiser University. The nominees are listed on the Education Foundation of Martin County website. The A-rated Martin County School District serves approximately 16,000 students with opportunities. entry.title: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street gang has led to nearly 40 arrests and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash, law enforcement officials said Thursday. The multi-agency investigation, called Operation Score Board, focused on alleged gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas. Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also found that gang members allegedly kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. "Hundreds of shootings over the last decade, violent crime terrorizing the north end of this county, and our community deserves better, and they're getting better because of the hard work of the men and women with the special investigation units that the chief mentioned, and our federal partners here," said Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Officials said about 70 to 80 people are documented as members of the gang. The investigation focused on people police described as shot callers who allegedly directed its activities. Authorities said the 23rd Street gang has been a problem in the Fort Pierce area for decades and was the most violent of several gangs in the city. 4, officers served five search warrants four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie beginning around 5 a.m. The operation led to 11 arrests on racketeering charges, with two people still wanted on warrants, and four additional probable-cause arrests, officials said. Authorities said some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages. 4 searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474. Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV. "We remain committed to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those responsible for bringing violence and criminal activity into our neighborhoods," Chief Smith said. "Our message is clear: We will not tolerate organized criminal activity that threatens the safety of our residents." Authorities did not identify the people they believe led the gang, but said they believe they have arrested most of the key players. They said some people connected to the investigation have faced murder charges, but declined to discuss active cases. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro called the operation an unusually large collaboration among local, state and federal agencies. He said investigators took significant players off the streets and that more operations are expected. The sheriff said the case took extensive work to connect years of records and evidence, and involved a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case. History of problems CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie recovery efforts continue after record breaking floods    WPEC
entry.article_text: Flooding continues in parts of St. Lucie County as recovery efforts move forward. Lucie police department is getting another look at flooding across the city as the sun rises. Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including : SW Cashmere Boulevard Lake Forest HOA St. Bernadette Church NW Country Club Drive Tradition Parkway SW Community Boulevard Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also working to support recovery efforts and restore normal conditions safely. Officials are reminding residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage people to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. The city thanked residents for their patience and support, noting that helping one another can make a difference as the community recovers. Lucie County moves temporary shelters to new locations St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population and special medical needs shelters to new locations Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter, currently at the Fenn Center, is relocating to the Florida Department of Health’s St. Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s historic flooding. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways Officials warn that it could take several days for water levels to recede. Although public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain. For updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding, visit the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: Five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still dealing with several feet of standing water inside their homes, with little indication of when it will recede. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, with floodwaters reaching mailboxes and entering most homes along the road. For longtime resident Linda Weisbecker, the flooding has left decades of memories and belongings underwater. “Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said. Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, preventing her from beginning the cleanup process. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials told WPBF 25 News that crews will be working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. entry.summary: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. WATCH REPORT BELOW: County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

entry.title: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue    WPBF
entry.article_text: Floodwaters are receding in Indian River County, but some areas remain affected by standing water as crews and officials work to address the aftermath of this week’s severe downpours. Law enforcement officials said County Roads 510 and 512 were reduced to one lane at one point due to flooding. Crews installed an emergency pipe under the roadway Thursday night to help drain the area. Dave Kubacki, a resident of Sebastian, shared cellphone video of the flooding outside his home. "Holy smoke, I can't believe how much water was out there, and I can't believe how fast it disappeared," Kubacki said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates He said he was surprised by the flooding, noting that the only time it had been this bad was during a hurricane. "The hurricanes were bad, but I've never seen rain come down like this for such a long period of time and so heavy," Kubacki said. Officials shared video of flooded roads taken just after the severe downpours, along with body camera footage showing deputies responding to incidents caused by the high water. Deputies were called to a residential driveway to secure an alligator that had been pushed out of its usual habitat by the flooding. The alligator was safely relocated to another area within the county. County leaders said assessment teams were out Friday surveying the damage, and results are still pending. Schools in Indian River County were closed Friday but are expected to reopen Monday. Kubacki said he shared the news with his granddaughter. "I said, 'Are you mad that schools are closed?' and she said, 'Oh no!' I said, 'What about your friends?' She said, 'That's OK, I'll see them on Monday,'" Kubacki said. Officials are reminding residents to avoid flooded roads as cleanup efforts continue. entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: Jensen Beach neighborhood submerged as overwhelmed drainage system keeps flooding homes after rain stops
entry.summary: Much of a Jensen Beach neighborhood on Hyline Drive is underwater after this week's heavy rain overwhelmed the local drainage system. As of Wednesday afternoon, water levels inside some homes are still rising long after the rain stopped. For Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid, a kayak has become the way to get around their flooded community. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Jensen Beach neighborhood submerged as overwhelmed drainage system keeps flooding homes At Kincaid's home, the water level is waist-deep. entry.article_text: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. "If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies," Del Toro said. Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff. WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power Light's equipment remains underwater. "We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else," FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. "Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety." Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high. Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede. Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

entry.title: Guns, drugs and lots of money: 40 arrested in major Fort Pierce gang takedown - WPBF
entry.summary: Guns, drugs and lots of money: 40 arrested in major Fort Pierce gang takedown    WPBF
entry.article_text: Law enforcement officials in St. Lucie County announced Thursday that 40 suspected members of a Fort Pierce gang have been arrested following an 18-month investigation. The investigation, known as "Operation Score Board," targeted the 23rd Street Gang, which authorities say has operated in northern St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the gang has between 70 and 80 members and has been responsible for years of violence in the Fort Pierce community. "This gang has terrorized, basically created a hostage crisis for our community up there," Del Toro said. "There’s a lot of good people that are up there in Fort Pierce that have been just held hostage by this group for the last decade, living in fear." Investigators said the gang even maintained a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, a discovery that ultimately gave the operation its name. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said detectives reviewed a decade of criminal activity to identify connections between suspected gang members and violent crimes. "Detectives conducted an extensive review of criminal activity spanning ten years, examining incidents and identifying connections between individuals associated with the gang," Smith said. "This intensive analysis revealed a disturbing pattern of organized crime and violence." Authorities said investigators used Florida’s RICO law to connect years of alleged shootings, drug trafficking and other criminal activity to members of the 23rd Street Gang. The investigation involved multiple local and state law enforcement agencies working together over 18 months to build cases against suspected members of the organization. On Wednesday, law enforcement officers executed multiple search warrants throughout the Fort Pierce area, resulting in 11 arrests as part of the larger operation. Authorities said officers also seized multiple firearms, drugs and thousands of dollars in cash. Del Toro said the size of the operation and the cooperation between agencies could have a lasting impact on the community. "I’ve never seen an operation this large with this many agencies at the local and federal level," Del Toro said. "I think this is going to have a significant generational impact in this community." Authorities said similar investigations and operations are expected in the future. entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.title: Okeechobee family forced to rebuild after historic flooding destroys home
entry.summary: A family in Okeechobee is facing a long road to recovery after historic flooding sent more than two feet of water into their home, destroying much of what they spent years building. Jennifer McArthur says her family never expected to experience flooding like this, especially because their home is not in a designated flood zone. Ring camera video captured the frightening moments when the family rushed out of their home with backpacks on their shoulders as floodwaters quickly overtook the property. 'We really didn't have a warning, we knew it was going to rain but that was it. Within an hour everything was under water,' McArthur said. One week later, McArthur took WPTV reporter Brooke Chau inside the home, showing the damage left behind. 'For six years I worked so hard to give my family a beautiful home,' she said. Now, the family is left trying to figure out how to rebuild. 'We never thought we'd have to go through something like this and watch everything that we built and worked for be literally washed away,' McArthur said. The home is currently unlivable, and the family does not know when they will be able to return. McArthur's husband, Richard Maraj, also hopes the flooding will bring attention to drainage concerns in the area. 'This area especially we'd really like to improve the drainage; it's something that as taxpayers we'd really like to see an improvement,' Maraj said. For now, the family is focused on picking up the pieces and rebuilding their lives after losing the home they worked so hard to create. A friend of the family has also set up a GoFundMe to help Jennifer and her family cover home repairs and other essential needs as they navigate the difficult road ahead. Those who wish to help can find the fundraiser here .

Williams Elementary School Principal Sarah Tuthill was posted to the school’s Facebook page on Sunday morning: FAWE Families, This is Principal Tuthill writing to make you aware of a law enforcement investigation involving threatening statements posted on social media that included a reference to our school. entry.summary: St. Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie, St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. Lucie County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County asks residents to report flood damage County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. 20. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roads, leaving drivers stranded County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.
