entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie is providing financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners for critical home repairs caused by this week’s flooding through its Disaster Relief Program, funded by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. The program, part of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), offers support to low- and moderate-income homeowners for emergency repairs to their primary residences in Port St. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, payment of homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. These repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, temporary structural stabilization, and other actions necessary to protect the home from additional damage. Eligible homeowners may receive up to $25,000 through 0% interest deferred payment loans, with no monthly payments required. Loans are forgiven over a five-year period in accordance with program guidelines. All work must be directly related to the declared disaster, deemed necessary to preserve the safety and integrity of the property, and approved by the city before assistance is provided. Funding is not available for mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal, or remediation. Homeowners must complete any necessary mold remediation before approved repairs can proceed. Eligible repairs may be funded after remediation is complete. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or non-permitted work are not eligible for assistance. The city has allocated $1 million for the program, which will run until the funds are exhausted. The program’s pre-application will open at 8 a.m. To qualify, applicants must meet income guidelines, have owned and occupied their home within city limits for at least one year, have an assessed home value of $560,154 or less, and be current on mortgage and property tax payments. 5, residents may complete the pre-application online. Assistance is also available by contacting the city’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, emailing Housing@cityofpsl.com, or visiting City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.summary: Jensen Beach families still surrounded by floodwater a week after historic rainfall    WPEC
entry.article_text: Eight days after historic rainfall flooded communities across the Treasure Coast, some Jensen Beach families remain trapped by standing water that is several feet deep in parts of their neighborhood. Many homeowners along Hyline Drive say the flooding is unlike anything they've seen before. They estimate water levels remain as high as five feet in some areas, and they say the floodwater is mixed with sewage because many homes in the neighborhood rely on septic systems. "It's just a shame that this happened," said homeowner Todd Doss who's lived in the neighborhood for more than two decades. For Doss and his partner, Susan Boeve, getting to their front door has become more like a game of leapfrog as they carefully step across concrete cinder blocks to avoid the water. See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end "The smell is bad," Doss said. "It has been very uncomfortable, but we're managing. It's kind of like camping." The couple, like many of their neighbors , say they cannot move their cars, take showers or flush their toilets. Despite those challenges, Doss says they consider themselves lucky compared to some of their neighbors. "Some of these people, our neighbors, have lost everything in their house, everything," Doss said. "The flooding in some my neighbors' homes are up to three, four feet high." So far, Doss has managed to keep floodwater out of his home. However, water has entered his Florida room and spilled into his pool. "It's dirty water," Doss said. Leaving is not an option for the family, which includes two dogs, a cat and a pet tortoise named Walter. "We were hopeful that it would drain," Doss said. "After the rain stopped, it started to drain and then the next morning it rose higher. That's when we got scared." See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end Neighbors gathered Sunday for a flood relief meeting with county leaders, hoping for answers about when conditions might improve. But officials told neighbors they do not know when the water will recede. With nowhere to put the water, some homeowners fear it could take months before the flooding fully subsides. "It's extremely frustrating," said homeowner Mike Bresette. Bresette said the neighborhood has experienced flooding before and believes infrastructure improvements should have been made years ago. "They've had since 2011 to make changes to the infrastructure for drainage and no one's done anything," Bresette said. "I went to that meeting this morning and I didn't get one iota of information about what they're going to do after this is over to fix the problem for long term." For many homeowners, the concern now is what happens if more rain falls before the standing water disappears. "If we have one more bad rain, we will definitely be flooded," Doss said. The neighborhood is not located in a designated flood zone, meaning many homeowners do not carry flood insurance. entry.article_text: A pedestrian was struck and killed by a Brightline train on Sunday afternoon in Port St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said. At approximately 1:10 p.m., deputies responded to a report of a pedestrian struck by a train on the railroad tracks about a mile north of Walton Road and near Savannas Preserve State Park. The tracks, which run east of U.S. 1, are operated by Florida East Coast Railway. Freight trains also use the route. Preliminary information indicates that a northbound train struck a person who entered the path of the approaching train, a sheriff's office spokesman told WPBF. The circumstances surrounding this incident remain under investigation. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the victim's family and friends during this difficult time," the agency said. Some other northbound trains were affected. Brightline trains go between Miami and Orlando. 22, 2023, the private company extended service from West Palm Beach to a new station at Orlando International Airport. Brightline trains reach maximum operating speeds of 110 mph from West Palm Beach to Cocoa, and up to 125 mph on the dedicated track between Cocoa and Orlando International Airport. They go at a maximum operating speed of 79 mph on the track segment between Miami and West Palm Beach. There are no train stations between West Palm Beach and Orlando. There are plans for a a Brightline station in downtown Stuart, though the project faces significant funding and operational hurdles.

entry.title: NTSB completes most on-scene work in Greenacres Learjet crash investigation
entry.summary: The National Transportation Safety Board has completed most of its on-scene investigative work following the deadly Nov. 1 Learjet 60 crash near Greenacres , though excavation of the impact site remains underway. The NTSB said in a Sunday evening post on X that investigators have cleared several areas involved in the investigation, including the Green Acres Mobile Home Community, Reading Truck, Silver Oaks Plaza, Value Store It Self Storage and John I. Leonard High School. PREVIOUS REPORT: Part of Learjet's engine recovered NTSB recovers part of Learjet engine after crash Investigators have recovered and identified numerous portions of the aircraft, including components from both wings and engines, the flight deck, vertical and horizontal stabilizers, the left elevator, sections of the ailerons and multiple flap track assemblies. Some of the recovered components have been sent to NTSB laboratories in Washington, D.C., for further examination. NTSB asks public to report debris As investigators continue their work, the NTSB urges anyone who finds debris believed to be from the crash not to keep, move, alter or throw it away. Anyone who has found or collected possible wreckage should contact the agency at witness@ntsb.gov to arrange for its recovery. The NTSB is asking people to include a photograph of the debris in the email, if possible. The agency said recovering all available wreckage is critical to determining what caused the crash. While most of the NTSB's on-scene investigative activities are complete, excavation at the impact site continues. Community members looking for information about ongoing recovery operations can visit Palm Beach County's website .

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him, and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Alexis Hodge said. Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain,' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

entry.summary: Cape Coral man arrested after threats against Martin County community    WPBF
entry.article_text: A southwest Florida resident is accused of making threats on TikTok against Felix A. Williams Elementary School in Stuart, law enforcement officers and members of the Martin County community. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said Sunday that 51-year-old Michael G. Davis, from Cape Coral, was arrested on Saturday night in Cape Coral on a Martin County warrant directly related to those threats. He was released from the Lee County Jail on Sunday after posting a $100,000 bond. "We know parents are concerned about his release," the sheriff's office posted on Facebook. "As a precaution, you’ll see more deputies at and around Felix A. Williams Elementary School and at several other Martin County schools. https://www.facebook.com/MartinCountySheriffsOffice/posts/pfbid0W4ynNVPAAJp4DsdSrU2tavXPhgo9MQ1cMjqw2P5oViBTvYXDeu5szmyp9zXirBVrl Davis uses a bicycle as his primary form of transportation, MCSO said. "If you think you see Davis in Martin County or notice anything suspicious, please call the Martin County Sheriff’s Office," the agency said. According to the Lee County Sheriff’s Office, Davis is facing a charge of resisting officers without violence along with an out-of-county warrant from Martin County. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it was contacted by a concerned citizen on Friday, Nov. 6, about a video that a man, later identified as Davis, posted on the social media platform TikTok threatening the lives of a local student, members of the community and Martin County law enforcement. Investigators reviewed the threats that targeted a school and were able to identify Davis, who posted the video. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said its criminal investigations division and warrants unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Service and the Cape Coral Police Department to arrest Davis. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office added that at first, Davis refused to surrender to law enforcement outside his home but was eventually taken into law enforcement custody. “If you threaten any of our students, our schools, anyone in our community or any of our law enforcement officers, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, find you and lock you up,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said in a statement on Sunday morning. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office noted it is undetermined why Davis targeted Martin County or the specific people he threatened. The following updated statement by Felix A. Williams Elementary School Principal Sarah Tuthill was posted to the school’s Facebook page on Sunday night: Dear FAWE Families and Staff. Please pardon our interruption this evening. We want to provide an update regarding the individual recently arrested in connection with social media threats that included references to our school community. The individual has since been released on bond. We understand that this news may raise concerns among our families and employees, and we want to reassure you that the Martin County Sheriff’s Office is fully aware of the individual’s release and continues to monitor the situation closely. Out of an abundance of caution, the Sheriff’s Office will have an increased law enforcement presence on our campus. This is a proactive precaution being taken in coordination with our law enforcement partners, who remain actively engaged in monitoring the situation and protecting our school community. We appreciate our families and employees for remaining alert and taking matters involving school safety seriously. At the same time, we want to emphasize that our law enforcement partners are closely monitoring this matter and taking appropriate precautions to safeguard our campus. School will remain open, and teaching and learning will continue as planned. Our priority is to ensure that students and staff feel safe, supported, and able to focus on the important work taking place in our classrooms each day. Thank you for your continued trust, understanding, and partnership. We are grateful to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office for its vigilance and ongoing commitment to the safety of our students, employees, and families.

entry.title: WATCH: Small plane hits pickup truck during emergency landing on Florida road
entry.summary: A plane carrying two pilots crashed into the back of a pickup truck Saturday while attempting an emergency landing in Lee County, according to the sheriff's office. The crash happened around noon near Bayshore Road and Interstate 75. The sheriff's office said the two pilots experienced a mechanical issue and attempted to make an emergency landing. During the landing, the aircraft struck the rear of a pickup truck traveling east on Bayshore Road. Despite the collision, no injuries were reported at the scene, according to deputies. The Cessna Skyhawk departed Sebring Regional Airport at 11:01 a.m. Saturday and made the emergency landing about 50 minutes later, according to the FlightAware website. The Federal Aviation Administration responded to the scene and will lead the investigation into the crash. 'Thankfully, this incident had a positive outcome, and no one was injured,' Sheriff Carmine Marceno said in a statement. 'Given the recent tragic news involving aviation accidents, we are especially grateful that everyone is safe.' Marceno also thanked responding deputies, FDOT Southwest Florida and Bayshore Fire Rescue for their response. 'We will continue working closely with our partners at the FAA as they review the circumstances surrounding this incident,' Marceno said. Authorities did not immediately provide additional information about the aircraft, the nature of the reported mechanical problem or how much damage was caused to the plane and pickup truck.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: A week after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still facing several feet of standing water inside their homes, forcing evacuations and raising concerns about recovery. Lisa French, a resident of Skyline Heights, described how the flooding progressed since last week. "Tuesday you can kind of see the water creep towards the house, and then we started having water come out of our toilets and our showers, so we decided to leave. Wednesday, we got back here, and there’s flooding inside the house, and this all came," French said. The affected neighborhood is located near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water naturally flows south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. French said officials explained that flooding in her area is caused by water being pumped into the Savannas Preserve from Port St. "We're at level with the Savannas, so if they try to pump, it's like how they explain it is they, they're pumping us and the Savannas at the same time," French said. Lucie, they can dump all their water from their streets into the Savanna Preserve, and it's going to come down to us." French said no one in her neighborhood, including herself, had flood insurance because the area is not designated as a flood zone. As the days went on, her home became inundated with water, and now fecal matter is floating around the house, creating strong odors. "It's like a total teardown; we had people come, and everything in there has been sewer water sitting in hot heat," French said. "Right now, it’s like a hot box because there’s sewer water 4-6 inches high everywhere. My floors are up… my husband was cutting out the walls to see how far the moisture got up. It’s gross inside; we can’t go inside anymore." Martin County officials said crews are working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. On Sunday, frustrated Jensen Beach residents brought their concerns directly to county leaders. District 1 County Commissioner Eileen Vargas said, "Habitat for Humanity is working with United Way right now for a shelter... plus other help." Jim Gorton, Martin County Public Works, added, "We are working on temporary housing... Make sure you have your contact information out there; next week is tomorrow. So that's being worked on." French said while emergency services, resources, and local and federal leaders are reaching out to help her family, she hopes to rebuild her home and return to normalcy. "The first thing you think of is Thanksgiving is coming up; we’re supposed to host Thanksgiving. Then I’m supposed to do Christmas for my boys, and we don’t have a home… It’s just hard," French said. "A lot of these neighbors have become our family, like our close family, and my goal is to keep this property and live on this property. Make sure this doesn't happen again."

entry.title: Jensen Beach families still surrounded by floodwater a week after historic rainfall - WPEC
entry.summary: Jensen Beach families still surrounded by floodwater a week after historic rainfall    WPEC
entry.article_text: Eight days after historic rainfall flooded communities across the Treasure Coast, some Jensen Beach families remain trapped by standing water that is several feet deep in parts of their neighborhood. Many homeowners along Hyline Drive say the flooding is unlike anything they've seen before. They estimate water levels remain as high as five feet in some areas, and they say the floodwater is mixed with sewage because many homes in the neighborhood rely on septic systems. "It's just a shame that this happened," said homeowner Todd Doss who's lived in the neighborhood for more than two decades. For Doss and his partner, Susan Boeve, getting to their front door has become more like a game of leapfrog as they carefully step across concrete cinder blocks to avoid the water. See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end "The smell is bad," Doss said. "It has been very uncomfortable, but we're managing. It's kind of like camping." The couple, like many of their neighbors , say they cannot move their cars, take showers or flush their toilets. Despite those challenges, Doss says they consider themselves lucky compared to some of their neighbors. "Some of these people, our neighbors, have lost everything in their house, everything," Doss said. "The flooding in some my neighbors' homes are up to three, four feet high." So far, Doss has managed to keep floodwater out of his home. However, water has entered his Florida room and spilled into his pool. "It's dirty water," Doss said. Leaving is not an option for the family, which includes two dogs, a cat and a pet tortoise named Walter. "We were hopeful that it would drain," Doss said. "After the rain stopped, it started to drain and then the next morning it rose higher. That's when we got scared." See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end Neighbors gathered Sunday for a flood relief meeting with county leaders, hoping for answers about when conditions might improve. But officials told neighbors they do not know when the water will recede. With nowhere to put the water, some homeowners fear it could take months before the flooding fully subsides. "It's extremely frustrating," said homeowner Mike Bresette. Bresette said the neighborhood has experienced flooding before and believes infrastructure improvements should have been made years ago. "They've had since 2011 to make changes to the infrastructure for drainage and no one's done anything," Bresette said. "I went to that meeting this morning and I didn't get one iota of information about what they're going to do after this is over to fix the problem for long term." For many homeowners, the concern now is what happens if more rain falls before the standing water disappears. "If we have one more bad rain, we will definitely be flooded," Doss said. The neighborhood is not located in a designated flood zone, meaning many homeowners do not carry flood insurance. While Florida has declared a state of emergency that includes Martin County, homeowners say they are hoping the governor requests a federal disaster declaration that could allow FEMA to provide assistance.

entry.title: Brightline train strikes, kills pedestrian in St. Lucie County - WPBF
entry.summary: Brightline train strikes, kills pedestrian in St. Lucie County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A pedestrian was struck and killed by a Brightline train on Sunday afternoon in Port St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said. At approximately 1:10 p.m., deputies responded to a report of a pedestrian struck by a train on the railroad tracks about a mile north of Walton Road and near Savannas Preserve State Park. The tracks, which run east of U.S. 1, are operated by Florida East Coast Railway. Freight trains also use the route. Preliminary information indicates that a northbound train struck a person who entered the path of the approaching train, a sheriff's office spokesman told WPBF. The circumstances surrounding this incident remain under investigation. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the victim's family and friends during this difficult time," the agency said. Some other northbound trains were affected. Brightline trains go between Miami and Orlando. 22, 2023, the private company extended service from West Palm Beach to a new station at Orlando International Airport. Brightline trains reach maximum operating speeds of 110 mph from West Palm Beach to Cocoa, and up to 125 mph on the dedicated track between Cocoa and Orlando International Airport. They go at a maximum operating speed of 79 mph on the track segment between Miami and West Palm Beach. There are no train stations between West Palm Beach and Orlando. There are plans for a a Brightline station in downtown Stuart, though the project faces significant funding and operational hurdles.

entry.title: Cooking up confidence: Program helps adults with disabilities gain independence
entry.summary: A recent cooking class in Port St. Lucie is helping adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities learn valuable life skills and gain more independence. The participants are part of the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach Countys Guardian Advocacy Program, which provides guardianship support to people with developmental disabilities. WATCH: Cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills for independent living Cooking up confidence: Port St. Lucie program helps adults with disabilities gain independence Some of the participants are young adults who have aged out of foster care and don't have family members to rely on for support. Through a partnership with GL Homes that has lasted nearly a decade, participants are given hands-on experiences and opportunities to develop skills that can help them in everyday life. During the latest class in October, participants learned how to prepare a healthier meal, with Mediterranean chicken on the menu. From chopping vegetables and preparing ingredients to following a recipe and practicing kitchen safety, the lesson was about more than just cooking. Organizers say the goal is to give participants experiences and opportunities that are often not readily available to them while helping them become more self-sufficient. 'We wanted to give them these experiences that they just don't have and the rest of us take for granted,' said Sarah Alsofrom, Vice President of Community Relations at GL Homes. Jessica Kelson with the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County says watching participants learn new skills and take part in activities can make a meaningful difference. 'Being able to watch them learn a new skill or participate in something that's not typically offered to them is just really heartwarming and nice to see them be able to grow,' Kelson said. By the end of the class, participants had prepared their meal and sat down to enjoy what they made. For one participant, the accomplishment was something to be proud of. 'I'm proud of it,' she said. 'I am going to try this at home.' Organizers hope these experiences will give participants the confidence and practical skills to take greater control of their daily lives one meal at a time.

entry.title: After months of concerns, Lake Worth neighbors get answers about collapsing Brooklyn Lane
entry.summary: For months, Ive been seeking answers for residents along Brooklyn Lane in Lake Worth after they reached out to me about a collapsing section of road that serves as the only way in and out of their neighborhood. Now, neighbors are finally seeing action. Im WPTV Traffic Reporter Johann Hoffend, and I first connected with residents in August, when they told me the deteriorating road was getting worse and they feared it could eventually become impassable. Hopefully with the help from WPTV Channel 5, were getting some action, one resident said. I think theyre gonna do something about it. Another neighbor described how difficult navigating the damaged section had become. This is nonsense. I cant drive one of my cars out because it bottoms out trying to go through this, the resident said. Neighbors told me repairs had been made before, but the problem kept returning. Every time they come out here, they do a little fixing, but it doesnt take long for it to keep going down, another resident said. After recent heavy rains, I returned to Brooklyn Lane and found the hole had grown larger and deeper. Residents believed the bigger problem was underground and involved a drainage pipe beneath the roadway. Within 24 hours of my visit, the road was patched, and the pipe underneath was being assessed. Now, the county has taken the repair a step further. Crews removed water from the pipe and filled a section beneath the roadway with concrete, addressing the area below the surface rather than simply placing another patch over the damaged road. For neighbors who say they have dealt with the problem for years, the latest work represents progress. Now, theyre hoping the repair beneath Brooklyn Lane will finally provide the long-term solution theyve been waiting for. WPTV Traffic Reporter Johann Hoffend will continue following the repairs and whether they hold up over time.

But officials told neighbors they do not know when the water will recede. With nowhere to put the water, some homeowners fear it could take months before the flooding fully subsides. "It's extremely frustrating," said homeowner Mike Bresette. Bresette said the neighborhood has experienced flooding before and believes infrastructure improvements should have been made years ago. "They've had since 2011 to make changes to the infrastructure for drainage and no one's done anything," Bresette said. "I went to that meeting this morning and I didn't get one iota of information about what they're going to do after this is over to fix the problem for long term." For many homeowners, the concern now is what happens if more rain falls before the standing water disappears. "If we have one more bad rain, we will definitely be flooded," Doss said. The neighborhood is not located in a designated flood zone, meaning many homeowners do not carry flood insurance. While Florida has declared a state of emergency that includes Martin County, homeowners say they are hoping the governor requests a federal disaster declaration that could allow FEMA to provide assistance.

The 15th annual event runs from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. and brings together more than 30 teams of firefighters, public safety personnel and community sponsors for an afternoon organizers describe as a combination of chili competition, entertainment and patriotism. Tequesta Chili Cook-Off moves to Carlin Park After 14 years, the cook-off is moving to a larger location at Carlin Park. Captain David McGovern of Tequesta Fire Rescue told WPTV the venue gives the growing event more room while offering easier parking and a different atmosphere near the ocean. Bigger, beautiful location, easier to park, and just that lovely little sea breeze coming in as well, McGovern said. The Seabreeze Amphitheater also offers paved walkways, permanent restrooms, a permanent stage and additional space for the chili teams, entertainment and guests, according to event organizers. We'll have (around) 4,000 people show up on Saturday to honor our veterans, give medals to our veterans, McGovern said. So we say thank you for all their sacrifices and everything else. entry.title: Lake Worth neighbors see action on collapsing Brooklyn Lane after months of concerns
entry.summary: For months, WPTV has been seeking answers for residents along Brooklyn Lane in Lake Worth after they reached out to me about a collapsing section of road that serves as the only way in and out of their neighborhood. Now, neighbors are finally seeing action. WATCH REPORT BELOW: BROOKLYN LANE LAKE WORTH UPDATE WPTV traffic reporter Johann Hoffend first connected with residents in August, when they told me the deteriorating road was getting worse and they feared it could eventually become impassable. 'Hopefully with the help from WPTV Channel 5, we're getting some action,' one resident said. 'I think they're gonna do something about it.' Another neighbor described how difficult navigating the damaged section had become. 'This is nonsense. I can't drive one of my cars out because it bottoms out trying to go through this,' the resident said. Neighbors told me repairs had been made before, but the problem kept returning. 'Every time they come out here, they do a little fixing, but it doesnt take long for it to keep going down,' another resident said. After recent heavy rains, I returned to Brooklyn Lane and found the hole had grown larger and deeper. Residents believed the bigger problem was underground and involved a drainage pipe beneath the roadway. Within 24 hours of my visit, the road was patched, and the pipe underneath was being assessed. Now, the county has taken the repair a step further. Crews removed water from the pipe and filled a section beneath the roadway with concrete, addressing the area below the surface rather than simply placing another patch over the damaged road. For neighbors who say they have dealt with the problem for years, the latest work represents progress. Now, they're hoping the repair beneath Brooklyn Lane will finally provide the long-term solution they've been waiting for. WPTV traffic reporter Johann Hoffend will continue following the repairs and whether they hold up over time.

entry.title: NTSB completes most on-scene work in Greenacres Learjet crash investigation
entry.summary: The National Transportation Safety Board has completed most of its on-scene investigative work following the deadly Nov. 1 Learjet 60 crash near Greenacres , though excavation of the impact site remains underway. The NTSB said in a Sunday evening post on X that investigators have cleared several areas involved in the investigation, including the Green Acres Mobile Home Community, Reading Truck, Silver Oaks Plaza, Value Store It Self Storage and John I. Leonard High School. WATCH REPORT BELOW: NTSB completes most on-scene work in Learjet crash Investigators have recovered and identified numerous portions of the aircraft, including components from both wings and engines, the flight deck, vertical and horizontal stabilizers, the left elevator, sections of the ailerons and multiple flap track assemblies. Some of the recovered components have been sent to NTSB laboratories in Washington, D.C., for further examination. PREVIOUS REPORT: Part of Learjet's engine recovered NTSB recovers part of Learjet engine after crash NTSB asks public to report debris As investigators continue their work, the NTSB urges anyone who finds debris believed to be from the crash not to keep, move, alter or throw it away. Anyone who has found or collected possible wreckage should contact the agency at witness@ntsb.gov to arrange for its recovery. The NTSB is asking people to include a photograph of the debris in the email, if possible. The agency said recovering all available wreckage is critical to determining what caused the crash. While most of the NTSB's on-scene investigative activities are complete, excavation at the impact site continues. Community members looking for information about ongoing recovery operations can visit Palm Beach County's website .

entry.title: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    WPEC
entry.article_text: Williams Elementary School in Martin County will remain open with an increased law enforcement presence after a man arrested in connection with social media threats was released from jail on bond. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families and staff that the Martin County Sheriff’s Office knows the man has been released and is monitoring the situation. The added law enforcement presence on campus is a precaution, she said. School will remain open, and teaching and learning will continue as planned, Tuthill wrote. Some parents responding to the school’s message said they were considering keeping their children home until they learn what conditions apply to the man’s release and how he is being monitored. Others asked whether absences would be excused and whether students could get assignments to complete at home. The school’s message did not specify the release conditions or address attendance questions. A Lee County booking record shows Michael George Davis, 51, was released at noon Sunday, Nov. The record lists a $1,000 cash or surety bond for a charge of resisting an officer without violence, and a $100,000 cash or surety bond for an out-of-county warrant from Martin County. 24 county court hearing for the resisting charge. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said a concerned person alerted the agency late Friday, Nov. 6, to a TikTok video threatening a local student, community members and Martin County law enforcement officers. Investigators said the threats also targeted a school. The sheriff’s office said investigators identified Davis as the person who posted the video and tracked him to Cape Coral. The agency’s Criminal Investigations Division and Warrants Unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Fugitive Task Force and Cape Coral police to arrest him Saturday night. Davis initially refused to leave his home, the sheriff’s office said, but was ultimately taken into custody on a Martin County warrant. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff’s office said it remains unclear why Davis targeted Martin County or the people named in the threats. His motive remains under investigation. If you threaten any of our students, our schools, anyone in our community or any of our law enforcement officers, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, find you and lock you up, Sheriff John Budensiek said. The school previously told families that the social media posts referenced a specific student and included vague threats against the school. Officials urged families to rely on school and law enforcement updates rather than unverified information circulating online.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: A week after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still facing several feet of standing water inside their homes, forcing evacuations and raising concerns about recovery. Lisa French, a resident of Skyline Heights, described how the flooding progressed since last week. "Tuesday you can kind of see the water creep towards the house, and then we started having water come out of our toilets and our showers, so we decided to leave. Wednesday, we got back here, and there’s flooding inside the house, and this all came," French said. The affected neighborhood is located near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water naturally flows south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. French said officials explained that flooding in her area is caused by water being pumped into the Savannas Preserve from Port St. "We're at level with the Savannas, so if they try to pump, it's like how they explain it is they, they're pumping us and the Savannas at the same time," French said. Lucie, they can dump all their water from their streets into the Savanna Preserve, and it's going to come down to us." French said no one in her neighborhood, including herself, had flood insurance because the area is not designated as a flood zone. As the days went on, her home became inundated with water, and now fecal matter is floating around the house, creating strong odors. "It's like a total teardown; we had people come, and everything in there has been sewer water sitting in hot heat," French said. "Right now, it’s like a hot box because there’s sewer water 4-6 inches high everywhere. My floors are up… my husband was cutting out the walls to see how far the moisture got up. It’s gross inside; we can’t go inside anymore." Martin County officials said crews are working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. On Sunday, frustrated Jensen Beach residents brought their concerns directly to county leaders. District 1 County Commissioner Eileen Vargas said, "Habitat for Humanity is working with United Way right now for a shelter... plus other help." Jim Gorton, Martin County Public Works, added, "We are working on temporary housing... Make sure you have your contact information out there; next week is tomorrow. So that's being worked on." French said while emergency services, resources, and local and federal leaders are reaching out to help her family, she hopes to rebuild her home and return to normalcy. "The first thing you think of is Thanksgiving is coming up; we’re supposed to host Thanksgiving. Then I’m supposed to do Christmas for my boys, and we don’t have a home… It’s just hard," French said. "A lot of these neighbors have become our family, like our close family, and my goal is to keep this property and live on this property. Make sure this doesn't happen again."

entry.title: Brightline train strikes, kills pedestrian in St. Lucie County - WPBF
entry.summary: Brightline train strikes, kills pedestrian in St. Lucie County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A pedestrian was struck and killed by a Brightline train on Sunday afternoon in Port St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said. At approximately 1:10 p.m., deputies responded to a report of a pedestrian struck by a train on the railroad tracks about a mile north of Walton Road and near Savannas Preserve State Park. The tracks, which run east of U.S. 1, are operated by Florida East Coast Railway. Freight trains also use the route. Preliminary information indicates that a northbound train struck a person who entered the path of the approaching train, a sheriff's office spokesman told WPBF. The circumstances surrounding this incident remain under investigation. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the victim's family and friends during this difficult time," the agency said. Some other northbound trains were affected. Brightline trains go between Miami and Orlando. 22, 2023, the private company extended service from West Palm Beach to a new station at Orlando International Airport. Brightline trains reach maximum operating speeds of 110 mph from West Palm Beach to Cocoa, and up to 125 mph on the dedicated track between Cocoa and Orlando International Airport. They go at a maximum operating speed of 79 mph on the track segment between Miami and West Palm Beach. There are no train stations between West Palm Beach and Orlando. There are plans for a a Brightline station in downtown Stuart, though the project faces significant funding and operational hurdles.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills, independence
entry.summary: A recent cooking class in Port St. Lucie is helping adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities learn valuable life skills and gain more independence. The participants are part of the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach Countys Guardian Advocacy Program, which provides guardianship support to people with developmental disabilities. WATCH: Cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills for independent living Cooking up confidence: Port St. Lucie program helps adults with disabilities gain independence Some of the participants are young adults who have aged out of foster care and don't have family members to rely on for support. Through a partnership with GL Homes that has lasted nearly a decade, participants are given hands-on experiences and opportunities to develop skills that can help them in everyday life. During the latest class in October, participants learned how to prepare a healthier meal, with Mediterranean chicken on the menu. From chopping vegetables and preparing ingredients to following a recipe and practicing kitchen safety, the lesson was about more than just cooking. Organizers say the goal is to give participants experiences and opportunities that are often not readily available to them while helping them become more self-sufficient. 'We wanted to give them these experiences that they just don't have and the rest of us take for granted,' said Sarah Alsofrom, Vice President of Community Relations at GL Homes. Jessica Kelson with the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County says watching participants learn new skills and take part in activities can make a meaningful difference. 'Being able to watch them learn a new skill or participate in something that's not typically offered to them is just really heartwarming and nice to see them be able to grow,' Kelson said. By the end of the class, participants had prepared their meal and sat down to enjoy what they made. For one participant, the accomplishment was something to be proud of. 'I'm proud of it,' she said. 'I am going to try this at home.' Organizers hope these experiences will give participants the confidence and practical skills to take greater control of their daily lives one meal at a time.

entry.title: Jensen Beach families still surrounded by floodwater a week after historic rainfall - WPEC
entry.summary: Jensen Beach families still surrounded by floodwater a week after historic rainfall    WPEC
entry.article_text: Eight days after historic rainfall flooded communities across the Treasure Coast, some Jensen Beach families remain trapped by standing water that is several feet deep in parts of their neighborhood. Many homeowners along Hyline Drive say the flooding is unlike anything they've seen before. They estimate water levels remain as high as five feet in some areas, and they say the floodwater is mixed with sewage because many homes in the neighborhood rely on septic systems. "It's just a shame that this happened," said homeowner Todd Doss who's lived in the neighborhood for more than two decades. For Doss and his partner, Susan Boeve, getting to their front door has become more like a game of leapfrog as they carefully step across concrete cinder blocks to avoid the water. See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end "The smell is bad," Doss said. "It has been very uncomfortable, but we're managing. It's kind of like camping." The couple, like many of their neighbors , say they cannot move their cars, take showers or flush their toilets. Despite those challenges, Doss says they consider themselves lucky compared to some of their neighbors. "Some of these people, our neighbors, have lost everything in their house, everything," Doss said. "The flooding in some my neighbors' homes are up to three, four feet high." So far, Doss has managed to keep floodwater out of his home. However, water has entered his Florida room and spilled into his pool. "It's dirty water," Doss said. Leaving is not an option for the family, which includes two dogs, a cat and a pet tortoise named Walter. "We were hopeful that it would drain," Doss said. "After the rain stopped, it started to drain and then the next morning it rose higher. That's when we got scared." See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end Neighbors gathered Sunday for a flood relief meeting with county leaders, hoping for answers about when conditions might improve. But officials told neighbors they do not know when the water will recede. With nowhere to put the water, some homeowners fear it could take months before the flooding fully subsides. "It's extremely frustrating," said homeowner Mike Bresette. Bresette said the neighborhood has experienced flooding before and believes infrastructure improvements should have been made years ago. "They've had since 2011 to make changes to the infrastructure for drainage and no one's done anything," Bresette said. "I went to that meeting this morning and I didn't get one iota of information about what they're going to do after this is over to fix the problem for long term." For many homeowners, the concern now is what happens if more rain falls before the standing water disappears. "If we have one more bad rain, we will definitely be flooded," Doss said. The neighborhood is not located in a designated flood zone, meaning many homeowners do not carry flood insurance. While Florida has declared a state of emergency that includes Martin County, homeowners say they are hoping the governor requests a federal disaster declaration that could allow FEMA to provide assistance.

entry.article_text: Some parents kept their children home from Felix A. Williams Elementary School on Monday after the man accused of posting TikTok threats involving the school was released on $100,000 bond. Jessica and Jon Greisen were among them. Their daughter, Teigan, is in third grade. My child is not going to school, Jessica Greisen recalled thinking when she learned he was out. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the school entrance. Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would add deputies at and around the campus and at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The Greisens said they want to know whether 51-year-old Michael George Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. She wants to know what precautions will be in place in the days ahead. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. What led to the arrest The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said a tip late Friday led investigators to a TikTok video they say threatened a student, community members and law enforcement officers. Tuthill said the posts referenced a specific student and included vague threats against the school. Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night. The sheriff’s office said he initially refused to come outside. Davis was released from the Lee County Jail on Sunday after posting $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant, the sheriff’s office said. Lee County jail records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. Investigators say they still don’t know why Davis singled out Martin County or the people named in the threats.

According to James, the Hamal Community Development District (CDD) is responsible for maintaining the area's surface water management system, which has two pumps that currently cannot operate simultaneously. James said the city has offered personnel, equipment and technical assistance, but both districts have indicated there is nothing further the city can do to assist with drainage operations at this time. entry.summary: Cape Coral man arrested after TikTok threats against Martin County student, deputies    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Cape Coral man was arrested Saturday night after Martin County investigators said he posted TikTok videos threatening a student, community members and law enforcement officers. A concerned resident alerted the Martin County Sheriff’s Office late Friday about the first video, the agency said. Investigators reviewed the threats, which also targeted a school, identified the person who posted them as 51-year-old Micheal George Davis and tracked him to Cape Coral. The sheriff’s office Criminal Investigations Division and Warrants Unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Fugitive Task Force and Cape Coral police to arrest Davis at his home. See also: Boynton Beach man becomes third arrested in alleged $32M Delray Beach THC scheme Davis initially refused to come outside but was ultimately taken into custody on a Martin County warrant with a $100,000 bond, the sheriff’s office said. Investigators have not determined why Davis targeted Martin County or the people named in the threats. His motive remains under investigation. If you threaten any of our students, our schools, anyone in our community or any of our law enforcement officers, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, find you and lock you up, Sheriff John Budensiek said. Along with the Martin County warrant, Davis was also arrested for resisting arrest, according to booking records.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: A week after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still facing several feet of standing water inside their homes, forcing evacuations and raising concerns about recovery. Lisa French, a resident of Skyline Heights, described how the flooding progressed since last week. "Tuesday you can kind of see the water creep towards the house, and then we started having water come out of our toilets and our showers, so we decided to leave. Wednesday, we got back here, and there’s flooding inside the house, and this all came," French said. The affected neighborhood is located near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water naturally flows south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. French said officials explained that flooding in her area is caused by water being pumped into the Savannas Preserve from Port St. "We're at level with the Savannas, so if they try to pump, it's like how they explain it is they, they're pumping us and the Savannas at the same time," French said. Lucie, they can dump all their water from their streets into the Savanna Preserve, and it's going to come down to us." French said no one in her neighborhood, including herself, had flood insurance because the area is not designated as a flood zone. As the days went on, her home became inundated with water, and now fecal matter is floating around the house, creating strong odors. "It's like a total teardown; we had people come, and everything in there has been sewer water sitting in hot heat," French said. "Right now, it’s like a hot box because there’s sewer water 4-6 inches high everywhere. My floors are up… my husband was cutting out the walls to see how far the moisture got up. It’s gross inside; we can’t go inside anymore." Martin County officials said crews are working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. On Sunday, frustrated Jensen Beach residents brought their concerns directly to county leaders. District 1 County Commissioner Eileen Vargas said, "Habitat for Humanity is working with United Way right now for a shelter... plus other help." Jim Gorton, Martin County Public Works, added, "We are working on temporary housing... Make sure you have your contact information out there; next week is tomorrow. So that's being worked on." French said while emergency services, resources, and local and federal leaders are reaching out to help her family, she hopes to rebuild her home and return to normalcy. "The first thing you think of is Thanksgiving is coming up; we’re supposed to host Thanksgiving. Then I’m supposed to do Christmas for my boys, and we don’t have a home… It’s just hard," French said. "A lot of these neighbors have become our family, like our close family, and my goal is to keep this property and live on this property. Make sure this doesn't happen again."

entry.title: Fort Pierce police union declares impasse, says city cited Amendment 3 in 0% raise offer - WPEC
entry.summary: Fort Pierce police union declares impasse, says city cited Amendment 3 in 0% raise offer    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Fort Pierce Police Officers Association says it declared an impasse in contract negotiations after the city proposed no raises or step increases for officers. In a Facebook post dated Nov. 7, the association said officers and representatives from the Coastal Florida Police Benevolent Association met with the city Nov. 5 for a fourth round of negotiations. The union said the city’s proposal included 0% raises and no step increases. The association said city representatives cited Amendment 3 and an anticipated $6 million budget shortfall. It also said representatives indicated city employees could potentially go without raises for two to three years. The city’s website estimates Amendment 3 could reduce Fort Pierce’s property-tax revenue by about $3.5 million in fiscal year 2028 and an additional $1.5 million in fiscal year 2029, for a combined estimated reduction of about $5 million. The city says it may consider cost reductions and other revenue sources to address the impact. 3 election, Florida law enforcement groups warned that the amendment could reduce money available for public safety and lead to fewer deputies, slower 911 response times and service cuts. The Florida Sheriffs Association ran an ad campaign opposing the measure, while police and fire leaders also raised concerns about the lack of a replacement funding plan. Those were warnings about potential effects, not announcements of specific cuts to Fort Pierce’s police department. Declaring an impasse moves negotiations into a formal process for resolving disagreements. The association said it will continue advocating for what it called fair and competitive wages and keep members and the community updated. The negotiations come as Fort Pierce police have been part of a major multi-agency operation targeting the 23rd Street gang . Officials said the nearly two-year investigation led to nearly 40 arrests, five search warrants and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash. Fort Pierce police said investigators linked people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings over the past decade.

I saw several snakes in the water," Pahzoor said.Robin Williams described a week without basic city services."Since Halloween we've not received mail. We've not had garbage pickup. First time I've seen something like this," Pahzoor said.To find answers, I got on the phone, connecting with officials at Palm Beach County, the City of West Palm Beach, Hamilton Bay's property management company, and the Hamal Community Development District — which includes several flooded neighborhoods off of Okeechobee Boulevard.Dwayne Barrett, Hamal's operations manager, told me the district has been working with the county and the city, and is currently pumping water into a canal that the county allowed them to use."This is at least 16 inches (deep) right here," Pahzoor said as he drove his SUV around his neighborhood.West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James sent the following statement Monday afternoon:“I understand the frustration and hardship that residents of Briar Bay, The Cove at Briar Bay, and Hamilton Bay continue to experience following last week's historic rainfall. With significant standing water remaining in these communities, the City is focused on residents’ safety and is continuing to coordinate with the agencies responsible for drainage while providing direct assistance where possible.The Hamal Community Development District (CDD) is responsible for maintaining the community’s surface water management system. Its existing system has two pumps that currently cannot operate simultaneously. The Northern Palm Beach County Improvement District (NPBCID) has provided two additional pumps, and Hamal CDD informed the City this morning that an electrician is being brought in to enable its two pumps to operate concurrently.Since the beginning of this event, the City has maintained ongoing communication with the NPBCID and has also made direct outreach to Hamal CDD, offering personnel, equipment, and technical assistance. Both districts have informed us that there is nothing further the City can do at this time to assist with drainage operations. The City is not withholding permits, delaying improvements on the current pumping and drainage efforts. We will continue monitoring conditions, coordinating with the responsible agencies and offering assistance as needs change.While the drainage system is outside our jurisdiction, our commitment to these residents is not. The City partially activated its Emergency Operations Center on November 2. Since then, City crews have been working around the clock to respond to flooding throughout West Palm Beach, while continuing to provide direct assistance to residents in these communities. This includes offering transportation to shelters for residents unable to leave their neighborhoods and helping hospice nurses reach patients when they were flooded in. The City will continue monitoring conditions and resume regular collection as soon as it is safe to do so.I recognize the significant impact this prolonged flooding has had on residents. The City will continue coordinating with the responsible agencies, monitoring conditions, and providing assistance wherever possible. Our priority remains the safety and well-being of every resident.” For questions regarding drainage operations and floodwater removal, residents should contact the Hamal Community Development District:District Manager: Jamie OteroPhone: (561) 571-0010Email: info@hamalcdd.comWebsite: https://hamalcdd.com/contactResidents experiencing a medical emergency should call 911. entry.title: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    WPEC
entry.article_text: Some parents kept their children home from Felix A. Williams Elementary School on Monday after the man accused of posting TikTok threats involving the school was released on $100,000 bond. Jessica and Jon Greisen were among them. Their daughter, Teigan, is in third grade. My child is not going to school, Jessica Greisen recalled thinking when she learned he was out. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the school entrance. Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would add deputies at and around the campus and at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The Greisens said they want to know whether 51-year-old Michael George Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. She wants to know what precautions will be in place in the days ahead. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Sheriff says parents have reason to be concerned At a news conference Monday, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said he understood parents’ concerns and acknowledged that Davis’s release creates an opportunity for a threat. I wish I could tell them, hey, the guy’s sitting in jail, he’s in custody, there’s no threat, Budensiek said. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat. Budensiek said parents must decide what is best for their children and that his office would support them. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams Elementary and continue working with Cape Coral police on the investigation. The sheriff said the student named in the posts has not attended the school for years. But he said investigators could not disregard the threats, in part because Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. Budensiek encouraged parents to stay vigilant and call the sheriff’s office if they see Davis. What led to the arrest The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said a tip late Friday led investigators to TikTok posts threatening law enforcement officers. While reviewing the account, investigators found another post that referred to Jewish people and a family associated with Felix A. Williams Elementary, Budensiek said. Principal Sarah Tuthill said the posts referenced a specific student and included vague threats against the school. The sheriff’s office said the posts threatened a student, community members and law enforcement officers. The posts were repeatedly uploaded and taken down, Budensiek said. Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night. The sheriff’s office said he initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said investigators are trying to determine why Davis focused on Martin County and the family he referenced. He said Davis allegedly told investigators he had surfed in Martin County sometime between 2006 and 2014 and had an altercation with people he associated with the family. Davis allegedly described a later incident at a gym in which people connected to a surf group failed to spot him while he lifted weights, causing a significant amount of weight to fall on his chest. The sheriff said investigators have found no direct connection between that account and the family. The family does not know Davis and could not recall an incident with him, Budensiek said. Davis was released from the Lee County Jail on Sunday after posting $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant, the sheriff’s office said. Lee County jail records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. The Martin County warrant charges Davis with written threats to kill, Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators have recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to review its contents. The office also sent preservation requests to TikTok, he said. Budensiek said the investigation could lead to additional charges in Martin County and other jurisdictions, but those charges had not been filed as of Monday’s news conference.

Williams Elementary School in Stuart, law enforcement officers and members of the Martin County community. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said Sunday that 51-year-old Michael G. Davis, from Cape Coral, was arrested on Saturday night in Cape Coral on a Martin County warrant directly related to those threats. We understand that this news may raise concerns among our families and employees, and we want to reassure you that the Martin County Sheriff’s Office is fully aware of the individual’s release and continues to monitor the situation closely. Out of an abundance of caution, the Sheriff’s Office will have an increased law enforcement presence on our campus. This is a proactive precaution being taken in coordination with our law enforcement partners, who remain actively engaged in monitoring the situation and protecting our school community. We appreciate our families and employees for remaining alert and taking matters involving school safety seriously. At the same time, we want to emphasize that our law enforcement partners are closely monitoring this matter and taking appropriate precautions to safeguard our campus. Our priority is to ensure that students and staff feel safe, supported, and able to focus on the important work taking place in our classrooms each day. entry.title: NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet that crashed near Greenacres
entry.summary: Federal investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres earlier this month. The National Transportation Safety Board said in a Monday evening post on X that investigators found the cockpit voice recorder, commonly known as a CVR, at the site of the plane's initial impact. PREVIOUS REPORT: NTSB completes most on-scene work related to crash NTSB completes most on-scene work in Learjet crash The recorder has been sent to the NTSB's Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C., where it is being evaluated. Cockpit voice recorders can provide investigators with information about sounds and conversations inside an aircrafts cockpit leading up to a crash. The NTSB also announced that excavation work at the initial impact site has been completed. The Learjet 60 crashed near Greenacres on Nov. 1. The NTSB did not provide additional details about what may have been captured on the recorder or when information from its examination could become available. The agency said Sunday that it had completed most of its on-scene investigative work. The investigation into the crash remains ongoing.

entry.title: Palm Beach County school district employee accused of soliciting person he believed was 14-year-old boy
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County School District employee was arrested after police said he had sexually explicit conversations with an undercover detective posing as a 14-year-old boy. Boynton Beach police said Donald Rush, 65, of Lake Worth was arrested following an investigation by the department's Human Exploitation Task Force. According to police, detectives posed as a 14-year-old boy advertising lawn mowing services on Craigslist's Community messaging board. Investigators said they were contacted by someone using the screen name 'Palm Guy,' who was later identified by police as Rush. Police said Rush asked the person his age, whether adult men had approached him about sexual activity and whether he had told his parents about those interactions. The conversation later moved to text messages, according to police. Detectives said they again made clear that the person Rush was communicating with was supposedly 14 years old. Despite the stated age, police allege Rush continued the conversation, asking sexually explicit questions and making statements about his own sexual activity. With assistance from the Palm Beach County School Board Police Department, detectives located and interviewed Rush. Boynton Beach police said Rush admitted his involvement during that interview. Police said Rush also claimed during the investigation that he was a youth pastor. The department did not identify a church or organization with which he was allegedly affiliated. Rush faces charges of solicitation of a minor to engage in sexual conduct and unlawful use of a two-way communications device, according to police. He was being held at the Palm Beach County Jail. Police identified Rush as an employee of the Palm Beach County School District. However, the department did not specify his position with the district. Investigators said they believe there could be additional victims. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized by Rush or has information about similar incidents involving him is asked to contact Boynton Beach police Detective Joseph at 561-742-6158.

It has now been closed for more than a week following the crash.The closure has been particularly difficult for a business with 15 employees and bills that did not stop when customers could no longer get through."Financially wise, it's been a pretty economical impact, considering we've got 15 employees and we've got a lot of businesses in the area," Rivera said.Add on the lost sales, customers, food waste, rent and payroll continuing to add up."Anything helps at this point, especially if it comes to payroll because we've got 15 employees trying to survive as well and help out as much as we can personally, but if we can have the county do some sort of grant program or maybe talk to the state or maybe talk to some at federal level that they can have some sort of help with us, that'll be great," Rivera said.Now, Palm Beach County is preparing to offer some of that help.The county's proposed Military Trail Business Interruption Grant Program would set aside $250,000 in Ad Valorem funds for eligible businesses affected by the incident and the associated Military Trail closure. Businesses could receive up to $5,000, depending on eligibility, available funding and the county's calculation of each award.Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said the program was created after businesses began reaching out about the financial strain caused by the closure."We've been receiving hundreds of calls about when are we gonna reopen. You know, we have employees, we have people that need to get paid that are not getting paid," Flores said. "We need to be able to cover our own rent, and a lot of these are small businesses. These are mom-and-pop shops, and we wanna make sure that we take care of them."For businesses like Rivera's, even that amount could make a meaningful difference."Absolutely. That at least helps out for half of the payroll so we can get, you know, at least help them go on because I've got employees that got bills to pay as well," Rivera said.Businesses will have to apply through the County's Housing and Economic Development Department.The money can be used for expenses including rent or mortgage payments, employee payroll, utilities, essential inventory and supplies and other approved operating costs. It cannot be used for personal expenses, expansion, owner distributions or expenses already covered by insurance or other assistance.The grants are capped at $5,000. Only one award is allowed per legal business as they take steps to return to normalcy.The county’s proposed $250,000 business grant program is not the only financial assistance being brought into the recovery effort. Flores said more than $50,000 has also been raised through United Way from the private sector, with funding going to Catholic Charities to help provide temporary housing, rental cars and Uber and Lyft vouchers for people affected by the crash.Separate from the county’s proposed assistance for businesses, the Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, is offering $1,000 cash grants to eligible residents impacted by the crash through its People First Fund. The organization previously told WPTV it had enough funding to help 18 people and was working to raise enough to provide grants to all 68 impacted individuals it had identified.Flores said water had been turned back on and Florida Power & Light was conducting a final assessment before residents could return to their homes. He said the county's goal was to get residents back within the coming days, or by the end of the week at the latest, as long as officials determine the area is safe.Businesses could also begin reopening within days, according to Flores, although work remains underway around the crash site and there is not yet a firm date for Military Trail to completely reopen.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Flood-damaged Florida homeowners may qualify for property tax break. Here's what to know
entry.summary: In some areas of South Florida and the Treasure Coast, the flooding from last week's heavy rains persists. 'It's been a definite challenge,' says Jesse Cabral in the Grand Isles condos, located off Haverhill Road in West Palm Beach. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flood damage could qualify homeowners for tax break The water around his condo is still over ankle - deep and laps up to his garage. 'It didnt come into the unit itself, but it did flood my garage and did do a lot of damage in there,' Cabral said. For some homeowners, flood damage can lead to a break on property taxes. 'Under Florida law, homeowners whose residences are uninhabitable for at least 30 consecutive days due to a catastrophic event may qualify for a partial property tax refund,' according to an email from Palm Beach County Appraiser Dorothy Jacks. Homeowners seeking a refund for damage must submit an Application for Catastrophic Event Tax Refund (Form DR-465) and supporting documentation by March 1, 2027. Damage sustained during this flooding will not change a property's 2026 assessment but may affect its 2027 assessment if repairs remain incomplete as of Jan. 1, 2027. Having flood insurance is still the best protection from sudden flooding events, even in areas not known for flooding in the past. 'This isn't a designated flood zone, and I didn't get flood insurance, so it might be a problem,' Cabral said.
