entry.title: West Palm Beach neighbors say they've been flooded in for a week with no answers on who will help them recover
entry.summary: Eight days after the rain stopped, neighbors in a West Palm Beach community remain flooded, and they say they are not getting the answers they need to get their lives back on track. In communities like Hamilton Bay, located off of Jog Road, people know they need help a week after record rainfall moved out. But they say their requests are falling on deaf ears. So I set out to answer one of their biggest questions: Who is accountable for providing that help? WATCH REPORT BELOW: West Palm Beach residents still flooded 8 days after rain 'I don't know if who's responsible, the HOA, the city,' Juliet Bradford said as she drove a rented Jeep through floodwaters. She told me her car had been totaled in those same floodwaters. 'It's unacceptable,' Bradford said. Jackie Copan, standing on the dry upper portion of her driveway, said she hadn't left her home since last Tuesday, when she waded through floodwaters to vote. 'We brought a stick in case we saw a gator,' Copan noted. By Monday, the water had somewhat subsided in Hamilton Bay since last week. But the frustration among neighbors has not. Sal Pahzoor said at one point, water had gotten into his garage, where he now stores the inflatable canoe and life vests he bought last week. 'The water has been mixed with the sewage. I saw several snakes in the water,' Pahzoor said. Robin Williams described a week without basic city services. 'Since Halloween we've not received mail. We've not had garbage pickup. We've not had bulk pick up all week long,' Williams said. 'We are very disappointed about this. I know I am.' 'I've been living in West Palm Beach for 30 years. First time I've seen something like this,' Pahzoor said. I saw several snakes in the water," Pahzoor said.Robin Williams described a week without basic city services."Since Halloween we've not received mail. We've not had garbage pickup. First time I've seen something like this," Pahzoor said.To find answers, I got on the phone, connecting with officials at Palm Beach County, the City of West Palm Beach, Hamilton Bay's property management company, and the Hamal Community Development District — which includes several flooded neighborhoods off of Okeechobee Boulevard.Dwayne Barrett, Hamal's operations manager, told me the district has been working with the county and the city, and is currently pumping water into a canal that the county allowed them to use."This is at least 16 inches (deep) right here," Pahzoor said as he drove his SUV around his neighborhood.West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James sent the following statement Monday afternoon:“I understand the frustration and hardship that residents of Briar Bay, The Cove at Briar Bay, and Hamilton Bay continue to experience following last week's historic rainfall. With significant standing water remaining in these communities, the City is focused on residents’ safety and is continuing to coordinate with the agencies responsible for drainage while providing direct assistance where possible.The Hamal Community Development District (CDD) is responsible for maintaining the community’s surface water management system. Its existing system has two pumps that currently cannot operate simultaneously. The Northern Palm Beach County Improvement District (NPBCID) has provided two additional pumps, and Hamal CDD informed the City this morning that an electrician is being brought in to enable its two pumps to operate concurrently.Since the beginning of this event, the City has maintained ongoing communication with the NPBCID and has also made direct outreach to Hamal CDD, offering personnel, equipment, and technical assistance. Both districts have informed us that there is nothing further the City can do at this time to assist with drainage operations. The City is not withholding permits, delaying improvements on the current pumping and drainage efforts. We will continue monitoring conditions, coordinating with the responsible agencies and offering assistance as needs change.While the drainage system is outside our jurisdiction, our commitment to these residents is not. The City partially activated its Emergency Operations Center on November 2. Since then, City crews have been working around the clock to respond to flooding throughout West Palm Beach, while continuing to provide direct assistance to residents in these communities. This includes offering transportation to shelters for residents unable to leave their neighborhoods and helping hospice nurses reach patients when they were flooded in. Our Police and Fire Rescue personnel remain available to assist residents with medical emergencies or other urgent needs, including assistance leaving their communities. Residents facing an immediate emergency should call 911.Our sanitation crews have continued assessing conditions in these neighborhoods twice daily. Due to significant standing water, garbage trucks cannot safely access certain areas without creating wakes that could push water into homes and garages. To provide residents with an alternative, the City is placing two temporary six-cubic-yard dumpsters in the community clubhouse parking lot for excess bagged household garbage. The City will continue monitoring conditions and resume regular collection as soon as it is safe to do so.I recognize the significant impact this prolonged flooding has had on residents. The City will continue coordinating with the responsible agencies, monitoring conditions, and providing assistance wherever possible. Our priority remains the safety and well-being of every resident.” For questions regarding drainage operations and floodwater removal, residents should contact the Hamal Community Development District:District Manager: Jamie OteroPhone: (561) 571-0010Email: info@hamalcdd.comWebsite: https://hamalcdd.com/contactResidents experiencing a medical emergency should call 911. City emergency services remain available to assist residents in the impacted communities.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    WPEC
entry.article_text: Less than 12 hours after he was booked into jail, a Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats involving a Stuart elementary school was out on a $100,000 bond. By Monday morning, deputies were watching the school entrance, and Jessica and John Greisen had decided to keep their third grader home. Wanted to vomit, Jessica Greisen said. She recalled thinking, My child is not going to school. Their daughter, Teigan, attends Felix A. Williams Elementary School. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the entrance. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would also add deputies at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. How detectives found the threats A tip late Friday led detectives to TikTok videos in which Michael George Davis, 51, threatened to kill law enforcement officers, the sheriff’s office said. Sheriff John Budensiek said the videos were repeatedly posted and taken down. In one video reviewed by CBS12 News, Davis said he was going to shoot people. As many as I can, dawg, as soon as I get there, he said. Budensiek said the threat in that video was directed at law enforcement officers. As detectives looked through the account, they found a separate post naming Felix A. So it went from threatening law enforcement to threatening Jews to threatening one of our students here in Martin County, Budensiek said. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff said the post also threatened a local family. Tuthill described the threats against the school as vague and said the posts referenced a specific student. Budensiek said the student hasn’t attended Felix A. Williams in years, but Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. An alleged dispute dating back to 2006 2014 Davis lives in Cape Coral, but Budensiek said he surfed in Martin County years ago. The sheriff said Davis appeared to link the family he named online to a dispute he claims happened sometime between 2006 and 2014. Budensiek also described a later incident Davis claims happened at a gym. According to that account, people Davis associated with a surf group were supposed to spot him while he lifted weights. Davis claims they failed to do so and a significant amount of weight fell on his chest. Budensiek said investigators found no direct connection between the alleged dispute and the family. They have no idea what he’s talking about, he said. Arrested Saturday night, released Sunday afternoon Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night on a felony warrant for written threats to kill. The sheriff’s office said Davis initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said deputies found no weapons when they arrested Davis. He said investigators were unaware of any prior arrests or any instances in which Davis was taken for an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. Lee County jail records show Davis was booked at 2:53 a.m. Sunday and released at 2:12 p.m. on a $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant. The records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. I was hoping that $100,000 bond he would still be sitting in jail, and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry, Budensiek said. The Greisens said they want to know whether Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Why was he even released first off? Budensiek said Davis rides an e-bike, his driver’s license was suspended and deputies don’t know of a car he uses. The sheriff said that makes it harder to track his movements. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat, Budensiek said. What happens next Budensiek urged parents to stay vigilant and asked anyone who sees Davis in Martin County to call the sheriff’s office. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams and that his office would support parents as they decide what’s best for their children. Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers about the precautions in place. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Detectives are still working with Cape Coral police. Budensiek said investigators recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to search it. His office also sent preservation requests to TikTok. We are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that, but we are not there yet, Budensiek said. He said he expects more charges in Martin County and that other jurisdictions could also bring charges.

entry.title: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond - cw34.com
entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Some parents kept their children home from Felix A. Williams Elementary School on Monday after the man accused of posting TikTok threats involving the school was released on $100,000 bond. Jessica and Jon Greisen were among them. Their daughter, Teigan, is in third grade. My child is not going to school, Jessica Greisen recalled thinking when she learned he was out. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the school entrance. Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would add deputies at and around the campus and at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The Greisens said they want to know whether 51-year-old Michael George Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. She wants to know what precautions will be in place in the days ahead. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Sheriff says parents have reason to be concerned At a news conference Monday, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said he understood parents’ concerns and acknowledged that Davis’s release creates an opportunity for a threat. I wish I could tell them, hey, the guy’s sitting in jail, he’s in custody, there’s no threat, Budensiek said. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat. Budensiek said parents must decide what is best for their children and that his office would support them. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams Elementary and continue working with Cape Coral police on the investigation. The sheriff said the student named in the posts has not attended the school for years. But he said investigators could not disregard the threats, in part because Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. Budensiek encouraged parents to stay vigilant and call the sheriff’s office if they see Davis. What led to the arrest The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said a tip late Friday led investigators to TikTok posts threatening law enforcement officers. While reviewing the account, investigators found another post that referred to Jewish people and a family associated with Felix A. Williams Elementary, Budensiek said. Principal Sarah Tuthill said the posts referenced a specific student and included vague threats against the school. The sheriff’s office said the posts threatened a student, community members and law enforcement officers. The posts were repeatedly uploaded and taken down, Budensiek said. Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night. The sheriff’s office said he initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said investigators are trying to determine why Davis focused on Martin County and the family he referenced. He said Davis allegedly told investigators he had surfed in Martin County sometime between 2006 and 2014 and had an altercation with people he associated with the family. Davis allegedly described a later incident at a gym in which people connected to a surf group failed to spot him while he lifted weights, causing a significant amount of weight to fall on his chest. The sheriff said investigators have found no direct connection between that account and the family. The family does not know Davis and could not recall an incident with him, Budensiek said. Davis was released from the Lee County Jail on Sunday after posting $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant, the sheriff’s office said. Lee County jail records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. The Martin County warrant charges Davis with written threats to kill, Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators have recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to review its contents. The office also sent preservation requests to TikTok, he said. Budensiek said the investigation could lead to additional charges in Martin County and other jurisdictions, but those charges had not been filed as of Monday’s news conference.

entry.title: Cape Coral man arrested after threats against Martin County community - WPBF
entry.summary: Cape Coral man arrested after threats against Martin County community    WPBF
entry.article_text: A southwest Florida resident is accused of making threats on TikTok against Felix A. Williams Elementary School in Stuart, law enforcement officers and members of the Martin County community. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said Sunday that 51-year-old Michael G. Davis, from Cape Coral, was arrested on Saturday night in Cape Coral on a Martin County warrant directly related to those threats. He was released from the Lee County Jail on Sunday after posting a $100,000 bond. "We know parents are concerned about his release," the sheriff's office posted on Facebook. "As a precaution, you’ll see more deputies at and around Felix A. Williams Elementary School and at several other Martin County schools. Davis uses a bicycle as his primary form of transportation, MCSO said. "If you think you see Davis in Martin County or notice anything suspicious, please call the Martin County Sheriff’s Office," the agency said. According to the Lee County Sheriff’s Office, Davis is facing a charge of resisting officers without violence along with an out-of-county warrant from Martin County. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it was contacted by a concerned citizen on Friday, Nov. 6, about a video that a man, later identified as Davis, posted on the social media platform TikTok threatening the lives of a local student, members of the community and Martin County law enforcement. Investigators reviewed the threats that targeted a school and were able to identify Davis, who posted the video. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said its criminal investigations division and warrants unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Service and the Cape Coral Police Department to arrest Davis. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office added that at first, Davis refused to surrender to law enforcement outside his home but was eventually taken into law enforcement custody. “If you threaten any of our students, our schools, anyone in our community or any of our law enforcement officers, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, find you and lock you up,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said in a statement on Sunday morning. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office noted it is undetermined why Davis targeted Martin County or the specific people he threatened. The following updated statement by Felix A. Williams Elementary School Principal Sarah Tuthill was posted to the school’s Facebook page on Sunday night: Dear FAWE Families and Staff. Please pardon our interruption this evening. We want to provide an update regarding the individual recently arrested in connection with social media threats that included references to our school community. The individual has since been released on bond. We understand that this news may raise concerns among our families and employees, and we want to reassure you that the Martin County Sheriff’s Office is fully aware of the individual’s release and continues to monitor the situation closely. Out of an abundance of caution, the Sheriff’s Office will have an increased law enforcement presence on our campus. This is a proactive precaution being taken in coordination with our law enforcement partners, who remain actively engaged in monitoring the situation and protecting our school community. We appreciate our families and employees for remaining alert and taking matters involving school safety seriously. At the same time, we want to emphasize that our law enforcement partners are closely monitoring this matter and taking appropriate precautions to safeguard our campus. School will remain open, and teaching and learning will continue as planned. Our priority is to ensure that students and staff feel safe, supported, and able to focus on the important work taking place in our classrooms each day. Thank you for your continued trust, understanding, and partnership. We are grateful to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office for its vigilance and ongoing commitment to the safety of our students, employees, and families.

entry.title: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary recovers after historic flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary recovers after historic flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: Save the Chimps, a 150-acre chimpanzee sanctuary in Fort Pierce, is recovering after 19 inches of rain caused historic flooding, disrupting operations and making it difficult for staff to care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. Mark Yohannan, facilities director at Save the Chimps, said water levels have dropped significantly, allowing staff to regain access to most of the sanctuary’s roads. "We've probably lost at least 7 or 8 inches of water. Now we have 1.2 miles of road here on property, 90% of that we can actually see and drive on. We expect the last little bit to dry up overnight," Yohannan said. Before the water began receding, staff faced challenges, including delivering food to a chimpanzee via drone. The sanctuary has 12 islands that house 11-21 chimpanzees in a family group. In total, there are 211 chimpanzees on the property. "We saw that we had a situation. Caleb was the one that stayed out; he loves his island as many others do," said Ana Paula Tavares, CEO of Save the Chimps. "He decided he was going to stay out until he realized that he was not going to be able to go indoors anymore because of the land bridge that connects the island to his indoor house got flooded as well. Not on all the islands, but on that island. That's when we had to get creative and think, how can we drop fluid and food?" The sanctuary’s chimps live on islands with care houses situated on higher ground, but staff struggled to navigate the flooded property. "We have a lot of golf carts that care staff use to move themselves, staff, 3,000 pounds of food a day, and so, those were rendered inoperable because you couldn't see the road; they're battery carts... Not to mention some were damaged," Yohannan said. Employees have been relying on tractors, trailers, and large off-road vehicles to access the sanctuary. An overflowing header canal has slowed the water’s recession. On Monday, Yohannan met with the St. Lucie Water River District to discuss the flooding. "We left with the understanding that everyone already knows. This rain event was a 200-year event, and I think that the county's working as hard as they can to get stuff moving," Yohannan said. Despite the historic flood, rescue leaders felt they were mostly prepared but acknowledged areas for improvement. "The one thing that came to mind is we have insurance...very good insurance but not flood insurance because we didn't have floods in Florida. So now we do, or now we will look into that...that was one lesson learned," Tavares said. Yohannan added, "We would have needed some very large pumps, watched the forecast a little better maybe...but other than that I think we're in the same boat as all the other neighbors. It's the first thing that's rained this hard in 200 years; I don't know what we could've done to be more prepared." entry.title: Vero Beach family citrus grove reels after historic South Florida flooding damages crops - WPEC
entry.summary: Vero Beach family citrus grove reels after historic South Florida flooding damages crops    WPEC
entry.article_text: Many businesses are reeling in the effects of last week’s historic flooding event across South Florida, including a local Vero Beach citrus grove farm. CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and we’re anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

entry.title: Fire heavily damages India Grill and Bar in Royal Palm Beach
entry.summary: A fire heavily damaged India Grill and Bar in Royal Palm Beach, but firefighters prevented the flames from spreading to neighboring businesses, according to Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. Crews responded to reports of a commercial fire on Royal Palm Beach Boulevard, just north of Southern Boulevard. Watch video of the fire: Fire heavily damages India Grill and Bar in Royal Palm Beach When firefighters arrived, they found the restaurant heavily involved in flames. PBCFR said a large fire was visible from the front of the building, while thick, dark smoke billowed from the rear. Firefighters prevent flames from spreading It took firefighters about 30 minutes to bring the fire under control. An aggressive attack prevented the fire from going to neighboring businesses or running along the overhead space, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said in a statement. Adjacent businesses experienced some smoke intrusion, according to PBCFR, but no injuries were reported. India Grill and Bar sustained considerable fire damage. Cause remains under investigation PBCFR fire investigators remained at the scene throughout the night as they worked to determine where and how the fire started. The fire remains under investigation, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said.

entry.title: Keiser football faces must-win season finale with playoff streak on the line
entry.summary: Since 2019, the Keiser University football team has made the NAIA football playoffs each season, including making it to the title game the last four years, but that streak could be in jeopardy. 'We always talk about process over results, and I know the results have shown us going to countless amount of national championships but we continue to focus on the process of what got us there,' said head coach Myles Russ. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Keiser's playoff streak comes down to season finale Keiser's push to national prominence is thanks to an all-in approach by every man on the team, and for the last few years the leader of that attack was Shea Spencer, the former quarterback who led Keiser to two straight national title appearances. These days, however, a new signal caller, JT Tabora, has taken over. 'It's been awesome being the quarterback here at Keiser. I've been backup for the past two years, and it's been great learning behind him, and giving me the opportunity to start this year has been great,' said Tabora. In seven games this season, the sophomore has passed for 1,300 yards and 13 touchdowns. While his numbers are strong, the Seahawks find themselves in uncharted waters. They're 6-3 and ranked 15th overall in the country, and after suffering a loss Saturday, the fellas could fall out of the top 15. Sounds like no problem, right? Well, only the top 15 teams are guaranteed a spot in the NAIA Playoffs, making Saturday's season finale against Warner a must-win. 'I think we can clean up some things, that's our mindset: just clean up some things, and once we get those things (fixed), were a tough team to beat,' Tabora said.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council approved the site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One , clearing another step for the project planned near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. The stadium is proposed to stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, while field-light poles could rise to 135 feet. The project is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The site-plan approval comes as the city advances related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. The city’s agenda listed those measures for second reading Monday. Staff recommended approval of the site plan subject to recording a replat; the project also has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. RELATED: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC , a United Soccer League League One team. The club is expected to begin play in 2027, with matches at the new stadium planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The stadium is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and that the stadium is intended to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. entry.title: Residents wait for FEMA assistance after Florida puts in request after widespread flooding
entry.summary: Historic flooding has damaged 66 homes in Martin County, including 25 that were destroyed, according to new county numbers, as displaced residents wait to learn whether federal assistance will be made available. The flooding has left damage across WPTV's five-county viewing area, stretching from Indian River County through Palm Beach County. But in Martin County's Jensen Beach community, the latest numbers show just how destructive the flooding has been. Jensen Beach residents describe unlivable conditions. West Palm Beach residents still flooded 8 days after rain Michael Drawdy is among the Jensen Beach residents dealing with severe flooding inside his home. 'Right now I've got 6 to 8 inches of water depending on the level of the house inside the house, and you can see the fecal matter that's coming through the house,' Drawdy told WPTV. Drawdy and his neighbors now face conditions they say have made their homes unlivable. Residents also told WPTV much of their immediate help has come from one another, along with churches and community donations. 'All these neighbors have all pulled together. They've brought us donations here every day. People have fed us from the churches. Everybody's really been really good that way,' resident Suzie Keith said. 'No one else has really helped us. I mean, we've all been helping ourselves.' Florida has formally requested federal disaster assistance to help communities recover from recent flooding across Central and South Florida. At the request of Gov. Ron DeSantis, the Florida Division of Emergency Management announced Monday that the state submitted a Major Disaster Declaration request seeking federal assistance for communities impacted by the flooding. The request comes after heavy rainfall caused significant flooding in portions of the state, leaving communities dealing with lingering water and damage more than a week later. 'We remain committed to working with our federal partners to ensure impacted Floridians receive the assistance they need to recover,' the Florida Division of Emergency Management said in a post on X. A Major Disaster Declaration must receive federal approval before the requested assistance becomes available. The state's announcement did not specify which counties are included in the request or detail what types of federal assistance Florida is seeking. Davis reportedly made multiple threats in TikTok videos, referencing the Martin County Sheriff’s Office, Stuart Police, and a student at Felix Williams Elementary School who no longer attends the school. “You don’t ever threaten our deputies. You don’t threaten the citizens of Martin County. You certainly don’t threaten our youth and expect us just to sit on our worlds and not take action,” Budensiek said. The sheriff said Davis appears to have lived in Martin County between 2006 and 2014 and claims to have had a fight with the family he is accused of threatening. “The question we had is why is he fixated on Martin County? Why is he fixated on this family?” Budensiek said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 However, the sheriff noted that the family has no recollection of Davis or any incident involving him. “They have no idea who this guy is. They don’t know of an incident that happened at the beach. They are as confused as we are trying to make these connections,” Budensiek said. Davis was arrested on a Martin County warrant and booked into the Lee County Jail on a $100,000 bond. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. “I was hoping that $100,000 bond, he would still be sitting in jail and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry. entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Less than 12 hours after he was booked into jail, a Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats involving a Stuart elementary school was out on a $100,000 bond. By Monday morning, deputies were watching the school entrance, and Jessica and John Greisen had decided to keep their third grader home. Wanted to vomit, Jessica Greisen said. She recalled thinking, My child is not going to school. Their daughter, Teigan, attends Felix A. Williams Elementary School. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the entrance. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would also add deputies at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. How detectives found the threats A tip late Friday led detectives to TikTok videos in which Michael George Davis, 51, threatened to kill law enforcement officers, the sheriff’s office said. Sheriff John Budensiek said the videos were repeatedly posted and taken down. In one video reviewed by CBS12 News, Davis said he was going to shoot people. As many as I can, dawg, as soon as I get there, he said. Budensiek said the threat in that video was directed at law enforcement officers. As detectives looked through the account, they found a separate post naming Felix A. So it went from threatening law enforcement to threatening Jews to threatening one of our students here in Martin County, Budensiek said. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff said the post also threatened a local family. Tuthill described the threats against the school as vague and said the posts referenced a specific student. Budensiek said the student hasn’t attended Felix A. Williams in years, but Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. An alleged dispute dating back to 2006 2014 Davis lives in Cape Coral, but Budensiek said he surfed in Martin County years ago. The sheriff said Davis appeared to link the family he named online to a dispute he claims happened sometime between 2006 and 2014. Budensiek also described a later incident Davis claims happened at a gym. According to that account, people Davis associated with a surf group were supposed to spot him while he lifted weights. Davis claims they failed to do so and a significant amount of weight fell on his chest. Budensiek said investigators found no direct connection between the alleged dispute and the family. They have no idea what he’s talking about, he said. Arrested Saturday night, released Sunday afternoon Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night on a felony warrant for written threats to kill. The sheriff’s office said Davis initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said deputies found no weapons when they arrested Davis. He said investigators were unaware of any prior arrests or any instances in which Davis was taken for an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. Lee County jail records show Davis was booked at 2:53 a.m. Sunday and released at 2:12 p.m. on a $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant. The records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. I was hoping that $100,000 bond he would still be sitting in jail, and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry, Budensiek said. The Greisens said they want to know whether Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Why was he even released first off? Budensiek said Davis rides an e-bike, his driver’s license was suspended and deputies don’t know of a car he uses. The sheriff said that makes it harder to track his movements. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat, Budensiek said. What happens next Budensiek urged parents to stay vigilant and asked anyone who sees Davis in Martin County to call the sheriff’s office. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams and that his office would support parents as they decide what’s best for their children. Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers about the precautions in place. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Detectives are still working with Cape Coral police. Budensiek said investigators recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to search it. His office also sent preservation requests to TikTok. We are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that, but we are not there yet, Budensiek said. He said he expects more charges in Martin County and that other jurisdictions could also bring charges.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills, independence
entry.summary: A recent cooking class in Port St. Lucie is helping adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities learn valuable life skills and gain more independence. The participants are part of the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach Countys Guardian Advocacy Program, which provides guardianship support to people with developmental disabilities. WATCH: Cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills for independent living Cooking up confidence: Port St. Lucie program helps adults with disabilities gain independence Some of the participants are young adults who have aged out of foster care and don't have family members to rely on for support. Through a partnership with GL Homes that has lasted nearly a decade, participants are given hands-on experiences and opportunities to develop skills that can help them in everyday life. During the latest class in October, participants learned how to prepare a healthier meal, with Mediterranean chicken on the menu. From chopping vegetables and preparing ingredients to following a recipe and practicing kitchen safety, the lesson was about more than just cooking. Organizers say the goal is to give participants experiences and opportunities that are often not readily available to them while helping them become more self-sufficient. 'We wanted to give them these experiences that they just don't have and the rest of us take for granted,' said Sarah Alsofrom, Vice President of Community Relations at GL Homes. Jessica Kelson with the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County says watching participants learn new skills and take part in activities can make a meaningful difference. 'Being able to watch them learn a new skill or participate in something that's not typically offered to them is just really heartwarming and nice to see them be able to grow,' Kelson said. By the end of the class, participants had prepared their meal and sat down to enjoy what they made. For one participant, the accomplishment was something to be proud of. 'I'm proud of it,' she said. 'I am going to try this at home.' Organizers hope these experiences will give participants the confidence and practical skills to take greater control of their daily lives one meal at a time.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him, and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Alexis Hodge said. Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain,' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council approved the site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One , clearing another step for the project planned near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. The stadium is proposed to stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, while field-light poles could rise to 135 feet. The project is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The site-plan approval comes as the city advances related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. The city’s agenda listed those measures for second reading Monday. Staff recommended approval of the site plan subject to recording a replat; the project also has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. RELATED: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC , a United Soccer League League One team. The club is expected to begin play in 2027, with matches at the new stadium planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The stadium is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and that the stadium is intended to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could be reimbursed for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

entry.article_text: Lucie Public Schools will reopen all schools Monday, Nov. 9, after historic flooding across the county. The district said most bus stops will operate as usual, but some may be temporarily relocated because of road conditions. Families whose stops are affected will receive a call from the SLPS Transportation Department on Sunday. If they don’t receive a call, their child’s regular stop is not affected. See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end Superintendent Dr. Prince thanked families for their patience and praised bus drivers and school staff who worked beyond their usual hours to help students get home safely. The district has also posted recovery resources for families affected by flooding, including information about government assistance.
